సెక్షన్ 5: అంగీకారం అంగీకరించినవారి అధీనం దాటిపోయే వరకు ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు తన ఆఫర్‌ను వెనక్కు తీసుకోవచ్చు. అంగీకారం ఆఫర్ చేసినవారికి చేరే వరకు అంగీకరించినవారు తన అంగీకారాన్ని వెనక్కు తీసుకోవచ్చు. UP సవరణ: ఉత్తరప్రదేశ్‌లో, ఆఫర్లు నిర్ణీత కాలం తెరిచి ఉంచాలని టెండర్ నోటీసు చెబితే, ఆ షరతుతో మీరు ఆఫర్ చేస్తే, ఆ కాలంలో దాన్ని వెనక్కు తీసుకోలేరు. సెక్షన్ 6: ఆఫర్ (1) రద్దు నోటీసు తో, (2) గడువు ముగియడం తో, (3) అంగీకరించే ముందు నెరవేర్చాల్సిన షరతును అంగీకరించేవారు నెరవేర్చకపోవడం తో, లేదా (4) ఆఫర్ చేసినవారి మరణం లేదా మతిస్థిమితం కోల్పోవడం తో, అంగీకరించే ముందే అంగీకరించేవారికి తెలిస్తే, ముగుస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 4: రద్దు చేసే వ్యక్తికి వ్యతిరేకంగా అతను దాన్ని పంపినప్పుడు ; అవతలి పక్షానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా అది అతనికి తెలిసినప్పుడు రద్దు పూర్తవుతుంది. IT Act, సెక్షన్ 10A: ఈమెయిల్ లేదా ఎలక్ట్రానిక్ మార్గంలో చేసిన రద్దు కాగితంపై చేసినంత మంచిదే. IT Act, సెక్షన్ 13(1): ఈమెయిల్ పంపినవారి నియంత్రణ దాటినప్పుడు పంపినట్టు .
te.meaning:
రద్దు అంటే

రద్దు అంటే ప్రతిపాదనను గానీ అంగీకారాన్ని గానీ, అది కట్టుబడేలా అయ్యే ముందే, చేసిన వ్యక్తే వెనక్కు తీసుకోవడం. ఇది వీటికి భిన్నం:

తిరస్కరణ : offeree ఆఫర్‌కు "వద్దు" అనడం; మరియు గడువు ముగియడం (lapse) : ఎవరూ ఏమీ చేయకుండానే, సమయం అయిపోవడంతో ఆఫర్ ముగియడం.

చట్టం రద్దును ఎందుకు అనుమతిస్తుంది

ఆఫర్ కేవలం ప్రతిపాదన. అంగీకరించే వరకు వాగ్దానం లేదు, కాబట్టి ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు వెనక్కు తీసుకోవచ్చు. పోస్టు ద్వారా అంగీకారం పోస్ట్ చేయగానే ఆఫర్ చేసినవారిని కట్టుబడేలా చేస్తుంది, కానీ అంగీకరించినవారు అది చేరినప్పుడే కట్టుబడతారు. ఆ ఖాళీలో అంగీకరించినవారు వెనక్కు తీసుకోవడానికి చట్టం అనుమతిస్తుంది; ఇలా రెండు పక్షాలకూ కొంత రక్షణ ఉంటుంది.

రద్దు గడువులు ఒక పట్టికలో

ఎవరు రద్దు చేస్తారు దేన్ని గడువు (సెక్షన్ 5) పోస్టులో ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు తన ప్రతిపాదనను అంగీకారం ఆఫర్ చేసినవారికి వ్యతిరేకంగా పూర్తయ్యే ముందు అంగీకారం పోస్ట్ అయ్యే వరకు అంగీకరించినవారు తన అంగీకారాన్ని అంగీకారం అంగీకరించినవారికి వ్యతిరేకంగా పూర్తయ్యే ముందు అంగీకారం ఆఫర్ చేసినవారికి చేరే వరకు

మన ఉదాహరణ

మీనా (హైదరాబాద్) తన కుట్టు మిషన్, మోడల్ XL-200, ను ₹8,000 కి అమ్ముతానని రవి (విజయవాడ) కి పోస్టులో ఆఫర్ చేసింది, "శుక్రవారం వరకు తెరిచి ఉంటుంది" అని.

సోమవారం: మీనా ఆఫర్‌ను పోస్ట్ చేసింది. బుధవారం: రవి దాన్ని చదివాడు. గురువారం, ఉదయం 10 గం.: రవి అంగీకార ఉత్తరాన్ని పోస్ట్ చేశాడు. శనివారం, ఉదయం 11 గం.: రవి ఉత్తరం మీనాకు అందింది.

selfTest.q: 1. అంగీకారం పోస్టు ద్వారా అయితే, ఆఫర్ చేసినవారు ఆఫర్‌ను ఎప్పటి వరకు రద్దు చేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: అంగీకార ఉత్తరం పోస్ట్ అయ్యే వరకు (సెక్షన్ 5, ఉదాహరణ).

selfTest.q: 2. పోస్టులో అంగీకరించినవారు తన అంగీకారాన్ని ఎప్పటి వరకు రద్దు చేయవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: అంగీకార ఉత్తరం ఆఫర్ చేసినవారికి చేరే వరకు (సెక్షన్ 5, ఉదాహరణ).

selfTest.q: 3. రద్దు పోస్ట్ చేసినప్పుడే ప్రభావం చూపుతుందా?
selfTest.a: రద్దు చేసినవారికి వ్యతిరేకంగా మాత్రమే. అవతలి పక్షానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా, అతనికి తెలిసినప్పుడే (సెక్షన్ 4; Byrne v. Van Tienhoven ).

selfTest.q: 5. ఆఫర్‌ను ఒక వారం తెరిచి ఉంచుతాననే వాగ్దానం కట్టుబడుతుందా?
selfTest.a: ప్రతిఫలం లేకుండా కట్టుబడదు ( Routledge v. Grant ); ఆహ్వానంలోని "తెరిచి ఉంచాలి" షరతును అంగీకరిస్తూ చేసిన ప్రతిపాదనకు UP సవరణ మినహాయింపు.

selfTest.q: 6. ఈమెయిల్ ద్వారా రద్దు చెల్లుతుందా?
selfTest.a: చెల్లుతుంది (IT Act, సెక్షన్ 10A).

selfTest.q: 7. ఈమెయిల్ రద్దు ఎప్పుడు పంపినట్టు?
selfTest.a: పంపినవారి నియంత్రణ బయట ఉన్న computer resource లోకి ప్రవేశించినప్పుడు (IT Act, సెక్షన్ 13(1)).

law-of-contract-i-u1-t6.subtitle: Articles 298 and 299 of the Constitution of India; section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The Union and the States can make contracts like anyone else (Article 298), and can sue and be sued on them (Article 300). The Indian Contract Act applies to these contracts. But the Constitution adds formalities in Article 299(1) : a contract made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or a State must be expressed to be made by the President or the Governor , and executed on his behalf by such persons and in such manner as he directs or authorises . These formalities are mandatory . A contract that does not follow them is void and cannot be enforced by either side; there can be no implied contract with the Government, and no ratification or estoppel can cure the defect ( K.P. Chowdhary ; Mulamchand ). But if the Government has enjoyed the benefit of goods or work, it must pay compensation under Section 70 ( State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal ). Neither the President, the Governor nor the officer who signs is personally liable (Article 299(2)). When awarding contracts, the State must act fairly and non-arbitrarily (Article 14; Ramana Dayaram Shetty ; Kasturi Lal ). In exams, marks come from Article 299 quoted and broken into its three requirements, the effect of non-compliance with cases, the Section 70 remedy, and Article 14. In real life, it tells a supplier or contractor how to make sure a government order is binding.
legalProvision: Constitution of India

Article 298. Power to carry on trade, etc. The executive power of the Union and of each State shall extend to the carrying on of any trade or business and to the acquisition, holding and disposal of property and the making of contracts for any purpose: Provided that— (a) the said executive power of the Union shall, in so far as such trade or business or such purpose is not one with respect to which Parliament may make laws, be subject in each State to legislation by the State; and (b) the said executive power of each State shall, in so far as such trade or business or such purpose is not one with respect to which the State Legislature may make laws, be subject to legislation by Parliament.

Article 299. Contracts. (1) All contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State shall be expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor of the State, as the case may be, and all such contracts and all assurances of property made in the exercise of that power shall be executed on behalf of the President or the Governor by such persons and in such manner as he may direct or authorise. (2) Neither the President nor the Governor shall be personally liable in respect of any contract or assurance made or executed for the purposes of this Constitution, or for the purposes of any enactment relating to the Government of India heretofore in force, nor shall any person making or executing any such contract or assurance on behalf of any of them be personally liable in respect thereof.

Article 300(1). Suits and proceedings. The Government of India may sue or be sued by the name of the Union of India and the Government of a State may sue or be sued by the name of the State and may, subject to any provisions which may be made by Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of such State enacted by virtue of powers conferred by this Constitution, sue or be sued in relation to their respective affairs in the like cases as the Dominion of India and the corresponding Provinces or the corresponding Indian States might have sued or been sued if this Constitution had not been enacted.
Indian Contract Act, 1872

Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered.

Section 65. Obligation of person who has received advantage under void agreement, or contract that becomes void. When an agreement is discovered to be void, or when a contract becomes void, any person who has received any advantage under such agreement or contract is bound to restore it, or to make compensation for it to the person from whom he received it.

Section 230 (relevant part). In the absence of any contract to that effect, an agent cannot personally enforce contracts entered into by him on behalf of his principal, nor is he personally bound by them. … Such a contract shall be presumed to exist in the following cases:— … (3) where the principal, though disclosed, cannot be sued.
In simple words

Article 298: the Government can do business, deal in property and make contracts for any purpose. Article 299(1): a government contract must say it is made by the President (or the Governor) and must be signed on his behalf by an authorised officer in the authorised manner . Article 299(2): the President, the Governor and the officer who signs are not personally liable on such contracts. Article 300: the Union is sued as " Union of India ", and a State by its name (for example, "State of Andhra Pradesh"). Section 70: if you lawfully do work or deliver goods to someone, not as a gift, and he enjoys the benefit , he must pay for it or return it , even without a valid contract. Section 65: a person who received an advantage under an agreement found to be void must restore it or pay for it. Section 230: an agent is normally not personally bound, but is presumed bound where his principal cannot be sued .
en.meaning:
What a government contract is

A government contract is a contract made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State, for example: buying supplies, awarding construction works, leasing government land, selling forest produce, or granting licences by auction.

Why the Constitution adds formalities

Public money is at stake. The formalities make sure that only authorised officers bind the Government, and only in the authorised manner. Certainty. It must be clear that the contract is the Government's, not the officer's private deal. Protection of the public interest. The Supreme Court has said the provisions are mandatory and "enacted in the public interest" ( Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria ).

Article 299(1) broken into parts

Requirement What it means Example "expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor" The contract must say it is made in the name of the President or the Governor "This agreement is made by the Governor of Andhra Pradesh …" "executed on behalf of the President or the Governor" It must be signed on his behalf "For and on behalf of the Governor of Andhra Pradesh" "by such persons … as he may direct or authorise" The signing officer must be authorised (usually by a notification or rules of business) The District Collector, if authorised for such contracts "in such manner as he may direct or authorise" The authorised form must be followed A written deed in the authorised form

Because the contract must be "expressed" to be made and "executed", the Supreme Court has held that there can be no implied contract with the Government ( K.P. Chowdhary v. State of M.P. ).

Which contracts are covered

Article 299 covers contracts made in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State . A company or corporation set up by the Government that contracts in its own name is a separate legal person; on the words of the Article, such a contract is not one made "in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State".

Running example

The District Collector, Krishna (Andhra Pradesh), wants 500 school desks. Ravi Furniture quotes ₹2,500 a desk, total ₹12,50,000 (500 × ₹2,500). We will test three versions of the deal:

Version A: a written agreement "made by the Governor of Andhra Pradesh", signed "for and on behalf of the Governor" by the Collector, who is authorised by notification to sign such contracts. Version B: the Collector simply writes a letter in his own name: "Supply 500 desks at ₹2,500 each." Version C: the same as Version B, and Ravi Furniture delivers all 500 desks, which the schools start using.
keyPoints: The Government can contract for any purpose (Article 298) and sue or be sued (Article 300). Article 299(1): in the name of the President or Governor, executed on his behalf, by an authorised person in the authorised manner . The formalities are mandatory ( Bikhraj Jaipuria ); there is no implied contract ( K.P. Chowdhary ). A non-complying contract is void ; no ratification or estoppel ( Mulamchand ). The Government must pay for benefits it enjoys under Section 70 ( B.K. Mondal ). No personal liability of the President, Governor or signing officer (Article 299(2)). A valid government contract is enforced on its terms ( Alopi Parshad ). The State must not act arbitrarily in awarding contracts (Article 14; Ramana Dayaram Shetty ; Kasturi Lal ).

caseLaws.name: State of West Bengal v
caseLaws.facts: B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. Contractors built structures at Arambagh and Khanakul in 1944 for the Civil Supplies Department under contracts that did not follow the required form. They sued for Rs. 19,325. Principle. A non-complying contract is invalid, but the State must pay under Section 70 for work lawfully done, not gratuitously, whose benefit it enjoyed. AIR 1962 SC 779 : 1962 Supp (1) SCR 876. Why it matters. It is the leading case on the Section 70 remedy against the Government. Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria v. Union of India (1961) Facts. A railway officer placed orders for foodgrains in 1943 that were not made in the name of the Governor-General. The Railway stopped accepting deliveries, and the supplier sued. Principle. The formalities are mandatory and "enacted in the public interest"; a contract not complying with them does not bind the Government. AIR 1962 SC 113 : (1962) 2 SCR 880. Why it matters. It establishes that the formalities are mandatory . K.P. Chowdhary v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1966) Facts. The highest bidder at a 1959 forest auction refused to complete; no written contract had been executed. The State re-auctioned and tried to recover the deficiency of Rs. 51,500 from him. Principle. "in view of Art. 299(1) there can be no implied contract between the Government and another person"; the State could not recover. AIR 1967 SC 203 : (1966) 3 SCR 919. Why it matters. It shows non-compliance binds neither side. Mulamchand v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1968) Facts. A contract for forest produce with the Deputy Commissioner did not comply with Article 299(1). The contractor sought a refund of his deposit of Rs. 10,000. Principle. The provisions are mandatory; "There is no question of estoppel or ratification in such a case"; Section 70 may apply, but the claimant must account for the benefit he received. AIR 1968 SC 1218 : (1968) 3 SCR 214. Why it matters. It settles that there is no ratification or estoppel . Chatturbhuj Vithaldas Jasani v. Moreshwar Parashram (1954) Facts. Contracts to supply bidis to the Government were not made in the form required by Article 299(1). Principle. The Court said such contracts were "not void simply because the Union Government could not have been sued on them by reason of article 299(1)" and could be ratified. AIR 1954 SC 236 : 1954 SCR 817. Why it matters. It is the earlier view , later not followed on ratification ( Mulamchand ). Alopi Parshad & Sons Ltd. v. Union of India (1960) Facts. Agents appointed by agreement with the Governor-General to supply ghee to the Army from 1937 claimed higher rates when wartime costs rose. Principle. A contract is not frustrated merely because circumstances change, and quantum meruit cannot be awarded where the contract fixes the price. Supreme Court, decided 20 January 1960, (1960) 2 SCR 793. Why it matters. It shows a valid government contract is enforced on its terms , like any other contract. Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India (1979) Facts. A tender for a restaurant at Bombay airport was awarded to a person who did not meet the eligibility condition in the tender notice. Principle. The State must act according to a standard that is not arbitrary, irrational or irrelevant; departure from its own conditions violated Article 14. AIR 1979 SC 1628 : (1979) 3 SCC 489. Why it matters. It brings Article 14 into the award of government contracts.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the three requirements of Article 299(1)?
selfTest.a: Expressed to be made by the President or Governor; executed on his behalf; by a person and in a manner he directs or authorises.

selfTest.q: 2. Can there be an oral or implied contract with the Government?
selfTest.a: No ( K.P. Chowdhary v. State of M.P. ).

selfTest.q: 3. Can the Government ratify a contract that does not comply with Article 299(1)?
selfTest.a: No. "There is no question of estoppel or ratification in such a case" ( Mulamchand ).

selfTest.q: 4. A contractor builds a structure for the State without a valid contract, and the State uses it. Can he recover anything?
selfTest.a: Yes, compensation under Section 70 ( State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 5. Is the officer who signs a government contract personally liable?
selfTest.a: No, for a contract made in the required form (Article 299(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. In whose name is a State Government sued?
selfTest.a: In the name of the State (Article 300(1)).

selfTest.q: 7. Which Article limits the State's choice in awarding contracts?
selfTest.a: Article 14 ( Ramana Dayaram Shetty ; Kasturi Lal ).

సులభమైన మాటల్లో

ఆర్టికల్ 298: ప్రభుత్వం ఏ ప్రయోజనం కోసమైనా వ్యాపారం చేయవచ్చు, ఆస్తి కొనవచ్చు అమ్మవచ్చు, కాంట్రాక్టులు చేసుకోవచ్చు . ఆర్టికల్ 299(1): ప్రభుత్వ కాంట్రాక్టు రాష్ట్రపతి (లేదా గవర్నర్) చేసినట్టు చెప్పాలి , అధికారం ఉన్న అధికారి, అనుమతించిన పద్ధతిలో, ఆయన తరఫున సంతకం చేయాలి . ఆర్టికల్ 299(2): అలాంటి కాంట్రాక్టులపై రాష్ట్రపతి, గవర్నర్, సంతకం చేసిన అధికారి వ్యక్తిగతంగా బాధ్యులు కారు . ఆర్టికల్ 300: కేంద్రంపై " Union of India " పేరుతో, రాష్ట్రంపై దాని పేరుతో (ఉదా: "State of Andhra Pradesh") దావా వేస్తారు. సెక్షన్ 70: ఎవరికైనా ఉచితంగా కాకుండా, చట్టబద్ధంగా పని చేసినా లేదా సరుకు ఇచ్చినా, అతను దాని ప్రయోజనం అనుభవిస్తే , చెల్లుబాటు అయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు లేకపోయినా, అతను డబ్బు చెల్లించాలి లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి . సెక్షన్ 65: void అని తేలిన ఒప్పందం కింద ప్రయోజనం పొందిన వ్యక్తి దాన్ని తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి లేదా పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి. సెక్షన్ 230: ఏజెంట్ సాధారణంగా వ్యక్తిగతంగా కట్టుబడడు, కానీ అతని principal పై దావా వేయలేని చోట కట్టుబడినట్టు భావిస్తారు.
te.meaning:
ప్రభుత్వ కాంట్రాక్టు అంటే

కేంద్రం లేదా రాష్ట్రం కార్యనిర్వాహక అధికారాన్ని వినియోగించి చేసే కాంట్రాక్టే ప్రభుత్వ కాంట్రాక్టు . ఉదాహరణకు: సామగ్రి కొనడం, నిర్మాణ పనులు అప్పగించడం, ప్రభుత్వ భూమిని లీజుకు ఇవ్వడం, అటవీ ఉత్పత్తులు అమ్మడం, వేలం ద్వారా లైసెన్సులు ఇవ్వడం.

రాజ్యాంగం లాంఛనాలు ఎందుకు చేర్చింది

ప్రజాధనం ప్రమాదంలో ఉంటుంది. అధికారం ఉన్న అధికారులు మాత్రమే, అనుమతించిన పద్ధతిలో మాత్రమే ప్రభుత్వాన్ని కట్టుబడేలా చేయాలని లాంఛనాలు చూసుకుంటాయి. నిశ్చితత్వం. కాంట్రాక్టు ప్రభుత్వానిదే, అధికారి సొంత వ్యవహారం కాదని స్పష్టంగా ఉండాలి. ప్రజా ప్రయోజన రక్షణ. ఈ నిబంధనలు తప్పనిసరి అని, "enacted in the public interest" అని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది ( Seth Bikhraj Jaipuria ).

ఆర్టికల్ 299(1) ను భాగాలుగా

అవసరం అర్థం ఉదాహరణ "expressed to be made by the President, or by the Governor" కాంట్రాక్టు రాష్ట్రపతి లేదా గవర్నర్ పేరుతో చేసినట్టు చెప్పాలి "This agreement is made by the Governor of Andhra Pradesh …" "executed on behalf of the President or the Governor" ఆయన తరఫున సంతకం చేయాలి "For and on behalf of the Governor of Andhra Pradesh" "by such persons … as he may direct or authorise" సంతకం చేసే అధికారికి అధికారం ఉండాలి (సాధారణంగా నోటిఫికేషన్ లేదా rules of business ద్వారా) అలాంటి కాంట్రాక్టులకు అధికారం ఉంటే జిల్లా కలెక్టర్ "in such manner as he may direct or authorise" అనుమతించిన రూపాన్ని పాటించాలి అనుమతించిన రూపంలో రాతపూర్వక దస్తావేజు

కాంట్రాక్టును "expressed" చేయాలి, "executed" చేయాలి కాబట్టి, ప్రభుత్వంతో సూచిత (implied) కాంట్రాక్టు ఉండదని సుప్రీంకోర్టు తీర్పు ఇచ్చింది ( K.P. Chowdhary v. State of M.P. ).

ఏ కాంట్రాక్టులకు వర్తిస్తుంది

కేంద్రం లేదా రాష్ట్రం కార్యనిర్వాహక అధికారాన్ని వినియోగించి చేసే కాంట్రాక్టులకు ఆర్టికల్ 299 వర్తిస్తుంది. ప్రభుత్వం స్థాపించిన కంపెనీ లేదా కార్పొరేషన్ తన సొంత పేరుతో కాంట్రాక్టు చేస్తే, అది వేరే చట్టపరమైన వ్యక్తి; ఆర్టికల్ మాటల ప్రకారం, అలాంటి కాంట్రాక్టు "in the exercise of the executive power of the Union or of a State" చేసినది కాదు.

మన ఉదాహరణ

కృష్ణా జిల్లా కలెక్టర్ (ఆంధ్రప్రదేశ్) కు 500 పాఠశాల బెంచీలు కావాలి. రవి ఫర్నిచర్ ఒక్కో బెంచీకి ₹2,500, మొత్తం ₹12,50,000 (500 × ₹2,500) కోట్ చేసింది. ఈ బేరాన్ని మూడు రకాలుగా పరీక్షిద్దాం:

రూపం A: "made by the Governor of Andhra Pradesh" అని రాసిన ఒప్పందం; అలాంటి కాంట్రాక్టులపై సంతకం చేయడానికి నోటిఫికేషన్ ద్వారా అధికారం ఉన్న కలెక్టర్ "for and on behalf of the Governor" అని సంతకం చేశారు. రూపం B: కలెక్టర్ తన సొంత పేరుతో "500 బెంచీలు ఒక్కోటి ₹2,500 కి సరఫరా చేయండి" అని ఉత్తరం మాత్రమే రాశారు. రూపం C: రూపం B లాగే; రవి ఫర్నిచర్ 500 బెంచీలూ అందజేసింది, పాఠశాలలు వాటిని వాడడం మొదలుపెట్టాయి.

selfTest.q: 1. ఆర్టికల్ 299(1) లోని మూడు అవసరాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: రాష్ట్రపతి లేదా గవర్నర్ చేసినట్టు వ్యక్తం చేయాలి; ఆయన తరఫున అమలు చేయాలి; ఆయన నిర్దేశించిన లేదా అధికారం ఇచ్చిన వ్యక్తి, ఆ పద్ధతిలో.

selfTest.q: 2. ప్రభుత్వంతో నోటి లేదా సూచిత కాంట్రాక్టు ఉండవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: ఉండదు ( K.P. Chowdhary v. State of M.P. ).

selfTest.q: 3. ఆర్టికల్ 299(1) ను పాటించని కాంట్రాక్టును ప్రభుత్వం ratify చేయగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. "There is no question of estoppel or ratification in such a case" ( Mulamchand ).

selfTest.q: 4. చెల్లుబాటు అయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు లేకుండా ఒక కాంట్రాక్టరు రాష్ట్రం కోసం నిర్మాణం చేశాడు, రాష్ట్రం దాన్ని వాడుతోంది. అతను ఏమైనా పొందగలడా?
selfTest.a: పొందగలడు, సెక్షన్ 70 కింద పరిహారం ( State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 5. ప్రభుత్వ కాంట్రాక్టుపై సంతకం చేసిన అధికారి వ్యక్తిగతంగా బాధ్యుడా?
selfTest.a: కాదు, అవసరమైన రూపంలో చేసిన కాంట్రాక్టుకు (ఆర్టికల్ 299(2)).

selfTest.q: 6. రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వంపై ఏ పేరుతో దావా వేస్తారు?
7. కాంట్రాక్టులు ఇవ్వడంలో ప్రభుత్వ ఎంపికను ఏ ఆర్టికల్ పరిమితం చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: ఆర్టికల్ 14 ( Ramana Dayaram Shetty ; Kasturi Lal ).

law-of-contract-i-u1-t7.subtitle: Sections 2(d), 23 and 25 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A promise is enforced by law only when something is given in return for it. That "something in return" is consideration . It is the price of the promise . Under Section 2(d), consideration is an act, abstinence or promise , done at the desire of the promisor , by the promisee or any other person . It may be past, present or future . It need not be adequate , but it must be real and lawful . Without it, an agreement is void (Section 25), except in a few cases. Indian law is wider than English law on two points: who may give consideration, and past consideration. This is a favourite long-answer topic. In real life, it explains why a gift promise cannot be enforced but a sale can.
legalProvision: Section 2(d). When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise.
Section 2(f). Promises which form the consideration or part of the consideration for each other are called reciprocal promises.

Section 10 (relevant part). All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Section 23 (opening words). The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless it is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy.
Section 25 (opening words). An agreement made without consideration is void, unless … (the three exceptions are in the note Exception to consideration ).

Section 25, Explanation 2. An agreement to which the consent of the promisor is freely given is not void merely because the consideration is inadequate; but the inadequacy of the consideration may be taken into account by the Court in determining the question whether the consent of the promisor was freely given.
In simple words

Section 2(d) says what consideration is. Section 2(f) says that two promises given for each other are reciprocal promises . Section 10 says a valid contract needs lawful consideration . Section 23 says when consideration is unlawful . Section 25 says an agreement without consideration is void , except in a few cases. Its Explanation 2 says a small consideration is still consideration.
en.meaning:
The idea: something for something Consideration is what each side gives or promises in exchange for the other's promise. The Latin phrase is quid pro quo , "something for something". The law enforces bargains , not bare promises. A bare promise without consideration is a nudum pactum (a naked promise). The maxim ex nudo pacto non oritur actio means no action arises from a bare promise . Why the law asks for consideration. It separates a bargain from a gift. In a bargain, each side has given or risked something, so it is fair to enforce it. A bare promise to give a gift has nothing behind it. The classic English definition In Currie v. Misa (1875), consideration was described as some right, interest, profit or benefit to one party, or some forbearance, detriment, loss or responsibility given, suffered or undertaken by the other. Put simply, it is either a benefit to the promisor or a detriment (loss or burden) to the promisee. The Indian definition, broken into parts Read Section 2(d) as five questions. Part of Section 2(d) Question to ask Answer in simple words "at the desire of the promisor" Who asked for it? The promisor must have wanted it "the promisee or any other person" Who gave it? The promisee, or even a third person "has done … does … promises to do" When was it given? Past, present or future "done or abstained from doing" What kind of thing? An act, an abstinence, or a promise "something" How much ? Anything of some value in law, even if small Running example Ravi promises to pay Sita ₹15,000 for her used scooter. Sita promises to hand over the scooter next Sunday. Ravi is the promisor of the promise to pay. Sita is the promisee . Sita's promise to hand over the scooter is the consideration for Ravi's promise. Ravi's promise to pay ₹15,000 is the consideration for Sita's promise. Each promise is the price of the other. These are reciprocal promises (Section 2(f)). See Diagram 1 (when consideration is given: past, present, future). Diagram 1. Section 2(d): "has done", "does", "promises to do". flowchart LR P["PAST · 'has done'
Done before the promise,
at the promisor's request
Bala repairs Arjun's tractor in March;
Arjun promises ₹4,000 in May"] N(["THE PROMISE"]) E["PRESENT · executed · 'does'
Given at the same time
Ravi pays ₹15,000 and
takes the scooter on the spot"] F["FUTURE · executory · 'promises to do'
To be given later
Both promise to perform on Sunday"] P -- "before" --> N N -- "at the same time" --> E N -- "after" --> F Text description Three boxes along a time line around the moment of the promise. Past: done before the promise, at the promisor's request (Bala repairs Arjun's tractor in March; Arjun promises ₹4,000 in May). Present, executed: given at the same time (Ravi pays ₹15,000 and takes the scooter). Future, executory: to be given later (both promise to perform on Sunday).
keyPoints: Consideration is the price of the promise : something for something. Section 2(d): an act, abstinence or promise , done at the desire of the promisor , by the promisee or any other person . It may be past, present or future . It need not be adequate (Section 25, Explanation 2), but inadequacy may show that consent was not free. It must be real (not impossible, uncertain, or an existing duty) and lawful (Sections 10, 23). Promises given for each other are reciprocal promises (Section 2(f)). Consideration need not be money. Motive is not consideration. Indian law is wider than English law on third-party and past consideration. An agreement without consideration is void , except in the Section 25 cases.

caseLaws.name: Durga Prasad v
caseLaws.facts: Baldeo (1880) Facts. Durga Prasad built shops in a market at Etawah at the Collector's request. The shopkeepers who occupied them signed an agreement to pay him a commission on goods sold there. Principle. An act done at the desire of a third person, not the promisor, is not consideration. Nor was it done "for the promisor" under Section 25(2). (1881) ILR 3 All 221. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian case on "at the desire of the promisor". Chinnaya v. Ramayya (1882) Facts. An old lady gifted her property to her daughter on condition that the daughter pay an annuity to the old lady's sister. The daughter promised but did not pay. Principle. Under Section 2(d), consideration may move from "any other person". The sister could recover. ILR (1882) 4 Mad 137. Why it matters. It shows that Indian law is wider than English law on who may give consideration. Sindha Shri Ganpatsingji v. Abraham (1895) Facts. Services were done for the defendant at his request. He later promised to pay for them. Principle. Past services done at the promisor's request are good consideration for a later promise. ILR (1895) 20 Bom 755. Why it matters. It confirms that past consideration is valid in India. Lalman Shukla v. Gauri Dutt (1913) Facts. A servant was already sent to search for his master's missing nephew. He found the boy and claimed a reward announced after he had left. Principle. Doing what one is already bound to do is not fresh consideration. Allahabad High Court, 1913. Why it matters. It applies the existing-duty rule in India. It is also studied under acceptance (knowledge of the offer). Thomas v. Thomas (1842) Facts. Executors let a widow live in her late husband's house for life at a rent of £1 a year. Principle. Consideration need not be adequate, and motive is not consideration. (1842) 2 QB 851. Why it matters. It supports the inadequacy rule in Section 25, Explanation 2. Currie v. Misa (1875) Facts. A dispute over a cheque given to a bank for an existing debt. Principle. Consideration is some benefit to one party or some detriment to the other. (1875) LR 10 Ex 153. Why it matters. It gives the classic definition of consideration. Tweddle v. Atkinson (1861) Facts. After the plaintiff's marriage, his father and his father-in-law agreed in writing to pay him £100 and £200. The father-in-law died without paying, and the plaintiff sued his executor. Principle. In English law, consideration must move from the promisee. The plaintiff gave none and could not sue. 121 ER 762. Why it matters. It marks the English rule that Indian law does not follow on this point.

selfTest.q: 1. A does work at B's request. Later C promises to pay A. Is there consideration for C's promise?
selfTest.a: No. The work was not done at C's desire (Section 2(d); Durga Prasad v. Baldeo ).

selfTest.q: 2. Which words of Section 2(d) allow a third party to give consideration?
selfTest.a: "The promisee or any other person".

selfTest.q: 3. A freely agrees to sell a Rs. 1,000 horse for Rs. 10. Is it a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. Inadequacy alone does not make it void (Section 25, Explanation 2 and illustration (f)).

selfTest.q: 4. Is past consideration valid in India?
selfTest.a: Yes, if the past act was done at the promisor's desire ( Sindha Shri Ganpatsingji v. Abraham ).

selfTest.q: 5. A police officer is promised ₹1,000 to investigate a theft he is already assigned to. Is there consideration?
selfTest.a: No. Performing an existing legal duty is not fresh consideration.

selfTest.q: 6. What are reciprocal promises?
selfTest.a: Promises which form the consideration, or part of it, for each other (Section 2(f)).

legalProvision: Section 2(d). When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise.
Section 2(f). Promises which form the consideration or part of the consideration for each other are called reciprocal promises.

Section 10 (relevant part). All agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not hereby expressly declared to be void.

Section 23 (opening words). The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless it is forbidden by law; or is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat the provisions of any law; or is fraudulent; or involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or the Court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy.
Section 25 (opening words). An agreement made without consideration is void, unless … (మూడు మినహాయింపులు Exception to consideration నోట్‌లో ఉన్నాయి).

Section 25, Explanation 2. An agreement to which the consent of the promisor is freely given is not void merely because the consideration is inadequate; but the inadequacy of the consideration may be taken into account by the Court in determining the question whether the consent of the promisor was freely given.

సెక్షన్ 2(d): consideration అంటే ఏమిటో చెబుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 2(f): ఒకదానికొకటి బదులుగా ఇచ్చిన రెండు వాగ్దానాలను reciprocal promises (పరస్పర వాగ్దానాలు) అంటారు. సెక్షన్ 10: చెల్లుబాటు అయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టుకు చట్టబద్ధమైన consideration ఉండాలి. సెక్షన్ 23: consideration ఎప్పుడు చట్టవిరుద్ధం అవుతుందో చెబుతుంది. సెక్షన్ 25: consideration లేని ఒప్పందం void , కొన్ని సందర్భాలు తప్ప. దాని Explanation 2 ప్రకారం, తక్కువ consideration అయినా అది consideration నే.

మూల భావన: ఒకదానికి బదులు మరొకటి ఒకరి వాగ్దానానికి బదులుగా మరొకరు ఇచ్చేది లేదా చేస్తానని మాట ఇచ్చేదే consideration. లాటిన్‌లో దీన్ని quid pro quo అంటారు. అంటే "ఒకదానికి బదులు మరొకటి". చట్టం బేరాలను అమలు చేస్తుంది, ఉత్త మాటలను కాదు. బదులుగా ఏమీ లేని వాగ్దానాన్ని nudum pactum (ఉత్త వాగ్దానం) అంటారు. ex nudo pacto non oritur actio అనే సూత్రం ప్రకారం ఉత్త వాగ్దానం మీద దావా వేయలేం . చట్టం consideration ఎందుకు అడుగుతుంది? బేరానికీ బహుమతికీ తేడా చూపడానికి. బేరంలో ఇద్దరూ ఏదో ఒకటి ఇస్తారు లేదా వదులుకుంటారు. అందుకే దాన్ని అమలు చేయడం న్యాయం. బహుమతి ఇస్తానన్న మాట వెనుక బదులుగా ఏమీ ఉండదు. ఇంగ్లీష్ చట్టంలోని ప్రసిద్ధ నిర్వచనం Currie v. Misa (1875) కేసులో consideration ను ఇలా వివరించారు: ఒక పక్షానికి కలిగే హక్కు, ప్రయోజనం, లాభం , లేదా మరో పక్షం భరించే నష్టం, బాధ్యత, వదులుకోవడం . సులభంగా: promisor కు లాభం , లేదా promisee కు నష్టం/భారం . భారత నిర్వచనాన్ని భాగాలుగా చూద్దాం సెక్షన్ 2(d) ను ఐదు ప్రశ్నలుగా చదవండి. సెక్షన్ 2(d) లోని భాగం అడగాల్సిన ప్రశ్న సులభమైన జవాబు "at the desire of the promisor" ఎవరు కోరారు? promisor కోరి ఉండాలి "the promisee or any other person" ఎవరు ఇచ్చారు? promisee, లేదా మూడో వ్యక్తి అయినా సరే "has done … does … promises to do" ఎప్పుడు ఇచ్చారు? గతం, వర్తమానం లేదా భవిష్యత్తు "done or abstained from doing" ఏ రకమైనది? ఒక పని, మానుకోవడం, లేదా వాగ్దానం "something" ఎంత? చట్టం విలువ ఇచ్చే ఏదైనా, చిన్నదైనా సరే మనం వాడే ఉదాహరణ రవి , సీత పాత స్కూటర్‌ను ₹15,000 కు కొంటానని వాగ్దానం చేశాడు. వచ్చే ఆదివారం స్కూటర్ అప్పగిస్తానని సీత మాట ఇచ్చింది. డబ్బు చెల్లిస్తానన్న వాగ్దానానికి రవి promisor (వాగ్దానం చేసిన వ్యక్తి). సీత promisee (వాగ్దానం పొందిన వ్యక్తి). స్కూటర్ అప్పగిస్తానన్న సీత వాగ్దానమే రవి వాగ్దానానికి consideration . ₹15,000 చెల్లిస్తానన్న రవి వాగ్దానమే సీత వాగ్దానానికి consideration. ఒక్కో వాగ్దానం మరో దానికి ధర. ఇవే reciprocal promises (సెక్షన్ 2(f)). selfTest.q: 1. B అడగగా A ఒక పని చేశాడు. తర్వాత C, A కి డబ్బు ఇస్తానని మాట ఇచ్చాడు. C వాగ్దానానికి consideration ఉందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ఆ పని C కోరిక మేరకు జరగలేదు (సెక్షన్ 2(d); Durga Prasad v. Baldeo ).

selfTest.q: 2. మూడో వ్యక్తి consideration ఇవ్వడానికి వీలు కల్పించే సెక్షన్ 2(d) లోని మాటలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: "The promisee or any other person".

selfTest.q: 3. రూ. 1,000 గుర్రాన్ని రూ. 10 కి అమ్మడానికి A స్వేచ్ఛగా ఒప్పుకున్నాడు. ఇది కాంట్రాక్టా?
selfTest.a: అవును. తక్కువ consideration ఒక్కటే దాన్ని void చేయదు (సెక్షన్ 25, Explanation 2, illustration (f)).

selfTest.q: 4. భారతదేశంలో గత consideration చెల్లుతుందా?
selfTest.a: అవును, ఆ పని promisor కోరిక మేరకు జరిగి ఉంటే ( Sindha Shri Ganpatsingji v. Abraham ).

selfTest.q: 5. తనకు ఇప్పటికే అప్పగించిన దొంగతనం కేసును దర్యాప్తు చేసినందుకు ఒక పోలీసు అధికారికి ₹1,000 ఇస్తామన్నారు. consideration ఉందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ముందే ఉన్న చట్టపరమైన బాధ్యత నెరవేర్చడం కొత్త consideration కాదు.

selfTest.q: 6. పరస్పర వాగ్దానాలు అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఒకదానికొకటి consideration గా గానీ, consideration లో భాగంగా గానీ ఉండే వాగ్దానాలు (సెక్షన్ 2(f)).

law-of-contract-i-u1-t8.subtitle: Section 25 and section 185 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: The general rule is "no consideration, no contract" . Section 25 says an agreement made without consideration is void . Section 25 itself makes three exceptions . A promise without consideration is still a contract if it is: in writing, registered, and made out of natural love and affection between near relations (Section 25(1)); a promise to compensate a person who voluntarily did something for the promisor in the past (Section 25(2)); or a written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt (Section 25(3)). A gift actually made cannot be undone for want of consideration (Explanation 1). No consideration is needed to create an agency (Section 185). Examiners love this list. In real life, it explains when a family promise or a thank-you payment can be enforced.
legalProvision: Section 25. An agreement made without consideration is void, unless— (1) it is expressed in writing and registered under the law for the time being in force for the registration of documents, and is made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other; or unless (2) it is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor, or something which the promisor was legally compellable to do; or unless (3) it is a promise, made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith, or by his agent generally or specially authorized in that behalf, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law for the limitation of suits. In any of these cases, such an agreement is a contract. Explanation 1. Nothing in this section shall affect the validity, as between the donor and donee, of any gift actually made. Explanation 2. An agreement to which the consent of the promisor is freely given is not void merely because the consideration is inadequate; but the inadequacy of the consideration may be taken into account by the Court in determining the question whether the consent of the promisor was freely given.
Section 185. No consideration is necessary to create an agency.
Illustration (a) to Section 25. A promises, for no consideration, to give to B Rs. 1,000. This is a void agreement.
In simple words

The rule: a bare promise to give something for nothing is void. Exception 1: a family promise made out of love, if it is written and registered . Exception 2: a promise to pay someone who already helped you on his own . Exception 3: a written and signed promise to pay an old debt that can no longer be sued on. Explanation 1: a gift already handed over stays valid. Section 185: an agent can be appointed without consideration .
en.meaning:
An exception to consideration is a case where the law enforces a promise even though nothing was given in return for it. In each case Section 25 says: "such an agreement is a contract ". Why the law makes exceptions. The rule "no consideration, no contract" protects people from careless, one-sided promises. But in some cases there is good reason to enforce a promise without consideration. Love and affection within a family is a real reason. Writing and registration show the promise was serious. Gratitude for a past voluntary service rests on a real benefit already received. An old debt is still a moral duty. The law of limitation takes away only the remedy, not the debt itself. Section 25, illustration (a)"] Text description A promise made without consideration. If it is in writing, registered, and made out of natural love and affection between near relations, it is a contract under Section 25(1). Otherwise, if it promises to compensate a past act done voluntarily for the promisor, or something he was legally compellable to do, Section 25(2). Otherwise, if it is a written, signed promise to pay a time-barred debt, Section 25(3). Otherwise, if a gift has already been made, the gift stands (Explanation 1). If it creates an agency, no consideration is needed (Section 185). Otherwise the agreement is void.
keyPoints: An agreement without consideration is void (Section 25). Section 25(1): written + registered + natural love and affection + near relation. Section 25(2): promise to compensate a past voluntary act done for the promisor, or what he was legally compellable to do. Section 25(3): written and signed promise to pay a time-barred debt , wholly or in part. A mere acknowledgment is not enough. Before the limitation period ends, a signed acknowledgment (Section 18) or an acknowledged payment (Section 19) of the Limitation Act gives a fresh period. Explanation 1: a completed gift stands. Explanation 2: inadequacy alone does not make an agreement void. Section 185: no consideration is needed for agency . Section 63: a promisee may remit performance without consideration. A subscription promise binds only after the promisee acts on it.

caseLaws.name: Rajlukhy Dabee v
caseLaws.facts: Bhootnath Mookerjee (1900) Facts. A husband agreed in writing to pay his wife a monthly allowance. The document recited their quarrels and her claim to live separately. Principle. The agreement was not made out of natural love and affection, and no consideration moved from the wife. (1900) 4 CWN 488. Why it matters. Section 25(1) needs real love and affection, not just a near relationship. Durga Prasad v. Baldeo (1880) Facts. Shops were built at the Collector's request. The occupying shopkeepers later promised a commission to the builder. Principle. No consideration, and not within Section 25(2), because the act was not done for the promisors. (1881) ILR 3 All 221. Why it matters. It marks the limit of Section 25(2): the act must be done for the promisor. Debi Prasad v. Bhagwati Prasad (1942) Facts. A debtor executed a document covering an old time-barred debt together with a small fresh advance, with interest. Principle. A mere acknowledgment of a debt, without more, is not enough under Section 25(3). There must be a promise to pay, express or implied. AIR 1943 All 63. Why it matters. It separates an acknowledgment from a promise to pay. Kedarnath Bhattacharji v. Gorie Mahomed (1886) Facts. The defendant signed for ₹100 towards a Town Hall at Howrah. Relying on the subscriptions, the Commissioners contracted with a builder. Principle. A subscriber who knows that liability will be incurred on the faith of his subscription is bound to pay. (1886) ILR 14 Cal 64. Why it matters. A charitable promise can be enforced once the promisee has acted on it. Abdul Aziz v. Masum Ali (1914) Facts. A person promised ₹500 for repairing a mosque. Nothing was done on the faith of the promise, and the committee sued his heirs. Principle. A mere gratuitous promise without consideration is not enforceable. (1914) ILR 36 All 268. Why it matters. It is the contrast case to Kedarnath .

selfTest.q: 1. What are the four conditions of Section 25(1)?
selfTest.a: Writing, registration, natural love and affection, and near relation.

selfTest.q: 2. A finds B's lost purse and returns it. B promises A Rs. 50. Is it enforceable?
selfTest.a: Yes. It is a promise to compensate a past voluntary act (Section 25(2), illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 3. Is an oral promise to pay a time-barred debt valid?
selfTest.a: No. It must be in writing and signed (Section 25(3)).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a donor take back a completed gift because the donee gave nothing?
selfTest.a: No. A gift actually made is not affected by Section 25 (Explanation 1).

selfTest.q: 5. Which case held a charitable subscription enforceable, and why?
selfTest.a: Kedarnath Bhattacharji v. Gorie Mahomed , because the promisee took on liability on the faith of the subscription.

నియమం: బదులుగా ఏమీ లేకుండా ఏదైనా ఇస్తానన్న ఉత్త మాట void. మినహాయింపు 1: ప్రేమతో కుటుంబ సభ్యుడికి ఇచ్చిన మాట, అది రాసి, రిజిస్టర్ చేస్తే . మినహాయింపు 2: మనం అడగకుండానే మనకు సహాయం చేసిన వ్యక్తికి డబ్బు ఇస్తానన్న మాట. మినహాయింపు 3: ఇక దావా వేయలేని పాత అప్పు తీరుస్తానని రాసి, సంతకం చేసిన మాట. "Consideration లేకపోతే కాంట్రాక్టు లేదు" అనే నియమం, ఆలోచించకుండా ఇచ్చే ఏకపక్ష మాటల నుంచి ప్రజలను కాపాడుతుంది. కానీ కొన్ని సందర్భాల్లో consideration లేకపోయినా మాటను అమలు చేయడానికి బలమైన కారణం ఉంటుంది. కుటుంబంలోని ప్రేమాభిమానాలు నిజమైన కారణం. రాసి రిజిస్టర్ చేయడం ఆ మాట గంభీరంగా ఇచ్చినదని చూపిస్తుంది. గతంలో స్వచ్ఛందంగా చేసిన సేవకు కృతజ్ఞత , అప్పటికే పొందిన నిజమైన ప్రయోజనం మీద ఆధారపడుతుంది. పాత అప్పు తీర్చడం ఇంకా నైతిక బాధ్యతే. కాలపరిమితి చట్టం దావా వేసే హక్కును మాత్రమే తీసేస్తుంది, అప్పును కాదు. selfTest.q: 2. B పోగొట్టుకున్న పర్సును A కనిపెట్టి ఇచ్చాడు. A కి రూ. 50 ఇస్తానని B మాట ఇచ్చాడు. అది అమలవుతుందా?
selfTest.a: అవును. ఇది గతంలో స్వచ్ఛందంగా చేసిన పనికి పరిహారం ఇస్తానన్న వాగ్దానం (సెక్షన్ 25(2), illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 3. కాలదోషం పట్టిన అప్పు తీరుస్తానన్న నోటి మాట చెల్లుతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అది రాసి, సంతకం చేసి ఉండాలి (సెక్షన్ 25(3)).

selfTest.q: 4. దానగ్రహీత బదులుగా ఏమీ ఇవ్వలేదని, పూర్తయిన దానాన్ని దాత వెనక్కి తీసుకోవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. ఇప్పటికే చేసిన దానం మీద సెక్షన్ 25 ప్రభావం ఉండదు (Explanation 1).

selfTest.q: 5. ఏ కేసులో చందా వాగ్దానం అమలవుతుందని చెప్పారు, ఎందుకు?
selfTest.a: Kedarnath Bhattacharji v. Gorie Mahomed లో. ఆ చందాను నమ్మి promisee బాధ్యత తీసుకున్నాడు కాబట్టి.

law-of-contract-i-u1-t9.subtitle: Section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 and the common law rule that only parties can sue

en.inOneMinute: The doctrine of privity of contract says that only the parties to a contract can sue on it , and only they can be sued on it. A person who is not a party, a "third party" or "stranger", has no right to enforce the contract, even if it was made for his benefit. The Indian Contract Act does not state the rule in one section, but it follows from the definitions: the promisor is the person making the proposal and the promisee is the person accepting it (Section 2(c)), and Section 37 says "the parties to a contract" must perform their promises. The Supreme Court confirmed the rule in M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore (1969), following Dunlop v. Selfridge and Jamna Das v. Ram Autar . Keep two ideas apart: privity of contract (who is a party?) applies in India; but privity of consideration (must consideration come from the plaintiff?) does not , because Section 2(d) allows consideration to move from "the promisee or any other person ". There are recognised exceptions (trust or charge, family arrangement, acknowledgment, agency, assignment , covenants running with land). They are covered in Exceptions to the privity of contract . In exams, marks come from the meaning, the statutory basis, the two aspects of privity, Tweddle , Dunlop and M.C. Chacko , and a short note on exceptions. In real life, it tells you whether you can sue on a contract you did not sign.
legalProvision: Section 2(b). When the person to whom the proposal is made signifies his assent thereto, the proposal is said to be accepted. A proposal, when accepted, becomes a promise;
Section 2(c). The person making the proposal is called the "promisor", and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promisee";

Section 2(d). When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise;
Section 2(e). Every promise and every set of promises, forming the consideration for each other, is an agreement;
Section 2(h). An agreement enforceable by law is a contract;

Section 37 (first paragraph). Obligation of parties to contracts. The parties to a contract must either perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the provisions of this Act, or of any other law.
In simple words

Section 2(c): the promisor is the one who makes the proposal; the promisee is the one who accepts it. These two are the parties . Section 2(d): the consideration may be given by the promisee or by someone else . Sections 2(e), 2(h): promises exchanged between the parties form an agreement; if enforceable, a contract . Section 37: it is the parties who must perform; the duty and the right lie between them. Read together, these sections make the contract a link between the parties . A third person is outside that link.
en.meaning:
What "privity" means

"Privity" means a relationship that exists between the parties to a transaction. Privity of contract is the relationship between the parties to a contract. The doctrine of privity draws two consequences from it:

A stranger to a contract cannot sue on it , even if the contract was made for his benefit. A stranger to a contract cannot be sued on it : the parties cannot impose duties on a person who did not agree.

The two aspects of privity

Aspect Question English law Indian law Privity of contract Is the plaintiff a party to the contract? Only a party can sue ( Dunlop ) Only a party can sue ( M.C. Chacko ; Jamna Das ) Privity of consideration Did the consideration move from the plaintiff? It must ( Tweddle ; Dunlop ) Not needed: "the promisee or any other person" (Section 2(d))

So in India a promisee can sue even if a third person gave the consideration; but a third person who is not a promisee cannot sue, even if he gave consideration or was meant to benefit. The Calcutta High Court explained this in Krishna Lal Sadhu v. Pramila Bala Dasi (Rankin CJ), quoted with approval by the Supreme Court in M.C. Chacko : Section 2(d) widens consideration, but "there is nothing in s. 2 to encourage the idea that contracts can be enforced by a person who is not a party to the contract, but this notion is rightly excluded by the definition of 'promisor' and 'promisee'."

Why the law has this rule

Freedom of contract. The parties chose each other. A stranger should not be able to step in and enforce, or be burdened by, a bargain he did not make. Mutuality. In Tweddle v. Atkinson , Crompton J said it would be "a monstrous proposition to say that a person was a party to the contract for the purpose of suing upon it for his own advantage, and not a party to it for the purpose of being sued." Freedom to vary. The parties may wish to change or cancel their contract. If third parties had rights, they could not do so freely.

Running example

Kavya sells her car to Madhu for ₹4,00,000 . As part of the price, Madhu promises Kavya that he will pay ₹1,00,000 directly to Suresh , to whom Kavya owes money, and pay the balance of ₹3,00,000 to Kavya (₹1,00,000 + ₹3,00,000 = ₹4,00,000). Madhu pays Kavya ₹3,00,000 but never pays Suresh.

Parties: Kavya (promisee of Madhu's promise to pay) and Madhu (promisor). Third party: Suresh, who benefits from the promise but did not make or accept it.
keyPoints: Only parties to a contract can sue or be sued on it. Statutory basis: promisor and promisee are the parties (Section 2(c)); parties must perform (Section 37). Tweddle v. Atkinson (1861): stranger to consideration cannot sue. Dunlop v. Selfridge (1915): "only a person who is a party to a contract can sue on it." M.C. Chacko (1969): rule applies in India, except a beneficiary under a trust or a family arrangement. Privity of consideration does not apply in India (Section 2(d)); privity of contract does. The promisee can sue even if the benefit was for a third person. Exceptions: trust/charge, family arrangement, acknowledgment, assignment, agency, covenants running with land.

caseLaws.name: Tweddle v
caseLaws.facts: Atkinson (1861) Facts. The fathers of a newly married couple agreed in writing that each would pay a sum to the bridegroom, who was given "full power to sue". The bride's father died without paying, and the bridegroom sued his executor. Principle. "no stranger to the consideration can take advantage of a contract, although made for his benefit." (1861) 121 ER 762 (Queen's Bench). Why it matters. It is the starting point of the privity doctrine in English law. Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co. Ltd. v. Selfridge & Co. Ltd. (1915) Facts. Selfridge promised Dew & Co. not to sell Dunlop tyres below list price and to pay Dunlop £5 per tyre for any breach. Selfridge sold below list price, and Dunlop sued. Principle. "only a person who is a party to a contract can sue on it. Our law knows nothing of a jus quaesitum tertio arising by way of contract." [1915] AC 847 (House of Lords). Why it matters. It is the classic statement of the privity rule . M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore (1969) Facts. A father's family deed said his son would pay any amount due to a bank under the father's guarantee. The bank sued the son and his properties under the deed. Principle. A person not a party to a contract cannot enforce it, except a beneficiary under a trust created by the contract or in the case of a family arrangement. AIR 1970 SC 500 : (1969) 2 SCC 343. Why it matters. It is the leading Indian Supreme Court case on privity. Jamna Das v. Ram Autar Pande (1911) Facts. A purchaser promised the seller to pay off the seller's mortgage debt. The mortgagee sued the purchaser on that promise. Principle. The mortgagee, not being a party to the sale, could not enforce the promise. (1911) 39 IA 7 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It applies privity to Indian law and is followed in M.C. Chacko .

selfTest.q: 1. What is the doctrine of privity of contract?
selfTest.a: Only the parties to a contract can sue or be sued on it.

selfTest.q: 2. Which sections form its basis in India?
selfTest.a: Sections 2(c) (promisor and promisee) and 37 (parties must perform).

selfTest.q: 3. Does privity of consideration apply in India?
selfTest.a: No. Under Section 2(d), consideration may move from the promisee or any other person.

selfTest.q: 4. A promises B to pay C ₹10,000. C is not a party. Can C sue A?
selfTest.a: No, unless an exception applies ( M.C. Chacko ). B can sue A.

selfTest.q: 5. Which Indian case states the rule and its two exceptions?
selfTest.a: M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore (1969): beneficiary under a trust; family arrangement.

selfTest.q: 6. Does Chinnaya v. Ramayya mean privity does not apply in India?
selfTest.a: No. It is about who may give consideration.

సెక్షన్ 2(c): ప్రతిపాదన చేసినవారు promisor ; దాన్ని అంగీకరించినవారు promisee . ఈ ఇద్దరే పక్షాలు . సెక్షన్ 2(d): ప్రతిఫలాన్ని promisee గానీ ఇంకెవరైనా గానీ ఇవ్వవచ్చు. సెక్షన్లు 2(e), 2(h): పక్షాల మధ్య మార్చుకున్న వాగ్దానాలు ఒప్పందం; అమలు చేయించగలిగితే కాంట్రాక్టు. సెక్షన్ 37: నెరవేర్చాల్సింది పక్షాలే ; బాధ్యత, హక్కు వారి మధ్యే ఉంటాయి. ఈ సెక్షన్లను కలిపి చదివితే, కాంట్రాక్టు పక్షాల మధ్య బంధం . మూడో వ్యక్తి ఆ బంధం బయట ఉంటాడు.
te.meaning:
"Privity" అంటే

"Privity" అంటే ఒక వ్యవహారంలోని పక్షాల మధ్య ఉండే సంబంధం . Privity of contract అంటే కాంట్రాక్టు పక్షాల మధ్య ఉండే సంబంధం. Privity సిద్ధాంతం దీని నుంచి రెండు ఫలితాలు తీస్తుంది:

కాంట్రాక్టుకు అపరిచితుడు దానిపై దావా వేయలేడు , కాంట్రాక్టు అతని ప్రయోజనం కోసమే చేసినా. కాంట్రాక్టుకు అపరిచితుడిపై దానిపై దావా వేయలేం : ఒప్పుకోని వ్యక్తిపై పక్షాలు బాధ్యతలు మోపలేవు.

Privity లోని రెండు అంశాలు

అంశం ప్రశ్న ఇంగ్లీష్ చట్టం భారత చట్టం Privity of contract వాది కాంట్రాక్టులో పక్షమా ? పక్షం మాత్రమే దావా వేయగలరు ( Dunlop ) పక్షం మాత్రమే దావా వేయగలరు ( M.C. Chacko ; Jamna Das ) Privity of consideration ప్రతిఫలం వాది నుంచే వచ్చిందా ? రావాలి ( Tweddle ; Dunlop ) అవసరం లేదు: "the promisee or any other person" (సెక్షన్ 2(d))

కాబట్టి భారతదేశంలో ప్రతిఫలం మూడో వ్యక్తి ఇచ్చినా promisee దావా వేయగలరు; కానీ promisee కాని మూడో వ్యక్తి , ప్రతిఫలం ఇచ్చినా లేదా ప్రయోజనం పొందాల్సినవాడైనా, దావా వేయలేడు. Krishna Lal Sadhu v. Pramila Bala Dasi లో కలకత్తా హైకోర్టు (Rankin CJ) దీన్ని వివరించింది; M.C. Chacko లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు దాన్ని ఆమోదిస్తూ ఉటంకించింది: సెక్షన్ 2(d) ప్రతిఫలాన్ని విస్తరిస్తుంది, కానీ "there is nothing in s. 2 to encourage the idea that contracts can be enforced by a person who is not a party to the contract, but this notion is rightly excluded by the definition of 'promisor' and 'promisee'."

చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది

కాంట్రాక్టు స్వేచ్ఛ. పక్షాలు ఒకరినొకరు ఎంచుకున్నారు. తాను చేయని బేరంలోకి అపరిచితుడు వచ్చి దాన్ని అమలు చేయించకూడదు, దాని భారమూ మోయకూడదు. పరస్పరత్వం. Tweddle v. Atkinson లో Crompton J ఇలా అన్నారు: "a monstrous proposition to say that a person was a party to the contract for the purpose of suing upon it for his own advantage, and not a party to it for the purpose of being sued." మార్చుకునే స్వేచ్ఛ. పక్షాలు తమ కాంట్రాక్టును మార్చుకోవాలని లేదా రద్దు చేసుకోవాలని అనుకోవచ్చు. మూడో వ్యక్తులకు హక్కులుంటే, అలా స్వేచ్ఛగా చేయలేరు.

మన ఉదాహరణ

కావ్య తన కారును మధు కు ₹4,00,000 కి అమ్మింది. ధరలో భాగంగా, కావ్య అప్పు ఉన్న సురేష్ కు నేరుగా ₹1,00,000 చెల్లిస్తానని, మిగిలిన ₹3,00,000 కావ్యకు చెల్లిస్తానని మధు కావ్యకు వాగ్దానం చేశాడు (₹1,00,000 + ₹3,00,000 = ₹4,00,000). మధు కావ్యకు ₹3,00,000 చెల్లించాడు, కానీ సురేష్‌కు ఎప్పుడూ చెల్లించలేదు.

పక్షాలు: కావ్య (మధు చెల్లిస్తానన్న వాగ్దానానికి promisee), మధు (promisor). మూడో వ్యక్తి: సురేష్; వాగ్దానం వల్ల అతనికి ప్రయోజనం, కానీ అతను దాన్ని చేయలేదు, అంగీకరించలేదు.

selfTest.q: 1. Privity of contract సిద్ధాంతం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టుపై దాని పక్షాలు మాత్రమే దావా వేయగలరు, వారిపైనే దావా వేయవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 2. భారతదేశంలో దీనికి ఏ సెక్షన్లు ఆధారం?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్లు 2(c) (promisor, promisee), 37 (పక్షాలు నెరవేర్చాలి).

selfTest.q: 3. భారతదేశంలో privity of consideration వర్తిస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. సెక్షన్ 2(d) కింద ప్రతిఫలం promisee నుంచి గానీ ఇంకెవరి నుంచైనా గానీ రావచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 4. C కి ₹10,000 చెల్లిస్తానని A, B కి వాగ్దానం చేశాడు. C పక్షం కాదు. C, A పై దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు, మినహాయింపు వర్తిస్తే తప్ప ( M.C. Chacko ). B, A పై దావా వేయగలడు.

selfTest.q: 5. నియమాన్ని, దాని రెండు మినహాయింపులను ఏ భారత కేసు చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore (1969): ట్రస్టు కింద లబ్ధిదారు; కుటుంబ ఏర్పాటు.

selfTest.q: 6. Chinnaya v. Ramayya అంటే భారతదేశంలో privity వర్తించదని అర్థమా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అది ఎవరు ప్రతిఫలం ఇవ్వవచ్చు అనే దాని గురించి.

law-of-contract-i-u1-t10.subtitle: Trusts, family arrangements, agency, assignment, estoppel, covenants running with land and statutes

en.inOneMinute: The general rule of privity is that only a party to a contract can sue on it ( Dunlop v. Selfridge ; M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore ). But the rule would cause injustice in some cases, so the courts recognise exceptions in which a person who is not a party can enforce the contract, or is treated as a party: Trust or charge : a beneficiary under a trust, or a person in whose favour a charge on property is created by the contract ( Khwaja Muhammad Khan v. Husaini Begam ). Marriage settlement, partition or other family arrangement , where provision is made for a family member ( M.C. Chacko recognises this exception). Acknowledgment or estoppel : where the promisor, by his conduct or acknowledgment, makes himself directly liable to the third person ( Narayani Devi v. Tagore Commercial Corporation ). Assignment : the benefit of a contract can be assigned, and the assignee can enforce it. Agency : a principal can sue and be sued on a contract made by his agent (Sections 182, 226, 230). Covenants running with land : a purchaser of land with notice of a restrictive covenant can be bound by it ( Tulk v. Moxhay ). In exams, marks come from stating the rule first, then each exception with its basis and a case. In real life, it tells a widow, a family member, a buyer of a debt or a principal when they can sue on a contract they did not sign.
legalProvision: There is no single section listing the exceptions. They come from case law and from the provisions below.
Section 2(c). The person making the proposal is called the "promisor", and the person accepting the proposal is called the "promisee";

Section 2(d). When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise;

Section 182. "Agent" and "principal" defined. An "agent" is a person employed to do any act for another, or to represent another in dealings with third persons. The person for whom such act is done, or who is so represented, is called the "principal".

Section 226. Enforcement and consequences of agent's contracts. Contracts entered into through an agent, and obligations arising from acts done by an agent, may be enforced in the same manner, and will have the same legal consequences, as if the contracts had been entered into and the acts done by the principal in person.

Section 230 (first paragraph). In the absence of any contract to that effect, an agent cannot personally enforce contracts entered into by him on behalf of his principal, nor is he personally bound by them.

The rule and its exceptions, in the words of the Supreme Court ( M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore , 1969): "It must therefore be taken as well settled that except in the case of a beneficiary under a trust created by a contract or in the case of a family arrangement, no right may be enforced by a person who is not a party to the contract."
In simple words

Sections 2(c), 2(d): the parties are the promisor and promisee; consideration may come from anyone. The privity rule comes from these definitions. Section 182: an agent acts for a principal . Section 226: a contract made through an agent is enforced as if the principal made it himself . So the principal, who did not sign, can sue and be sued. Section 230: the agent normally cannot sue or be sued on it. M.C. Chacko: the Supreme Court named two exceptions expressly: a beneficiary under a trust and a family arrangement . Other exceptions come from other cases and statutes.
en.meaning:
What an "exception to privity" is

An exception is a situation in which a person who is not the promisee can still enforce a promise, or is bound by it, because the law treats him as having a direct right or duty.

Why the exceptions exist

Justice to the intended beneficiary. Where the whole purpose of the contract is to provide for a person, such as a wife or a widow, it would be unjust to leave her without a remedy. Equity. A trust or charge gives the beneficiary an equitable right, not a contractual one. In M.C. Chacko , the Supreme Court explained that a beneficiary under a trust may enforce the rights the trust gives him because "though he is not a party to the contract his rights are equitable and not contractual." Representation. In agency, the principal is the real party; the agent is only his instrument. Commercial need. Debts and other contract rights must be transferable ( assignment ).

Running example (the rule)

Kavya sells her car to Madhu for ₹4,00,000 , and Madhu promises Kavya to pay ₹1,00,000 of the price directly to Kavya's creditor Suresh . Madhu does not pay. Under the rule, Suresh cannot sue Madhu ( M.C. Chacko ; Jamna Das v. Ram Autar ). Below, we change the facts to fit each exception.
keyPoints: The rule: only parties can sue ( Dunlop ; M.C. Chacko ). Trust or charge : beneficiary can enforce in equity ( Khwaja Muhammad Khan ). Family arrangement , marriage settlement or partition: family member provided for can enforce ( M.C. Chacko ). Acknowledgment or estoppel : promisor's conduct creates direct liability ( Narayani Devi ). Assignment : benefit, not burden, can be transferred (Transfer of Property Act, Section 130). Agency : principal sues and is sued (Section 226); agent normally not (Section 230). Covenants running with land : purchaser with notice bound ( Tulk v. Moxhay ). Chinnaya v. Ramayya is about consideration, not an exception to privity.

caseLaws.name: Khwaja Muhammad Khan v
caseLaws.facts: Husaini Begam (1910) Facts. Before the marriage of two minors in 1877, the bridegroom's father agreed with the bride's father to pay the bride Rs. 500 a month in perpetuity, charged on immovable property. The wife later sued for arrears. Principle. "although no party to the document, she is clearly entitled to proceed in equity to enforce her claim." (1910) 37 IA 152 (Privy Council). Why it matters. It is the leading case on the trust or charge and marriage settlement exceptions. M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore (1969) Facts. A father's family deed directed his son to pay any amount due to a bank under the father's guarantee. The bank sued to enforce the deed against the son and his properties. Principle. A non-party cannot enforce a contract "except in the case of a beneficiary under a trust created by a contract or in the case of a family arrangement"; the bank was neither. AIR 1970 SC 500 : (1969) 2 SCC 343. Why it matters. It states the rule and the two main exceptions for India, and shows their limits. Narayani Devi v. Tagore Commercial Corporation Ltd. (1972) Facts. A company agreed with a husband, who transferred shares to it, to pay Rs. 250 a month to his widow after his death. After he died, the widow sued for arrears. Principle. The company's acknowledgment and conduct towards the widow created privity, and she could recover. AIR 1973 Cal 401 (Calcutta High Court). Why it matters. It illustrates the acknowledgment or estoppel exception. Tulk v. Moxhay (1848) Facts. Land in Leicester Square was sold subject to a covenant to keep it as a garden. A later purchaser, Moxhay, who knew of the covenant, wanted to build on it. Principle. A purchaser with notice of a restrictive covenant is bound by it in equity and can be restrained by injunction. (1848) 41 ER 1143. Why it matters. It is the leading case on covenants running with land .

selfTest.q: 1. Which two exceptions did the Supreme Court name in M.C. Chacko?
selfTest.a: A beneficiary under a trust created by a contract, and a family arrangement.

selfTest.q: 2. Why could the wife sue in Khwaja Muhammad Khan?
selfTest.a: The allowance was charged on property for her benefit, so she could proceed in equity, though not a party.

selfTest.q: 3. Why did the bank lose in M.C. Chacko?
selfTest.a: It was not a party, and the deed created no trust or charge in its favour.

selfTest.q: 4. Can the burden of a contract be assigned?
selfTest.a: Not without the other party's consent; only the benefit can be assigned.

selfTest.q: 5. Under which section is a contract made by an agent enforced as if made by the principal?
selfTest.a: Section 226.

selfTest.q: 6. Which case is the authority for covenants running with land?
selfTest.a: Tulk v. Moxhay (1848).

Section 2(d). When, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise;
