రద్దు చేసుకుని
పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు"] B --> A B --> C A --> A1 C --> C1 C --> C2 C --> C3 వచన వివరణ కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘన (సెక్షన్లు 39, 53 నుంచి 55) కు రెండు రకాలు. ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘన: గడువు తేదీకి ముందే నిరాకరణ లేదా నెరవేర్చలేని స్థితి (సెక్షన్ 39); వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించి వెంటనే దావా వేయవచ్చు, లేదా గడువు తేదీ వరకు ఆగవచ్చు. వాస్తవ ఉల్లంఘనకు మూడు రూపాలు: గడువు సమయంలో నెరవేర్చకపోవడం (సెక్షన్ 55) – సమయం ప్రధానమైతే వాగ్దానగ్రహీత ఇష్టం మేరకు కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు చేయదగినది, లేకపోతే పరిహారం మాత్రమే; నెరవేర్చే సమయంలో నిరాకరణ (సెక్షన్ 39) – వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించవచ్చు; ఒక పక్షం అడ్డుకోవడం (సెక్షన్ 53) – అడ్డుకోబడిన పక్షం కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేసుకుని పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 1. ఉల్లంఘన కాంట్రాక్టును ఆటోమేటిక్‌గా ముగిస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అమాయక పక్షం దాన్ని ముగించడానికి లేదా కొనసాగించడానికి ఎంచుకోవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 39).

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 39 కింద వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించే హక్కు ఎప్పుడు కోల్పోతాడు?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు కొనసాగడాన్ని మాటలతో గానీ ప్రవర్తనతో గానీ అంగీకరించినప్పుడు.

selfTest.q: 3. ఉల్లంఘన ఫ్రస్ట్రేషన్‌కు ఎలా భిన్నం?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన ఒక పక్షం సొంత లోపం నుంచి వస్తుంది; అమాయక పక్షానికి ఎంపిక, నష్టపరిహారం ఇస్తుంది. ఫ్రస్ట్రేషన్ బయటి సంఘటన నుంచి వస్తుంది; కాంట్రాక్టును ఆటోమేటిక్‌గా శూన్యం చేస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. ఆరో రాత్రి గాయని రాకపోవడంతో మేనేజర్ కాంట్రాక్టును ముగిస్తాడు. అతను ఆమెకు ఏమైనా చెల్లించాలా?
selfTest.a: అవును. ఆమె పాడిన ఐదు రాత్రులకు చెల్లించాలి (సెక్షన్ 65, Illustration (c)).

selfTest.q: 5. ఉల్లంఘనకు పరిహారం దావా ఎంత కాలంలో వేయాలి?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘించబడినప్పటి నుంచి మూడేళ్లలో (లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, ఆర్టికల్ 55).

law-of-contract-i-u3-t10.subtitle: Section 39 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An anticipatory breach happens when a party refuses to perform, or makes himself unable to perform, before the time for performance arrives. The other party need not wait for the due date. He has two choices: He may accept the refusal, end the contract and sue at once. Or he may keep the contract alive and wait. The choice has risks. In exams, the meaning, the two choices and the cases earn the marks. In real life, it decides whether you can act the day a supplier says he will not deliver.
legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance. Illustrations. (a) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her 100 rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night A wilfully absents herself from the theatre. B is at liberty to put an end to the contract. (b) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two night's in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her at the rate of 100 rupees for each night. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself. With the assent of B, A sings on the seventh night. B has signified his acquiescence in the continuance of the contract, and cannot now put an end to it, but is entitled to compensation for the damage sustained by him through A's failure to sing on the sixth night.
Related provisions

Section 73, Illustration (c). A contracts to buy of B, at a stated price, 50 maunds of rice, no time being fixed for delivery. A afterwards informs B that he will not accept the rice if tendered to him. B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the amount, if any, by which the contract price exceeds that which B can obtain for the rice at the time when A informs B that he will not accept it.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 16(c). Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person— ... (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant. Explanation. —For the purposes of clause (c),— ... (ii) the plaintiff must prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
In simple words

Section 39 covers both a refusal and a disabling act, if it goes to the whole promise. The promisee "may" end the contract. He loses that right if he shows, by words or conduct, that he accepts the contract's continuance. Section 73, Illustration (c) measures the loss at the time the defaulter announces his refusal.
en.meaning:
Anticipatory breach is a breach committed before the time fixed for performance. It takes two forms: Form What happens Example Express repudiation The party says he will not perform A seller writes, "I will not deliver" Implied repudiation His conduct makes performance impossible He sells to another buyer the very goods he promised The words of the Act. The Act does not use the words "anticipatory breach". Section 39 covers it in the words "refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing". The English case Hochster v. De La Tour gave the doctrine its shape. Why the law lets the innocent party act early. Waiting helps no one. He can look for another supplier at once and so reduce his loss. See Diagram 1 for the moments in order. Diagram 1. Read from top to bottom. After the refusal, follow the branch the promisee chooses. flowchart TD M["Contract made"] R["Before the due date:
refusal or disabling act
covering the whole promise (s.39)"] Q{"What does the
promisee choose?"} A["Accept the repudiation:
contract ends; sue at once
for damages (s.73); mitigate"] A2["Cannot later ask for
specific performance"] W["Affirm and wait:
contract binds both sides;
the other party may withdraw"] W2["At the due date: must be
ready and willing; an event in
between may defeat the claim"] M --> R R --> Q Q -->|"Accept"| A A --> A2 Q -->|"Affirm"| W W --> W2 Text description The contract is made. Before the due date, one party refuses to perform, or disables himself from performing, his whole promise (Section 39). The promisee then chooses. If he accepts the repudiation, the contract ends, he may sue at once for damages under Section 73 and must mitigate his loss, but he cannot later ask for specific performance. If he affirms and waits, the contract stays binding on both sides and the other party may withdraw his refusal; at the due date the promisee must be ready and willing to perform, and an event in between may defeat his claim (Avery v. Bowden).
keyPoints: Anticipatory breach is a refusal or disabling act before the due date (Section 39). The refusal must be clear and cover the whole promise. The promisee may accept it, end the contract and sue at once ( Hochster ). Or he may affirm the contract and wait, staying ready and willing. If he waits, an intervening event may defeat his claim ( Avery v. Bowden ). After accepting the repudiation he can claim damages but not specific performance ( Jawahar Lal Wadhwa ). Section 39 covers refusal and also disabling oneself from performing. Specific performance needs proof of readiness and willingness (Specific Relief Act, Section 16(c)).

caseLaws.name: Hochster v
caseLaws.facts: De La Tour (1853) Facts. In April 1852 De La Tour engaged Hochster as a courier for a three-month tour from 1 June 1852. On 11 May 1852 he wrote that he had changed his mind and declined Hochster's services. Hochster sued on 22 May. Principle. The injured party has "an option ... either to sue immediately, or to wait till the time when the act was to be done, still holding it as prospectively binding". Judgment for the plaintiff. (1853) 2 E & B 678 : 118 ER 922 (Queen's Bench, 25 June 1853). Why it matters. It is the origin of the doctrine. Frost v. Knight (1872) Facts. Knight promised to marry Miss Frost on his father's death. While the father was still alive, he told her he would not marry her. LR 7 Ex 111. Principle. She could sue once he made clear he would not perform, without waiting for the father's death. Why it matters. It confirms Hochster for a promise with an uncertain date. Avery v. Bowden (1855) Facts. A charterer's agent told the ship's master at Odessa that no cargo would be supplied. The master stayed on. War made performance illegal before the time for loading ended. (1855) 5 E & B 714. Principle. A promisee who does not accept the repudiation keeps the contract alive and takes the risk. The shipowner lost. Why it matters. It shows the risk of waiting. Jawahar Lal Wadhwa v. Haripada Chakroberty (1988) Facts. Under an agreement of 6 September 1973, an advance of Rs 5,000 was paid and monthly payments of Rs 105 followed. On 16 January 1976 notice was given repudiating the agreement. The dispute went to arbitration, and an award of 18 March 1988 granted Rs 58,498.60. Principle. A party who accepts an anticipatory breach and treats the contract as ended may claim damages, not specific performance. A party who keeps the contract alive must show that he was ready and willing to perform. AIR 1989 SC 606 : (1989) 1 SCC 76 (Supreme Court, 14 October 1988). Why it matters. It states the two courses in Indian law.

selfTest.q: 1. What is anticipatory breach?
selfTest.a: A refusal to perform, or an act disabling performance, made before the time for performance arrives (Section 39).

selfTest.q: 2. What two choices does the promisee have?
selfTest.a: He may accept the repudiation, end the contract and sue at once, or keep the contract alive and wait for the due date.

selfTest.q: 3. Why is waiting risky?
selfTest.a: An event before the due date may discharge the contract, as war did in Avery v. Bowden , and then the promisee loses his claim.

selfTest.q: 4. A builder says he may be a week late because labour is short. Is this an anticipatory breach?
selfTest.a: No. It is not a clear refusal of the whole promise.

selfTest.q: 5. After accepting the repudiation, can the promisee sue for specific performance?
selfTest.a: No. He may claim damages only ( Jawahar Lal Wadhwa ).

legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance. Illustrations. (a) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her 100 rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night A wilfully absents herself from the theatre. B is at liberty to put an end to the contract. (b) A, a singer, enters into a contract with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre two night's in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her at the rate of 100 rupees for each night. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself. With the assent of B, A sings on the seventh night. B has signified his acquiescence in the continuance of the contract, and cannot now put an end to it, but is entitled to compensation for the damage sustained by him through A's failure to sing on the sixth night.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు

Section 73, Illustration (c). A contracts to buy of B, at a stated price, 50 maunds of rice, no time being fixed for delivery. A afterwards informs B that he will not accept the rice if tendered to him. B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the amount, if any, by which the contract price exceeds that which B can obtain for the rice at the time when A informs B that he will not accept it.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Specific Relief Act, 1963, Section 16(c). Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person— ... (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant. Explanation. —For the purposes of clause (c),— ... (ii) the plaintiff must prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే

సెక్షన్ 39 నిరాకరణకూ, నెరవేర్చలేని స్థితికి తెచ్చుకోవడానికీ వర్తిస్తుంది, అది వాగ్దానం మొత్తానికి సంబంధించినదైతే. వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించ "వచ్చు". కాంట్రాక్టు కొనసాగడాన్ని మాటలతో గానీ ప్రవర్తనతో గానీ అంగీకరించినట్టు చూపితే ఆ హక్కు పోతుంది. సెక్షన్ 73, Illustration (c) ప్రకారం నష్టాన్ని, ఎగవేతదారు తన నిరాకరణను తెలియజేసిన సమయాన్ని బట్టి లెక్కిస్తారు.

ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘన అంటే నెరవేర్చడానికి నిర్ణయించిన సమయానికి ముందే జరిగే ఉల్లంఘన. దీనికి రెండు రూపాలు: రూపం ఏం జరుగుతుంది ఉదాహరణ స్పష్టమైన నిరాకరణ (repudiation) తాను నెరవేర్చనని పక్షం చెబుతాడు "నేను సరుకు ఇవ్వను" అని అమ్మకందారు రాస్తాడు సూచిత నిరాకరణ అతని ప్రవర్తనే నెరవేర్పును అసాధ్యం చేస్తుంది వాగ్దానం చేసిన అవే సరుకులను వేరే కొనుగోలుదారుకు అమ్మేస్తాడు చట్టంలోని మాటలు. చట్టం "ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘన" అనే మాటను వాడదు. సెక్షన్ 39 దీన్ని "refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing" అనే మాటలతో కవర్ చేస్తుంది. ఈ సిద్ధాంతానికి రూపం ఇచ్చింది ఇంగ్లీష్ కేసు Hochster v. De La Tour . అమాయక పక్షానికి ముందుగానే చర్య తీసుకోవడానికి చట్టం ఎందుకు అనుమతిస్తుంది? ఆగడం వల్ల ఎవరికీ లాభం లేదు. అతను వెంటనే వేరే సరఫరాదారు కోసం చూసి తన నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించుకోవచ్చు. ఈ దశలు ఏ క్రమంలో వస్తాయో చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. ఉండాలి; మధ్యలో జరిగే సంఘటన
దావాను దెబ్బతీయవచ్చు"] M --> R R --> Q Q -->|"అంగీకరిస్తే"| A A --> A2 Q -->|"ధృవీకరిస్తే"| W W --> W2 వచన వివరణ కాంట్రాక్టు కుదురుతుంది. గడువు తేదీకి ముందే ఒక పక్షం తన వాగ్దానం మొత్తాన్ని నెరవేర్చడానికి నిరాకరిస్తాడు, లేదా నెరవేర్చలేని స్థితికి తనను తాను తెచ్చుకుంటాడు (సెక్షన్ 39). అప్పుడు వాగ్దానగ్రహీత ఎంచుకుంటాడు. నిరాకరణను అంగీకరిస్తే కాంట్రాక్టు ముగుస్తుంది; సెక్షన్ 73 కింద వెంటనే నష్టపరిహారం కోసం దావా వేయవచ్చు, నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించుకోవాలి, కానీ తర్వాత నిర్దిష్ట అమలు కోరలేడు. ధృవీకరించి ఆగితే కాంట్రాక్టు ఇరు పక్షాలపై కట్టుబడి ఉంటుంది, అవతలి పక్షం నిరాకరణను వెనక్కి తీసుకోవచ్చు; గడువు తేదీన వాగ్దానగ్రహీత నెరవేర్చడానికి సిద్ధంగా, సుముఖంగా ఉండాలి, మధ్యలో జరిగే సంఘటన అతని దావాను దెబ్బతీయవచ్చు (Avery v. Bowden).

selfTest.q: 1. ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘన అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: నెరవేర్చాల్సిన సమయం రాకముందే నెరవేర్చడానికి నిరాకరించడం, లేదా నెరవేర్పును అసాధ్యం చేసే చర్య (సెక్షన్ 39).

selfTest.q: 2. వాగ్దానగ్రహీతకు ఏ రెండు ఎంపికలు ఉన్నాయి?
selfTest.a: నిరాకరణను అంగీకరించి, కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించి, వెంటనే దావా వేయవచ్చు. లేదా కాంట్రాక్టును కొనసాగించి గడువు తేదీ వరకు ఆగవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 3. ఆగడం ఎందుకు ప్రమాదకరం?
selfTest.a: గడువు తేదీకి ముందు జరిగే సంఘటన కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించవచ్చు, Avery v. Bowden లో యుద్ధం చేసినట్టు. అప్పుడు వాగ్దానగ్రహీత తన దావాను కోల్పోతాడు.

selfTest.q: 4. కూలీలు తక్కువగా ఉన్నందున ఒక వారం ఆలస్యం కావచ్చని ఒక బిల్డర్ చెబుతాడు. ఇది ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘనా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. ఇది వాగ్దానం మొత్తాన్ని స్పష్టంగా నిరాకరించడం కాదు.

selfTest.q: 5. నిరాకరణను అంగీకరించిన తర్వాత వాగ్దానగ్రహీత నిర్దిష్ట అమలు కోసం దావా వేయవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అతను నష్టపరిహారం మాత్రమే కోరవచ్చు ( Jawahar Lal Wadhwa ).

law-of-contract-i-u3-t11.subtitle: Sections 39, 53 to 55 and 73 to 75 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: An actual breach happens when a party fails to perform at the time performance is due, or performs badly or only in part, or refuses during performance. The other party can always claim compensation. He can end the contract only if the breach goes to the whole promise or time was of the essence. Compensation follows Sections 73 to 75. In exams, the line between a breach that ends the contract and one that gives damages only earns the marks. In real life, it tells a buyer or owner whether to cancel or to claim the cost of putting things right.
legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance.

Section 53. Liability of party preventing event on which the contract is to take effect. When a contract contains reciprocal promises, and one party to the contract prevents the other from performing his promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented; and he is entitled to compensation from the other party for any loss which he may sustain in consequence of the non-performance of the contract.

Section 54. Effect of default as to that promise which should be first performed, in contract consisting of reciprocal promises. When a contract consists of reciprocal promises, such that one of them cannot be performed, or that its performance cannot be claimed till the other has been performed, and the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it, such promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise, and must make compensation to the other party to the contract for any loss which such other party may sustain by the non-performance of the contract.

Section 55. Effect of failure to perform at fixed time, in contract in which time is essential. When a party to a contract promises to do a certain thing at or before a specified time, or certain things at or before specified times, and fails to do any such thing at or before the specified time, the contract, or so much of it as has not been performed, becomes voidable at the option of the promisee, if the intention of the parties was that time should be of the essence of the contract. Effect of such failure when time is not essential. —If it was not the intention of the parties that time should be of the essence of the contract, the contract does not become voidable by the failure to do such thing at or before the specified time; but the promisee is entitled to compensation from the promisor for any loss occasioned to him by such failure.

Section 65, Illustration (b). A contracts with B to deliver to him 250 maunds of rice before the first of May. A delivers 130 maunds only before that day, and none after. B retains the 130 maunds after the first of May. He is bound to pay A for them.

Section 73. Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract. When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Explanation. —In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74. Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.
Related provisions

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 11. Stipulations as to time. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to time of payment are not deemed to be of the essence of a contract of sale. Whether any other stipulation as to time is of the essence of the contract or not depends on the terms of the contract.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 12. Condition and warranty. (1) A stipulation in a contract of sale with reference to goods which are the subject thereof may be a condition or a warranty. (2) A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated. (3) A warranty is a stipulation collateral to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a claim for damages but not to a right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. (4) Whether a stipulation in a contract of sale is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition, though called a warranty in the contract.
In simple words

Section 39. Where a party refuses to perform, or disables himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract unless he has accepted its continuance. Section 53. If one party prevents the other from performing, the contract becomes voidable at the prevented party's option. He may claim compensation. Section 54. A party who fails in the promise that had to be performed first cannot claim the other party's performance and must compensate him. Section 55. Where time is of the essence and performance is late, the contract is voidable at the promisee's option. Otherwise the promisee may claim compensation for the delay. Section 65, Illustration (b). A delivers 130 maunds of the 250 maunds of rice he promised before the date. B keeps the 130 maunds after that date. He must pay A for them. Section 73. Compensation for loss that naturally arose from the breach, or that the parties knew was likely. No compensation for remote and indirect loss. The means of remedying the inconvenience must be taken into account. Section 74. Where a sum is named for breach, or a penalty is stipulated , the court awards reasonable compensation not exceeding that amount. Section 75. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for the damage he has sustained.
en.meaning:
Actual breach is a breach committed at the time performance is due or during performance. It differs from an anticipatory breach, which comes before the due date. The Act does not give it a separate name. It deals with it in the sections above. An actual breach may take four forms: Failure to perform at the time fixed. Defective or incomplete performance. Refusal in the course of performance. Prevention of the other party's performance. The law gives the innocent party a remedy for each. Diagram 1 shows the questions to ask. Diagram 1. Start at the top. Each box must be answered "yes" to move down. A "no" shows where the claim to end the contract fails. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Did a party fail to perform when due,
perform defectively, or refuse
during performance?"} N1["No actual breach"] Q2{"2. Was the failure without lawful excuse?
(not frustration, not a refused tender,
not the promisee's own prevention)"} N2["The promisor is excused:
no breach"] Q3{"3. Does the breach go to the whole promise,
or was time of the essence? (ss.39, 55)"} N3["Compensation only (ss.55, 73);
he must still perform his own part"] R["Result (ss.39, 55, 65, 73, 75):
end the contract and claim compensation;
pay for any benefit received;
if he accepts continuance,
he can still claim compensation"] Q1 -->|"No"| N1 Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2 Q2 -->|"No"| N2 Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3 Q3 -->|"No"| N3 Q3 -->|"Yes"| R Text description Question 1: did a party fail to perform when due, perform defectively, or refuse during performance? If no, there is no actual breach. Question 2: was the failure without lawful excuse (not frustration, not a refused tender, not the promisee's own prevention)? If no, the promisor is excused and there is no breach. Question 3: does the breach go to the whole promise, or was time of the essence (Sections 39, 55)? If no, the promisee may claim compensation only (Sections 55, 73) and must still perform his own part. If yes, the result (Sections 39, 55, 65, 73, 75): the promisee may end the contract and claim compensation; he must pay for any benefit received; if he accepts the contract's continuance, he can still claim compensation.
keyPoints: Actual breach is a breach at the due time or during performance. Every actual breach gives a right to compensation (Section 73). The right to end the contract needs a breach of the whole promise or time of the essence (Sections 39, 55). Remote and indirect loss is not compensated. The innocent party must reduce his loss. Where a sum is named for breach, the court awards reasonable compensation not above it (Section 74). A party who rescinds must pay for benefits received and may claim compensation (Sections 65, 75). Condition v warranty in sale of goods: Sale of Goods Act, Section 12. Compensation suit: three years from the breach (Limitation Act, Article 55). Compensation may be claimed with specific performance (Specific Relief Act, Section 21).

caseLaws.name: Fateh Chand v
caseLaws.facts: Balkishan Das (1963) Facts. By an agreement of 21 March 1949 the seller agreed to sell leasehold rights in land and a building in Delhi. He received Rs 25,000 (Rs 1,000 as earnest money and Rs 24,000 towards the price). The sale was not completed, and the contract said the whole sum would be forfeited. Principle. Section 74 covers forfeiture of money already paid. Proof of actual loss is not needed, but a breach causing no legal injury gives no compensation. The seller kept only the Rs 1,000 earnest money. [1964] 1 SCR 515 : AIR 1963 SC 1405 (Supreme Court, Constitution Bench, 15 January 1963). Why it matters. It limits what a wronged party may keep. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) Facts. Millers in Gloucester sent a broken crank shaft by carrier to Greenwich to be copied for a new one. The carrier delayed delivery and the mill stayed idle. Principle. Damages are those arising naturally from the breach, or reasonably contemplated by both parties. Special circumstances count only if "communicated by the plaintiffs to the defendants, and thus known to both parties". (1854) 9 Ex 341 : 156 ER 145 (Court of Exchequer, Alderson B., 23 February 1854). Why it matters. It is the source of the rule on remote loss in Section 73. Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi (2011) Facts. Under an agreement of 17 January 1981 a buyer agreed to buy 24 acres 95 cents at Rs 15,000 an acre. The balance was payable in three instalments , and clause 6 said "payments on due dates is the essence of this contract". She paid part and missed the last payment dates. The sellers cancelled the agreement by notice of 2 August 1981. Principle. The clauses made time for payment the essence, so her default justified the cancellation (paras 17, 19 and 20). The money she paid was ordered to be refunded with interest. [2011] 8 SCR 874 (Supreme Court, 4 July 2011). Why it matters. A breach of a time-essential term lets the seller end the contract.

selfTest.q: 1. When can a promisee end the contract after an actual breach?
selfTest.a: When the breach goes to the whole promise (Section 39) or time was of the essence (Section 55).

selfTest.q: 2. What loss does Section 73 compensate?
selfTest.a: Loss that arose naturally from the breach, or that the parties knew to be likely when they made the contract. Remote and indirect loss is excluded.

selfTest.q: 3. A debtor does not pay on the day, and the creditor is ruined. What does the debtor owe?
selfTest.a: Only the principal and interest up to the day of payment (Section 73, Illustration (n)).

selfTest.q: 4. A builder finishes the house but uses cheaper paint on one wall. Can the owner cancel the contract?
selfTest.a: No. He may claim the cost of repainting, but the breach does not go to the whole promise.

selfTest.q: 5. Under the Sale of Goods Act, what is the difference between a condition and a warranty?
selfTest.a: Breach of a condition gives a right to treat the contract as repudiated. Breach of a warranty gives a claim for damages only (Section 12).

legalProvision: Section 39. Effect of refusal of party to perform promise wholly. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance.

Section 53. Liability of party preventing event on which the contract is to take effect. When a contract contains reciprocal promises, and one party to the contract prevents the other from performing his promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented; and he is entitled to compensation from the other party for any loss which he may sustain in consequence of the non-performance of the contract.

Section 54. Effect of default as to that promise which should be first performed, in contract consisting of reciprocal promises. When a contract consists of reciprocal promises, such that one of them cannot be performed, or that its performance cannot be claimed till the other has been performed, and the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it, such promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise, and must make compensation to the other party to the contract for any loss which such other party may sustain by the non-performance of the contract.

Section 55. Effect of failure to perform at fixed time, in contract in which time is essential. When a party to a contract promises to do a certain thing at or before a specified time, or certain things at or before specified times, and fails to do any such thing at or before the specified time, the contract, or so much of it as has not been performed, becomes voidable at the option of the promisee, if the intention of the parties was that time should be of the essence of the contract. Effect of such failure when time is not essential. —If it was not the intention of the parties that time should be of the essence of the contract, the contract does not become voidable by the failure to do such thing at or before the specified time; but the promisee is entitled to compensation from the promisor for any loss occasioned to him by such failure.

Section 65, Illustration (b). A contracts with B to deliver to him 250 maunds of rice before the first of May. A delivers 130 maunds only before that day, and none after. B retains the 130 maunds after the first of May. He is bound to pay A for them.

Section 73. Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract. When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach. Explanation. —In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Section 74. Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.

Section 75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation. A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.
సంబంధిత నిబంధనలు

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 11. Stipulations as to time. Unless a different intention appears from the terms of the contract, stipulations as to time of payment are not deemed to be of the essence of a contract of sale. Whether any other stipulation as to time is of the essence of the contract or not depends on the terms of the contract.

Sale of Goods Act, 1930, Section 12. Condition and warranty. (1) A stipulation in a contract of sale with reference to goods which are the subject thereof may be a condition or a warranty. (2) A condition is a stipulation essential to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a right to treat the contract as repudiated. (3) A warranty is a stipulation collateral to the main purpose of the contract, the breach of which gives rise to a claim for damages but not to a right to reject the goods and treat the contract as repudiated. (4) Whether a stipulation in a contract of sale is a condition or a warranty depends in each case on the construction of the contract. A stipulation may be a condition, though called a warranty in the contract.
సరళంగా చెప్పాలంటే

సెక్షన్ 39. ఒక పక్షం తన వాగ్దానం మొత్తాన్ని నెరవేర్చడానికి నిరాకరిస్తే, లేదా నెరవేర్చలేని స్థితికి తనను తాను తెచ్చుకుంటే, కాంట్రాక్టు కొనసాగడాన్ని వాగ్దానగ్రహీత అంగీకరించి ఉండకపోతే, అతను కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 53. ఒక పక్షం అవతలి పక్షాన్ని నెరవేర్చకుండా అడ్డుకుంటే, అడ్డుకోబడిన పక్షం ఇష్టం మేరకు కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు చేయదగినది అవుతుంది. అతను పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 54. ముందు నెరవేర్చాల్సిన వాగ్దానంలో విఫలమైన పక్షం అవతలి పక్షం నెరవేర్పును కోరలేడు, అతనికి పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి. సెక్షన్ 55. సమయమే ప్రధానమై నెరవేర్పు ఆలస్యమైతే, వాగ్దానగ్రహీత ఇష్టం మేరకు కాంట్రాక్టు రద్దు చేయదగినది. లేకపోతే ఆలస్యానికి వాగ్దానగ్రహీత పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 65, Illustration (b). తేదీకి ముందు ఇస్తానన్న 250 మణుగుల బియ్యంలో A 130 మణుగులు మాత్రమే ఇస్తాడు. ఆ తేదీ తర్వాత కూడా B ఆ 130 మణుగులను ఉంచుకుంటాడు. వాటికి B, A కు చెల్లించాలి. సెక్షన్ 73. ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చిన నష్టానికి, లేదా వచ్చే అవకాశం ఉందని పక్షాలకు తెలిసిన నష్టానికి పరిహారం. దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టానికి పరిహారం లేదు. అసౌకర్యాన్ని సరిదిద్దడానికి ఉన్న మార్గాలను లెక్కలోకి తీసుకోవాలి. సెక్షన్ 74. ఉల్లంఘనకు ఒక మొత్తాన్ని పేర్కొన్నా, జరిమానా షరతు పెట్టినా, ఆ మొత్తాన్ని మించకుండా సహేతుక పరిహారాన్ని కోర్టు ఇస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 75. కాంట్రాక్టును సక్రమంగా రద్దు చేసిన వ్యక్తికి తనకు కలిగిన నష్టానికి పరిహారం వస్తుంది.
te.meaning:
వాస్తవ ఉల్లంఘన అంటే నెరవేర్చాల్సిన సమయంలో గానీ, నెరవేర్చే మధ్యలో గానీ జరిగే ఉల్లంఘన. గడువు తేదీకి ముందే వచ్చే ముందస్తు ఉల్లంఘనకు ఇది భిన్నం. చట్టం దీనికి వేరే పేరు పెట్టలేదు. పై సెక్షన్లలో దీని గురించి చెబుతుంది. వాస్తవ ఉల్లంఘనకు నాలుగు రూపాలు ఉండవచ్చు: నిర్ణీత సమయానికి నెరవేర్చకపోవడం. లోపభూయిష్టంగా లేదా అసంపూర్తిగా నెరవేర్చడం. నెరవేర్చే మధ్యలో నిరాకరించడం. అవతలి పక్షం నెరవేర్చకుండా అడ్డుకోవడం. ప్రతి దానికీ చట్టం అమాయక పక్షానికి పరిష్కారం ఇస్తుంది. అడగాల్సిన ప్రశ్నలను చిత్రం 1 చూపిస్తుంది. Diagram 1. పై నుంచి మొదలుపెట్టండి. కిందికి వెళ్లాలంటే ప్రతి పెట్టెకూ "అవును" అని సమాధానం రావాలి. "కాదు" వచ్చిన చోట కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించే హక్కు ఆగిపోతుంది. flowchart TD Q1{"1. ఒక పక్షం గడువు సమయానికి నెరవేర్చలేదా,
లోపభూయిష్టంగా నెరవేర్చాడా, లేదా
మధ్యలో నిరాకరించాడా?"} N1["వాస్తవ ఉల్లంఘన లేదు"] Q2{"2. చట్టబద్ధమైన కారణం లేదా?
(ఫ్రస్ట్రేషన్ కాదు, తిరస్కరించిన టెండర్ కాదు,
వాగ్దానగ్రహీత సొంత అడ్డంకి కాదు)"} N2["వాగ్దానకర్తకు మినహాయింపు:
ఉల్లంఘన లేదు"] Q3{"3. ఉల్లంఘన వాగ్దానం మొత్తానికి వర్తిస్తుందా,
లేదా సమయమే ప్రధానమా? (సె.39, 55)"} N3["పరిహారం మాత్రమే (సె.55, 73);
తన భాగాన్ని ఇంకా నెరవేర్చాలి"] R["ఫలితం (సె.39, 55, 65, 73, 75):
కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించి పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు;
పొందిన లాభానికి చెల్లించాలి;
కొనసాగడాన్ని అంగీకరిస్తే,
అప్పటికీ పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు"] Q1 -->|"కాదు"| N1 Q1 -->|"అవును"| Q2 Q2 -->|"కాదు"| N2 Q2 -->|"అవును"| Q3 Q3 -->|"కాదు"| N3 Q3 -->|"అవును"| R వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: ఒక పక్షం గడువు సమయానికి నెరవేర్చలేదా, లోపభూయిష్టంగా నెరవేర్చాడా, లేదా మధ్యలో నిరాకరించాడా? కాదు అయితే వాస్తవ ఉల్లంఘన లేదు. ప్రశ్న 2: ఆ వైఫల్యానికి చట్టబద్ధమైన కారణం లేదా (ఫ్రస్ట్రేషన్ కాదు, తిరస్కరించిన టెండర్ కాదు, వాగ్దానగ్రహీత సొంత అడ్డంకి కాదు)? కాదు అయితే వాగ్దానకర్తకు మినహాయింపు, ఉల్లంఘన లేదు. ప్రశ్న 3: ఉల్లంఘన వాగ్దానం మొత్తానికి వర్తిస్తుందా, లేదా సమయమే ప్రధానమా (సెక్షన్లు 39, 55)? కాదు అయితే వాగ్దానగ్రహీత పరిహారం మాత్రమే కోరవచ్చు (సెక్షన్లు 55, 73), తన భాగాన్ని ఇంకా నెరవేర్చాలి. అవును అయితే ఫలితం (సెక్షన్లు 39, 55, 65, 73, 75): వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ముగించి పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు; పొందిన లాభానికి చెల్లించాలి; కాంట్రాక్టు కొనసాగడాన్ని అంగీకరిస్తే, అప్పటికీ పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 1. వాస్తవ ఉల్లంఘన తర్వాత వాగ్దానగ్రహీత కాంట్రాక్టును ఎప్పుడు ముగించవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన వాగ్దానం మొత్తానికి వర్తించినప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 39), లేదా సమయమే ప్రధానమైనప్పుడు (సెక్షన్ 55).

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 73 ఏ నష్టానికి పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చిన నష్టానికి, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు చేసేటప్పుడు వచ్చే అవకాశం ఉందని పక్షాలకు తెలిసిన నష్టానికి. దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టం మినహాయింపు.

selfTest.q: 3. రుణగ్రహీత నిర్ణీత రోజున చెల్లించడు, రుణదాత నాశనమవుతాడు. రుణగ్రహీత ఎంత చెల్లించాలి?
selfTest.a: అసలు మొత్తం, చెల్లించిన రోజు వరకు వడ్డీ మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 73, Illustration (n)).

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక బిల్డర్ ఇల్లు పూర్తి చేస్తాడు, కానీ ఒక గోడకు చౌక రంగు వేస్తాడు. యజమాని కాంట్రాక్టును రద్దు చేయవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మళ్లీ రంగు వేయించే ఖర్చు కోరవచ్చు, కానీ ఉల్లంఘన వాగ్దానం మొత్తానికి వర్తించదు.

selfTest.q: 5. సరుకుల అమ్మకం చట్టం కింద షరతుకూ హామీకీ తేడా ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: షరతు ఉల్లంఘన కాంట్రాక్టును తిరస్కరించినట్టు భావించే హక్కు ఇస్తుంది. హామీ ఉల్లంఘన నష్టపరిహారం దావా మాత్రమే ఇస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 12).

en.meaning:
What does Section 37 of the Indian Contract Act require of the parties to a contract?

Explanation. Section 37 states that the parties to a contract must perform, or offer to perform, their respective promises, unless such performance is dispensed with or excused under the Act or any other law.

Which of the following is NOT one of the six recognised modes of discharge of a contract?

Explanation. The six modes are performance, agreement, impossibility, lapse of time, operation of law, and breach. Registration is not a recognised mode of discharge.

Novation, rescission, and alteration are all examples of discharge by:

Explanation. Section 62 covers novation, rescission, and alteration together as discharge by mutual agreement between the parties.

Explanation. A tender is valid even if refused — Section 38 discharges the promisor from liability once a valid tender is proved, regardless of whether the promisee accepts it.

What is the legal effect of a valid tender that the promisee wrongfully refuses to accept?

Explanation. Section 38 provides that a promisor who has made a valid tender is not responsible for non-performance and does not lose any rights under the contract.

Under Section 40, who must perform a contract requiring personal skill, such as painting a portrait?

Explanation. Section 40 requires personal performance where the contract shows the parties intended it, or where the nature of the contract requires personal skill or credit.

Explanation. Section 59 gives the debtor the first right to direct which debt a payment should be applied to, either expressly or by clear implication.

If the debtor does not specify which debt a payment is for, Section 60 allows the creditor to apply it to:

Explanation. Section 60 gives the creditor discretion to apply an unspecified payment to any lawful debt, including one barred by the Limitation Act.

If neither the debtor nor the creditor appropriates a payment, Section 61 applies it:

Explanation. Section 61 applies unappropriated payments to debts in chronological order — the earliest debt is treated as discharged first.

law-of-contract-i-u4-t1.subtitle: Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872: relations resembling those created by contract

en.inOneMinute: A quasi contract is not a contract. It is a duty that the law puts on one person to pay or to return something, although the parties never made an agreement. The law does this so that nobody keeps a benefit at another person's cost. Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 list the cases, in a chapter headed "Of Certain Relations Resembling Those Created by Contract". The idea behind all five sections is unjust enrichment . In exams, the meaning, the idea of unjust enrichment, the five sections and Moses v. Macferlan earn the marks. In real life, it decides who pays when work, goods or money change hands and there is no valid contract.
legalProvision: Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person.

Section 69. Reimbursement of person paying money due by another, in payment of which he is interested. A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other.

Section 70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act. Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered.
Section 71. Responsibility of finder of goods. A person who finds goods belonging to another, and takes them into his custody, is subject to the same responsibility as a bailee.

Section 72. Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion. A person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it.
Related provision

Section 73 (third paragraph). Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract. When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract.
In simple words

Section 68: a person who supplies necessaries suited to the condition in life of a person unable in law to contract , or of anyone that person must support, is paid back from the property of the incapable person. Section 69: a person who is interested in the payment of money that another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is paid back by the other. Section 70: where a person lawfully does anything for another, or delivers anything to him, not meaning to do it free of charge, and the other enjoys the benefit, the other must pay compensation or restore the thing. Section 71: a person who finds goods belonging to another and takes them into his keeping has the same responsibility as a bailee . Section 72: a person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion must repay or return it. Section 73, third paragraph: when such an obligation is not discharged, the injured person gets the same compensation as if he had contracted for it and the contract had been broken.
en.meaning:
The Act does not define quasi contract. It speaks only of "relations resembling those created by contract". The word "quasi" means "as if". The law treats the parties as if they had made a contract, but only to enforce a duty to pay or to restore. Where the duty comes from. The Supreme Court explained the source of the duty in Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968). It is "not founded upon any contract or tort but upon a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution". In plain words, the duty comes from the law, not from the parties' promise. The same idea is called restitution : giving back a benefit received. Why the law has it. The idea behind the chapter is unjust enrichment . The Latin maxim nemo debet locupletari ex aliena jactura means that no one should be made richer at another's loss. Contract law cannot help here, because there is no promise to enforce. The law therefore creates the duty itself. In State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons the Supreme Court said: "What s. 70 prevents is unjust enrichment and it applies as much to individuals as to corporations and Government." See Diagram 1 for the five situations. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. Each bottom box is one situation in which the law makes a person pay or return something. flowchart TD Q["Quasi contract

or under coercion (s. 72): repay or return"] Q --> A Q --> B A --> S68 A --> S69 B --> S70 B --> S71 B --> S72 Text description Quasi contract, Sections 68 to 72, branches into two groups. Claims by a supplier or payer: necessaries for an incapable person, Section 68, paid from that person's property; payment by an interested person, Section 69, reimbursed by the person bound by law to pay. Claims for a benefit received: non-gratuitous act with benefit enjoyed, Section 70, compensation or restoration; goods found and taken into custody, Section 71, the finder is treated as a bailee; money paid or thing delivered by mistake or under coercion, Section 72, must be repaid or returned.
keyPoints: A quasi contract is a duty imposed by law, with no agreement between the parties. It rests on unjust enrichment: no one should be enriched at another's loss. Sections 68 to 72 cover necessaries, an interested payer, a non-gratuitous act, a finder and a payment by mistake or coercion. The claim is for reimbursement, compensation or restoration, not damages for breach. Section 73, third paragraph, gives the same compensation as on a breach when such an obligation is not discharged. Section 70 applies even where a Government contract is invalid for want of form ( B.K. Mondal ). The duty rests on "a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution" ( Mulamchand ). It does not apply where a valid contract governs the dispute ( MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

caseLaws.name: Moses v
caseLaws.facts: Macferlan (1760) Facts. Moses endorsed promissory notes to Macferlan on his promise not to sue Moses on them. Macferlan sued him on them in the Court of Conscience, and Moses had to pay. Moses then sued to get the money back. Principle. Where a defendant is obliged by the ties of natural justice and equity to refund money, the law implies a debt and gives an action to recover it. (1760) 2 Burr 1005 : 97 ER 676 (Court of King's Bench, Lord Mansfield CJ). Why it matters. It is the foundation of the law on unjust enrichment, which Sections 68 to 72 apply. State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. In 1944 a firm of contractors built a road, offices and storage sheds at Arambagh and Khanakul for the Civil Supplies Department, on its officers' requests. No contract was made in the form required by Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The State refused to pay Rs. 19,325. Principle. Section 70 "deals with cases where there is no valid contract". The State must pay when it voluntarily accepts and enjoys the work. AIR 1962 SC 779 : 1962 Supp (1) SCR 876 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It is the leading authority that a quasi-contractual claim does not depend on any contract, and that the State is bound like a citizen. Mulamchand v. State of M.P. (1968) Facts. A Section 70 claim was made against a State on a contract that did not comply with Section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935. The Court held Section 175(3) mandatory and based on public policy. Principle. If the three conditions of Section 70 are met, the claim lies. It rests on "a third category of law, namely, quasi-contract or restitution", and not on any contract. (1968) 3 SCR 214 (Supreme Court). Why it matters. It states the legal basis of every quasi-contractual claim. Sales Tax Officer, Banaras v. Kanhaiya Lal Mukundlal Saraf (1958) Facts. A Banaras firm dealing in bullion and in forward contracts in silver paid sales tax for 1948-49 to 1950-51, in all Rs. 1,365-12-0 as stated in the judgment. The Allahabad High Court later held the tax on forward transactions beyond the State's power. The firm asked for a refund. Principle. "Mistake" in Section 72 covers a mistake of law as well as a mistake of fact. AIR 1959 SC 135 : 1959 SCR Supp (1) 1350 (Supreme Court, 23 September 1958). Why it matters. It applies unjust enrichment to a refund from the State. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. MTNL deducted money from Tata Communications' bills. Clause 16.2(c) of the purchase order limited liquidated damages to a maximum of 12 per cent. The Supreme Court decided Civil Appeal No. 1766 of 2019 on 27 February 2019. Principle. Each section of this chapter assumes there is no contractual relationship. The dispute was governed by Section 74, so only the contract figure could be claimed and the excess had to be refunded. Why it matters. It shows the limit of quasi contract: a claim under the chapter cannot override a valid contract.

selfTest.q: 1. Is a quasi contract a contract?
selfTest.a: No. It is a duty imposed by law, resembling a contract. No offer, acceptance or consent is needed.

selfTest.q: 2. Which principle lies behind Sections 68 to 72?
selfTest.a: Unjust enrichment: no one should be enriched at another's loss.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a person claiming under Section 70 sue for damages for breach?
selfTest.a: No. He can claim only compensation for the benefit, or restoration of the thing, because there is no contract ( Mulamchand ).

selfTest.q: 4. Can a State escape a Section 70 claim because its officers did not make the contract in the required form?
selfTest.a: No. If it voluntarily accepted and enjoyed the work, it must pay ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 5. A valid purchase order fixes liquidated damages. Can a party add a quantum meruit claim under Section 70?
selfTest.a: No. Where a valid contract governs the dispute, the claim lies under the contract ( MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

సెక్షన్ 68: చట్టప్రకారం కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేని వ్యక్తికి, లేదా అతను పోషించాల్సిన వారికి, వారి జీవన స్థితికి తగిన అవసరమైన వస్తువులు (necessaries) సరఫరా చేసిన వ్యక్తికి, ఆ అసమర్థుడి ఆస్తి నుంచి డబ్బు తిరిగి వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 69: మరొకరు చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సిన డబ్బు చెల్లింపులో ఆసక్తి ఉండి, అందుకే దాన్ని చెల్లించిన వ్యక్తికి ఆ మరొకరు తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి. సెక్షన్ 70: ఒకరు మరొకరి కోసం చట్టబద్ధంగా ఏదైనా పని చేసినా, ఏదైనా అందజేసినా, అది ఉచితంగా చేయాలనే ఉద్దేశం లేకపోయి, ఆ మరొకరు దాని ప్రయోజనాన్ని అనుభవిస్తే, అతను పరిహారం చెల్లించాలి లేదా ఆ వస్తువును తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. సెక్షన్ 71: మరొకరికి చెందిన వస్తువులను కనుగొని తన అధీనంలోకి తీసుకున్న వ్యక్తికి బెయిలీ (bailee) కి ఉన్న బాధ్యతే ఉంటుంది. సెక్షన్ 72: పొరపాటు (mistake) వల్ల గానీ, బలవంతం (coercion) వల్ల గానీ ఎవరికైనా డబ్బు చెల్లించినా, ఏదైనా అందజేసినా, అతను దాన్ని తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. సెక్షన్ 73, మూడో పేరా: అలాంటి బాధ్యత నెరవేరకపోతే, నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తికి, అతను కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకుని ఆ కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనకు గురైనట్లే అదే పరిహారం వస్తుంది.

క్లెయిమ్‌లు"] S68["అసమర్థుడికి అవసరమైన వస్తువులు (సె. 68):
అతని ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లింపు"] S69["ఆసక్తి ఉన్న వ్యక్తి చెల్లింపు (సె. 69):
చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సినవారు తిరిగి ఇస్తారు"] S70["ఉచితం కాని పని, ప్రయోజనం అనుభవించడం (సె. 70):
పరిహారం, లేదా వస్తువు తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం"] S71["కనుగొని అధీనంలోకి తీసుకున్న వస్తువులు (సె. 71):
కనుగొన్నవారు బెయిలీలాగే బాధ్యులు"] S72["పొరపాటు లేదా బలవంతంతో చెల్లించిన డబ్బు,
అందజేసిన వస్తువు (సె. 72): తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి"] Q --> A Q --> B A --> S68 A --> S69 B --> S70 B --> S71 B --> S72 వచన వివరణ క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు, సెక్షన్లు 68 నుంచి 72, రెండు గుంపులుగా చీలుతుంది. సరఫరాదారు లేదా చెల్లింపుదారు క్లెయిమ్‌లు: అసమర్థుడికి అవసరమైన వస్తువులు, సెక్షన్ 68, అతని ఆస్తి నుంచి చెల్లింపు; ఆసక్తి ఉన్న వ్యక్తి చెల్లింపు, సెక్షన్ 69, చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సినవారు తిరిగి చెల్లిస్తారు. పొందిన ప్రయోజనానికి క్లెయిమ్‌లు: ఉచితం కాని పని, ప్రయోజనం అనుభవించడం, సెక్షన్ 70, పరిహారం లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం; కనుగొని అధీనంలోకి తీసుకున్న వస్తువులు, సెక్షన్ 71, కనుగొన్నవారు బెయిలీ; పొరపాటు లేదా బలవంతంతో చెల్లించిన డబ్బు లేదా అందజేసిన వస్తువు, సెక్షన్ 72, తిరిగి చెల్లించాలి లేదా తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి.

selfTest.q: 1. క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు కాంట్రాక్టా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. ఇది కాంట్రాక్టును పోలిన, చట్టం విధించే బాధ్యత. ప్రతిపాదన, అంగీకారం, సమ్మతి అవసరం లేదు.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్లు 68 నుంచి 72 వెనుక ఏ సూత్రం ఉంది?
selfTest.a: అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత: మరొకరి నష్టంతో ఎవరూ సంపన్నులు కాకూడదు.

selfTest.q: 3. సెక్షన్ 70 కింద క్లెయిమ్ చేసే వ్యక్తి ఉల్లంఘనకు నష్టపరిహారం కోసం దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కాంట్రాక్టు లేదు కాబట్టి ప్రయోజనానికి పరిహారం, లేదా వస్తువు తిరిగి ఇవ్వడం మాత్రమే కోరగలడు ( Mulamchand ).

selfTest.q: 4. అధికారులు కోరిన రూపంలో కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేదని రాష్ట్రం సెక్షన్ 70 క్లెయిమ్ నుంచి తప్పించుకోగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పనిని స్వచ్ఛందంగా అంగీకరించి అనుభవిస్తే చెల్లించాలి ( B.K. Mondal ).

selfTest.q: 5. చెల్లుబాటయ్యే purchase order ముందే నష్టపరిహారాన్ని నిర్ణయించింది. ఒక పక్షం సెక్షన్ 70 కింద క్వాంటమ్ మెరిట్ క్లెయిమ్ జోడించగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. చెల్లుబాటయ్యే కాంట్రాక్టు వివాదాన్ని నియంత్రిస్తే క్లెయిమ్ ఆ కాంట్రాక్టు కిందే ఉంటుంది ( MTNL v. Tata Communications ).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t2.subtitle: Section 68 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: A minor or a person of unsound mind cannot make a binding contract. Yet he must eat, dress and stay healthy. Section 68 lets a person who supplies him with necessaries be paid back from his property. The supplier cannot sue the incapable person on a promise, because there is none. He claims under the law, and only against the property. In exams, the two tests for necessaries and the property-only rule earn the marks. In real life, it protects the grocer, the doctor and the school that serve a minor.
legalProvision: Section 68. Claim for necessaries supplied to person incapable of contracting, or on his account. If a person, incapable of entering into a contract, or any one whom he is legally bound to support, is supplied by another person with necessaries suited to his condition in life, the person who has furnished such supplies is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of such incapable person. Illustrations. (a) A supplies B, a lunatic, with necessaries suitable to his condition in life. A is entitled to be reimbursed from B's property. (b) A supplies the wife and children of B, a lunatic, with necessaries suitable to their condition in life. A is entitled to be reimbursed from B's property.
Related provisions

Section 11. Who are competent to contract. Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which he is subject, and who is of sound mind, and is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which he is subject.

Section 12 (first sentence). What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting. A person is said to be of sound mind for the purpose of making a contract, if, at the time when he makes it, he is capable of understanding it and of forming a rational judgment as to its effect upon his interests.
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 26 (second paragraph). Minor. —A minor may draw, indorse, deliver and negotiate such instrument so as to bind all parties except himself.
In simple words

If a person who cannot contract , or anyone he must support by law, is supplied with necessaries that suit his condition in life, the supplier is paid back from that person's property. "Lunatic" is the Act's old word for a person of unsound mind. A person can contract only if he is a major, of sound mind , and not disqualified by law (Section 11). A minor may sign a promissory note , but the note binds everyone except the minor (Section 26, Negotiable Instruments Act).
en.meaning:
Section 68 is one of the five situations in which the law imposes a duty without agreement (a quasi contract ). It applies to a person who is "incapable of entering into a contract". That means a person who fails the test of Section 11: a minor, a person of unsound mind, or a person disqualified by law. What are necessaries. The Act does not define necessaries. It gives the test in the section itself: they must be "suited to his condition in life". The courts add a second test, which is the person's actual need at the time of supply. Why the law has this rule. The reason is fairness to both sides. The law protects a minor from bad bargains by making his agreements void . It does not want him to starve for that reason. So it lets the supplier recover, but only from the minor's own property. This prevents unjust enrichment . See Diagram 1 for the questions a court asks. Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. A "No" answer sends you to the result beside the box. flowchart TD Q1["1. Is the person supplied incapable of contracting,
or someone such a person must support? (s. 68)"] Q2["2. Are the goods or services necessaries,
suited to his condition in life? (s. 68)"] Q3["3. Did he actually need them when supplied,
and was he not already enough supplied?"] Q4["4. Does the incapable person own property?"] Y["Supplier is reimbursed from the
incapable person's property.
The person himself is not liable."] N1["s. 68 does not apply.
Ordinary contract law decides."] N2["No claim."] N3["No claim."] N4["Nothing from which
to be reimbursed."] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2 Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3 Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4 Q4 -->|"Yes"| Y Q1 -->|"No"| N1 Q2 -->|"No"| N2 Q3 -->|"No"| N3 Q4 -->|"No"| N4 Text description Question 1: is the person supplied incapable of entering into a contract, or someone whom such a person must support? If no, Section 68 does not apply and ordinary contract law decides. Question 2: are the goods or services necessaries, suited to his condition in life? If no, there is no claim. Question 3: did he actually need them when they were supplied, and was he not already enough supplied? If no, there is no claim. Question 4: does the incapable person own property? If no, there is nothing from which to be reimbursed. If every answer is yes, the supplier is reimbursed from the incapable person's property; the person himself is not liable.
keyPoints: Section 68 repays a person who supplies necessaries to someone incapable of contracting. Persons incapable of contracting are those who fail Section 11: a minor, a person of unsound mind, a disqualified person. Necessaries must suit the person's condition in life and his actual need. The supplier is repaid from the incapable person's property only. The incapable person is not personally liable ( Mohori Bibee ). Dependants of the incapable person are covered (Illustration (b)). A promissory note signed by a minor does not bind him, so the supplier claims under Section 68. A minor is outside Section 70, because Section 68 provides for his case ( B.K. Mondal ).

caseLaws.name: Mohori Bibee v
caseLaws.facts: Dharmodas Ghose (1903) Facts. On 20 July 1895 Dharmodas Ghose, a minor, mortgaged his houses to Brahmo Dutt, a moneylender, to secure Rs. 20,000. The lender's attorney knew he was a minor. The Privy Council decided the appeal on 4 March 1903. Principle. A minor is not competent to contract, and his agreement is void. Sections 64 and 65 do not apply, because they assume a contract between competent parties. Under Section 68 the infant is not liable even for necessaries, "though a statutory claim is created against his property". [1903] UKPC 12 (Privy Council, 4 March 1903). Why it matters. It is the reason a supplier of necessaries has no contract claim and must use Section 68. State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons (1961) Facts. The State argued that it was like a minor, and so could not be made to pay under Section 70 where its contract was invalid. Principle. The Court said a minor is outside Section 70 because "his case has been specifically provided for by s. 68", and because he cannot voluntarily accept a benefit. The State was not in that position. AIR 1962 SC 779 (Supreme Court, 5 December 1961). Why it matters. It confirms that Section 68 is the special rule for incapable persons. Nash v. Inman (1908) Facts. A Savile Row tailor sued Inman, a Cambridge undergraduate who was a minor, for clothes that included eleven fancy waistcoats. The trial judge found that Inman was already amply supplied with clothes. [1908] 2 KB 1 (Court of Appeal). Principle. The supplier must prove that the goods suited the minor's condition in life and that he was not already sufficiently supplied with them. Why it matters. It supplies the second test for necessaries. Kanhayalal Bisandayal Bhiwapurkar v. Indarchandji Hamirmalji Sisodia (1947) Facts. An eye specialist sued a husband for Rs. 188 for removing his wife's cataract, under an agreement with her and her son-in-law. Principle. Section 68 covers "the dependent of a person incompetent to contract". The husband "was not incompetent to contract", so it did not apply. AIR 1947 Nag 84 (Nagpur High Court). Why it matters. It marks the limit of Section 68.

selfTest.q: 1. From whom is a supplier of necessaries reimbursed under Section 68?
selfTest.a: From the property of the incapable person. The person himself is not liable.

selfTest.q: 2. What two tests decide whether goods are necessaries?
selfTest.a: They must suit his condition in life, and they must meet his actual requirements at the time of supply.

selfTest.q: 3. A grocer holds a minor's promissory note for necessaries. Can he sue on the note?
selfTest.a: No. The note does not bind the minor. The grocer claims the price of the necessaries under Section 68 from the minor's property.

selfTest.q: 4. A supplies food to the wife and children of B, a person of unsound mind. Can A recover?
selfTest.a: Yes. A is reimbursed from B's property (Section 68, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 5. A doctor treats a woman under an agreement with her and sues her husband, who is a competent adult, under Section 68. Will he succeed?
selfTest.a: No. Section 68 applies only where the person bound to support is incapable of contracting ( Kanhayalal ).

కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేని వ్యక్తికి, లేదా అతను చట్టప్రకారం పోషించాల్సిన ఎవరికైనా, అతని జీవన స్థితికి తగిన అవసరమైన వస్తువులు సరఫరా అయితే, సరఫరాదారుకు ఆ వ్యక్తి ఆస్తి నుంచి డబ్బు తిరిగి వస్తుంది. "Lunatic" అనేది మతిస్థిమితం లేని వ్యక్తికి చట్టంలోని పాత పదం. మేజర్ అయి, స్థిరమైన మనస్సు (sound mind) ఉండి, ఏ చట్టం ద్వారానూ అనర్హుడు కాని వ్యక్తి మాత్రమే కాంట్రాక్టు చేయగలడు (సెక్షన్ 11). మైనర్ ప్రామిసరీ నోటుపై సంతకం చేయవచ్చు, కానీ ఆ నోటు మైనర్‌ను తప్ప మిగతా అందరినీ బంధిస్తుంది (Negotiable Instruments Act, సెక్షన్ 26).
te.meaning:
ఒప్పందం లేకుండా చట్టం బాధ్యత విధించే ఐదు సందర్భాల్లో ( క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు ) సెక్షన్ 68 ఒకటి. ఇది "incapable of entering into a contract " (కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేని) వ్యక్తికి వర్తిస్తుంది. అంటే సెక్షన్ 11 పరీక్షలో నెగ్గని వ్యక్తి: మైనర్, మతిస్థిమితం లేని వ్యక్తి, లేదా చట్టం ద్వారా అనర్హుడైన వ్యక్తి. అవసరమైన వస్తువులు అంటే ఏమిటి. చట్టం necessaries ని నిర్వచించలేదు. సెక్షన్‌లోనే పరీక్ష ఇచ్చింది: అవి "suited to his condition in life" (అతని జీవన స్థితికి తగినవి) అయి ఉండాలి. కోర్టులు రెండో పరీక్షను జోడిస్తాయి: సరఫరా సమయంలో ఆ వ్యక్తికి నిజంగా ఉన్న అవసరం. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం రెండు పక్షాలకూ న్యాయం. మైనర్ ఒప్పందాలను చెల్లనివి (void) గా చేసి, చట్టం అతన్ని చెడ్డ బేరాల నుంచి కాపాడుతుంది. ఆ కారణంగా అతను ఆకలితో ఉండాలని చట్టం కోరుకోదు. కాబట్టి సరఫరాదారు డబ్బు వసూలు చేసుకోవచ్చు, కానీ మైనర్ సొంత ఆస్తి నుంచి మాత్రమే. ఇది అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత ను నివారిస్తుంది. కోర్టు అడిగే ప్రశ్నలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. పెట్టెలను వరుసగా కిందికి చదవండి. "కాదు" అనే జవాబు మిమ్మల్ని పక్కన ఉన్న ఫలితానికి పంపుతుంది. flowchart TD Q1["1. సరఫరా పొందినవారు కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేనివారా,

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 68 కింద అవసరమైన వస్తువులు సరఫరా చేసినవారికి ఎవరి నుంచి తిరిగి చెల్లింపు వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: అసమర్థుడి ఆస్తి నుంచి. ఆ వ్యక్తి స్వయంగా బాధ్యుడు కాడు.

selfTest.q: 2. సరుకులు అవసరమైన వస్తువులా కాదా అని ఏ రెండు పరీక్షలు నిర్ణయిస్తాయి?
selfTest.a: అవి అతని జీవన స్థితికి తగినవి కావాలి, సరఫరా సమయంలో అతని నిజమైన అవసరాలను తీర్చాలి.

selfTest.q: 3. అవసరమైన వస్తువుల కోసం ఒక కిరాణా వ్యాపారి దగ్గర మైనర్ ప్రామిసరీ నోటు ఉంది. ఆ నోటుపై దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. నోటు మైనర్‌ను బంధించదు. వ్యాపారి సెక్షన్ 68 కింద మైనర్ ఆస్తి నుంచి అవసరమైన వస్తువుల ధరను క్లెయిమ్ చేస్తాడు.

selfTest.q: 4. మతిస్థిమితం లేని B భార్యాపిల్లలకు A ఆహారం సరఫరా చేస్తాడు. A కు డబ్బు వస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: వస్తుంది. B ఆస్తి నుంచి A కు తిరిగి చెల్లింపు వస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 68, Illustration (b)).

selfTest.q: 5. ఒక డాక్టరు ఒక స్త్రీతో ఒప్పందం ప్రకారం ఆమెకు చికిత్స చేసి, సమర్థుడైన పెద్దవాడైన ఆమె భర్తపై సెక్షన్ 68 కింద దావా వేస్తాడు. గెలుస్తాడా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. పోషించాల్సిన వ్యక్తి కాంట్రాక్టు చేయలేనివాడు అయినప్పుడే సెక్షన్ 68 వర్తిస్తుంది ( Kanhayalal ).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t3.subtitle: Section 69 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes a person must pay another's debt to save his own interest. Section 69 gives him a right to be paid back by the person who should have paid. Two things must be present. The payer has a real interest in the payment, and the other person is bound by law to pay. The payer must pay "therefore", that is, because of that interest. In exams, the two conditions and the Act's illustration of the Bengal lease earn the marks. In real life, it protects a tenant, buyer or co-owner who pays a landlord's or seller's dues to stop a forced sale.
legalProvision: Section 69. Reimbursement of person paying money due by another, in payment of which he is interested. A person who is interested in the payment of money which another is bound by law to pay, and who therefore pays it, is entitled to be reimbursed by the other. Illustration. B holds land in Bengal, on a lease granted by A, the zamindar. The revenue payable by A to the Government being in arrear, his land is advertised for sale by the Government. Under the revenue law, the consequence of such sale will be the annulment of B's lease. B, to prevent the sale and the consequent annulment of his own lease, pays to the Government the sum due from A. A is bound to make good to B the amount so paid.
Related provisions

Section 43 (second and third paragraphs). Each promisor may compel contribution. —Each of two or more joint promisors may compel every other joint promisor to contribute equally with himself to the performance of the promise, unless a contrary intention appears from the contract. Sharing of loss by default in contribution. —If any one of two or more joint promisors makes default in such contribution, the remaining joint promisors must bear the loss arising from such default in equal shares.

Section 145. Implied promise to indemnify surety. In every contract of guarantee there is an implied promise by the principal debtor to indemnify the surety, and the surety is entitled to recover from the principal debtor whatever sum he has rightfully paid under the guarantee, but, no sums which he has paid wrongfully.
Section 72, Illustration (a). A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C, A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B.
In simple words

A person who is interested in the payment of money that another is bound by law to pay, and who pays it for that reason, gets the money back from the other. In the illustration, B, the lessee , pays the revenue that A, the zamindar, owed, to stop a sale that would end B's lease. A must make good to B what B paid. "In arrear" means unpaid after it fell due.
en.meaning:
Section 69 is one of the five situations of quasi contract . The Act does not define "interested". It does not need to, because the section describes the whole claim: an interested person pays what another must pay by law, and the other reimburses him. Why the law has this rule. The reason is fairness. The payer saved the debtor from the result of his own default. If the law let the debtor keep that saving for free, the debtor would be made richer at the payer's cost. This is unjust enrichment , and the law prevents it. Not a promise. The claim does not come from any promise by the debtor. It comes from the law. English source. The English earlier form of the rule is Exall v. Partridge (1799). See Diagram 1 for the parties in the Act's own illustration. Diagram 1. The boxes are the parties. The arrows say what each one does. The dotted arrow shows what the law gives B. flowchart LR A["A, the zamindar
owes land revenue, unpaid"] G["The Government
advertises A's land for sale"] B["B, the lessee
a sale would annul his lease"] A -->|"owes revenue"| G B -->|"pays the revenue due from A,
to save his lease"| G B -.->|"s. 69: A must make good
the amount paid"| A N["If B had no interest and paid out of kindness:
no right to be reimbursed"] B --- N Text description A, the zamindar, owes land revenue to the Government and has not paid. The Government advertises A's land for sale; the sale would annul the lease of B, the lessee. B pays the Government the revenue due from A, to save his lease. The Government's claim for that revenue ends. Under Section 69, A must make good to B the amount paid. If B had no interest and paid only out of kindness, he would have no right to be reimbursed.
keyPoints: Section 69 reimburses a person who pays money that another was bound by law to pay. The payer must be interested in the payment; a legal proprietary interest is not needed ( Seksaria ). The payment must be made "therefore", to protect that interest. The other person's duty may come from a statute, a contract or a decree. The right is to the sum paid and nothing more. A volunteer with no interest has no claim. The debtor's promise is not needed; the right comes from the law.

caseLaws.name: Govindram Gordhandas Seksaria v
caseLaws.facts: State of Gondal (1949) Facts. The State of Gondal sold two Bombay mills (the Currimbhoy and Mahomedbhoy Mills) to Seksaria, who sub-sold them to a company. Municipal taxes of Rs. 1,24,092-1-0 were outstanding on the mills. Neither the seller nor the debenture trustees in possession paid. On 23 February 1939 the company paid Rs. 78,466-12-0 to the Municipality to avoid a forced sale, and claimed reimbursement. Principle. "Interested" does not require a legal proprietary interest. "Bound by law to pay" extends "to any obligation which is an effective bond in law", including one arising by contract. The company recovered under Section 69. Privy Council, 19 December 1949 : (1950) 52 Bom LR 450. Why it matters. It gives the widest reading of the two conditions of Section 69. Radha Madhub Samonta v. Sasti Ram Sen (1899) Facts. The plaintiff bought a putni (a kind of tenure) at a sale in May 1892. On 12 May 1894 the sale was set aside, and the zamindar's appeal against that order was pending. During the appeal the zamindar demanded the rent that had fallen due, and on 16 May 1895 the plaintiff paid about Rs. 2,000. He then sued the defaulting putnidars (the tenure holders) for reimbursement under Section 69. Principle. Maclean CJ said: "It is difficult to say that, at the time the plaintiff made the payment, he was not interested." He was not "a mere volunteer". The putnidars' liability for the rent "cannot be disputed", so they were bound by law to pay. (1899) ILR 26 Cal 826 (Calcutta High Court, 22 February 1899). Why it matters. A doubtful title does not defeat the payer's interest. Exall v. Partridge (1799) Facts. Exall left his carriage at the premises of Partridge, a coachbuilder, for repair. The landlord seized the carriage as distress for rent that Partridge and his co-tenants owed. Exall paid the rent to recover the carriage and sued Partridge and the others. (1799) 8 TR 308 (Court of King's Bench). Principle. The payment was compulsory and not voluntary, so Exall could recover the money. Why it matters. It is the English forerunner of Section 69.

selfTest.q: 1. What two conditions does Section 69 require?
selfTest.a: The payer must be interested in the payment, and the other person must be bound by law to pay the money.

selfTest.q: 2. Can a stranger who pays a debt out of kindness recover under Section 69?
selfTest.a: No. He has no interest in the payment, so the section does not apply.

selfTest.q: 3. In the Act's illustration, why is B entitled to be reimbursed?
selfTest.a: B paid the Government the revenue that A owed, to prevent a sale that would end B's lease. B was interested and A was bound by law to pay.

selfTest.q: 4. Does "bound by law to pay" cover a duty that arises from a contract?
selfTest.a: Yes. It extends to any obligation which is an effective bond in law, including one under a contract ( Seksaria ).

selfTest.q: 5. Mohan pays ₹1,20,000 of Lata's property tax to save his lease. How much can he recover?
selfTest.a: ₹1,20,000, the sum he paid. Section 69 gives reimbursement, not profit or damages.

Illustration లో, కౌలుదారు B, తన కౌలును రద్దు చేసే అమ్మకాన్ని ఆపడానికి, జమీందారు A బాకీ పడిన శిస్తును చెల్లిస్తాడు. B చెల్లించినదాన్ని A తిరిగి ఇవ్వాలి. "In arrear" అంటే గడువు తీరినా చెల్లించనిది.
te.meaning:
క్వాసి-కాంట్రాక్టు లోని ఐదు సందర్భాల్లో సెక్షన్ 69 ఒకటి. చట్టం "interested" (ఆసక్తి ఉన్న) ను నిర్వచించలేదు. నిర్వచించాల్సిన అవసరం కూడా లేదు, ఎందుకంటే సెక్షన్ మొత్తం క్లెయిమ్‌ను వివరిస్తుంది: మరొకరు చట్టప్రకారం చెల్లించాల్సినదాన్ని ఆసక్తి ఉన్న వ్యక్తి చెల్లిస్తాడు, ఆ మరొకరు అతనికి తిరిగి చెల్లిస్తాడు. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. కారణం న్యాయం. అప్పుదారు (debtor) తన సొంత పొరపాటు ఫలితం నుంచి చెల్లింపుదారు అతన్ని కాపాడాడు. ఆ మేలును అప్పుదారు ఉచితంగా ఉంచుకోనిస్తే, చెల్లింపుదారు ఖర్చుతో అప్పుదారు ధనవంతుడవుతాడు. ఇదే అన్యాయమైన సంపన్నత , చట్టం దాన్ని నివారిస్తుంది. వాగ్దానం కాదు. క్లెయిమ్ అప్పుదారు చేసిన ఏ వాగ్దానం నుంచీ రాదు. చట్టం నుంచి వస్తుంది. ఇంగ్లిష్ మూలం. ఈ నియమానికి ముందున్న ఇంగ్లిష్ రూపం Exall v. Partridge (1799). చట్టంలోని Illustration లోని పక్షాలను చిత్రం 1 లో చూడండి.
