సెక్షన్ 73"] X4 --> OK వచన వివరణ 1 నష్టం ఉల్లంఘన వల్లేనా? 2 సహజంగా వచ్చిందా, లేదా ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలుసా? లేకపోతే దూరపు నష్టం. 3 నిరూపించారా? లేకపోతే నామమాత్రం. 4 సహేతుక చర్యలతో తగ్గించగలిగేవాడా? అవునైతే ఆ భాగం తీసివేస్తారు. ఆ నష్టం ఉల్లంఘన వల్లే వచ్చిందా? అది సహజంగా వచ్చిందా, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు జరగవచ్చని ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలుసా ? లేకపోతే అది దూరపు నష్టం. క్లెయిమ్ చేసినవాడు నష్టాన్నీ దాని మొత్తాన్నీ నిరూపించాడా ? లేకపోతే నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం మాత్రమే. సహేతుక చర్యలతో అతను దాన్ని తగ్గించగలిగేవాడా ? అవునైతే, తప్పించుకోగలిగిన భాగం తీసివేస్తారు.

selfTest.q: 1. Hadley v. Baxendale నియమంలోని రెండు భాగాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సహజంగా వచ్చే నష్టం; కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల జరగవచ్చని ఇరుపక్షాలూ సహేతుకంగా ఊహించిన నష్టం.

selfTest.q: 2. ₹2,000 చొప్పున 100 బస్తాల బియ్యాన్ని రవి డెలివరీ చేయలేదు. గడువు తేదీ నాటి మార్కెట్ ధర ₹2,300. సాధారణ నష్టపరిహారం ఎంత?
3. ప్రత్యేక నష్టపరిహారం ఎప్పుడు వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడే ప్రత్యేక పరిస్థితులు ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలిసి ఉంటేనే.

selfTest.q: 4. కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనకు సాధారణంగా శిక్షాత్మక నష్టపరిహారం ఇస్తారా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. కాంట్రాక్టు నష్టపరిహారం నష్టాన్ని పూడుస్తుంది. పెళ్లి వాగ్దానం ఉల్లంఘన, చెక్కును తప్పుగా తిరస్కరించడం మినహాయింపులుగా పాఠ్యపుస్తకాలు చెబుతాయి.

selfTest.q: 5. నామమాత్ర నష్టపరిహారం అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఉల్లంఘన నిరూపితమై, నిజమైన నష్టం చూపించనప్పుడు ఇచ్చే చిన్న మొత్తం.

law-of-contract-i-u4-t10.subtitle: Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, read with section 73

en.inOneMinute: Sometimes a contract fixes in advance what a party must pay if he breaks it. That is a liquidated sum, or, if it is meant to frighten, a penalty . Sometimes the contract says nothing, and the court works out the loss after the breach. Those are unliquidated damages, under Section 73. Section 74 governs every sum named for breach. The injured party gets reasonable compensation, never more than the sum named . Indian law does not split the named sum into a valid "liquidated damages" clause and a void "penalty" clause. Both are treated alike ( Fateh Chand , 1963). Loss is still essential, and where loss can be proved it must be proved ( Kailash Nath , 2015). In exams, Section 74, Fateh Chand , Kailash Nath , the upper limit and proof of loss earn the marks. In real life, the rule decides how much a seller can keep of an advance, or how much a buyer can deduct for late delivery.
legalProvision: Section 74. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for. Explanation. A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by way of penalty. Exception. When any person enters into any bail-bond, recognizance or other instrument of the same nature, or, under the provisions of any law, or under the orders of the Central Government or of any State Government, gives any bond for the performance of any public duty or act in which the public are interested, he shall be liable, upon breach of the condition of any such instrument, to pay the whole sum mentioned therein. Explanation. A person who enters into a contract with Government does not necessarily thereby undertake any public duty, or promise to do an act in which the public are interested.

Section 73 (summary). Compensation is given for loss that naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or that the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from it. It is not given for remote and indirect loss.
In simple words

Section 74: if the contract names a sum for breach, or contains any other penalty (such as forfeiting money already paid), the court gives reasonable compensation , and the sum named is the ceiling . Explanation: a jump in interest on default may be a penalty. Exception: bail-bonds, recognizances and bonds for a public duty are payable in full . A contract with the Government is not, by itself, a public duty. Section 73: where nothing is named, the court assesses the loss itself.
en.meaning:
Liquidated damages are a sum the contract fixes in advance as payable on breach, as a genuine pre-estimate of the likely loss. Unliquidated damages are not fixed in advance. The court assesses them after the breach, under Section 73 . A penalty is a sum fixed mainly to frighten a party into performing ( in terrorem ). It is out of proportion to any likely loss. Earnest money is a deposit paid when the contract is made, as a sign that the payer means to perform. It usually goes towards the price. The English background. Under English common law, a genuine pre-estimate was enforced in full as liquidated damages , and a penalty was not enforced at all. In Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1963), the Supreme Court said Section 74 is "an attempt to eliminate the somewhat elaborate refinements" of that English distinction. India has one rule for both : reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named. Why the law has this rule. Damages compensate and do not punish. A party should not get a windfall just because the contract named a large figure. But a fair pre-estimate saves the trouble of proving a loss that is hard to measure. See Diagram 1 (how a court applies Section 74). Diagram 1. One rule for liquidated damages and penalties: reasonable compensation, never above the sum named. flowchart TD A["Breach of contract"] --> Q1{"Contract names a sum for breach,
or a penalty such as forfeiture?"} Q1 -- "No" --> U["Unliquidated damages
court assesses · Section 73"] Q1 -- "Yes" --> Q2{"Bail-bond, recognizance,
or public duty bond?"} Q2 -- "Yes" --> W["Whole sum payable
Exception to Section 74"] Q2 -- "No" --> Q3{"Any loss at all?"} Q3 -- "No" --> Z["Nothing payable
loss is a sine qua non · Kailash Nath"] Q3 -- "Yes" --> Q4{"Can the loss be proved?"} Q4 -- "Yes" --> P["Proved loss as reasonable compensation
capped at the sum named"] Q4 -- "No, hard to prove" --> G["Sum may be awarded if a genuine
pre-estimate · ONGC v. Saw Pipes"] P --> CAP["Never above the sum named
MTNL v. Tata Communications"] G --> CAP Text description Does the contract name a sum for breach, or a penalty such as forfeiture? No: unliquidated damages under Section 73. Yes: is it a bail-bond or public duty bond? Yes: whole sum payable (Exception). No: was there any loss? No: nothing (Kailash Nath). Yes: can the loss be proved? Yes: actual proved loss, capped at the sum named. No, hard to prove, and the sum is a genuine pre-estimate: the sum may be awarded (ONGC v. Saw Pipes). Never above the sum named (MTNL).
keyPoints: Section 74 applies to a named sum and to any penalty , including forfeiture. The court awards reasonable compensation . The sum named is the upper limit . India does not distinguish liquidated damages from a penalty ( Fateh Chand ). Loss is a sine qua non. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved ( Kailash Nath ). Proof is excused where loss is hard to prove and the sum is a genuine pre-estimate ( ONGC v. Saw Pipes ). Forfeiture of reasonable earnest money: two lines of authority. Increased interest on default may be a penalty. An acceleration clause for a real debt is not. Bail-bonds and public duty bonds are payable in full . Unliquidated damages are assessed by the court under Section 73 .

caseLaws.name: Fateh Chand v
caseLaws.facts: Balkishan Dass (1963) Facts. A buyer agreed to buy a Delhi property for Rs. 1,12,500, paid Rs. 1,000 earnest money and Rs. 24,000 towards the price, and failed to complete. The contract said Rs. 25,000 would be forfeited. Principle. Section 74 applies to every stipulation by way of penalty, including forfeiture of money paid. Only reasonable compensation up to the sum named is given. AIR 1963 SC 1405. Why it matters. It removed the English distinction in India. The seller kept only the Rs. 1,000. Maula Bux v. Union of India (1969) Facts. A supplier of potatoes, and of poultry, eggs and fish, to the Government gave deposits of Rs. 10,000 and Rs. 8,500 as security. On his default, the Government forfeited them without proving loss. Principle. Reasonable earnest money may be forfeited. But a security deposit is not earnest money. Where loss can be measured in money, it must be proved. AIR 1970 SC 1955. Why it matters. It limits forfeiture of deposits to real, proved loss. ONGC Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd. (2003) Facts. Saw Pipes supplied casing pipes late. The contract fixed liquidated damages at 1% per week of delay, up to 10%, and ONGC deducted them. Principle. A genuine pre-estimate is payable without proof of actual loss, unless the other side shows it is unreasonable. (2003) 5 SCC 705. Why it matters. It explains when proof of loss is not required. Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA (2015) Facts. DDA forfeited ₹78 lakh earnest money (25% of a ₹3.12 crore bid). It later re-auctioned the plot for ₹11.78 crore. Principle. Loss is a sine qua non under Section 74. Where loss can be proved, it must be proved. Section 74 applies to forfeiture of earnest money. (2015) 4 SCC 136. Why it matters. It is the leading summary of Section 74. DDA, with no loss, had to refund. Construction and Design Services v. Delhi Development Authority (2015) Facts. A contractor was late in building a sewage pumping station. DDA claimed the agreed compensation for delay. Principle. Loss may be presumed for a delayed public utility project. Where only a maximum is fixed, the court may award part as reasonable compensation. Half the claim was awarded. Supreme Court, decided 4 February 2015. Why it matters. It shows how the burden of proof works. Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd. v. Tata Communications Ltd. (2019) Facts. A purchase order capped liquidated damages at 12%. MTNL deducted more from the bills. Principle. A higher amount than the contract fixes cannot be awarded. The excess had to be refunded. Why it matters. It applies the upper limit under Section 74. K.R. Suresh v. R. Poornima (2025) Facts. Under a 2007 agreement to sell property for ₹55,50,000, the buyer paid ₹20,00,000 and failed to pay the balance. The vendors forfeited the advance. Principle. The earnest money clause was not penal, so Section 74 did not apply. Even if it did, the vendors' proved losses exceeded the sum forfeited. 2025 INSC 617. Why it matters. It is the latest Supreme Court word on earnest money.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the upper limit of compensation under Section 74?
selfTest.a: The sum named in the contract, or the penalty stipulated .

selfTest.q: 2. Does Indian law treat liquidated damages and a penalty differently?
selfTest.a: No. Section 74 gives reasonable compensation up to the sum named in both ( Fateh Chand ).

selfTest.q: 3. A contract fixes ₹500 for each month of delay. The seller is six months late and the buyer's loss is ₹6,500. What can the buyer recover?
selfTest.a: At most ₹3,000, because the sum named is the upper limit.

selfTest.q: 4. Is any compensation payable under Section 74 if there is no loss at all?
selfTest.a: No. Loss is a sine qua non ( Kailash Nath ).

selfTest.q: 5. Which instruments are enforced for the whole sum?
selfTest.a: Bail-bonds, recognizances and bonds for a public duty (the Exception to Section 74).

Section 73 (సారాంశం). ఉల్లంఘన నుంచి సాధారణ పరిస్థితుల్లో సహజంగా వచ్చిన నష్టానికి, లేదా కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నప్పుడు జరగవచ్చని పక్షాలకు తెలిసిన నష్టానికి పరిహారం ఇస్తారు. దూరపు, పరోక్ష నష్టానికి ఇవ్వరు.
సులభమైన మాటల్లో

సెక్షన్ 74: ఉల్లంఘనకు కాంట్రాక్టు ఒక మొత్తం పేర్కొంటే, లేదా వేరే ఏదైనా జరిమానా (ఇప్పటికే చెల్లించిన డబ్బును జప్తు చేయడం వంటిది) ఉంటే, కోర్టు సహేతుక పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది. పేర్కొన్న మొత్తం గరిష్ట పరిమితి . Explanation: ఉల్లంఘన జరిగినప్పటి నుంచి వడ్డీ పెంచడం జరిమానా కావచ్చు . Exception: బెయిల్ బాండ్లు, recognizances, ప్రజా విధికి ఇచ్చే బాండ్ల మొత్తాన్ని పూర్తిగా చెల్లించాలి. ప్రభుత్వంతో కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకున్నంత మాత్రాన అది ప్రజా విధి కాదు. సెక్షన్ 73: ఏ మొత్తమూ పేర్కొనని చోట, కోర్టే నష్టాన్ని అంచనా వేస్తుంది.
te.meaning:
Liquidated damages (ముందే నిర్ణయించిన నష్టపరిహారం ) అంటే జరగబోయే నష్టానికి నిజాయితీగా ముందుగా వేసిన అంచనాగా (genuine pre-estimate), ఉల్లంఘనపై చెల్లించాల్సినదిగా కాంట్రాక్టు ముందుగానే నిర్ణయించిన మొత్తం. Unliquidated damages (నిర్ణయించని నష్టపరిహారం) ముందుగా నిర్ణయించినవి కావు . ఉల్లంఘన తర్వాత సెక్షన్ 73 కింద కోర్టు వాటిని అంచనా వేస్తుంది. జరిమానా (penalty) అంటే ఒక పక్షాన్ని భయపెట్టి కాంట్రాక్టు అమలు చేయించడానికే ( in terrorem ) ప్రధానంగా నిర్ణయించిన మొత్తం. జరగవచ్చిన ఏ నష్టానికీ ఇది సరితూగదు. బయానా (earnest money) అంటే కాంట్రాక్టు చేసుకునేటప్పుడు, చెల్లించేవాడు కాంట్రాక్టు అమలు చేయాలనుకుంటున్నాడని చూపడానికి చెల్లించే డిపాజిట్. సాధారణంగా ఇది ధరలో భాగంగా లెక్కకు వస్తుంది. ఇంగ్లీష్ నేపథ్యం. ఇంగ్లీష్ common law కింద, నిజాయితీ అంచనాను liquidated damages గా పూర్తిగా అమలు చేసేవారు, జరిమానాను అసలు అమలు చేసేవారు కాదు. Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Dass (1963) లో, సెక్షన్ 74 ఆ ఇంగ్లీష్ తేడాలోని "somewhat elaborate refinements" ను తొలగించే ప్రయత్నమని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది. భారతదేశంలో రెండింటికీ ఒకే నియమం : పేర్కొన్న మొత్తానికి మించని సహేతుక పరిహారం. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. నష్టపరిహారం నష్టాన్ని పూడుస్తుంది, శిక్షించదు. కాంట్రాక్టులో పెద్ద సంఖ్య రాసినంత మాత్రాన ఒక పక్షానికి అనుకోని లాభం రాకూడదు. కానీ కొలవడం కష్టమైన నష్టాన్ని నిరూపించే శ్రమను న్యాయమైన ముందస్తు అంచనా తప్పిస్తుంది. selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 74 కింద పరిహారానికి గరిష్ట పరిమితి ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టులో పేర్కొన్న మొత్తం, లేదా నిర్ణయించిన జరిమానా.

selfTest.q: 2. భారత చట్టం liquidated damages ను, జరిమానాను వేర్వేరుగా చూస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. రెండింటిలోనూ సెక్షన్ 74 పేర్కొన్న మొత్తం వరకు సహేతుక పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది ( Fateh Chand ).

selfTest.q: 3. ఆలస్యమైన ప్రతి నెలకు ₹500 అని కాంట్రాక్టు నిర్ణయించింది. అమ్మకందారు ఆరు నెలలు ఆలస్యం చేశాడు, కొనుగోలుదారు నష్టం ₹6,500. కొనుగోలుదారుకు ఎంత వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: గరిష్టంగా ₹3,000, ఎందుకంటే పేర్కొన్న మొత్తమే గరిష్ట పరిమితి.

selfTest.q: 4. ఏ నష్టమూ లేకపోతే సెక్షన్ 74 కింద ఏదైనా పరిహారం వస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. నష్టం sine qua non ( Kailash Nath ).

selfTest.q: 5. ఏ పత్రాలకు మొత్తం సొమ్ము చెల్లించాలి?
selfTest.a: బెయిల్ బాండ్లు, recognizances, ప్రజా విధికి ఇచ్చే బాండ్లు (సెక్షన్ 74 కి Exception).

law-of-contract-i-u4-t11.subtitle: Explanation to section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: When a contract is broken, the injured party must act sensibly. He must take reasonable steps to keep his loss small . He cannot sit still, let the loss grow, and then bill the wrongdoer for all of it. Loss that reasonable steps would have avoided is not paid . The rule comes from the Explanation to Section 73 : in estimating the loss, "the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience" must be taken into account. It is a limit on what he can claim , not a duty anyone can sue him for. Reasonable costs of mitigating are recoverable, and gains made by mitigating are deducted. In exams, the meaning, the rules (reasonable steps, nothing extraordinary, costs, gains, burden of proof) and the cases ( Murlidhar Chiranjilal , Jamal , British Westinghouse , Payzu ) earn the marks. In real life, the rule decides how much of a large loss a court will actually award.
legalProvision: Section 73 (first two paragraphs). When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach.

Explanation. In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

Illustration (a). A contracts to sell and deliver 50 maunds of saltpetre to B, at a certain price to be paid on delivery. A breaks his promise. B is entitled to receive from A, by way of compensation, the sum, if any, by which the contract price falls short of the price for which B might have obtained 50 maunds of saltpetre of like quality at the time when the saltpetre ought to have been delivered.

Illustration (b). A hires B's ship to go to Bombay, and there take on board, on the first of January, a cargo, which A is to provide, and to bring it to Calcutta, the freight to be paid when earned. B's ship does not go to Bombay, but A has opportunities of procuring suitable conveyance for the cargo upon terms as advantageous as those on which he had chartered the ship. A avails himself of those opportunities, but is put to trouble and expense in doing so. A is entitled to receive compensation from B in respect of such trouble and expense.
In simple words

Section 73 pays for loss that arises naturally from the breach, and for loss both sides knew was likely. It does not pay for remote loss. The Explanation says: count what the injured party could have done to reduce the loss. Illustration (a) measures the loss by the price at which the buyer might have bought elsewhere, so he is expected to buy elsewhere. Illustration (b) shows the other side: the reasonable trouble and expense of mitigating is paid by the wrongdoer. Illustrations (c), (d), (g) and (h) also measure loss by the market price, which shows what the injured party could have got elsewhere.
en.meaning:
Mitigation means taking reasonable steps to reduce the loss caused by a breach. The Supreme Court stated the rule in Murlidhar Chiranjilal v. Harishchandra Dwarkadas (1961). It said there are two settled principles under Section 73 read with its Explanation: the injured party is to be placed, as far as money can do it, in as good a situation as if the contract had been performed; but he has a duty to take all reasonable steps to mitigate the loss, and he cannot claim any part of the damage that is due to his neglect to take such steps. The Privy Council said the same earlier in Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915). Why the law has this rule. Fairness. The wrongdoer should pay for the loss his breach caused, not for the part the injured party could easily have avoided. It is not a true "duty". The injured party is not liable to anyone for failing to mitigate. The wrongdoer cannot sue him. He only loses the right to recover the avoidable part of the loss. See Diagram 1 (from breach to the claim: where mitigation fits). Diagram 1. Damages are fixed at the date of breach. Loss caused by later delay is cut; reasonable costs are added; gains are set off. flowchart LR B["1 June · BREACH
Ravi does not deliver
100 bags at ₹2,000"] M["Market price on 1 June ₹2,300
Loss at breach = ₹30,000"] Q{"Did Sita take
reasonable steps?"} Y["Yes: bought on 1 June
+ ₹2,000 lorry cost
(illustration (b))"] N["No: waited to 1 July, paid ₹2,600
extra ₹30,000 avoidable · NOT paid"] G["Any gain from mitigating
is set off"] R["Claim allowed
₹30,000 + ₹2,000 = ₹32,000"] BP["Burden of proving failure
to mitigate: the wrongdoer"] B --> M --> Q Q -- "Yes" --> Y --> G --> R Q -- "No" --> N --> R BP -.-> Q Text description 1 June: Ravi fails to deliver 100 bags at ₹2,000; market price ₹2,300; loss at breach ₹30,000. Sita waits to 1 July and pays ₹2,600; extra ₹30,000 is avoidable and not paid. Reasonable cost of mitigation, ₹2,000 lorry, is added. Any gain from mitigation is set off. Claim allowed ₹32,000. Burden of proving failure to mitigate is on the wrongdoer.
keyPoints: The injured party must take reasonable steps to reduce his loss (Explanation to Section 73). Avoidable loss cannot be recovered. He need not take extraordinary or risky steps, or accept a lower-status job. The reasonable cost of mitigation is recoverable (illustration (b)). A gain made by mitigating is set off against the damages. The wrongdoer must prove the failure to mitigate. For goods, the loss is fixed at the date of breach . Delay is at the injured party's risk. Failure to mitigate only reduces the damages. No one can sue for it.

caseLaws.name: Murlidhar Chiranjilal v
caseLaws.facts: Harishchandra Dwarkadas (1961) Facts. A seller failed to supply canvas under a contract for delivery at Kanpur, to be sent to Calcutta. The buyer claimed damages at the Calcutta price. Principle. Under Section 73 and its Explanation, the buyer must take all reasonable steps to mitigate. Damages are the Kanpur market price on the date of breach minus the contract price. The buyer did not prove the Kanpur price and got nothing. AIR 1962 SC 366. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court authority on the duty to mitigate. Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915) Facts. Buyers failed to take 23,500 shares on 30 December 1911. The seller sold them later, mostly at higher prices. Principle. The loss is the difference between the contract price and the market price on the date of breach. Later market movements are the seller's own risk. (1915) LR 43 IA 6; ILR 43 Cal 493 (PC). Why it matters. It fixes the date of assessment and states the duty to mitigate. British Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Co. v. Underground Electric Railways Co. of London (1912) Facts. Turbines supplied for a power station were less efficient than promised. The buyers replaced them with better turbines from another maker. Principle. The injured party must take all reasonable steps to reduce his loss, but need not take steps a prudent person would not ordinarily take. A gain from reasonable mitigation is set off. [1912] AC 673. Why it matters. It states the main rules of mitigation and was relied on by the Supreme Court in Murlidhar Chiranjilal . Payzu Ltd. v. Saunders (1919) Facts. A seller refused to continue supplying on credit but offered the same goods at the same price for cash. The buyer refused and bought elsewhere at a higher price. Principle. The buyer should have accepted the reasonable offer. His damages were limited to what he would have lost by accepting it. [1919] 2 KB 581. Why it matters. Mitigation may include accepting an offer from the wrongdoer. Harichand & Co. v. Gosho Kabushiki Kaisha (1924) Facts. The buyer refused goods on 5 April 1921. The sellers resold only on 25 May 1921, while the market kept falling. Principle. Undue delay in reselling in a falling market is a failure to mitigate. The sellers got only the market difference on the day after the breach. (1924) 26 Bom LR 921; AIR 1925 Bom 28. Why it matters. It applies the rule to an Indian sale of goods. Prafulla Ranjan Sarkar v. Hindusthan Building Society Ltd. (1959) Facts. A society's Secretary was dismissed with only one month's salary. The court found he was entitled to nine months' notice. Principle. Failure to mitigate is a question of fact, and the burden of proving it is on the defendant. With no evidence from the defendant, he got nine months' salary in full. AIR 1960 Cal 214. Why it matters. It places the burden of proof on the wrongdoer.

selfTest.q: 1. Where is the duty to mitigate found in the Act?
selfTest.a: In the Explanation to Section 73.

selfTest.q: 2. Sita could buy rice on the due date at ₹2,300 a bag, but waited and paid ₹2,600. The contract price was ₹2,000 for 100 bags. How much does Ravi pay?
selfTest.a: ₹30,000, that is (₹2,300 − ₹2,000) × 100. The extra ₹30,000 was avoidable.

selfTest.q: 3. Can the wrongdoer sue the injured party for failing to mitigate?
selfTest.a: No. Failure to mitigate only reduces the damages by the avoidable part.

selfTest.q: 4. What happens to a gain made while mitigating?
selfTest.a: It is set off against the damages ( British Westinghouse ).

selfTest.q: 5. Who must prove that the injured party failed to mitigate?
selfTest.a: The wrongdoer (defendant) ( Prafulla Ranjan Sarkar ).

సెక్షన్ 73 ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల సహజంగా వచ్చే నష్టానికీ, జరగవచ్చని ఇరుపక్షాలకూ తెలిసిన నష్టానికీ పరిహారం ఇస్తుంది. దూరపు నష్టానికి ఇవ్వదు. Explanation ఇలా చెబుతుంది: నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించడానికి నష్టపోయిన పక్షం ఏమి చేయగలిగేవాడో లెక్కలోకి తీసుకోండి. Illustration (a) నష్టాన్ని కొనుగోలుదారు బయట కొనుక్కోగలిగిన ధరతో కొలుస్తుంది. అంటే అతను బయట కొనుక్కుంటాడని ఆశిస్తుంది. Illustration (b) మరో వైపు చూపిస్తుంది: నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించుకోవడానికి పడిన సహేతుకమైన శ్రమ, ఖర్చు ఉల్లంఘించినవాడే చెల్లిస్తాడు. Illustrations (c), (d), (g), (h) కూడా నష్టాన్ని మార్కెట్ ధరతో కొలుస్తాయి. నష్టపోయిన పక్షం బయట ఏమి పొందగలిగేవాడో అది చూపిస్తుంది.
te.meaning:
Mitigation (నష్ట నివారణ) అంటే ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల వచ్చిన నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించడానికి సహేతుకమైన చర్యలు తీసుకోవడం . Murlidhar Chiranjilal v. Harishchandra Dwarkadas (1961) లో సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఈ నియమాన్ని చెప్పింది. సెక్షన్ 73, దాని Explanation కలిపి చదివితే రెండు స్థిరపడిన సూత్రాలు ఉన్నాయని చెప్పింది: డబ్బుతో సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు, కాంట్రాక్టు అమలైతే ఉండేంత మంచి స్థితిలో నష్టపోయిన పక్షాన్ని ఉంచాలి; కానీ నష్టాన్ని తగ్గించడానికి అన్ని సహేతుకమైన చర్యలూ తీసుకోవాల్సిన బాధ్యత అతనిది. అలాంటి చర్యలు తీసుకోవడంలో అతని నిర్లక్ష్యం వల్ల వచ్చిన నష్టంలో ఏ భాగాన్నీ అతను కోరలేడు. అంతకు ముందే Jamal v. Moolla Dawood, Sons & Co. (1915) లో Privy Council ఇదే చెప్పింది. చట్టం ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు పెట్టింది. న్యాయం కోసం. ఉల్లంఘించినవాడు తన ఉల్లంఘన వల్ల వచ్చిన నష్టానికి చెల్లించాలి. నష్టపోయిన పక్షం సులభంగా తప్పించుకోగలిగిన భాగానికి కాదు. ఇది నిజమైన "బాధ్యత" కాదు. నష్టం తగ్గించుకోనందుకు నష్టపోయిన పక్షం ఎవరికీ జవాబుదారీ కాదు. ఉల్లంఘించినవాడు అతని మీద దావా వేయలేడు. నష్టంలో తప్పించుకోగలిగిన భాగాన్ని పొందే హక్కు మాత్రమే అతను కోల్పోతాడు. law-of-contract-i-u5-t1.subtitle: Specific Relief Act, 1963 and the Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018

en.inOneMinute: Damages give money for a broken promise. Sometimes the injured person needs the thing itself: the plot of land, the document set right, the wrong stopped. The Specific Relief Act, 1963 gives these remedies. They are called specific relief . The Act has seven kinds of relief: recovery of possession, specific performance , rectification, rescission, cancellation, declaration and injunction . The Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018 changed the Act by a large amount from 1 October 2018. Above all, specific performance of a contract is now the rule ("shall be enforced"), and no longer a matter of the court's choice. In exams, the scheme of the Act, Sections 3 and 4, and the 2018 changes earn the marks. Add the Supreme Court's answer on whether the 2018 changes apply to contracts made before 1 October 2018.
legalProvision: Section 1. Short title, extent and commencement. (1) This Act may be called the Specific Relief Act, 1963. (2) It extends to the whole of India [***]. (3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint.
(The date appointed was 1 March 1964. The words "except the State of Jammu and Kashmir" were omitted from sub-section (2) with effect from 31 October 2019.)

Section 2. Definitions. In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— (a) "obligation" includes every duty enforceable by law; (b) "settlement" means an instrument (other than a will or codicil as defined by the Indian Succession Act, 1925 (39 of 1925)), whereby the destination or devolution of successive interests in movable or immovable property is disposed of or is agreed to be disposed of; (c) "trust" has the same meaning as in section 3 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882 (2 of 1882), and includes an obligation in the nature of a trust within the meaning of Chapter IX of that Act; (d) "trustee" includes every person holding property in trust; (e) all other words and expressions used herein but not defined, and defined in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), have the meanings respectively assigned to them in that Act.

Section 3. Savings. Except as otherwise provided herein, nothing in this Act shall be deemed— (a) to deprive any person of any right to relief, other than specific performance, which he may have under any contract; or (b) to affect the operation of the Indian Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908), on documents.

Section 4. Specific relief to be granted only for enforcing individual civil rights and not for enforcing penal laws. Specific relief can be granted only for the purpose of enforcing individual civil rights and not for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law.

Section 10 (as substituted in 2018). Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.
Sections 5 to 42 contain the seven kinds of relief (see Diagram 1 ). Sections 43 and 44 were repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1974, with effect from 20 December 1974.
In simple words

Section 1: the Act applies to the whole of India. It came into force on 1 March 1964. Section 2: defines obligation, settlement, trust and trustee . Words the Act does not define, but the Indian Contract Act does, carry their Contract Act meaning. Section 3: the Act does not take away any right to relief, other than specific performance , that a person has under a contract. It does not affect the Indian Registration Act, 1908. Section 4: specific relief is given only to enforce a person's own civil rights. It is never given merely to enforce a penal (criminal) law. Section 10 (new): the court shall enforce specific performance of a contract. The only exceptions are those in Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16.
en.meaning:
Specific relief means relief in the exact form the person is entitled to. The court orders the actual thing: the land handed over, the contract performed, the document corrected, the right declared, the wrong stopped. Damages are only the money value of the loss. The Act does not define "specific relief", but its title and Section 4 show its scope. The Act's own description. The preamble calls it "An Act to define and amend the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief." It is the second law on the subject. It replaced the Specific Relief Act, 1877, and was made after the Law Commission's Ninth Report. Why the law has it. At common law in England, courts at first gave only damages. Courts of Equity began to order specific performance where damages would be inadequate. That is why these remedies come from equity (a branch of law based on fairness, as against strict rules) and why, before 2018, the court had a wide discretion (freedom to decide) whether to grant them. The 2018 Amendment made specific performance the rule. Many other reliefs in the Act, such as injunctions (Section 36) and declarations (Section 34), are still discretionary . The structure. The Act has three Parts and eight Chapters. Part I, Preliminary: Sections 1 to 4. Part II, Specific Relief: Chapters I to VI, Sections 5 to 35. Part III, Preventive Relief : Chapters VII and VIII, Sections 36 to 44 (Sections 43 and 44 repealed). The Schedule: the list of infrastructure projects, added in 2018. See Diagram 1 for the scheme of the Act. Diagram 1. Start at the top box and follow the lines down. Part II, Specific Relief, has six kinds of relief: recovery of possession (Sections 5 to 8), specific performance (Sections 9 to 25), rectification (Section 26), rescission (Sections 27 to 30), cancellation (Sections 31 to 33) and declaratory decrees (Sections 34 and 35). Part III, Preventive Relief, is injunctions (Sections 36 to 42; Sections 43 and 44 repealed). The Schedule, added in 2018, lists infrastructure projects.
keyPoints: Specific relief gives the thing itself. Damages give its money value. Act 47 of 1963, in force from 1 March 1964. It replaced the 1877 Act. It has three Parts, eight Chapters and a Schedule. Sections 43 and 44 are repealed. Seven kinds of relief: possession, specific performance, rectification, rescission, cancellation, declaration and injunction (Sections 5 to 42). Section 2(e) borrows Contract Act meanings. Section 3 saves other remedies. Section 4 limits the Act to individual civil rights. The 2018 Amendment came into force on 1 October 2018. Section 10 now says "shall be enforced", subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16. The old discretion in Section 20 was replaced by substituted performance. Katta Sujatha Reddy (2022) held the amendment prospective. The 2024 review recalled that judgment without deciding the point again.

caseLaws.name: Katta Sujatha Reddy v
caseLaws.facts: Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (2022) Facts. A purchaser under two agreements of 26 and 27 March 1997 for about 40 acres in Budvel Village, Ranga Reddy District, paid ₹34,80,850 of ₹40,20,000. The balance was due within three months. The purchaser sued in 2002. The High Court held the amended Section 10 retrospective and decreed the suit in part. Principle. The 2018 Amendment is prospective and "cannot apply to those transactions that took place prior to its coming into force". The Court also held the suit barred by limitation and the purchaser not ready and willing. Civil Appeal No. 5822 of 2022, decided 25 August 2022 (Ramana CJI, Krishna Murari and Hima Kohli JJ). On 8 November 2024 the Court recalled this judgment in review and restored the High Court's decree, without deciding the prospective point again (2024 INSC 861). Why it matters. It is the leading authority on whether the amended Section 10 applies to older contracts. K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan (1997) Facts. An agreement of 15 December 1978 to sell a house in Madurai for ₹60,000 required the sale within six months. The buyer paid ₹5,000 and did nothing for about two and a half years. He sent notice on 11 July 1981 and sued on 23 August 1981, after prices had risen sharply. Principle. Not every suit for specific performance must be decreed merely because it is filed within limitation. Total inaction for 2½ years together with a steep rise in prices made the relief inequitable . (1997) 3 SCC 1 : AIR 1997 SC 1751. Why it matters. It shows how the old discretion under Sections 10 and 20 worked before 2018, and why delay and readiness still matter. Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh (1967) Facts. Tenant-cultivators of agricultural land in Gwalior district said the landlord forcibly stopped them from cultivating and had the land cultivated by others. They sued for restoration of possession under a Gwalior law similar to Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. Principle. The Court approved the Privy Council's words: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession". In such a suit the question of title is irrelevant. AIR 1968 SC 620 : (1968) 2 SCR 203, decided 29 November 1967. Why it matters. It supports the rule now in Section 6 of the 1963 Act. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Two house sites in Matwada, Warangal were sold to the plaintiffs by Rukminibai in 1968 and the same land was sold to the defendant by her brother in 1977. The plaintiffs sued only for a permanent injunction. Principle. A suit for injunction alone lies where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and his title is not under a cloud. Where the title is in dispute, he must sue for declaration and consequential injunction. (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It shows how declaration and injunction under the Act work together.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 4 of the Act say?
selfTest.a: Specific relief can be granted only to enforce individual civil rights. It cannot be granted for the mere purpose of enforcing a penal law.

selfTest.q: 2. On what date did the 2018 Amendment come into force?
selfTest.a: On 1 October 2018.

selfTest.q: 3. What does the amended Section 10 say?
selfTest.a: The specific performance of a contract "shall be enforced" by the court, subject to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16.

selfTest.q: 4. What did the old Section 20 say, and what does the new Section 20 deal with?
selfTest.a: The old Section 20 made the jurisdiction to decree specific performance discretionary. The new Section 20 deals with substituted performance after at least 30 days' written notice.

selfTest.q: 5. Does the Act take away the right to claim damages under the Contract Act?
selfTest.a: No. Section 3 saves every right to relief under a contract other than specific performance.

సెక్షన్ 1: చట్టం భారతదేశం అంతటికీ వర్తిస్తుంది. ఇది 1 మార్చి 1964 నుంచి అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది. సెక్షన్ 2: obligation, settlement, trust, trustee అనే పదాలను నిర్వచిస్తుంది. ఈ చట్టం నిర్వచించని, కానీ కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం నిర్వచించిన పదాలకు కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం అర్థమే వర్తిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 3: కాంట్రాక్టు కింద ఒక వ్యక్తికి ఉన్న, నిర్దిష్ట అమలు తప్ప, మరే ఉపశమన హక్కునూ ఈ చట్టం తీసివేయదు. Indian Registration Act, 1908 ను ఇది ప్రభావితం చేయదు. సెక్షన్ 4: నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమనం ఒక వ్యక్తి సొంత పౌర హక్కులను అమలు చేయడానికి మాత్రమే. కేవలం శిక్షా (క్రిమినల్) చట్టాన్ని అమలు చేయడానికి దీన్ని ఎప్పుడూ ఇవ్వరు. సెక్షన్ 10 (కొత్తది): కోర్టు కాంట్రాక్టు నిర్దిష్ట అమలును తప్పనిసరిగా అమలు చేయాలి. మినహాయింపులు సెక్షన్ 11(2), సెక్షన్ 14, సెక్షన్ 16 లోనివి మాత్రమే.
te.meaning:
నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమనం అంటే వ్యక్తికి హక్కు ఉన్న అదే రూపంలో ఇచ్చే ఉపశమనం. కోర్టు అసలు వస్తువునే ఆదేశిస్తుంది: భూమిని అప్పగించడం, కాంట్రాక్టును నెరవేర్చడం, పత్రాన్ని సరిదిద్దడం, హక్కును ప్రకటించడం, తప్పును ఆపడం. నష్టపరిహారం నష్టానికి డబ్బు విలువ మాత్రమే. చట్టం "specific relief" ను నిర్వచించదు, కానీ దాని పేరు, సెక్షన్ 4 దాని పరిధిని చూపుతాయి. చట్టం తన గురించి చెప్పేది. ప్రవేశిక (preamble) దీన్ని "An Act to define and amend the law relating to certain kinds of specific relief." అంటుంది. ఈ విషయంపై ఇది రెండో చట్టం. ఇది Specific Relief Act, 1877 స్థానంలో వచ్చింది, లా కమిషన్ తొమ్మిదో నివేదిక తర్వాత రూపొందింది. చట్టంలో ఇది ఎందుకు ఉంది. ఇంగ్లండ్‌లో కామన్ లా కోర్టులు మొదట నష్టపరిహారం మాత్రమే ఇచ్చేవి. నష్టపరిహారం సరిపోని చోట Courts of Equity నిర్దిష్ట అమలును ఆదేశించడం మొదలుపెట్టాయి. అందుకే ఈ పరిష్కారాలు equity (కఠిన నియమాలకు బదులు న్యాయబద్ధతపై ఆధారపడిన చట్ట శాఖ) నుంచి వచ్చాయి. అందుకే 2018 కి ముందు వాటిని ఇవ్వాలా వద్దా అనే దానిపై కోర్టుకు విస్తృత విచక్షణ (నిర్ణయించే స్వేచ్ఛ) ఉండేది. 2018 సవరణ నిర్దిష్ట అమలును నియమంగా మార్చింది. చట్టంలోని ఇతర అనేక ఉపశమనాలు, ఉదాహరణకు injunctions (సెక్షన్ 36), declarations (సెక్షన్ 34), ఇప్పటికీ కోర్టు విచక్షణపైనే ఆధారపడతాయి. నిర్మాణం. చట్టంలో మూడు భాగాలు (Parts), ఎనిమిది అధ్యాయాలు (Chapters) ఉన్నాయి. Part I, Preliminary: సెక్షన్లు 1 నుంచి 4. Part II, Specific Relief: అధ్యాయాలు I నుంచి VI, సెక్షన్లు 5 నుంచి 35. Part III, Preventive Relief : అధ్యాయాలు VII, VIII, సెక్షన్లు 36 నుంచి 44 (సెక్షన్లు 43, 44 రద్దయ్యాయి). selfTest.q: 1. చట్టంలోని సెక్షన్ 4 ఏమి చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమనాన్ని వ్యక్తిగత పౌర హక్కులను అమలు చేయడానికి మాత్రమే ఇవ్వవచ్చు. కేవలం శిక్షా చట్టాన్ని అమలు చేసే ఉద్దేశంతో ఇవ్వలేం.

selfTest.q: 2. 2018 సవరణ ఏ తేదీన అమల్లోకి వచ్చింది?
selfTest.a: 1 అక్టోబర్ 2018 న.

selfTest.q: 3. సవరించిన సెక్షన్ 10 ఏమి చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్టు నిర్దిష్ట అమలును కోర్టు "shall be enforced", సెక్షన్ 11(2), సెక్షన్ 14, సెక్షన్ 16 కు లోబడి.

selfTest.q: 4. పాత సెక్షన్ 20 ఏమి చెప్పింది, కొత్త సెక్షన్ 20 దేని గురించి?
selfTest.a: పాత సెక్షన్ 20 నిర్దిష్ట అమలు డిక్రీ ఇచ్చే అధికారాన్ని విచక్షణాధికారంగా చేసింది. కొత్త సెక్షన్ 20 కనీసం 30 రోజుల లిఖిత నోటీసు తర్వాత ప్రత్యామ్నాయ నెరవేర్పు గురించి.

selfTest.q: 5. కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం కింద నష్టపరిహారం కోరే హక్కును ఈ చట్టం తీసివేస్తుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. నిర్దిష్ట అమలు తప్ప, కాంట్రాక్టు కింద ఉన్న ప్రతి ఉపశమన హక్కును సెక్షన్ 3 కాపాడుతుంది.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t2.subtitle: Sections 5 to 8 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: If someone throws you out of your land, the law gives you two doors. One asks you to prove that you own it (Section 5). The other asks only whether you were in possession and were removed without due process of law (Section 6). Sections 7 and 8 do the same work for goods. No one may force a person out of his property by self-help, not even the true owner. A person in settled possession can be removed only through a court. In exams, the six-month possessory suit under Section 6 is asked most often. In real life, it protects tenants, shopkeepers and farmers from being put on the street overnight.
legalProvision: Section 5. Recovery of specific immovable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).

Section 6. Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property. (1) If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. (2) No suit under this section shall be brought— (a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government. (3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed. (4) Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.
(The words "through whom he has been in possession or any person" were inserted in sub-section (1) by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 7. Recovery of specific movable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific movable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). Explanation 1. —A trustee may sue under this section for the possession of movable property to the beneficial interest in which the person for whom he is trustee is entitled. Explanation 2. —A special or temporary right to the present possession of movable property is sufficient to support a suit under this section.

Section 8. Liability of person in possession, not as owner, to deliver to persons entitled to immediate possession. Any person having the possession or control of a particular article of movable property, of which he is not the owner, may be compelled specifically to deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession, in any of the following cases:— (a) when the thing claimed is held by the defendant as the agent or trustee of the plaintiff; (b) when compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed; (c) when it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss; (d) when the possession of the thing claimed has been wrongfully transferred from the plaintiff. Explanation. —Unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall, in respect of any article of movable property claimed under clause (b) or clause (c) of this section, presume— (a) that compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed, or, as the case may be; (b) that it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss.
Related provisions (Limitation Act, 1963, Schedule)

Article 64. For possession of immovable property based on previous possession and not on title, when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed. – Twelve years. – The date of dispossession.
Article 65. For possession of immovable property or any interest therein based on title. – Twelve years. – When the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff.
In simple words

Section 5: a person entitled to possess particular land or a building may sue for it in the ordinary way under the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 6: a person put out of land or a building without his consent and without due process of law may sue to get it back. The defendant cannot defend by saying he owns it. The suit must be filed within six months and cannot be against the Government. There is no appeal or review. Anyone may still file a separate suit on title. Section 7: the same as Section 5, for particular goods. A trustee may sue, and a special or temporary right to present possession is enough. Section 8: a person who holds a particular article but does not own it can be made to hand over that very article, in four cases. In two of them the court presumes that money is not enough. Articles 64 and 65: an ordinary suit on earlier possession, or on title, may be filed within 12 years.
en.meaning:
Possession here means actual control of the property. Settled possession means possession that has continued for some time with the owner's knowledge. The law protects it even against the owner. In Krishna Ram Mahale (1989) the Supreme Court held that such a person "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law", even if he has no right to remain. The question this part of the Act answers. Who is entitled to possession, and how may he get it back? The answer for land is a choice between two suits. A title suit under Section 5 proves ownership and decides it for good. A possessory suit under Section 6 is quick, but it proves only earlier possession and unlawful removal. It does not decide who owns the land. Why the law has this rule. If every owner could retake property by force whenever he believed he was right, disputes would end in violence. The Privy Council's words, approved by the Supreme Court, are: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession; they must obtain such possession as they are entitled to through a Court." no appeal or review (s. 6(3));
title suit still open (s. 6(4))"] Text description Question 1: is the property immovable? If no, use Sections 7 and 8 for movable property. Question 2: was the plaintiff in possession and removed without his consent and without due process of law? If no, file a title suit under Section 5 (12 years, Article 65). Question 3: is the suit within six months of dispossession and not against the Government? If no, file a title suit under Section 5, or a suit on earlier possession within 12 years (Article 64), where the defendant may plead title. If all answers are yes, a Section 6 suit lies: title is no defence, there is no appeal or review, and a title suit remains open under Section 6(4).
keyPoints: Section 5 is a title suit under the Code of Civil Procedure (12 years, Article 65). Section 6 is a quick suit on possession. Section 6: six months, not against the Government, no appeal or review, title no defence. Since 2018, a person through whom the dispossessed person was in possession can also sue. Section 6(4) always saves a separate suit on title. After six months, a suit on earlier possession lies within 12 years (Article 64), but the defendant may plead title. Settled possession is protected even against the true owner ( Lallu Yeshwant Singh ; Krishna Ram Mahale ). Section 7: recovery of movables. A trustee may sue, and a special or temporary right to possession is enough. Section 8: four cases where a non-owner must deliver the article, with a presumption for the plaintiff in clauses (b) and (c).

caseLaws.name: Lallu Yeshwant Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Rao Jagdish Singh (1967) Facts. Gairdakhilkar (tenant) cultivators in Gwalior district said the landlord forcibly stopped them from cultivating and had the land cultivated by others. The landlord said their rights had ended because land revenue was not paid. They sued under Section 326 of the Gwalior Qanoon Mal, which is similar to Section 9 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. Principle. The tenants' rights did not end automatically. Under Section 9 the question of title is irrelevant, and a landlord cannot use force to throw out his tenant. AIR 1968 SC 620 : (1968) 2 SCR 203, decided 29 November 1967 (Sikri and Shah JJ). Why it matters. It is the foundation of the "no self-help" rule now in Section 6. Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao (1989) Facts. The owner of a restaurant in Parel, Bombay had let the plaintiff conduct it under a 1956 agreement. On 15 February 1959 he took possession behind her back, in collusion with others, relying on notices she said she never received. She sued within a few weeks. Principle. A person in settled possession "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law", even if he had no right to remain. The appeal was dismissed with costs, and the Court Receiver was appointed to take possession. (1989) 4 SCC 131 : AIR 1989 SC 2097, decided 9 August 1989. Why it matters. It states the "no self-help" rule in the clearest terms. Nair Service Society Ltd. v. K.C. Alexander (1968) Facts. The plaintiff sued in 1942 for possession of about 131 acres of Government poramboke land in former Travancore, from which he said the Society's men had removed him in October 1939. The suit was filed long after six months and was based on his earlier possession. Principle. In a suit under Section 9 of the 1877 Act the plaintiff need not prove title. After six months the defendant may raise title; the plaintiff may still sue on earlier possession within 12 years. AIR 1968 SC 1165 : (1968) 3 SCR 163 (Hidayatullah, Sikri, Hegde JJ). Why it matters. It explains how Section 6 relates to ordinary suits for possession. Sanjay Kumar Pandey v. Gulbahar Sheikh (2004) Facts. A trial court decreed a suit under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. The defendants filed a revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the High Court dismissed the suit. Principle. The unsuccessful party's remedy "is to file a suit based on title". A revision is available "only by way of an exception". The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and sent the revision back for a fresh hearing. (2004) 4 SCC 664 : AIR 2004 SC 3354, decided 2 April 2004. Why it matters. It shows how Section 6(3) and Section 6(4) work in practice.

selfTest.q: 1. Within what time must a Section 6 suit be filed?
selfTest.a: Within six months from the date of dispossession.

selfTest.q: 2. Can the defendant in a Section 6 suit plead that he is the owner?
selfTest.a: No. Section 6(1) says the suit lies notwithstanding any other title that may be set up.

selfTest.q: 3. Does an appeal lie from a decree in a Section 6 suit?
selfTest.a: No. Section 6(3) bars appeal and review. A suit on title remains open under Section 6(4).

selfTest.q: 4. A person dispossessed eight months ago has no title deed. Can he still sue?
selfTest.a: Yes. He may sue on his earlier possession within 12 years (Article 64). If the defendant proves a better title, he fails.

selfTest.q: 5. A hirer of a tractor loses it to a stranger. Can he sue under Section 7?
selfTest.a: Yes. Explanation 2 says a special or temporary right to present possession is enough.

legalProvision: Section 5. Recovery of specific immovable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific immovable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).

Section 6. Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property. (1) If any person is dispossessed without his consent of immovable property otherwise than in due course of law, he or any person through whom he has been in possession or any person claiming through him may, by suit, recover possession thereof, notwithstanding any other title that may be set up in such suit. (2) No suit under this section shall be brought— (a) after the expiry of six months from the date of dispossession; or (b) against the Government. (3) No appeal shall lie from any order or decree passed in any suit instituted under this section, nor shall any review of any such order or decree be allowed. (4) Nothing in this section shall bar any person from suing to establish his title to such property and to recover possession thereof.
("through whom he has been in possession or any person" అనే పదాలు 2018 చట్టం నం. 18 ద్వారా, 1 అక్టోబర్ 2018 నుంచి సబ్-సెక్షన్ (1) లో చేర్చబడ్డాయి.)

Section 7. Recovery of specific movable property. A person entitled to the possession of specific movable property may recover it in the manner provided by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). Explanation 1. —A trustee may sue under this section for the possession of movable property to the beneficial interest in which the person for whom he is trustee is entitled. Explanation 2. —A special or temporary right to the present possession of movable property is sufficient to support a suit under this section.

Section 8. Liability of person in possession, not as owner, to deliver to persons entitled to immediate possession. Any person having the possession or control of a particular article of movable property, of which he is not the owner, may be compelled specifically to deliver it to the person entitled to its immediate possession, in any of the following cases:— (a) when the thing claimed is held by the defendant as the agent or trustee of the plaintiff; (b) when compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed; (c) when it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss; (d) when the possession of the thing claimed has been wrongfully transferred from the plaintiff. Explanation. —Unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall, in respect of any article of movable property claimed under clause (b) or clause (c) of this section, presume— (a) that compensation in money would not afford the plaintiff adequate relief for the loss of the thing claimed, or, as the case may be; (b) that it would be extremely difficult to ascertain the actual damage caused by its loss.

Article 64. For possession of immovable property based on previous possession and not on title, when the plaintiff while in possession of the property has been dispossessed. – Twelve years. – The date of dispossession.
Article 65. For possession of immovable property or any interest therein based on title. – Twelve years. – When the possession of the defendant becomes adverse to the plaintiff.

సెక్షన్ 5: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట భూమిని లేదా భవనాన్ని స్వాధీనం చేసుకునే హక్కు ఉన్న వ్యక్తి, సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్ కింద సాధారణ పద్ధతిలో దాని కోసం దావా వేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 6: తన సమ్మతి లేకుండా, చట్ట ప్రక్రియ లేకుండా భూమి లేదా భవనం నుంచి బయటకు గెంటబడిన వ్యక్తి దాన్ని తిరిగి పొందడానికి దావా వేయవచ్చు. తానే యజమాని అని చెప్పి ప్రతివాది తప్పించుకోలేడు. దావా ఆరు నెలల్లో వేయాలి, ప్రభుత్వంపై వేయలేం. అప్పీల్ గానీ, రివ్యూ గానీ ఉండదు. ఎవరైనా టైటిల్‌పై వేరే దావా వేయవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 7: నిర్దిష్ట వస్తువుల కోసం సెక్షన్ 5 లాంటిదే. ట్రస్టీ దావా వేయవచ్చు; ప్రస్తుత స్వాధీనానికి ప్రత్యేక లేదా తాత్కాలిక హక్కు ఉన్నా చాలు. సెక్షన్ 8: ఒక నిర్దిష్ట వస్తువును యజమాని కాకుండా తన దగ్గర ఉంచుకున్న వ్యక్తిని, నాలుగు సందర్భాల్లో, అదే వస్తువును అప్పగించేలా చేయవచ్చు. వాటిలో రెండింటిలో డబ్బు సరిపోదని కోర్టు ఊహిస్తుంది. ఆర్టికల్స్ 64, 65: పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై లేదా టైటిల్‌పై సాధారణ దావాను 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో వేయవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
ఇక్కడ స్వాధీనం (possession) అంటే ఆస్తిపై వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ. స్థిరపడిన స్వాధీనం అంటే యజమానికి తెలిసి కొంతకాలం కొనసాగిన స్వాధీనం. యజమానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా కూడా చట్టం దాన్ని కాపాడుతుంది. Krishna Ram Mahale (1989) లో, అలాంటి వ్యక్తి "cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law" అని, అతనికి అక్కడ ఉండే హక్కు లేకపోయినా ఇదే నియమమని సుప్రీంకోర్టు చెప్పింది. చట్టంలోని ఈ భాగం సమాధానం చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. స్వాధీనానికి ఎవరు అర్హులు, దాన్ని ఎలా తిరిగి పొందవచ్చు? భూమికి సమాధానం రెండు దావాల మధ్య ఎంపిక. సెక్షన్ 5 కింది టైటిల్ దావా యాజమాన్యాన్ని రుజువు చేసి శాశ్వతంగా తేలుస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6 కింది స్వాధీన దావా త్వరితమైనది, కానీ అది పూర్వ స్వాధీనం, చట్టవిరుద్ధ తొలగింపులను మాత్రమే రుజువు చేస్తుంది. భూమి ఎవరిదో అది తేల్చదు. చట్టంలో ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు ఉంది. తాను సరైనవాడినని నమ్మిన ప్రతిసారీ ప్రతి యజమాని బలవంతంగా ఆస్తిని తిరిగి తీసుకోగలిగితే, వివాదాలు హింసలో ముగుస్తాయి. సుప్రీంకోర్టు ఆమోదించిన Privy Council మాటలు: "In India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession; they must obtain such possession as they are entitled to through a Court." ఏ దావా ఎంచుకోవాలో Diagram 1 లో చూడండి. Diagram 1. పై నుంచి ప్రతి ప్రశ్నకు సమాధానం ఇవ్వండి. "కాదు" అయితే పక్కన ఉన్న పెట్టెకు వెళ్లండి. flowchart TD Q1{"1. ఆస్తి స్థిరాస్తా

పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై దావా (ఆర్టి. 64);
ప్రతివాది టైటిల్ వాదించవచ్చు"] Q3 -->|"అవును"| S["సె. 6 దావా నిలుస్తుంది: టైటిల్ రక్షణ కాదు;

టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంది (సె. 6(4))"] వచన వివరణ ప్రశ్న 1: ఆస్తి స్థిరాస్తా? కాకపోతే, చరాస్తికి సెక్షన్లు 7, 8 వాడండి. ప్రశ్న 2: వాది స్వాధీనంలో ఉండి, తన సమ్మతి లేకుండా, చట్ట ప్రక్రియ లేకుండా తొలగించబడ్డాడా? కాకపోతే, సెక్షన్ 5 కింద టైటిల్ దావా (12 సంవత్సరాలు, ఆర్టికల్ 65). ప్రశ్న 3: స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన ఆరు నెలల్లో, ప్రభుత్వంపై కాకుండా దావా వేస్తున్నారా? కాకపోతే, సెక్షన్ 5 కింద టైటిల్ దావా, లేదా 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై దావా (ఆర్టికల్ 64); అందులో ప్రతివాది టైటిల్ వాదించవచ్చు. అన్నీ అవును అయితే, సెక్షన్ 6 దావా నిలుస్తుంది: టైటిల్ రక్షణ కాదు, అప్పీల్ లేదా రివ్యూ లేదు, సెక్షన్ 6(4) కింద టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాను ఎంత కాలంలో వేయాలి?
selfTest.a: స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన తేదీ నుంచి ఆరు నెలల్లో.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాలో ప్రతివాది తానే యజమానినని వాదించవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. మరే టైటిల్ వాదించినా దావా నిలుస్తుందని సెక్షన్ 6(1) చెబుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 3. సెక్షన్ 6 దావాలోని డిక్రీపై అప్పీల్ ఉంటుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. సెక్షన్ 6(3) అప్పీల్, రివ్యూలను నిషేధిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 6(4) కింద టైటిల్ దావా తెరిచే ఉంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. ఎనిమిది నెలల క్రితం స్వాధీనం కోల్పోయిన వ్యక్తికి టైటిల్ పత్రం లేదు. అతను ఇంకా దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును. 12 సంవత్సరాల్లో తన పూర్వ స్వాధీనంపై దావా వేయవచ్చు (ఆర్టికల్ 64). ప్రతివాది మెరుగైన టైటిల్ రుజువు చేస్తే, అతను ఓడిపోతాడు.

selfTest.q: 5. ట్రాక్టర్ అద్దెకు తీసుకున్న వ్యక్తి దాన్ని ఒక అపరిచితుడి వల్ల కోల్పోతాడు. అతను సెక్షన్ 7 కింద దావా వేయగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును. ప్రస్తుత స్వాధీనానికి ప్రత్యేక లేదా తాత్కాలిక హక్కు చాలని Explanation 2 చెబుతుంది.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t3.subtitle: Sections 9 to 25 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as amended in 2018

en.inOneMinute: When a party breaks a contract, the injured party can ask the court to make the other side keep its promise. That order is called specific performance . It is the most important remedy in the Specific Relief Act, 1963. Since 1 October 2018, the court shall enforce a contract as a rule, unless a section bars it. Three provisions can bar it: the kind of contract (Sections 11(2) and 14) and the plaintiff's own conduct (Section 16). Substituted performance under Section 20 works through Sections 14(a) and 16(a). In exams, you must know all of these, with the main cases. In real life, this is the remedy a buyer uses when a seller backs out of a land or flat sale because prices have gone up.
legalProvision: Section 9. Defences respecting suits for relief based on contract. Except as otherwise provided herein where any relief is claimed under this Chapter in respect of a contract, the person against whom the relief is claimed may plead by way of defence any ground which is available to him under any law relating to contracts.

Section 10. Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.
(Section 10 was substituted by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 11. Cases in which specific performance of contracts connected with trusts enforceable. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, specific performance of a contract shall, be enforced when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly of a trust. (2) A contract made by a trustee in excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced.
(In Section 11(1), " contract shall" replaced "contract may, in the discretion of the court" from 1 October 2018.)

Section 14. Contracts not specifically enforceable. The following contracts cannot be specifically enforced, namely:— (a) where a party to the contract has obtained substituted performance of contract in accordance with the provisions of section 20; (b) a contract, the performance of which involves the performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract which is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; and (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.
(Section 14 was substituted by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.)

Section 16. Personal bars to relief. Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person— (a) who has obtained substituted performance of contract under section 20; or (b) who has become incapable of performing, or violates any essential term of, the contract that on his part remains to be performed, or acts in fraud of the contract, or wilfully acts at variance with, or in subversion of, the relation intended to be established by the contract; or (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant. Explanation. —For the purposes of clause (c),— (i) where a contract involves the payment of money, it is not essential for the plaintiff to actually tender to the defendant or to deposit in court any money except when so directed by the court; (ii) the plaintiff must prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
(In 2018, clause (a) was substituted, "who fails to aver and prove" became "who fails to prove", and "must aver" in Explanation (ii) became "must prove".)

Section 20. Substituted performance of contract. (1) Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), and, except as otherwise agreed upon by the parties, where the contract is broken due to non-performance of promise by any party, the party who suffers by such breach shall have the option of substituted performance through a third party or by his own agency, and, recover the expenses and other costs actually incurred, spent or suffered by him, from the party committing such breach. (2) No substituted performance of contract under sub-section (1) shall be undertaken unless the party who suffers such breach has given a notice in writing, of not less than thirty days, to the party in breach calling upon him to perform the contract within such time as specified in the notice, and on his refusal or failure to do so, he may get the same performed by a third party or by his own agency: Provided that the party who suffers such breach shall not be entitled to recover the expenses and costs under sub-section (1) unless he has got the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency. (3) Where the party suffering breach of contract has got the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency after giving notice under sub-section (1), he shall not be entitled to claim relief of specific performance against the party in breach. (4) Nothing in this section shall prevent the party who has suffered breach of contract from claiming compensation from the party in breach.
Related provision ( Limitation Act, 1963 , Schedule)
Article 54. For specific performance of a contract. – Three years. – The date fixed for the performance, or, if no such date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.
In simple words

Section 9: the defendant may raise any defence that the law of contract allows. Section 10: specific performance shall be enforced, subject to Section 11(2), Section 14 and Section 16. Sections 11 to 13: contracts connected with trusts, part of a contract, and rights against a vendor with a defective title. Section 14: four kinds of contract that cannot be specifically enforced. Section 14A: the court may engage experts. Sections 15 to 19: who may sue and against whom, personal bars, no title, enforcement only with a variation. Section 20: substituted performance. Sections 20A to 20C: infrastructure projects, Special Courts, and a 12-month time limit for suits. Sections 21 to 25: compensation, possession and refund of earnest money , a sum named for breach, bar of a later suit, and awards. Article 54: the suit must be filed within three years.
en.meaning:
Specific performance is a court order that a party must actually do what he promised in the contract. It differs from damages , which give money. It is the natural remedy where the subject matter is one of a kind, such as land, because no sum of money buys exactly the same plot. The question this part of the Act answers. When will the court make a party actually perform his contract, instead of paying money? The answer since 2018. The Act does not say that the court has no freedom left. It says the court shall enforce the contract unless a named bar applies. A plaintiff must clear a series of tests. Is there a valid, subsisting contract, with no defence under the law of contract? If not, there is nothing to enforce (Section 9). Is the suit filed in time, within three years of the date fixed for performance or of refusal? If not, the suit is barred by Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Is the contract one that the Act allows to be enforced? If it is barred by Section 11(2) or Section 14, damages are the remedy. Is the plaintiff free of the personal bars? If he took substituted performance, cannot perform, or cannot prove readiness and willingness , he fails (Section 16). If all the tests are met, the court shall enforce the contract (Section 10). It may add compensation and possession (Sections 21 and 22). See Diagram 1 for the order of the tests. Diagram 1. may add compensation and possession (ss. 21, 22)"] Text description Question 1: is there a valid, subsisting contract with no defence under the law of contract? If no, there is nothing to enforce (Section 9). Question 2: is the suit within three years of the date fixed for performance or of refusal? If no, it is barred by Article 54 of the Limitation Act. Question 3: is the contract outside Section 11(2) and Section 14? If no, damages are the remedy. Question 4: is the plaintiff free of the personal bars in Section 16 (substituted performance, incapacity or misconduct, readiness and willingness)? If no, relief is refused. If all answers are yes, the court shall enforce the contract under Section 10 and may add compensation and possession under Sections 21 and 22.
keyPoints: Section 10 (after 2018): specific performance shall be enforced as a rule, subject to Sections 11(2), 14 and 16. Before 1 October 2018 it was "may", in the court's discretion. Katta Sujatha Reddy (2022): the amendment is prospective. The 2024 review recalled that judgment without deciding the point again. Section 14 has four classes: substituted performance obtained, continuous duty, personal qualifications, determinable contracts. Section 16(c): the plaintiff must prove continuous readiness and willingness. Readiness is financial capacity and willingness is conduct. Filing within limitation (three years, Article 54) is not enough. Delay and price rise can defeat relief. Section 20: substituted performance after 30 days' written notice. It bars a later claim for specific performance but not compensation. Sections 21 and 22: compensation, possession and refund of earnest money must be claimed in the plaint, but the court shall allow amendment. Sections 20A to 20C: no injunction that delays a listed infrastructure project; Special Courts; suits disposed of within 12 months (plus six).

caseLaws.name: Katta Sujatha Reddy v
caseLaws.facts: Siddamsetty Infra Projects Pvt. Ltd. (2022) Facts. A purchaser under two agreements of March 1997 for Acs. 40.08 in Budvel village, for a total of ₹40,20,000, paid ₹34,80,850 but did not pay the balance within the three months fixed. It sued in 2002 (O.S. No. 88 of 2002). Principle. The 2018 amendment to Section 10 is substantive and prospective; it does not apply to transactions made before it came into force. On the old law, the Court held the suit barred under Article 54 and the purchaser not ready and willing. Civil Appeal No. 5822 of 2022, decided 25 August 2022. The judgment was recalled in review on 8 November 2024 (2024 INSC 861), and the High Court's decree was restored. Why it matters. It is the leading statement on the date of effect of the amended Section 10, read with its 2024 review. Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi (2011) Facts. Under an agreement of 17 January 1981 for 24.95 acres at ₹3,75,000, the buyer paid ₹1,00,000 as advance and was to pay the balance of ₹2,75,000 in three instalments . The agreement said payment on the due dates was of the essence. He paid ₹1,25,000 of the balance and missed the rest. The sellers cancelled on 2 August 1981. Principle. Time for payment was of the essence, and the buyer was not ready and willing. Older cases holding time not of the essence in land sales "may no longer apply" because of steep rises in prices. The buyer got a refund with interest. (2011) 12 SCC 18 : AIR 2011 SC 3234. Why it matters. It links delay, price rise and Section 16(c). K.S. Vidyanadam v. Vairavan (1997) Facts. On 15 December 1978 a buyer agreed to buy a house in Madurai for ₹60,000, to be completed in six months, and paid ₹5,000. He gave notice only on 11 July 1981 and sued on 23 August 1981, after prices had risen. Principle. A suit need not be decreed merely because it is within limitation. "Total inaction" for two and a half years, with a steep rise in prices, made relief inequitable . (1997) 3 SCC 1 : AIR 1997 SC 1751. Why it matters. It shows that a court looks at all circumstances, not only the limitation period. J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao (2010) Facts. The owners of 30 acres 86 cents agreed on 3 February 2006 to sell for ₹5,55,48,000 and received ₹75,00,000. The land was mortgaged to a bank for a sister concern's loan. The buyers deposited ₹2,45,00,000 in a bank and sued. Principle. The buyers proved readiness and willingness. Readiness refers to financial capacity; willingness refers to the conduct of the plaintiff wanting performance. The plaintiff need not tender the money unless the court directs. Civil Appeal Nos. 9821-9822 of 2010, decided 22 November 2010. Why it matters. It explains the two limbs of Section 16(c). N.P. Thirugnanam v. R. Jagan Mohan Rao (1995) Facts. On 9 April 1979 a buyer agreed to buy a house in Madras for ₹2,30,000, paid ₹10,000 and was in possession as a tenant. He did not deposit ₹2,00,000 when the court directed it, and the lender he relied on had no cash. Principle. "Continuous readiness and willingness" is a condition precedent. The amount "must of necessity be proved to be available", judged by the plaintiff's conduct before and after the suit. The courts below rightly found him not ready and willing. (1995) 5 SCC 115 : AIR 1996 SC 116. Why it matters. It is a standard authority for readiness and willingness. K. Narendra v. Riviera Apartments (P) Ltd. (1999) Facts. In 1972 the owner of a bungalow at 6 Tolstoy Marg, New Delhi agreed to sell it to builders, who paid part of the price. The land was later caught by the urban land ceiling law and partly acquired. The builders sued in 1979. Principle. Performance would cause the seller hardship he did not foresee, so specific performance was refused. The buyers got the price paid back with 12% interest, and ₹3,25,000 as compensation under Section 21. Section 18 did not allow enforcement with a variation. (1999) 5 SCC 77 : AIR 1999 SC 2309. Why it matters. It shows compensation under Section 21 where performance is refused. Percept D'Mark (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Zaheer Khan (2006) Facts. A sports agency had a promotion agreement with the cricketer for 30 October 2000 to 29 October 2003. Clause 31(b) gave it a right to match third-party offers, which it said applied after the term. The cricketer signed with another agent, and the agency sought an injunction. Principle. At the interim stage, the Court held that a covenant restricting the cricketer after the term was a restraint of trade , hit by Section 27 of the Contract Act and void. The injunction would in substance be specific performance of a contract of personal service. The agency could be compensated in money. (2006) 4 SCC 227 : AIR 2006 SC 3426. Why it matters. It explains the bar on enforcing personal service contracts, now Section 14(c). Indian Oil Corporation v. Amritsar Gas Service (1991) Facts. Indian Oil terminated an LPG distributorship. The arbitrator ordered the distributorship to be restored. The agreement could be ended by either party on 30 days' notice. Principle. The agreement was revocable and for personal service, so it was determinable in nature and could not be specifically enforced. Restoration was contrary to Section 14(1). The only relief was compensation for the 30-day notice period. (1991) 1 SCC 533. Why it matters. It is the standard authority for determinable contracts, now Section 14(d).

selfTest.q: 2. What must the plaintiff prove under Section 16(c)?
selfTest.a: That he has performed, or has always been ready and willing to perform, the essential terms that are to be performed by him.

selfTest.q: 3. How much notice does Section 20 require before substituted performance?
selfTest.a: Written notice of not less than 30 days.

selfTest.q: 4. A seller owns 9.8 of the 10 acres he agreed to sell. Can the buyer get the 9.8 acres?
selfTest.a: Yes. The shortfall is small and can be compensated in money, so the court may order the sale of 9.8 acres with compensation for the rest (Section 12(2)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a court grant possession if the plaintiff asked only for specific performance?
selfTest.a: No. Section 22(2) requires possession to be specifically claimed, but the court shall allow the plaint to be amended at any stage.

selfTest.q: 6. Within what time must a suit for specific performance be filed?
selfTest.a: Three years from the date fixed for performance, or, if none is fixed, from notice of refusal (Article 54).

legalProvision: Section 9. Defences respecting suits for relief based on contract. Except as otherwise provided herein where any relief is claimed under this Chapter in respect of a contract, the person against whom the relief is claimed may plead by way of defence any ground which is available to him under any law relating to contracts.

Section 10. Specific performance in respect of contracts. The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in sub-section (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.

Section 11. Cases in which specific performance of contracts connected with trusts enforceable. (1) Except as otherwise provided in this Act, specific performance of a contract shall, be enforced when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly of a trust. (2) A contract made by a trustee in excess of his powers or in breach of trust cannot be specifically enforced.
(సెక్షన్ 11(1) లో " contract may, in the discretion of the court" స్థానంలో 1 అక్టోబర్ 2018 నుంచి "contract shall" వచ్చింది.)

Section 14. Contracts not specifically enforceable. The following contracts cannot be specifically enforced, namely:— (a) where a party to the contract has obtained substituted performance of contract in accordance with the provisions of section 20; (b) a contract, the performance of which involves the performance of a continuous duty which the court cannot supervise; (c) a contract which is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; and (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.

Section 16. Personal bars to relief. Specific performance of a contract cannot be enforced in favour of a person— (a) who has obtained substituted performance of contract under section 20; or (b) who has become incapable of performing, or violates any essential term of, the contract that on his part remains to be performed, or acts in fraud of the contract, or wilfully acts at variance with, or in subversion of, the relation intended to be established by the contract; or (c) who fails to prove that he has performed or has always been ready and willing to perform the essential terms of the contract which are to be performed by him, other than terms the performance of which has been prevented or waived by the defendant. Explanation. —For the purposes of clause (c),— (i) where a contract involves the payment of money, it is not essential for the plaintiff to actually tender to the defendant or to deposit in court any money except when so directed by the court; (ii) the plaintiff must prove performance of, or readiness and willingness to perform, the contract according to its true construction.
(2018 లో clause (a) కొత్తగా మార్చబడింది; "who fails to aver and prove" అనేది "who fails to prove" అయింది; Explanation (ii) లో "must aver" అనేది "must prove" అయింది.)

Section 20. Substituted performance of contract. (1) Without prejudice to the generality of the provisions contained in the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (9 of 1872), and, except as otherwise agreed upon by the parties, where the contract is broken due to non-performance of promise by any party, the party who suffers by such breach shall have the option of substituted performance through a third party or by his own agency, and, recover the expenses and other costs actually incurred, spent or suffered by him, from the party committing such breach. (2) No substituted performance of contract under sub-section (1) shall be undertaken unless the party who suffers such breach has given a notice in writing, of not less than thirty days, to the party in breach calling upon him to perform the contract within such time as specified in the notice, and on his refusal or failure to do so, he may get the same performed by a third party or by his own agency: Provided that the party who suffers such breach shall not be entitled to recover the expenses and costs under sub-section (1) unless he has got the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency. (3) Where the party suffering breach of contract has got the contract performed through a third party or by his own agency after giving notice under sub-section (1), he shall not be entitled to claim relief of specific performance against the party in breach. (4) Nothing in this section shall prevent the party who has suffered breach of contract from claiming compensation from the party in breach.
సంబంధిత నిబంధన ( Limitation Act, 1963 , Schedule)
Article 54. For specific performance of a contract. – Three years. – The date fixed for the performance, or, if no such date is fixed, when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.
