selfTest.q: 1. చట్టం నివారణ ఉపశమనాన్ని ఎలా ఇస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: తాత్కాలిక లేదా శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ద్వారా, కోర్టు విచక్షణతో (సెక్షన్ 36).

selfTest.q: 3. నిషేధాజ్ఞ నిరాకరణ, ప్రతికూల ఒప్పందాల గురించి ఏ సెక్షన్లు చెబుతాయి?
selfTest.a: నిరాకరణ గురించి సెక్షన్ 41. ప్రతికూల ఒప్పందం గురించి సెక్షన్ 42.

selfTest.q: 4. శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఎప్పుడు ఇవ్వవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: దావా విచారణలో, merits పై ఇచ్చే డిక్రీ ద్వారా మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 37(2)).

selfTest.q: 5. కేవలం శిక్షా చట్టాన్ని అమలు చేయడానికి నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. వ్యక్తిగత పౌర హక్కులను అమలు చేయడానికి మాత్రమే నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమనం ఇస్తారు (సెక్షన్ 4).

law-of-contract-i-u5-t9.subtitle: Sections 36 to 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: An injunction is a court order that tells a person to stop doing something, or to do something. It prevents a wrong, so it is called preventive relief. The court grants it at its discretion (the court's freedom to decide), not as of right. The Specific Relief Act, 1963 recognises temporary injunctions, which last for a time, and perpetual injunctions, which come with the final decree. A perpetual injunction may also be mandatory. In exams, you must be able to classify injunctions, state the grounds for granting them, and list when they are refused. In real life, injunctions stop a wall from collapsing, waste from being dumped, or a passage from being blocked, before money can only count the loss.
legalProvision: Section 36. Preventive relief how granted. Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual.

Section 37. Temporary and perpetual injunctions. (1) Temporary injunctions are such as are to continue until a specific time, or until the further order of the court, and they may be granted at any stage of a suit, and are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). (2) A perpetual injunction can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit; the defendant is thereby perpetually enjoined from the assertion of a right, or from the commission of an act, which would be contrary to the rights of the plaintiff.

Section 38. Perpetual injunction when granted. (1) Subject to the other provisions contained in or referred to by this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication. (2) When any such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions contained in Chapter II. (3) When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.

Section 39. Mandatory injunctions. When, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts.

Section 40. Damages in lieu of, or in addition to, injunction. (1) The plaintiff in a suit for perpetual injunction under section 38, or mandatory injunction under section 39, may claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction and the court may, if it thinks fit, award such damages. (2) No relief for damages shall be granted under this section unless the plaintiff has claimed such relief in his plaint: Provided that where no such damages have been claimed in the plaint, the court shall, at any stage of the proceedings, allow the plaintiff to amend the plaint on such terms as may be just for including such claim. (3) The dismissal of a suit to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff shall bar his right to sue for damages for such breach.

Section 41. Injunction when refused. An injunction cannot be granted— (a) to restrain any person from prosecuting a judicial proceeding pending at the institution of the suit in which the injunction is sought, unless such restraint is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of proceedings; (b) to restrain any person from instituting or prosecuting any proceeding in a court not sub-ordinate to that from which the injunction is sought; (c) to restrain any person from applying to any legislative body; (d) to restrain any person from instituting or prosecuting any proceeding in a criminal matter; (e) to prevent the breach of a contract the performance of which would not be specifically enforced; (f) to prevent, on the ground of nuisance, an act of which it is not reasonably clear that it will be a nuisance; (g) to prevent a continuing breach in which the plaintiff has acquiesced; (h) when equally efficacious relief can certainly be obtained by any other usual mode of proceeding except in case of breach of trust; (ha) if it would impede or delay the progress or completion of any infrastructure project or interfere with the continued provision of relevant facility related thereto or services being the subject matter of such project. (i) when the conduct of the plaintiff or his agents has been such as to disentitle him to the assistance of the court; (j) when the plaintiff has no personal interest in the matter.

Section 42. Injunction to perform negative agreement. Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (e) of section 41, where a contract comprises an affirmative agreement to do a certain act, coupled with a negative agreement, express or implied, not to do a certain act, the circumstance that the court is unable to compel specific performance of the affirmative agreement shall not preclude it from granting an injunction to perform the negative agreement: Provided that the plaintiff has not failed to perform the contract so far as it is binding on him.
Clause (ha) of Section 41 was inserted by Act 18 of 2018, with effect from 1 October 2018.
In simple words

Section 36: preventive relief is granted at the court's discretion, by injunction , temporary or perpetual. Section 37: temporary injunctions last until a set time or further order, may be granted at any stage, and are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. A perpetual injunction comes only by decree at the hearing, on the merits (the real issues of the case, not procedure). Section 38: a perpetual injunction prevents the breach of an obligation in the plaintiff's favour. For property rights it is given in four cases. Section 39: a mandatory injunction compels (forces) acts that the court can enforce, as well as preventing the breach. Section 40: damages may come with, or instead of, a perpetual or mandatory injunction. Section 41: the cases in which an injunction cannot be granted. Section 42: a negative agreement may be enforced by injunction, even where the affirmative one cannot be specifically enforced.
en.meaning:
An injunction is a court order that stops (restrains) a person from an act, or compels a person to do one. Damages repair a wrong that has happened. An injunction stops a wrong from happening or continuing. It is equitable relief (based on fairness) and acts on the person ordered. Lawyers say equity acts in personam (on the person). Even where the plaintiff proves a right, the court may refuse it if Section 41 or the plaintiff's conduct stands in the way. The question this part of the Act answers. What kinds of injunction can a court grant, on what grounds, and when must it refuse? Why the law has this rule. Some wrongs cannot be undone by money: a collapsed wall, a blocked passage, a secret once leaked. The law lets the court stop them in time, but keeps the remedy discretionary so that it is not used unfairly. Kinds of injunction. The Act gives two kinds by time (temporary and perpetual) and, within perpetual injunctions, an ordinary one that only stops an act and a mandatory one that also compels an act. See Diagram 1 . A perpetual injunction is either an ordinary (prohibitory) injunction under Section 38, which stops an act (the Act does not use the word "prohibitory"), or a mandatory injunction under Section 39, which also compels acts that the court can enforce.
keyPoints: Injunction = preventive relief, granted at the court's discretion (Section 36). Temporary: any stage, until a time or further order (Section 37(1)). Perpetual: only by decree on the merits (Section 37(2)). Three tests for a temporary injunction: prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury. Section 38(3) lists four cases for a perpetual injunction on property rights. Section 39: mandatory injunction. Section 40: damages. Section 41: refusals, with clause (ha) added in 2018. Section 42: negative agreements. Section 20A: no injunction that would impede or delay a Schedule infrastructure project.

caseLaws.name: American Cyanamid v
caseLaws.facts: Ethicon (1975) Facts. American Cyanamid held a patent on absorbable surgical sutures. Ethicon planned to launch a rival suture in the United Kingdom, and Cyanamid sought an interim injunction. Principle. The court need only be satisfied that there is a serious question to be tried. It then weighs the adequacy of damages and the balance of convenience. The House of Lords found the balance in Cyanamid's favour and allowed its appeal. [1975] AC 396 (HL). Why it matters. It is the English interim-injunction test, a useful contrast with the Indian three-fold test. Gujarat Bottling v. Coca Cola (1995) Facts. A bottler agreed (para 14 of its 1993 agreement) not to deal in any other brand during its agreement with Coca Cola. Pepsi-linked concerns bought its shares, and the Bombay High Court granted an interim injunction restraining the use of its Ahmedabad and Rajkot plants for other beverages. Principle. The Supreme Court upheld it and dismissed the appeals. The three tests (prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury) guide an interlocutory injunction. A negative covenant that operates only during the agreement is not a restraint of trade under Section 27. Decided 4 August 1995; (1995) 5 SCC 545 : AIR 1995 SC 2372. Why it matters. It shows temporary injunctions and Section 42 at work. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Buyers of two sites in Matwada, Warangal, under sale deeds of 9 December 1968 from Rukminibai, sued only for a permanent injunction. The defendants claimed title through a sale by Rukminibai's brother. Principle. A bare suit for injunction lies only where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and there is no real cloud on title. Where title is disputed, the plaintiff must sue for declaration as well (paras 11 and 12). The suit was dismissed. (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It tells you when an injunction suit alone is the right remedy. Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh (1992) Facts. In the fourth round of litigation over a Jaipur house that the first appellant claimed to have agreed to buy on 14 June 1979 for ₹51,000, the High Court granted a temporary injunction against dispossession. Principle. A prima facie case is not enough. Refusal must cause irreparable injury, and there must be "no other remedy available to the party except one to grant injunction". The balance of convenience must favour the plaintiff (para 5). The Supreme Court set the injunction aside (para 7). Decided 16 December 1991; (1992) 1 SCC 719 : AIR 1993 SC 276. Why it matters. It is the standard Indian authority for the three tests.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the two kinds of injunction in Section 37?
selfTest.a: Temporary (until a specific time or further order, at any stage) and perpetual (by decree on the merits).

selfTest.q: 2. What three things must a plaintiff show for a temporary injunction?
selfTest.a: A prima facie case, a balance of convenience in his favour, and irreparable injury if the order is refused.

selfTest.q: 3. Which section lists the cases where an injunction cannot be granted?
selfTest.a: Section 41 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

selfTest.q: 5. Can a plaintiff who forgot to claim damages in the plaint still get them under Section 40?
selfTest.a: Yes, if he amends the plaint. The court must allow the amendment at any stage of the proceedings.

సెక్షన్ 36: నివారణ ఉపశమనం కోర్టు విచక్షణతో, తాత్కాలిక లేదా శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ద్వారా ఇస్తారు. సెక్షన్ 37: తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞలు నిర్ణీత సమయం లేదా తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వు వరకు ఉంటాయి, ఏ దశలోనైనా ఇవ్వవచ్చు, సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1908 వాటిని నియంత్రిస్తుంది. శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ విచారణలో, merits పై (విధానం కాకుండా కేసులోని అసలు అంశాలపై) ఇచ్చే డిక్రీ ద్వారా మాత్రమే వస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 38: శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ వాదికి అనుకూలంగా ఉన్న బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపుతుంది. ఆస్తి హక్కులకు నాలుగు సందర్భాల్లో ఇస్తారు. సెక్షన్ 39: తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపడంతో పాటు, కోర్టు అమలు చేయగల పనులను చేయమని బలవంతం చేస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 40: శాశ్వత లేదా తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞతో పాటు, లేదా దానికి బదులుగా నష్టపరిహారం రావచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 41: నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వలేని సందర్భాలు. సెక్షన్ 42: సానుకూల ఒప్పందాన్ని నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయలేకపోయినా, ప్రతికూల ఒప్పందాన్ని నిషేధాజ్ఞ ద్వారా అమలు చేయవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
నిషేధాజ్ఞ అంటే ఒక వ్యక్తిని ఒక పని చేయకుండా ఆపే, లేదా ఒక పని చేయమని బలవంతం చేసే కోర్టు ఉత్తర్వు. నష్టపరిహారం జరిగిన తప్పును సరిచేస్తుంది. నిషేధాజ్ఞ తప్పు జరగకుండా లేదా కొనసాగకుండా ఆపుతుంది. ఇది equity (న్యాయబద్ధత) ఆధారిత ఉపశమనం, ఆదేశం పొందిన వ్యక్తిపై పనిచేస్తుంది. Equity acts in personam (వ్యక్తిపై) అని న్యాయవాదులు అంటారు. వాది హక్కును రుజువు చేసినా, సెక్షన్ 41 గానీ, వాది ప్రవర్తన గానీ అడ్డు వస్తే కోర్టు నిరాకరించవచ్చు. ఈ భాగం జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. కోర్టు ఏ రకాల నిషేధాజ్ఞలు ఇవ్వగలదు, ఏ కారణాలపై, ఎప్పుడు తప్పనిసరిగా నిరాకరించాలి? చట్టంలో ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు. కొన్ని తప్పులను డబ్బుతో సరిచేయలేం: కూలిన గోడ, మూసుకుపోయిన దారి, ఒకసారి బయటపడిన రహస్యం. వాటిని సమయానికి ఆపడానికి చట్టం కోర్టును అనుమతిస్తుంది, కానీ అన్యాయంగా వాడకుండా ఈ పరిష్కారాన్ని విచక్షణాధీనంగా ఉంచుతుంది. నిషేధాజ్ఞల రకాలు. కాలాన్ని బట్టి చట్టం రెండు రకాలు ఇస్తుంది (తాత్కాలికం, శాశ్వతం). శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞల్లో, పనిని ఆపే మాత్రమే సాధారణమైనది, పనిని చేయమని కూడా బలవంతం చేసే తప్పనిసరిది ఉంటాయి. selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 37 లోని రెండు రకాల నిషేధాజ్ఞలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: తాత్కాలికం (నిర్ణీత సమయం లేదా తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వు వరకు, ఏ దశలోనైనా), శాశ్వతం (merits పై డిక్రీ ద్వారా).

selfTest.q: 2. తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞకు వాది ఏ మూడు విషయాలు చూపాలి?
selfTest.a: prima facie case, తనకు అనుకూలమైన సౌలభ్యం సమతుల్యత, ఉత్తర్వు నిరాకరిస్తే సరిచేయలేని హాని.

selfTest.q: 3. నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వలేని సందర్భాలను ఏ సెక్షన్ చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 41.

selfTest.q: 5. plaint లో నష్టపరిహారం కోరడం మర్చిపోయిన వాది సెక్షన్ 40 కింద ఇంకా పొందగలడా?
selfTest.a: అవును, plaint సవరిస్తే. ప్రక్రియలో ఏ దశలోనైనా సవరణకు కోర్టు అనుమతించాలి.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t10.subtitle: Sections 37 and 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 and Order XXXIX of the Code of Civil Procedure

en.inOneMinute: An injunction can come early in a suit or at its end. A temporary injunction protects the plaintiff while the case is going on. A perpetual injunction is the final order that ends the case in the plaintiff's favour. Section 37 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 draws the line. Temporary injunctions are governed by the Code of Civil Procedure. Perpetual injunctions are granted only by a decree on the merits. In exams, the six-point comparison and the three tests are the core. In real life, the temporary order is what stops a wall or a sale today; the perpetual order is what the plaintiff takes home after the trial.
legalProvision: Section 36. Preventive relief how granted. Preventive relief is granted at the discretion of the court by injunction, temporary or perpetual.

Section 37. Temporary and perpetual injunctions. (1) Temporary injunctions are such as are to continue until a specific time, or until the further order of the court, and they may be granted at any stage of a suit, and are regulated by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908). (2) A perpetual injunction can only be granted by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit; the defendant is thereby perpetually enjoined from the assertion of a right, or from the commission of an act, which would be contrary to the rights of the plaintiff.

Section 38. Perpetual injunction when granted. (1) Subject to the other provisions contained in or referred to by this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication. (2) When any such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions contained in Chapter II. (3) When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX (" Temporary Injunctions and Interlocutory Orders") – stated closely, not quoted

Rule 1: where it is proved by affidavit or otherwise that (a) any property in dispute in a suit is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated by any party to the suit; (b) the defendant threatens, or intends, to remove or dispose of his property with a view to defrauding his creditors; or (c) the defendant threatens to dispossess the plaintiff or otherwise cause injury to him in relation to any property in dispute, the court may grant a temporary injunction , until the disposal of the suit or until further orders. Rule 2: in a suit to restrain a breach of contract or other injury, the plaintiff may, at any time after the suit begins and before or after judgment, apply for a temporary injunction to restrain the breach or injury complained of, on such terms as the court thinks fit. Rule 2A: on disobedience or breach of an injunction, the court may order the property of the person guilty to be attached, and may order him to be detained in civil prison for a term not exceeding three months. An attachment cannot remain in force for more than one year; after that, the property may be sold and compensation paid to the injured party. Rule 3: before granting an injunction, the court shall direct notice to the opposite party, except where the object of granting the injunction would be defeated by the delay. If it grants one without notice, it must record its reasons, and the applicant must at once send the other side copies of the application, the affidavit, the plaint and the documents relied on, and file an affidavit that he has done so. Rule 3A: where an injunction is granted without notice, the court shall make an endeavour to finally dispose of the application within thirty days; if it cannot, it must record its reasons. Rule 4: any order for an injunction may be discharged, varied or set aside by the court on the application of a party dissatisfied with it.
In simple words

Section 36: preventive relief is given by injunction, temporary or perpetual, at the court's discretion . Section 37(1): a temporary injunction lasts until a specific time, or until the court's further order. It may be granted at any stage of a suit. The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 regulates it. Section 37(2): a perpetual injunction can be granted only by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits. The defendant is perpetually enjoined (ordered to refrain) from asserting a right, or committing an act, contrary to the plaintiff's rights. Section 38: a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation in the plaintiff's favour, and in four cases of invasion of property rights. Order XXXIX: Rules 1 and 2 give the grounds for a temporary injunction. Rule 2A deals with disobedience. Rule 3 requires notice. Rule 4 allows the order to be discharged, varied or set aside.
en.meaning:
A temporary injunction is an order that holds the position until a set time or further order. It does not decide who is right. A perpetual injunction is the final order granted by the decree. It decides the dispute on the merits and binds the defendant for good. The word "perpetual" refers to the permanence of the decree, not to a different kind of act. The question this topic answers. At what stage of a suit can each kind of injunction be granted, on what basis, and what is its effect? Why the law has two kinds. A trial takes time. If nothing could be done until the decree, the property in dispute might be sold, a wall might be built, or a secret might be leaked. The temporary injunction keeps things as they are until the court can decide. The perpetual injunction then gives the final answer. The two in one suit. The timeline shows how the two fit into the life of one suit. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Read the boxes from top to bottom. Green marks the final order. flowchart TD S1["1. Plaint

Step 2, application: he applies in the suit for a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX, Rules 1 and 2. Step 3, notice and order: the court hears the other side under Rule 3; in urgent cases it may pass an ad interim order without notice, recording reasons. Step 4, temporary injunction: the order lasts until a stated time or further order under Section 37(1). Step 5, decree: after the hearing on the merits, the court may grant a perpetual injunction under Section 37(2).
keyPoints: Temporary: any stage, until a time or further order, Order XXXIX. Perpetual: decree on the merits only. Three tests for a temporary injunction: prima facie case, balance of convenience, irreparable injury. A temporary order does not decide the suit. Section 38(3): four cases of invasion of property rights for a perpetual injunction. A bare suit for a perpetual injunction needs possession and no real cloud on title. Disobedience: Order XXXIX, Rule 2A for a temporary injunction; Order XXI, Rule 32 for a decree.

caseLaws.name: Dalpat Kumar v
caseLaws.facts: Prahlad Singh (1992) Facts. In the fourth round of litigation over a Jaipur house that the first appellant claimed to have agreed to buy on 14 June 1979 for ₹51,000, the Supreme Court considered a temporary injunction against dispossession, which the trial court had refused and the High Court had granted. Decided 16 December 1991; (1992) 1 SCC 719 : AIR 1993 SC 276. Principle. A prima facie case alone is not enough. The court must also find that refusal would cause irreparable injury and that the balance of convenience favours the plaintiff (para 5). The High Court's order was set aside (para 7). Why it matters. It is the standard Indian authority for the three tests. Wander Ltd. v. Antox India (1990) Facts. Wander owned the trade mark "Cal-De-Ce" for calcium tablets that Antox had made for it. In Antox's passing off suit, the single judge of the Madras High Court refused an interim injunction; the Division Bench granted it on appeal. Decided 26 April 1990; 1990 Supp SCC 727. Principle. An appellate court should not interfere with a trial court's discretionary order "except where the discretion has been shown to have been exercised arbitrarily, or capriciously or perversely", or where settled principles were ignored (para 9). The single judge's order was restored. Why it matters. It limits appeals against temporary orders. American Cyanamid v. Ethicon (1975) Facts. A patent holder for absorbable surgical sutures sought an interim injunction to stop a rival from launching a suture in the United Kingdom before trial. Principle. The court asks whether there is a serious question to be tried, then weighs damages and the balance of convenience. [1975] AC 396 (HL). Why it matters. It is the English approach, a contrast with the Indian three tests. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Two sites in Matwada, Warangal, were claimed under two lines of sale from one family: the plaintiffs bought from Rukminibai by deeds of 9 December 1968, and the defendants claimed through her brother. The plaintiffs sued only for a perpetual injunction. Principle. A bare injunction suit lies only where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and there is no real cloud on title. Otherwise a declaration is also needed (paras 11 and 12). (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It marks when a perpetual injunction alone is the right suit.

selfTest.q: 1. When can a perpetual injunction be granted?
selfTest.a: Only by the decree made at the hearing and upon the merits of the suit (Section 37(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. What law regulates temporary injunctions?
selfTest.a: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, mainly Order XXXIX (Section 37(1)).

selfTest.q: 4. What must a court do if it grants a temporary injunction without notice?
selfTest.a: Record its reasons (Order XXXIX, Rule 3), and try to decide the application within 30 days (Rule 3A).

selfTest.q: 5. When will an appellate court interfere with a trial court's temporary order?
selfTest.a: Only where the discretion was exercised arbitrarily, capriciously or perversely, or settled principles were ignored ( Wander v. Antox ).

Rule 1: అఫిడవిట్ ద్వారా గానీ మరో విధంగా గానీ ఇది రుజువైతే: (a) దావాలో వివాదంలో ఉన్న ఏదైనా ఆస్తి దావాలోని ఏ పక్షం వల్లనైనా వృథా, నష్టం లేదా అన్యాక్రాంతం (alienation) అయ్యే ప్రమాదంలో ఉంది; (b) ప్రతివాది తన రుణదాతలను మోసగించే ఉద్దేశంతో తన ఆస్తిని తొలగిస్తానని లేదా అమ్మేస్తానని బెదిరిస్తున్నాడు, లేదా ఉద్దేశిస్తున్నాడు; లేదా (c) ప్రతివాది వాదిని స్వాధీనం నుంచి తొలగిస్తానని, లేదా వివాదంలోని ఆస్తికి సంబంధించి అతనికి హాని చేస్తానని బెదిరిస్తున్నాడు – అప్పుడు కోర్టు, దావా పరిష్కారం అయ్యే వరకు లేదా తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వుల వరకు తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వవచ్చు. Rule 2: కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనను లేదా ఇతర హానిని ఆపే దావాలో, దావా మొదలైన తర్వాత ఏ సమయంలోనైనా, తీర్పుకు ముందు లేదా తర్వాత, ఫిర్యాదు చేసిన ఉల్లంఘన లేదా హానిని ఆపడానికి వాది తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ కోసం దరఖాస్తు చేయవచ్చు; కోర్టు తగిన షరతులపై ఇవ్వవచ్చు. Rule 2A: నిషేధాజ్ఞను ఉల్లంఘిస్తే, తప్పు చేసిన వ్యక్తి ఆస్తిని జప్తు చేయమని కోర్టు ఆదేశించవచ్చు, మూడు నెలలకు మించని కాలం సివిల్ జైలులో నిర్బంధించమని ఆదేశించవచ్చు. జప్తు ఒక సంవత్సరానికి మించి అమలులో ఉండదు; ఆ తర్వాత ఆస్తిని అమ్మి, నష్టపోయిన పక్షానికి పరిహారం చెల్లించవచ్చు. Rule 3: నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇచ్చే ముందు, ఆలస్యం వల్ల నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఉద్దేశం దెబ్బతినే సందర్భంలో తప్ప, కోర్టు ఎదుటి పక్షానికి నోటీసు ఇవ్వాలి. నోటీసు లేకుండా ఇస్తే, కారణాలు నమోదు చేయాలి; దరఖాస్తుదారు వెంటనే దరఖాస్తు, అఫిడవిట్, plaint , ఆధారపడిన పత్రాల ప్రతులను ఎదుటి పక్షానికి పంపి, పంపినట్లు అఫిడవిట్ దాఖలు చేయాలి. Rule 3A: నోటీసు లేకుండా నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇస్తే, ముప్పై రోజుల్లో దరఖాస్తును తుదిగా పరిష్కరించడానికి కోర్టు ప్రయత్నించాలి; చేయలేకపోతే కారణాలు నమోదు చేయాలి. Rule 4: నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఉత్తర్వుతో అసంతృప్తి చెందిన పక్షం దరఖాస్తుపై, కోర్టు దాన్ని రద్దు చేయవచ్చు, మార్చవచ్చు లేదా పక్కన పెట్టవచ్చు.

సెక్షన్ 36: నివారణ ఉపశమనం కోర్టు విచక్షణతో, తాత్కాలిక లేదా శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ద్వారా ఇస్తారు. సెక్షన్ 37(1): తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ నిర్ణీత సమయం వరకు, లేదా కోర్టు తదుపరి ఉత్తర్వు వరకు ఉంటుంది. దావాలో ఏ దశలోనైనా ఇవ్వవచ్చు. సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1908 దాన్ని నియంత్రిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 37(2): శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ విచారణలో, merits పై ఇచ్చే డిక్రీ ద్వారా మాత్రమే ఇవ్వవచ్చు. వాది హక్కులకు వ్యతిరేకంగా హక్కు చెప్పుకోకుండా, లేదా పని చేయకుండా ప్రతివాదిని శాశ్వతంగా ఆపుతుంది (perpetually enjoined ). సెక్షన్ 38: వాదికి అనుకూలమైన బాధ్యత ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపడానికి, ఆస్తి హక్కుల ఆక్రమణలో నాలుగు సందర్భాల్లో శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వవచ్చు. selfTest.q: 1. శాశ్వత నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఎప్పుడు ఇవ్వవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: దావా విచారణలో, merits పై ఇచ్చే డిక్రీ ద్వారా మాత్రమే (సెక్షన్ 37(2)).

selfTest.q: 2. తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞలను ఏ చట్టం నియంత్రిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1908, ముఖ్యంగా Order XXXIX (సెక్షన్ 37(1)).

selfTest.q: 4. నోటీసు లేకుండా తాత్కాలిక నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇస్తే కోర్టు ఏమి చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: కారణాలు నమోదు చేయాలి (Order XXXIX, Rule 3), 30 రోజుల్లో దరఖాస్తును నిర్ణయించడానికి ప్రయత్నించాలి (Rule 3A).

selfTest.q: 5. ట్రయల్ కోర్టు తాత్కాలిక ఉత్తర్వులో అప్పీలు కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు జోక్యం చేసుకుంటుంది?
selfTest.a: విచక్షణను ఏకపక్షంగా, ఇష్టానుసారంగా లేదా వక్రంగా వాడినప్పుడు, లేదా స్థిరపడిన సూత్రాలను పట్టించుకోనప్పుడు మాత్రమే ( Wander v. Antox ).

law-of-contract-i-u5-t11.subtitle: Sections 38 and 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963

en.inOneMinute: A prohibitory injunction tells a person to stop doing something. A mandatory injunction tells him to do something, usually to undo what he has done. The first is the ordinary kind. The second is stronger, and the court grants it with more care. Section 38 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 covers the ordinary perpetual injunction. Section 39 covers the mandatory one. In exams, "Mandatory Injunction" is a short-note question. You must give Section 39, the difference from the prohibitory kind, and the test for interim relief. In real life, a prohibitory order stops a wall going up; a mandatory order makes the builder pull it down.
legalProvision: Section 38. Perpetual injunction when granted. (1) Subject to the other provisions contained in or referred to by this Chapter, a perpetual injunction may be granted to the plaintiff to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in his favour, whether expressly or by implication. (2) When any such obligation arises from contract, the court shall be guided by the rules and provisions contained in Chapter II. (3) When the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff’s right to, or enjoyment of, property, the court may grant a perpetual injunction in the following cases, namely:— (a) where the defendant is trustee of the property for the plaintiff; (b) where there exists no standard for ascertaining the actual damage caused, or likely to be caused, by the invasion; (c) where the invasion is such that compensation in money would not afford adequate relief; (d) where the injunction is necessary to prevent a multiplicity of judicial proceedings.

Section 39. Mandatory injunctions. When, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts.

Section 40. Damages in lieu of, or in addition to, injunction. (1) The plaintiff in a suit for perpetual injunction under section 38, or mandatory injunction under section 39, may claim damages either in addition to, or in substitution for, such injunction and the court may, if it thinks fit, award such damages. (2) No relief for damages shall be granted under this section unless the plaintiff has claimed such relief in his plaint: Provided that where no such damages have been claimed in the plaint, the court shall, at any stage of the proceedings, allow the plaintiff to amend the plaint on such terms as may be just for including such claim. (3) The dismissal of a suit to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in favour of the plaintiff shall bar his right to sue for damages for such breach.
In simple words

Section 38: a perpetual injunction may be granted to prevent the breach of an obligation existing in the plaintiff's favour, and where the defendant invades or threatens to invade the plaintiff's right to property, in the four cases listed. The Act does not use the word "prohibitory". Section 39: where, to prevent the breach of an obligation, it is necessary to compel the performance of certain acts which the court is capable of enforcing, the court may in its discretion grant an injunction to prevent the breach complained of, and also to compel performance of the requisite acts. Section 40: damages may be claimed in addition to, or in place of, an injunction under Section 38 or 39.
en.meaning:
A prohibitory injunction forbids an act. A mandatory injunction compels (forces) an act. Section 39 says the court may both "prevent the breach complained of" and "compel performance of the requisite acts". So a mandatory injunction has two parts: a restraint and a positive order. The question this topic answers. When will the court only say "do not", and when will it go further and say "do" or "undo"? Why the law has both. Stopping a wrong is not enough once the wrong is already in place. A wall already built across a passage keeps blocking it, even if the builder is forbidden to build more. Only an order to remove it gives real relief. But such an order can cost the defendant heavily, so the law asks for more before granting it. How the court decides. The decision tree shows how a court approaches a request for a mandatory injunction. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Go down the boxes in order. A "No" answer sends you to the result beside the box. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Is a positive act, such as removing
a wall, necessary to prevent the breach? s. 39"} Q1 -->|"No"| N1["A prohibitory injunction
under s. 38 is enough"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"2. Is the court capable of
enforcing the act? s. 39"} Q2 -->|"No"| N2["No mandatory
injunction"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"3. Asked only until the end
of the suit (interim)? Order XXXIX"} Q3 -->|"No"| N3["Decided at the hearing;
may be ordered by decree"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4{"4. Strong case, serious or irreparable injury,
balance of convenience? Dorab Cawasji Warden"} Q4 -->|"No"| N4["Interim mandatory
injunction refused"] Q4 -->|"Yes"| Y["Interim mandatory injunction may be granted:
restore the last non-contested status
or undo an act illegally done"] style Y fill:#d9f2d9,stroke:#2e7d32 Text description Question 1: is a positive act, such as removing a wall, necessary to prevent the breach (Section 39)? If no, a prohibitory injunction under Section 38 is enough. Question 2: is the act one that the court is capable of enforcing (Section 39)? If no, the court cannot grant a mandatory injunction. Question 3: is the plaintiff asking for it only until the end of the suit, that is interim relief (Order XXXIX)? If no, the court decides at the hearing and may order it by decree. Question 4: does the plaintiff show a strong case, serious or irreparable injury, and a balance of convenience in his favour (Dorab Cawasji Warden)? If no, the interim mandatory injunction is refused. If all answers are yes, the court may grant an interim mandatory injunction to restore the last non-contested status or to undo an act illegally done.
keyPoints: Prohibitory: "do not" (Section 38). Mandatory: "do" or "undo" (Section 39). Section 39 needs a necessary act that the court is capable of enforcing. Interim mandatory injunction: strong case, serious or irreparable injury, balance of convenience ( Dorab Cawasji Warden ). It is granted to restore the last non-contested status or to undo an illegal act. Damages may be claimed with or instead of the injunction (Section 40).

caseLaws.name: Dorab Cawasji Warden v
caseLaws.facts: Coomi Sorab Warden (1990) Facts. The widow and sons of one brother sold their undivided half of "Dorab Villa", Bandra, to an outsider by a sale deed of 16 April 1987, and he was let into possession. The trial court granted an interim mandatory injunction against his remaining in possession, but a High Court single judge set it aside. Principle. The Supreme Court restored the trial court's order and told the respondents "to undo what they have done". Such an injunction needs a strong case, serious or irreparable injury and balance of convenience. It restores the last non-contested status or undoes an illegal act. Decided 13 February 1990; (1990) 2 SCC 117 : AIR 1990 SC 867. Why it matters. It is the Indian standard for interim mandatory relief. Redland Bricks Ltd. v. Morris (1970) Facts. A brick company's excavation on its own land caused the neighbours' land to slip, and a mandatory injunction was granted below requiring the company to restore support. Principle. A mandatory injunction is discretionary and is granted only on "a very strong probability" that grave danger will accrue to the plaintiff in the future. The order must tell the defendant "exactly in fact what he has to do". The House of Lords discharged the order, which did not do so. [1970] AC 652 (HL). Why it matters. It shows the caution courts use with mandatory orders. Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) Facts. Two sites in Matwada, Warangal, were claimed under two lines of sale from one family: the plaintiffs bought from Rukminibai by deeds of 9 December 1968, and the defendants claimed through her brother. The plaintiffs sued only for a perpetual injunction. Principle. A bare injunction suit lies only where the plaintiff is in lawful possession and there is no real cloud on title (paras 11 and 12). (2008) 4 SCC 594 : AIR 2008 SC 2033. Why it matters. It shows when a prohibitory injunction is the right remedy in a title dispute.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section deals with mandatory injunctions?
selfTest.a: Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963.

selfTest.q: 2. What two conditions does Section 39 set?
selfTest.a: The performance of the acts must be necessary to prevent the breach, and the acts must be ones the court is capable of enforcing.

selfTest.q: 3. What is the standard for an interim mandatory injunction?
selfTest.a: A strong case of a higher standard than prima facie, necessity to prevent serious or irreparable injury, and balance of convenience in the plaintiff's favour.

selfTest.q: 4. Why must a mandatory order be precise?
selfTest.a: So that the defendant knows exactly in fact what he has to do ( Redland Bricks ).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a mandatory injunction be temporary?
selfTest.a: Yes. It may be granted before trial (interim) or by the decree (perpetual, Section 37(2)).

నిషేధాత్మక నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఒక పనిని నిషేధిస్తుంది. తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఒక పనిని బలవంతంగా చేయిస్తుంది. కోర్టు "prevent the breach complained of", "compel performance of the requisite acts" రెండూ చేయవచ్చని సెక్షన్ 39 చెబుతుంది. కాబట్టి తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞకు రెండు భాగాలు: ఒక నిరోధం, ఒక సానుకూల ఆదేశం. ఈ అంశం జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు "చేయవద్దు" అని మాత్రమే చెబుతుంది, ఎప్పుడు ఇంకా ముందుకు వెళ్లి "చేయి" లేదా "రద్దు చేయి" అంటుంది? రెండూ ఎందుకు. తప్పు ఇప్పటికే జరిగి ఉంటే, దాన్ని ఆపితే సరిపోదు. దారికి అడ్డంగా ఇప్పటికే కట్టిన గోడ, బిల్డర్‌ను ఇంకా కట్టవద్దని నిషేధించినా, దారిని అడ్డుకుంటూనే ఉంటుంది. దాన్ని తొలగించమనే ఉత్తర్వే నిజమైన ఉపశమనం ఇస్తుంది. కానీ అలాంటి ఉత్తర్వు ప్రతివాదికి భారీ ఖర్చు కలిగించవచ్చు, కాబట్టి ఇచ్చే ముందు చట్టం ఎక్కువ అడుగుతుంది. కోర్టు ఎలా నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞ అభ్యర్థనను కోర్టు ఎలా పరిశీలిస్తుందో decision tree చూపుతుంది. selfTest.q: 1. తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞల గురించి ఏ సెక్షన్ చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: నిర్దిష్ట ఉపశమన చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 39.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 39 ఏ రెండు షరతులు పెడుతుంది?
selfTest.a: పనులు చేయడం ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపడానికి అవసరం కావాలి, ఆ పనులను కోర్టు అమలు చేయగలగాలి.

selfTest.q: 3. మధ్యంతర తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞకు ప్రమాణం ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: prima facie కంటే ఉన్నత ప్రమాణం గల బలమైన కేసు, తీవ్రమైన లేదా సరిచేయలేని హానిని నివారించాల్సిన అవసరం, వాదికి అనుకూలమైన సౌలభ్యం సమతుల్యత.

selfTest.q: 4. తప్పనిసరి ఉత్తర్వు ఎందుకు ఖచ్చితంగా ఉండాలి?
selfTest.a: ప్రతివాది తాను ఏమి చేయాలో ఖచ్చితంగా తెలుసుకోవడానికి ( Redland Bricks ).

selfTest.q: 5. తప్పనిసరి నిషేధాజ్ఞ తాత్కాలికం కావచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. విచారణకు ముందు (మధ్యంతరం) గానీ, డిక్రీ ద్వారా (శాశ్వతం, సెక్షన్ 37(2)) గానీ ఇవ్వవచ్చు.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t12.subtitle: Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, read with section 41(e) and section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872

en.inOneMinute: Many contracts have two halves. One half says "I will work only for you". The other half, expressed or implied, says "I will not work for anyone else". A court cannot force a person to work. It can stop him from working for a rival. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 allows this. The court may enforce the negative promise by injunction even where it cannot enforce the positive one. In exams, you must explain Section 42, its proviso, and the limit set by Section 27 of the Contract Act. In real life, it is how a company keeps a trained employee from joining a rival in the middle of his contract, or a brand keeps its bottler from bottling a competitor's drink.
legalProvision: Section 42. Injunction to perform negative agreement. Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (e) of section 41, where a contract comprises an affirmative agreement to do a certain act, coupled with a negative agreement, express or implied, not to do a certain act, the circumstance that the court is unable to compel specific performance of the affirmative agreement shall not preclude it from granting an injunction to perform the negative agreement: Provided that the plaintiff has not failed to perform the contract so far as it is binding on him.
Section 41. Injunction when refused. An injunction cannot be granted— (e) to prevent the breach of a contract the performance of which would not be specifically enforced;

Section 14. Contracts not specifically enforceable. The following contracts cannot be specifically enforced, namely:— . . . (c) a contract which is so dependent on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce specific performance of its material terms; and (d) a contract which is in its nature determinable.

Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 27. Agreement in restraint of trade, void. Every agreement by which any one is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind, is to that extent void. Exception 1. —Saving of agreement not to carry on business of which good-will is sold.—One who sells the good-will of a business may agree with the buyer to refrain from carrying on a similar business, within specified local limits, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the good-will from him, carries on a like business therein, provided that such limits appear to the Court reasonable, regard being had to the nature of the business.
In simple words

Section 42: notwithstanding clause (e) of Section 41, a contract may contain an affirmative agreement to do an act, together with a negative agreement, express or implied, not to do an act. The court may be unable to compel specific performance of the affirmative agreement. That does not stop it from granting an injunction to perform the negative agreement. Proviso to Section 42: the plaintiff must not have failed to perform the contract so far as it is binding on him. Section 41(e): an injunction cannot be granted to prevent the breach of a contract whose performance would not be specifically enforced. Section 14(c) and (d): a contract that depends so much on the personal qualifications of the parties that the court cannot enforce its material terms, or that is in its nature determinable (can be ended at will), cannot be specifically enforced. Section 27, Contract Act: every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business is void to that extent ( void : having no legal effect).
en.meaning:
A negative covenant is a formal promise not to do a certain act. An affirmative (positive) agreement is a promise to do one. Section 41(e) says that no injunction lies where the contract itself could not be specifically enforced. Section 42 carves out an exception for the negative half. The question this section answers. If the court cannot make a person keep his positive promise, can it at least hold him to his promise not to do something? Why the law has this rule. Without Section 42, a person who promised to serve one employer only could walk away to a rival mid-contract, and the employer would get only damages . Section 42 lets the court enforce the part it can enforce, without forcing anyone to work. How the court decides. The flowchart shows the questions a court asks. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Start at the top. If an answer ends the claim, stop at the box beside it. Otherwise follow the arrow down to the next box. flowchart TD Q1{"1. Affirmative agreement plus a negative
agreement, express or implied?"} Q1 -->|"No"| N1["Section 42
does not apply"] Q1 -->|"Yes"| Q2{"2. Is the negative covenant lawful?
(operates only during the term;
not hit by s. 27, Contract Act)"} Q2 -->|"No: restrains trade after the term"| N2["Void: no injunction
can enforce it"] Q2 -->|"Yes"| Q3{"3. Has the plaintiff performed the
contract so far as it binds him?"} Q3 -->|"No"| N3["Proviso to s. 42
bars the injunction"] Q3 -->|"Yes"| Q4{"4. Any other bar in s. 41,
such as acquiescence or
the plaintiff's conduct?"} Q4 -->|"Yes"| N4["Court may refuse"] Q4 -->|"No"| Y["Court may grant an injunction to perform
the negative agreement, though it cannot
compel the affirmative one"] style Y fill:#d9f2d9,stroke:#2e7d32 Text description Question 1: does the contract contain an affirmative agreement and a negative agreement, express or implied? If no, Section 42 does not apply. Question 2: is the negative covenant lawful, for example because it operates only during the term and is not a restraint of trade under Section 27 of the Contract Act? If no, because it restrains a trade after the term, it is void and no injunction can enforce it. Question 3: has the plaintiff performed the contract so far as it binds him? If no, the proviso to Section 42 bars the injunction. Question 4: is any other bar in Section 41 present, such as acquiescence or the plaintiff's own conduct? If yes, the court may refuse. If all the tests are met, the court may grant an injunction to perform the negative agreement, even though it cannot compel the affirmative one.
keyPoints: Section 42: a negative agreement, express or implied, may be enforced by injunction even if the affirmative one cannot be. Proviso: the plaintiff must not have failed to perform his own part. A covenant during the term is generally valid. A covenant after the term is void under Section 27. Authorities: Lumley v. Wagner ; Golikari ; Gujarat Bottling ; Krishan Murgai ; Percept D'Mark . The other bars in Section 41 still apply.

caseLaws.name: Niranjan Shankar Golikari v
caseLaws.facts: Century Spinning (1967) Facts. A shift supervisor on a five-year contract, trained in the secret processes for tyre cord yarn, left after about nineteen months for a rival at a higher salary. The trial court restrained him from working as a shift supervisor in tyre cord yarn manufacture for the rest of the five years, and the High Court confirmed it. Principle. A negative covenant that applies only during the term of employment is generally not a restraint of trade under Section 27. The appeal was dismissed and the injunction stood. Decided 17 January 1967; AIR 1967 SC 1098 : [1967] 2 SCR 378. Why it matters. It is the leading authority on a negative covenant during service. Gujarat Bottling v. Coca Cola (1995) Facts. A bottler agreed (para 14 of its 1993 agreement) not to deal in any other brand during its agreement with Coca Cola. Its shares passed to Pepsi-linked concerns, and the Bombay High Court granted an interim injunction. Principle. A covenant that operates only while the contract lasts is not a restraint of trade under Section 27. The Supreme Court upheld the injunction and dismissed the appeals, enforcing the negative covenant. (1995) 5 SCC 545 : AIR 1995 SC 2372. Why it matters. It applies the principle of Section 42 to a commercial franchise. Superintendence Company of India v. Krishan Murgai (1980) Facts. An employer terminated a branch manager and then sought to enforce a two-year post-service restriction against him at his last place of posting. Principle. The Supreme Court refused to enforce it and dismissed the appeal. The majority held that "leave" in the clause did not cover termination. Sen J. alone held that a restraint operating after service is void under Section 27. AIR 1980 SC 1717 : [1980] 3 SCR 1278. Why it matters. It marks the limit of Section 42 for post-service covenants. Percept D'Mark v. Zaheer Khan (2006) Facts. A sports agency had a promotion agreement with a cricketer for 30 October 2000 to 29 October 2003, and claimed under clause 31(b) a right to match third-party offers after the term. Principle. A covenant enforced after the term is "clearly hit by Section 27 of the Contract Act and is void". An injunction would amount to specific performance of a personal service contract, which is barred. (2006) 4 SCC 227 : AIR 2006 SC 3426. Why it matters. It links Sections 14(c), 41(e) and 42.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 42 allow?
selfTest.a: An injunction to perform a negative agreement, even though the court cannot compel specific performance of the affirmative agreement in the same contract.

selfTest.q: 2. What is the condition in the proviso to Section 42?
selfTest.a: The plaintiff must not have failed to perform the contract so far as it is binding on him.

selfTest.q: 3. Why can a covenant after the term usually not be enforced?
selfTest.a: It is a restraint of trade and void under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

selfTest.q: 4. Must the negative promise be written in words?
selfTest.a: No. Section 42 says it may be express or implied.

selfTest.q: 5. Which clause of Section 41 does Section 42 override?
selfTest.a: Only clause (e). The other bars in Section 41 still apply.

సెక్షన్ 42: సెక్షన్ 41 clause (e) ఉన్నప్పటికీ, ఒక కాంట్రాక్టులో ఒక పని చేస్తానని సానుకూల ఒప్పందం, దానితో పాటు స్పష్టమైన లేదా సూచనప్రాయమైన, ఒక పని చేయనని ప్రతికూల ఒప్పందం ఉండవచ్చు. సానుకూల ఒప్పందాన్ని నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయమని కోర్టు బలవంతం చేయలేకపోవచ్చు. అది ప్రతికూల ఒప్పందాన్ని అమలు చేసే నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వకుండా కోర్టును ఆపదు. సెక్షన్ 42 proviso: వాది తనను కట్టుబడి ఉంచేంత వరకు కాంట్రాక్టును పాటించడంలో విఫలం కాకూడదు. సెక్షన్ 41(e): నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయని కాంట్రాక్టు ఉల్లంఘనను ఆపడానికి నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వలేరు. సెక్షన్ 14(c), (d): పక్షాల వ్యక్తిగత అర్హతలపై ఎంతగా ఆధారపడి ఉందంటే దాని ముఖ్యమైన నిబంధనలను కోర్టు అమలు చేయలేని కాంట్రాక్టును, లేదా స్వభావరీత్యా ముగించదగిన (ఇష్టానుసారం ముగించగల) కాంట్రాక్టును నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయలేరు. సెక్షన్ 27, కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం: ఎవరినైనా చట్టబద్ధమైన వృత్తి, వ్యాపారం చేయకుండా నిరోధించే ప్రతి ఒప్పందం ఆ మేరకు చెల్లనిది (void: చట్టపరమైన ప్రభావం లేనిది).

ప్రతికూల నిబంధన (negative covenant ) అంటే ఒక పని చేయనని ఇచ్చే అధికారిక వాగ్దానం. సానుకూల (affirmative) ఒప్పందం అంటే ఒక పని చేస్తానని వాగ్దానం. కాంట్రాక్టునే నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయలేని చోట నిషేధాజ్ఞ రాదని సెక్షన్ 41(e) చెబుతుంది. ప్రతికూల భాగానికి సెక్షన్ 42 మినహాయింపు ఇస్తుంది. ఈ సెక్షన్ జవాబు చెప్పే ప్రశ్న. ఒక వ్యక్తి తన సానుకూల వాగ్దానాన్ని నిలబెట్టుకునేలా కోర్టు చేయలేకపోతే, కనీసం ఏదైనా చేయనన్న అతని వాగ్దానానికి అతన్ని కట్టుబడి ఉంచగలదా? చట్టంలో ఈ నియమం ఎందుకు. సెక్షన్ 42 లేకపోతే, ఒక యజమాని కోసమే పని చేస్తానని వాగ్దానం చేసిన వ్యక్తి కాంట్రాక్టు మధ్యలో ప్రత్యర్థి దగ్గరకు వెళ్లిపోవచ్చు, యజమానికి నష్టపరిహారం మాత్రమే దక్కుతుంది. ఎవరినీ పని చేయమని బలవంతం చేయకుండా, తాను అమలు చేయగల భాగాన్ని అమలు చేయడానికి సెక్షన్ 42 కోర్టును అనుమతిస్తుంది. కోర్టు ఎలా నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. కోర్టు అడిగే ప్రశ్నలను flowchart చూపుతుంది. selfTest.q: 1. సెక్షన్ 42 దేన్ని అనుమతిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: అదే కాంట్రాక్టులోని సానుకూల ఒప్పందాన్ని నిర్దిష్టంగా అమలు చేయమని కోర్టు బలవంతం చేయలేకపోయినా, ప్రతికూల ఒప్పందాన్ని అమలు చేసే నిషేధాజ్ఞను.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 42 proviso లోని షరతు ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: వాది తనను కట్టుబడి ఉంచేంత వరకు కాంట్రాక్టును పాటించడంలో విఫలం కాకూడదు.

selfTest.q: 3. కాలం తర్వాతి నిబంధనను సాధారణంగా ఎందుకు అమలు చేయలేరు?
selfTest.a: అది వ్యాపార నిరోధం, భారత కాంట్రాక్టు చట్టం, 1872 సెక్షన్ 27 కింద చెల్లనిది.

selfTest.q: 4. ప్రతికూల వాగ్దానం మాటల్లో రాసి ఉండాలా?
selfTest.a: అవసరం లేదు. అది స్పష్టంగా లేదా సూచనప్రాయంగా ఉండవచ్చని సెక్షన్ 42 చెబుతుంది.

selfTest.q: 5. సెక్షన్ 42 సెక్షన్ 41 లోని ఏ clause ను అధిగమిస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: clause (e) ను మాత్రమే. సెక్షన్ 41 లోని ఇతర అడ్డంకులు ఇంకా వర్తిస్తాయి.

law-of-contract-i-u5-t13.subtitle: Sections 20A, 20B, 20C and 41(ha) of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, and the Schedule

en.inOneMinute: A single injunction can stall a road, a power plant or a metro line for years, over a private dispute between a contractor and a public body. The Specific Relief (Amendment) Act, 2018 (Act 18 of 2018), in force from 1 October 2018, built a small code to prevent this. It bars injunctions that would delay an infrastructure project, creates Special Courts, and sets a time limit for suits. The code is in Sections 20A, 20B, 20C and 41(ha), with a Schedule that lists the projects covered. In exams, you must state each section, name the five categories in the Schedule and explain why the bar is limited to injunctions.
legalProvision: Section 20A. Special provisions for contract relating to infrastructure project. (1) No injunction shall be granted by a court in a suit under this Act involving a contract relating to an infrastructure project specified in the Schedule, where granting injunction would cause impediment or delay in the progress or completion of such infrastructure project. Explanation. —For the purposes of this section, section 20B and clause (ha) of section 41, the expression “infrastructure project” means the category of projects and infrastructure Sub-Sectors specified in the Schedule. (2) The Central Government may, depending upon the requirement for development of infrastructure projects, and if it considers necessary or expedient to do so, by notification in the Official Gazette, amend the Schedule relating to any Category of projects or Infrastructure Sub-Sectors. (3) Every notification issued under this Act by the Central Government shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is issued, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session, for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the notification or both Houses agree that the notification should not be made, the notification shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; so, however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that notification.

Section 20B. Special Courts. The State Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, shall designate, by notification published in the Official Gazette, one or more Civil Courts as Special Courts, within the local limits of the area to exercise jurisdiction and to try a suit under this Act in respect of contracts relating to infrastructure projects.

Section 20C. Expeditious disposal of suits. Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), a suit filed under the provisions of this Act shall be disposed of by the court within a period of twelve months from the date of service of summons to the defendant: Provided that the said period may be extended for a further period not exceeding six months in aggregate after recording reasons in writing for such extension by the court.

Section 41. Injunction when refused. An injunction cannot be granted— . . . (ha) if it would impede or delay the progress or completion of any infrastructure project or interfere with the continued provision of relevant facility related thereto or services being the subject matter of such project.

The Schedule [See sections 20A and 41 (ha)] Category of projects and Infrastructure Sub-Sectors Sl. No. Category Infrastructure Sub-Sectors Transport (a) Road and bridges (b) Ports (including Capital Dredging) (c) Shipyards (including a floating or land-based facility with the essential features of waterfront, turning basin, berthing and docking facility, slipways or ship lifts, and which is self-sufficient for carrying on shipbuilding/repair/breaking activities) (d) Inland Waterways (e) Airports (f) Railway Track, tunnels, viaducts, bridges, terminal infrastructure including stations and adjoining commercial infrastructure (g) Urban Public Transport (except rolling stock in case of urban road transport) Energy (a) Electricity Generation (b) Electricity Transmission (c) Electricity Distribution (d) Oil pipelines (e) Oil/Gas/Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) storage facility(including strategic storage of crude oil) (f) Gas pipelines (including city gas distribution network) Water and Sanitation (a) Solid Waste Management (b) Water supply pipelines (c) Water treatment plants (d) Sewage collection, treatment and disposal system (e) Irrigation (dams, channels, embankments, etc.) (f) Storm Water Drainage System (g) Slurry pipelines Communication (a) Telecommunication (Fixed network including optic fibre/wire/cable networks which provide broadband/internet) (b) Telecommunication towers (c) Telecommunications and Telecom Services Social and Commercial Infrastructure (a) Education Institutions (capital stock) (b) Sports infrastructure (including provision of Sports Stadia and Infrastructure for Academies for Training/Research in Sports and Sports-relating activities) (c) Hospitals (capital stock including Medical Colleges, Para Medical Training Institutes and Diagnostic Centres) (d) Tourism infrastructure viz. (i) three-star or higher category classified hotels located outside cities with population of more than one million; (ii) ropeways and cable cars (e) Common infrastructure for industrial parks and other parks with industrial activity such as food parks, textile parks, Special Economic Zones, tourism facilities and agriculture markets (f) Post-harvest storage infrastructure for agriculture and horticulture produce including cold storage (g) Terminal markets (h) Soil-testing laboratories (i) Cold chain (including cold room facility for farm level pre-cooling, for preservation or storage of agriculture and allied produce, marine products and meat) (j) Affordable Housing (including a housing project using at least 50% of the Floor Area Ratio (FAR)/Floor Space Index (FSI) for dwelling units with carpet area of not more than 60 square meters Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-clause, the term “carpet area” shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in clause (k) of section 2 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (16 of 2016).
In simple words

Section 20A(1): no court shall grant an injunction in a suit under the Act involving a contract relating to an infrastructure project specified in the Schedule, where the injunction would cause impediment (obstacle) or delay in the progress or completion of the project. Explanation to Section 20A: for Sections 20A, 20B and 41(ha), "infrastructure project" means the category of projects and infrastructure sub-sectors specified in the Schedule. Section 20A(2): the Central Government may amend the Schedule by notification (official announcement) in the Official Gazette, depending on the needs of infrastructure development, if it considers it necessary or expedient (useful and suitable). Section 20A(3): every such notification is laid before each House of Parliament for a total of 30 days. If both Houses agree to modify it, it has effect only as modified. If both Houses agree it should not be made, it has no effect. Anything already done under it stays valid. Section 20B: the State Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, designates by notification one or more Civil Courts as Special Courts, within local limits, to try suits under the Act about contracts relating to infrastructure projects. Section 20C: notwithstanding the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, a suit filed under the Act shall be disposed of within 12 months from the date of service of summons on the defendant. The court may extend this by not more than six months in aggregate, after recording reasons in writing. The section speaks of "a suit filed under the provisions of this Act", so it is not limited to infrastructure suits. Section 41(ha): an injunction cannot be granted if it would impede or delay the progress or completion of any infrastructure project, or interfere with the continued provision of the related facility or services that are the subject matter of the project. The Schedule: five categories of projects (Transport; Energy; Water and Sanitation; Communication; Social and Commercial Infrastructure), each with listed sub-sectors.
en.meaning:
An infrastructure project, for this purpose, is a project listed in the Schedule. The Act does not use the ordinary meaning of the word. If a project is not in the Schedule, Sections 20A, 20B and 41(ha) do not apply to it. The Schedule has five categories, and each has sub-sectors. The tree shows the categories. See Diagram 1 . Transport: roads and bridges, ports, shipyards, inland waterways, airports, railways, urban public transport. 2. Energy: electricity generation, transmission and distribution; oil and gas pipelines; storage facilities. 3. Water and sanitation: solid waste management, water supply and treatment, sewage, irrigation, storm water drainage, slurry pipelines. 4. Communication: telecommunication networks, towers and services. 5. Social and commercial infrastructure: education institutions, sports infrastructure, hospitals, tourism infrastructure, industrial parks, cold storage and cold chain, terminal markets, soil-testing laboratories, affordable housing. The question these sections answer. When a dispute arises under a contract for a public project, can a court freeze the project by injunction while the dispute is decided? Why the law has this rule. The public needs the road, the power line or the water plant. The parties' quarrel is usually about money. The 2018 scheme lets the money dispute go on, by suit, damages or arbitration, while the project keeps moving.
keyPoints: Section 20A: no injunction that would impede or delay a Schedule infrastructure project. Schedule: five categories. The Central Government may amend it; Parliament supervises. Section 41(ha): the same bar in the list of refusals, plus protection of the facility or services. Section 20B: Special Courts. Section 20C: 12 months from service of summons, extendable by up to six months in aggregate. Only injunctions are barred. Damages, arbitration and other claims remain.

caseLaws.name: Roadway Solutions India Infra Ltd
caseLaws.facts: v. National Highways Authority of India (2023) Facts. The contractor had a ₹409.77 crore contract, signed on 19 July 2022, for six-laning part of NH-48 (Gurgaon-Kotputli-Jaipur), to be completed in 18 months. NHAI issued a termination notice under clause 63.1. The Court noted "a meagre physical progress of 3.08% in the last 8 months" (para 77). The contractor sought interim relief from the Delhi High Court under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Principle. Sections 20A and 41(ha) "squarely apply", and courts should "interfere to the minimum extent so that public work projects are not impeded or stalled" (para 76). The petition was "dismissed along with the pending applications" (para 83). Delhi High Court, Chandra Dhari Singh J., 24 May 2023; 2023:DHC:3610. Why it matters. It applies the bar to a highway dispute, even in a petition under the Arbitration Act. Energy Watchdog v. CERC (2017) Facts. Power generators won bids to supply electricity at fixed tariffs, using coal imported from Indonesia. A change in Indonesian law raised the price of that coal, and they sought relief for force majeure and change in law . Principle. "An unexpected rise in the price of coal will not absolve the generating companies from performing their part of the contract" (para 40). It was neither frustration nor force majeure . (2017) 14 SCC 80 (Supreme Court, 11 April 2017). The case came before the 2018 Amendment and did not concern Section 20A. Why it matters. Electricity generation is in the Energy category of the Schedule. The case shows the kind of dispute over an infrastructure contract that the 2018 scheme is meant to keep from stopping the project. Nabha Power v. PSPCL (2017) Facts. Under a "25 year Power Purchase Agreement ", the buyer, Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd., refused washing related costs of coal and road transportation costs in the generator's bills. Principle. The Supreme Court decided the dispute by reading the terms of the agreement. On implied terms , it quoted the test that "A term can only be implied if it is necessary in the business sense to give efficacy to the contract" (para 38). Relief was granted for part of the amount, including the washing cost of coal and transportation from the mine. Civil Appeal No. 179 of 2017, decided 5 October 2017; (2018) 11 SCC 508. This case also came before the 2018 Amendment and did not concern Section 20A. Why it matters. It shows how a major power contract dispute is settled on the contract's terms while the project continues.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 20A(1) bar?
selfTest.a: An injunction in a suit under the Act involving a contract relating to an infrastructure project in the Schedule, where it would cause impediment or delay in the progress or completion of the project.

selfTest.q: 2. What is the time limit in Section 20C?
selfTest.a: 12 months from the date of service of summons on the defendant, extendable by up to six months in aggregate, with reasons recorded in writing.

selfTest.q: 3. Who designates the Special Courts under Section 20B?
selfTest.a: The State Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court.

selfTest.q: 5. What does Section 41(ha) add to Section 20A?
selfTest.a: It also bars an injunction that would interfere with the continued provision of the facility or services that are the subject matter of the project.

legalProvision: Section 20A. Special provisions for contract relating to infrastructure project. (1) No injunction shall be granted by a court in a suit under this Act involving a contract relating to an infrastructure project specified in the Schedule, where granting injunction would cause impediment or delay in the progress or completion of such infrastructure project. Explanation. —For the purposes of this section, section 20B and clause (ha) of section 41, the expression “infrastructure project” means the category of projects and infrastructure Sub-Sectors specified in the Schedule. (2) The Central Government may, depending upon the requirement for development of infrastructure projects, and if it considers necessary or expedient to do so, by notification in the Official Gazette, amend the Schedule relating to any Category of projects or Infrastructure Sub-Sectors. (3) Every notification issued under this Act by the Central Government shall be laid, as soon as may be after it is issued, before each House of Parliament, while it is in session, for a total period of thirty days which may be comprised in one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the notification or both Houses agree that the notification should not be made, the notification shall thereafter have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; so, however, that any such modification or annulment shall be without prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that notification.

Section 20B. Special Courts. The State Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, shall designate, by notification published in the Official Gazette, one or more Civil Courts as Special Courts, within the local limits of the area to exercise jurisdiction and to try a suit under this Act in respect of contracts relating to infrastructure projects.

Section 20C. Expeditious disposal of suits. Notwithstanding anything contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908), a suit filed under the provisions of this Act shall be disposed of by the court within a period of twelve months from the date of service of summons to the defendant: Provided that the said period may be extended for a further period not exceeding six months in aggregate after recording reasons in writing for such extension by the court.

Section 41. Injunction when refused. An injunction cannot be granted— . . . (ha) if it would impede or delay the progress or completion of any infrastructure project or interfere with the continued provision of relevant facility related thereto or services being the subject matter of such project.

సెక్షన్ 20A(1): షెడ్యూల్‌లో పేర్కొన్న మౌలిక సదుపాయాల ప్రాజెక్టుకు సంబంధించిన కాంట్రాక్టుతో కూడిన, ఈ చట్టం కింది దావాలో, నిషేధాజ్ఞ ప్రాజెక్టు పురోగతికి లేదా పూర్తికి అడ్డంకి (impediment) లేదా ఆలస్యం కలిగిస్తే, ఏ కోర్టూ ఆ నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వకూడదు. సెక్షన్ 20A వివరణ (Explanation): సెక్షన్లు 20A, 20B, 41(ha) కోసం, "మౌలిక సదుపాయాల ప్రాజెక్టు" అంటే షెడ్యూల్‌లో పేర్కొన్న ప్రాజెక్టుల వర్గం, మౌలిక సదుపాయాల ఉప-రంగాలు. సెక్షన్ 20A(2): మౌలిక సదుపాయాల అభివృద్ధి అవసరాలను బట్టి, అవసరం లేదా తగినది (expedient) అని భావిస్తే, కేంద్ర ప్రభుత్వం Official Gazette లో నోటిఫికేషన్ (అధికారిక ప్రకటన) ద్వారా షెడ్యూల్‌ను సవరించవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ 20A(3): ప్రతి అలాంటి నోటిఫికేషన్‌ను పార్లమెంటులోని ప్రతి సభ ముందు మొత్తం 30 రోజులు ఉంచాలి. రెండు సభలూ దాన్ని మార్చడానికి అంగీకరిస్తే, మార్చిన రూపంలోనే అది అమలవుతుంది. అది చేయకూడదని రెండు సభలూ అంగీకరిస్తే, దానికి ప్రభావం ఉండదు. దాని కింద ఇప్పటికే చేసినది చెల్లుబాటులోనే ఉంటుంది. సెక్షన్ 20B: హైకోర్టు ప్రధాన న్యాయమూర్తితో సంప్రదించి, రాష్ట్ర ప్రభుత్వం నోటిఫికేషన్ ద్వారా ఒకటి లేదా అంతకంటే ఎక్కువ సివిల్ కోర్టులను, స్థానిక పరిధిలో, ప్రత్యేక కోర్టులుగా నియమిస్తుంది. మౌలిక సదుపాయాల ప్రాజెక్టుల కాంట్రాక్టుల గురించి ఈ చట్టం కింది దావాలను అవి విచారిస్తాయి. సెక్షన్ 20C: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 లో ఏమి ఉన్నప్పటికీ, ఈ చట్టం కింద వేసిన దావాను, ప్రతివాదికి సమన్లు అందిన తేదీ నుంచి 12 నెలల్లో పరిష్కరించాలి. కారణాలను లిఖితంగా నమోదు చేసి, కోర్టు మొత్తం మీద ఆరు నెలలకు మించకుండా పొడిగించవచ్చు. సెక్షన్ "a suit filed under the provisions of this Act" అంటుంది, కాబట్టి ఇది మౌలిక సదుపాయాల దావాలకు మాత్రమే పరిమితం కాదు. సెక్షన్ 41(ha): ఏదైనా మౌలిక సదుపాయాల ప్రాజెక్టు పురోగతిని లేదా పూర్తిని అడ్డుకుంటే లేదా ఆలస్యం చేస్తే, లేదా ఆ ప్రాజెక్టు విషయమైన సదుపాయం లేదా సేవల నిరంతర అందింపులో జోక్యం చేసుకుంటే, నిషేధాజ్ఞ ఇవ్వకూడదు. షెడ్యూల్: ప్రాజెక్టుల ఐదు వర్గాలు (రవాణా; ఇంధనం; నీరు, పారిశుధ్యం; కమ్యూనికేషన్; సామాజిక, వాణిజ్య మౌలిక సదుపాయాలు), ప్రతి దానికీ ఉప-రంగాల జాబితా.
