keyPoints: Section 13(1): adultery, cruelty, desertion (two years), conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation, presumed death. Section 13(1A): one year without cohabitation or restitution after the earlier decree; either party. Section 13(2): four grounds for a wife. Section 13B: one year apart, two motions, six to eighteen months; waivable; consent must continue. Section 14: one-year bar. Section 23: bars and reconciliation. Irretrievable breakdown: only the Supreme Court, under Article 142. Special Marriage Act, 1954: divorce in Sections 27 and 28; no conversion or renunciation ground, but imprisonment for seven years.

caseLaws.name: Dastane v
caseLaws.facts: Dastane (1975) Facts. Dr. Dastane, married in 1956, sought annulment , divorce or judicial separation. Only judicial separation for cruelty under the old Section 10(1)(b) reached the Supreme Court. Principle. Cruelty is proved on a preponderance of probabilities; danger to life, limb or health is not needed; trivialities are ignored. The wife was cruel, but the husband condoned it and it was not revived. (1975) 2 SCC 326 : AIR 1975 SC 1534. Why it matters. It fixes the standard of proof and the test for cruelty, and shows how condonation bars relief. Savitri Pandey v. Prem Chandra Pandey (2002) Facts. The parties, married on 6 May 1987, lived together only till 21 June 1987. The wife sought divorce for cruelty and desertion. Principle. Neither was proved; desertion needs separation and animus deserendi , and there is no desertion without previous cohabitation; a spouse cannot take advantage of his or her own wrong. Appeals dismissed. (2002) 2 SCC 73 : AIR 2002 SC 591. Why it matters. It states the elements of cruelty and desertion. Shilpa Sailesh (2023) read it down on the Supreme Court's power under Article 142. Sureshta Devi v. Om Prakash (1991) Facts. Married in 1968, the spouses filed a Section 13B petition at Hamirpur on 8 January 1985. On 15 January 1985 the wife applied to withdraw, saying her statement was obtained under pressure. The High Court granted divorce. Principle. Mutual consent must continue till the decree; either party may withdraw it before then. Appeal allowed and the decree set aside. (1991) 2 SCC 25 : AIR 1992 SC 1904. Why it matters. It is the leading case on withdrawal of consent and the meaning of "living separately". Amardeep Singh v. Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. The parties married in 1994 and lived apart from 2008. They settled all disputes, including alimony of ₹2.75 crore and custody, and asked to waive the six months. Principle. The six-month period in Section 13B(2) is directory; the court may waive it on four conditions. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It makes the waiting period flexible where the marriage is clearly over and everything is settled. Saroj Rani v. Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. The wife got a consent decree for restitution on 28 March 1978. With no cohabitation for over a year, the husband petitioned for divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii) on 19 April 1979. Principle. Divorce was granted; the consent decree was not collusive and the husband was not taking advantage of his own wrong. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It shows how a failed restitution decree leads to divorce. Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023) Facts. A transfer petition in which the Supreme Court referred questions on its power under Article 142 in matrimonial cases to a Constitution Bench, decided on 1 May 2023. Principle. The Supreme Court may dissolve a marriage on irretrievable breakdown, and may waive the Section 13B procedure on a settlement, but only with great care and caution. [2023] 5 SCR 165. Why it matters. It settles that irretrievable breakdown is a ground only before the Supreme Court, not before trial courts.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the period of desertion required?
selfTest.a: A continuous period of at least two years immediately before the petition.

selfTest.q: 2. Is the six-month period in Section 13B mandatory?
selfTest.a: No. It is directory ( Amardeep Singh ).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a spouse withdraw consent before the decree?
selfTest.a: Yes ( Sureshta Devi ).

selfTest.q: 4. Which section of the Special Marriage Act, 1954 provides divorce by mutual consent?
selfTest.a: Section 28.

selfTest.q: 5. Can the spouse against whom a restitution decree was passed seek divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii)?
selfTest.a: Yes. Either party may petition ( Saroj Rani ).

selfTest.q: 6. Can a Family Court grant divorce on irretrievable breakdown of marriage?
selfTest.a: No. It is not a ground in the Act; only the Supreme Court can do so under Article 142 ( Shilpa Sailesh ).

selfTest.q: 1. పరిత్యాగానికి ఎంత కాలం అవసరం?
selfTest.a: పిటిషన్‌కు వెంటనే ముందు కనీసం రెండేళ్లు నిరంతరంగా.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 13B లో ఆరు నెలల గడువు తప్పనిసరా?
selfTest.a: కాదు. అది నిర్దేశాత్మకం ( Amardeep Singh ).

selfTest.q: 3. డిక్రీకి ముందు జీవిత భాగస్వామి సమ్మతి ఉపసంహరించుకోవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును ( Sureshta Devi ).

selfTest.q: 4. ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం, 1954 లో పరస్పర సమ్మతితో విడాకులు ఏ సెక్షన్‌లో ఉన్నాయి?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 28.

selfTest.q: 5. ఎవరికి వ్యతిరేకంగా పునరుద్ధరణ డిక్రీ వచ్చిందో ఆ జీవిత భాగస్వామి సెక్షన్ 13(1A)(ii) కింద విడాకులు కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. ఏ పక్షమైనా పిటిషన్ వేయవచ్చు ( Saroj Rani ).

selfTest.q: 6. తిరిగి బాగుచేయలేని వివాహ విచ్ఛిన్నంపై కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానం విడాకులు ఇవ్వగలదా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అది చట్టంలో ఆధారం కాదు; ఆర్టికల్ 142 కింద సుప్రీంకోర్టు మాత్రమే ఇవ్వగలదు ( Shilpa Sailesh ).

family-law-i-u3-t6.subtitle: Section 24: interim maintenance and expenses, with a comparison to permanent alimony under section 25

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Maintenance pendente lite is interim support that the court orders while a matrimonial case is pending, together with the expenses of the case (Section 24). Who may claim. Either the wife or the husband, in any proceeding under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA). The test. The applicant has no independent income sufficient for his or her support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding. Speed. The application is to be decided, as far as possible, within sixty days of service of notice ( proviso to Section 24). After the case. The order ends with the proceeding. At or after the decree, the court may grant permanent alimony under Section 25.
legalProvision: Section 24, Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Maintenance pendente lite and expenses of proceedings. Where in any proceeding under this Act it appears to the court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding, and monthly during the proceeding such sum as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, it may seem to the court to be reasonable: Provided that the application for the payment of the expenses of the proceeding and such monthly sum during the proceeding, shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within sixty days from the date of service of notice on the wife or the husband, as the case may be.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Section 25: permanent alimony and maintenance at or after the decree. HMA Section 26: custody, maintenance and education of minor children, with a sixty-day target for interim maintenance and education. HMA Sections 21B, 28 and 28A: speedy trial, appeals and enforcement. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA), Sections 36, 37 and 38. Family Courts Act, 1984, Sections 7 and 9. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), Section 144 (earlier Section 125, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA), Sections 18(1) and 23(2). Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA), Sections 12, 20, 23 and 26.
en.meaning:
Maintenance pendente lite means maintenance while the suit is pending (" pendente lite " means "while the litigation is pending"). It lets a spouse with no means live during the case and carry on the case on fair terms. The order is temporary. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. A proceeding under the Act, an application by the wife or the husband, and no sufficient independent income lead to an order for expenses and a monthly sum, decided within sixty days as far as possible. flowchart TD A{"Proceeding under the
Hindu Marriage Act pending?"} A -->|"No"| N["Section 24 does not apply"] A -->|"Yes"| B["Application by
wife or husband"] B --> C{"Independent income sufficient
for support and expenses?"} C -->|"Yes"| F["Application fails"] C -->|"No"| O["Order: expenses of proceeding
+ reasonable monthly sum
(both incomes considered)"] O --> T["Decided within 60 days
of notice, as far as possible"] T --> E["Lasts until the
proceeding ends"] Text description First ask whether a proceeding under the Hindu Marriage Act is pending; if not, Section 24 does not apply. Then ask whether the wife or the husband has applied. Then ask whether the applicant has independent income sufficient for support and the expenses of the proceeding; if yes, the application fails. If no, the court orders the other spouse to pay the expenses of the proceeding and a reasonable monthly sum, having regard to both incomes, deciding as far as possible within sixty days of notice. The order lasts until the proceeding ends. Element What Section 24 says Proceeding Any proceeding under the Act Applicant The wife or the husband Condition No independent income sufficient for support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding What is ordered Expenses of the proceeding, and a monthly sum during the proceeding Measure Reasonable, having regard to the applicant's own income and the other spouse's income Time As far as possible, within sixty days of service of notice
keyPoints: Section 24: interim maintenance and expenses during any proceeding under the Act. Wife or husband may claim; the test is no independent income sufficient. Disposal within sixty days of notice, as far as possible. Section 25: permanent alimony at or after the decree, variable under Section 25(2) and (3). BNSS Section 144 also allows interim maintenance, within sixty days as far as possible. Special Marriage Act, 1954: interim maintenance (Section 36) and permanent alimony (Section 37) are for the wife only. Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Section 20: monetary relief, including maintenance, from a Magistrate.

caseLaws.name: Saroj Rani v
caseLaws.facts: Sudarshan Kumar Chadha (1984) Facts. In the wife's restitution case the Sub-Judge on 21 March 1978 granted ₹185 a month as maintenance pendente lite and ₹300 as litigation expenses; a consent decree followed on 28 March 1978. The husband later got divorce under Section 13(1A)(ii). Principle. The Supreme Court directed that maintenance continue after the divorce: ₹200 a month to the wife until she remarries and ₹300 a month to the daughter until her marriage. (1984) 4 SCC 90 : AIR 1984 SC 1562. Why it matters. It shows interim maintenance and expenses during a case, and continuing maintenance at the decree stage.

selfTest.q: 1. Can a husband claim maintenance pendente lite?
selfTest.a: Yes. The section says wife or husband.

selfTest.q: 2. What is the target time to decide a Section 24 application?
selfTest.a: Sixty days from service of notice, as far as possible.

selfTest.q: 3. Which section gives permanent alimony?
selfTest.a: Section 25.

selfTest.q: 4. Who may claim alimony pendente lite under Section 36 of the Special Marriage Act, 1954?
selfTest.a: The wife only.

selfTest.q: 5. Under which section is interim maintenance for minor children ordered?
selfTest.a: Section 26.

selfTest.q: 6. Does a Section 24 order continue after the decree?
selfTest.a: No. It runs during the proceeding; after the decree, Section 25 applies.

Where in any proceeding under this Act it appears to the court that either the wife or the husband, as the case may be, has no independent income sufficient for her or his support and the necessary expenses of the proceeding, it may, on the application of the wife or the husband, order the respondent to pay to the petitioner the expenses of the proceeding, and monthly during the proceeding such sum as, having regard to the petitioner's own income and the income of the respondent, it may seem to the court to be reasonable: Provided that the application for the payment of the expenses of the proceeding and such monthly sum during the proceeding, shall, as far as possible, be disposed of within sixty days from the date of service of notice on the wife or the husband, as the case may be.
ఈ నోట్‌లో వాడిన ఇతర నిబంధనలు:

HMA సెక్షన్ 25: డిక్రీ సమయంలో లేదా తర్వాత శాశ్వత భరణం, పోషణ. HMA సెక్షన్ 26: మైనర్ పిల్లల సంరక్షణ, పోషణ, చదువు; తాత్కాలిక పోషణ, చదువుకు అరవై రోజుల లక్ష్యం. HMA సెక్షన్లు 21B, 28, 28A: వేగవంతమైన విచారణ, అప్పీళ్లు, అమలు. ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం, 1954 (SMA), సెక్షన్లు 36, 37, 38. కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానాల చట్టం, 1984, సెక్షన్లు 7, 9. భారతీయ నాగరిక సురక్ష సంహిత, 2023 (BNSS), సెక్షన్ 144 (గతంలో క్రిమినల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1973, సెక్షన్ 125). హిందూ దత్తత, భరణ చట్టం, 1956 (HAMA), సెక్షన్లు 18(1), 23(2). గృహ హింస నుంచి మహిళల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2005 (PWDVA), సెక్షన్లు 12, 20, 23, 26.

Maintenance pendente lite అంటే దావా పెండింగ్‌లో ఉన్నప్పుడు భరణం (" pendente lite " అంటే "వ్యాజ్యం పెండింగ్‌లో ఉన్నప్పుడు"). ఆర్థిక వనరులు లేని జీవిత భాగస్వామి కేసు సమయంలో జీవించడానికి, న్యాయమైన పరిస్థితుల్లో కేసు నడపడానికి ఇది వీలిస్తుంది. ఉత్తర్వు తాత్కాలికం. Diagram 1 చూడండి. selfTest.q: 1. భర్త కేసు పెండింగ్‌లో భరణం కోరవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: అవును. సెక్షన్ భార్య లేదా భర్త అంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 2. సెక్షన్ 24 దరఖాస్తును నిర్ణయించడానికి లక్ష్య సమయం ఎంత?
selfTest.a: సాధ్యమైనంత వరకు, నోటీసు అందిన అరవై రోజులు.

selfTest.q: 3. శాశ్వత భరణం ఏ సెక్షన్ ఇస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 25.

selfTest.q: 4. ప్రత్యేక వివాహ చట్టం, 1954 సెక్షన్ 36 కింద కేసు పెండింగ్‌లో భరణం ఎవరు కోరవచ్చు?
selfTest.a: భార్య మాత్రమే.

selfTest.q: 5. మైనర్ పిల్లల తాత్కాలిక పోషణ ఏ సెక్షన్ కింద ఆదేశిస్తారు?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 26.

selfTest.q: 6. సెక్షన్ 24 ఉత్తర్వు డిక్రీ తర్వాత కొనసాగుతుందా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. అది కేసు సమయంలో అమలులో ఉంటుంది; డిక్రీ తర్వాత సెక్షన్ 25 వర్తిస్తుంది.

family-law-i-u3-t7.subtitle: Why the law makes the court try for settlement first: section 23(2), cooling-off and family courts

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Conciliation means helping the spouses to settle their dispute and, where possible, save the marriage. Duty of the court. Before granting any relief under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA), the court must make every endeavour to bring about reconciliation, where the nature of the case allows (Section 23(2)). It may adjourn up to fifteen days and refer the parties to a person for this (Section 23(3)). Exceptions. The duty does not apply where relief is sought on conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation or presumed death ( proviso to Section 23(2)). Family Courts. The Family Courts Act, 1984 was passed "with a view to promote conciliation"; a Family Court must first try to assist and persuade the parties to settle (Section 9). Why it matters. Breakdown of a marriage harms children and families. The six-month wait in a mutual-consent divorce and the duty to reconcile serve the same aim: peace first, decree last.
legalProvision: Section 23(2), Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Before proceeding to grant any relief under this Act, it shall be the duty of the court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible so to do consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to bring about reconciliation between the parties: Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall apply to any proceeding wherein relief is sought on any of the grounds specified in clause (ii), clause (iii), clause (iv), clause (v), clause (vi) or clause (vii) of sub-section (1) of section 13. (3) For the purpose of aiding the court in bringing about such reconciliation, the court may, if the parties so desire or if the court thinks it just and proper so to do, adjourn the proceedings for a reasonable period not exceeding fifteen days and refer the matter to any person named by the parties in this behalf or to any person nominated by the court if the parties fail to name any person, with directions to report to the court as to whether reconciliation can be and has been, effected and the court shall in disposing of the proceeding have due regard to the report.

Section 9(1), Family Courts Act, 1984. In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding and for this purpose a Family Court may, subject to any rules made by the High Court, follow such procedure as it may deem fit.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Section 13B(2): the second motion in a mutual-consent divorce comes six to eighteen months after the petition. Family Courts Act, 1984 (FCA): long title; Sections 4(4), 5, 6, 9(2), (3), 10(3), 11, 12, 13 and 21(2)(c). Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC): Order XXXIIA, Rules 1 to 5. Mediation Act, 2023: Sections 5(1), 6(1), 7, 22 and 27, and the First Schedule. Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996: Sections 61, 74 and 75. Special Marriage Act, 1954 (SMA): Section 34(2) and (3).
en.meaning:
Conciliation is a process in which the court or a neutral person helps the spouses to settle their dispute by agreement. It is not a ruling: the parties remain free to accept or reject the suggestions. In matrimonial law its first aim is reconciliation (the spouses live together again); if that fails, a fair settlement of maintenance, custody and property. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Before any relief the court checks the ground; on most grounds it must try reconciliation, with an optional fifteen-day reference; a Family Court also tries settlement under Section 9. flowchart TD P["Petition under the

s. 23(3)"] A -->|"Reconciled"| E["Case ends"] A -->|"Fails"| D["Trial and decree"] Text description A petition under the Hindu Marriage Act is filed. If a Family Court hears it, the Family Court first tries to assist and persuade the parties to settle under Section 9. Then the court asks whether relief is sought on a ground in Section 13(1)(ii) to (vii). If yes, the Section 23(2) duty does not apply and the case goes to trial. If no, the court must try reconciliation; it may adjourn up to fifteen days and refer the parties to a person who reports back (Section 23(3)). If reconciliation succeeds, the case ends. If it fails, the case goes to trial and decree. Stage Who acts Provision Before any relief The court tries reconciliation HMA s. 23(2) Reference for up to fifteen days A person named by the parties or the court HMA s. 23(3) First step in every Family Court case The Family Court assists and persuades the parties to settle FCA s. 9(1) Waiting period in mutual consent The parties themselves, with time to rethink HMA s. 13B(2)
keyPoints: Section 23(2): the court must try reconciliation before granting relief. Adjournment up to fifteen days and reference to a person (Section 23(3)). Duty excluded for conversion, mental disorder, venereal disease, renunciation and presumed death. Section 9, Family Courts Act: the Family Court must first assist and persuade the parties to settle, and may adjourn for that purpose. Amardeep Singh (para 18) lists Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA among the conciliation efforts that must fail before waiver. The Section 13B waiting period gives time to reconcile and is directory. Order XXXIIA CPC and the Mediation Act, 2023 support settlement of family disputes.

caseLaws.name: Amardeep Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. A couple married in 1994 had lived apart since 2008. They settled all disputes and sought waiver of the six months under Section 13B(2). Principle. The period is directory; it exists for a rethink and reconciliation, and may be waived only if conciliation efforts (including Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA) have failed and the other conditions are met. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It treats the waiting period as a chance for conciliation, not a rigid delay. Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023) Facts. A Constitution Bench answered questions on the Supreme Court's power under Article 142 in matrimonial cases, decided on 1 May 2023. Principle. Public policy in family matters is to encourage mutual settlement (Section 89 CPC, Section 23(2) HMA, Section 9 FCA); a settlement must be free of pressure, fraud or undue influence. [2023] 5 SCR 165. Why it matters. It places conciliation at the centre of matrimonial law at the highest level.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section requires the court to try reconciliation?
selfTest.a: Section 23(2) of the Hindu Marriage Act.

selfTest.q: 2. For how long may the court adjourn to reconcile under Section 23(3)?
selfTest.a: Up to fifteen days.

selfTest.q: 3. What does Section 9(1) of the Family Courts Act require?
selfTest.a: The Family Court must first try, where possible, to assist and persuade the parties to settle.

selfTest.q: 4. Which provisions does Amardeep Singh list among the conciliation efforts?
selfTest.a: Order XXXIIA Rule 3 CPC, Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 of the Family Courts Act (para 18, condition (ii)).

selfTest.q: 5. Must the court attempt reconciliation in a divorce petition on the ground of desertion?
selfTest.a: Yes. Desertion (Section 13(1)(ib)) is not among the excluded grounds.

selfTest.q: 6. Under the Family Courts Act, for how long may the Family Court adjourn for settlement?
selfTest.a: For such period as it thinks fit (Section 9(2)).

family-law-i-u3-t8.subtitle: Settlement first: the Family Courts Act, 1984 (jurisdiction, duty to assist settlement, procedure, appeals), Hindu Marriage Act procedure, Order XXXIIA, maintenance and mediation

en.inOneMinute: Aim. The Family Courts Act, 1984 (FCA) provides for Family Courts "with a view to promote conciliation in, and secure speedy settlement of, disputes relating to marriage and family affairs" (long title). Who hears what. A Family Court takes over the matrimonial , family property, maintenance, legitimacy and custody suits of its area, and the maintenance cases of a Magistrate (Sections 7 and 8). Settlement first. It must first try to assist and persuade the parties to settle (Section 9). The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (HMA) (Section 23(2)) and Order XXXIIA of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) say the same for other courts. Simple procedure. Hearings in camera on request (Section 11), help of counsellors and experts (Sections 6 and 12), no lawyer as of right (Section 13), flexible evidence (Sections 14 to 16). Appeal. To the High Court within thirty days; none from a consent decree (Section 19).
legalProvision: Section 9, Family Courts Act, 1984. Duty of Family Court to make efforts for settlement. (1) In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding and for this purpose a Family Court may, subject to any rules made by the High Court, follow such procedure as it may deem fit. (2) If, in any suit or proceeding, at any stage, it appears to the Family Court that there is a reasonable possibility of a settlement between the parties, the Family Court may adjourn the proceedings for such period as it thinks fit to enable attempts to be made to effect such a settlement. (3) The power conferred by sub-section (2) shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other power of the Family Court to adjourn the proceedings.

Section 13. Right to legal representation. Notwithstanding anything contained in any law, no party to a suit or proceeding before a Family Court shall be entitled, as of right, to be represented by a legal practitioner: Provided that if the Family Court considers it necessary in the interest of justice, it may seek the assistance of a legal expert as amicus curiae.
The scheme of the Family Courts Act, 1984 (Act 66 of 1984):

Sections 1 and 2: short title, extent, commencement by notification , and definitions. Sections 3 to 6: establishment of Family Courts, Judges, social welfare agencies, counsellors and staff. Sections 7 and 8: jurisdiction , and exclusion of other courts with transfer of pending cases. Sections 9 to 18: settlement, procedure, in camera hearings, experts, lawyers, evidence, judgment and execution. Section 19: appeals and revision. Section 20: overriding effect. Sections 21 to 23: rules.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMA Sections 3(b), 19, 21A, 21B, 22, 23(2), (3), 24 to 28. CPC Order XXXIIA , Rules 1 to 6. Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), Section 144 (earlier Chapter IX of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973). Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA), Section 26. Mediation Act, 2023, Section 7.
en.meaning:
A Family Court is a court established by the State Government under Section 3 of the Family Courts Act, 1984 (Section 2(d)). It is a specialised court for disputes about marriage and family affairs, built around conciliation and speed rather than a contest between lawyers. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. The Family Court takes the case from the civil court and Magistrate, tries settlement first, then hears it with a simple procedure; appeal lies to the High Court within thirty days. flowchart TD A["Family dispute in an area

s. 19"] Text description A matrimonial, property, maintenance, legitimacy or custody case arises in an area that has a Family Court. The district court, subordinate civil court and Magistrate cannot hear it (Section 8); it goes to the Family Court (Section 7). The Family Court first assists and persuades the parties to settle, and may adjourn for that (Section 9), with counsellors and experts (Sections 6 and 12). If they settle, a consent decree or order follows and no appeal lies (Section 19(2)). If they do not settle, the court hears the case: in camera if desired (Section 11), no lawyer as of right (Section 13), evidence not bound by the Evidence Act (Sections 14 to 16). It gives a judgment (Section 17). Appeal lies to the High Court within thirty days (Section 19). keyPoints: Family Courts Act, 1984: the aim is conciliation and speedy settlement of marriage and family disputes. Section 3: a Family Court for every city or town above one million people. Section 7: nullity, restitution, judicial separation, divorce, property, injunction, legitimacy, maintenance, guardianship and custody, plus Chapter IX maintenance. Section 9: the Family Court first assists the parties to settle. Section 11: in camera if the Court or either party so desires. Section 13: no lawyer as of right. Section 19: appeal to the High Court within thirty days; none from a consent decree. Section 20: overriding effect. Section 23(2) HMA: the court must try reconciliation. Order XXXIIA Rule 3: assist the parties to settle first. HMA Section 28(4): appeal within ninety days. Mediation Act, Section 7: the parties are not bound to settle.

caseLaws.name: Amardeep Singh v
caseLaws.facts: Harveen Kaur (2017) Facts. A couple married in 1994 had lived apart since 2008 and settled all disputes before the Family Court at Tis Hazari, Delhi. They asked to waive the six-month wait under Section 13B(2). Principle. The period is directory; waiver is allowed only if settlement efforts under Order XXXIIA Rule 3, Section 23(2) HMA and Section 9 FCA have failed and the other conditions are met. (2017) 8 SCC 746. Why it matters. It shows that a Family Court's duty to try settlement is a condition the court must check before relaxing the waiting period.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section of the Hindu Marriage Act requires the court to try reconciliation?
selfTest.a: Section 23(2).

selfTest.q: 2. Which Order of the Code of Civil Procedure deals with suits about the family?
selfTest.a: Order XXXIIA.

selfTest.q: 3. Which section of the Family Courts Act makes the Court assist the parties to settle?
selfTest.a: Section 9. Amardeep Singh names it at para 18, condition (ii).

selfTest.q: 4. What is the time limit to appeal from a Family Court to the High Court?
selfTest.a: Thirty days from the judgment or order (Section 19(3)).

selfTest.q: 5. Is a party entitled to a lawyer as of right before a Family Court?
selfTest.a: No (Section 13). The Court may seek a legal expert as amicus curiae.

selfTest.q: 6. Once a Family Court is set up for an area, can a Magistrate there still hear a maintenance case under Chapter IX?
selfTest.a: No (Section 8(b)). The Family Court hears it (Section 7(2)(a)).

legalProvision: Section 9, Family Courts Act, 1984. Duty of Family Court to make efforts for settlement. (1) In every suit or proceeding, endeavour shall be made by the Family Court in the first instance, where it is possible to do so consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case, to assist and persuade the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject-matter of the suit or proceeding and for this purpose a Family Court may, subject to any rules made by the High Court, follow such procedure as it may deem fit. (2) If, in any suit or proceeding, at any stage, it appears to the Family Court that there is a reasonable possibility of a settlement between the parties, the Family Court may adjourn the proceedings for such period as it thinks fit to enable attempts to be made to effect such a settlement. (3) The power conferred by sub-section (2) shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other power of the Family Court to adjourn the proceedings.

Section 13. Right to legal representation. Notwithstanding anything contained in any law, no party to a suit or proceeding before a Family Court shall be entitled, as of right, to be represented by a legal practitioner: Provided that if the Family Court considers it necessary in the interest of justice, it may seek the assistance of a legal expert as amicus curiae.

selfTest.q: 3. పక్షాలు రాజీకి రావడానికి సహాయం చేయమని కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానాల చట్టంలో ఏ సెక్షన్ చెబుతుంది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 9. Amardeep Singh దానిని పేరా 18, షరతు (ii) లో పేర్కొంటుంది.

selfTest.q: 4. కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానం నుంచి హైకోర్టుకు అప్పీలు గడువు ఎంత?
selfTest.a: తీర్పు లేదా ఉత్తర్వు నుంచి ముప్పై రోజులు (సెక్షన్ 19(3)).

selfTest.q: 5. కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానం ముందు పక్షానికి హక్కుగా న్యాయవాది ఉంటారా?
selfTest.a: లేదు (సెక్షన్ 13). కోర్టు అమికస్ క్యూరీగా న్యాయ నిపుణుడిని కోరవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 6. ఒక ప్రాంతానికి కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానం ఏర్పడిన తర్వాత, అక్కడి మేజిస్ట్రేట్ అధ్యాయం IX కింద భరణ కేసు విచారించగలరా?
selfTest.a: లేదు (సెక్షన్ 8(b)). కుటుంబ న్యాయస్థానం విచారిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 7(2)(a)).

Explanation. Section 10 of the Hindu Marriage Act deals with judicial separation.

Explanation. Judicial separation releases the parties from the duty to cohabit, but the marriage continues to exist.

Which section of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 deals with restitution of conjugal rights?

Explanation. Section 9 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 provides the remedy of restitution of conjugal rights.

What must the petitioner prove to succeed under Section 9?

Explanation. The core requirement under Section 9 is withdrawal from society without reasonable excuse.

Once withdrawal from society is proved, on whom does the burden shift to prove a reasonable excuse?

Explanation. The burden shifts to the respondent once withdrawal from society is established.

A marriage is void under Section 11 if it contravenes conditions in Section 5 relating to:

Explanation. Section 11 makes a marriage void if it contravenes Sec. 5(i) bigamy, 5(iv) prohibited relationship, or 5(v) sapinda relationship.

Explanation. A void marriage never had legal existence from the very moment it was performed.

Which of the following is a ground for a voidable marriage under Section 12?

Explanation. Impotence preventing consummation is a Section 12 ground for a voidable marriage.

A voidable marriage remains valid:

Explanation. A voidable marriage is fully valid and subsisting until a competent court annuls it by decree.

Under the fault theory of divorce, the petitioner must prove:

Explanation. The fault theory requires proof of a specific matrimonial offence committed by the respondent.

Which of the following is NOT currently a ground for divorce under Section 13(1)?

Explanation. Section 13(1) now lists adultery, cruelty, desertion for two years, conversion, mental disorder, communicable venereal disease, renunciation of the world and presumed death. Clause (iv) of section 13(1) was omitted by Act 6 of 2019.

How many special grounds does section 13(2) give to a wife?

Explanation. Section 13(2) gives a wife four more grounds: pre-1955 polygamy of the husband, rape, sodomy or bestiality by him, non-cohabitation for a year after a maintenance decree, and repudiation of a marriage solemnized before she was fifteen.

family-law-i-u4-t1.subtitle: Meaning, requisites of a valid adoption, who may give and take, and the effects under the 1956 Act

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Adoption moves a child for good from the family of birth to the adoptive family. From the date of adoption the child is the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes (Section 12, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA)). Four requisites. The taker has the capacity and right to take, the giver has the capacity to give, the child can be adopted, and the other conditions of Chapter II are met (Section 6). Void if the Act is broken. An adoption made in breach of Chapter II is void; it creates no new rights in the adoptive family and takes away none in the family of birth (Section 5). Final. A valid adoption cannot be cancelled, and the child cannot go back to the birth family (Section 15). No payment. Giving or taking payment for an adoption is punishable with up to six months' imprisonment, or fine, or both (Section 17).
legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Requisites of a valid adoption. No adoption shall be valid unless— (i) the person adopting has the capacity, and also the right, to take in adoption; (ii) the person giving in adoption has the capacity to do so; (iii) the person adopted is capable of being taken in adoption; and (iv) the adoption is made in compliance with the other conditions mentioned in this Chapter.

Section 12. Effects of adoption. An adopted child shall be deemed to be the child of his or her adoptive father or mother for all purposes with effect from the date of the adoption and from such date all the ties of the child in the family of his or her birth shall be deemed to be severed and replaced by those created by the adoption in the adoptive family: Provided that— (a) the child cannot marry any person whom he or she could not have married if he or she had continued in the family of his or her birth; (b) any property which vested in the adopted child before the adoption shall continue to vest in such person subject to the obligations, if any, attaching to the ownership of such property, including the obligation to maintain relatives in the family of his or her birth; (c) the adopted child shall not divest any person of any estate which vested in him or her before the adoption.
Chapter II of HAMA ( Adoption ) at a glance:

Section 5: adoption only as Chapter II provides; an adoption in breach is void. Section 6: the four requisites. Sections 7 and 8: capacity of a male and a female Hindu to take in adoption, with the spouse's consent. Section 9: who may give a child in adoption. Section 10: who may be adopted. Section 11: other conditions, including actual giving and taking. Sections 12 to 17: effects, power to dispose of property, adoptive mother, no cancellation, presumption from registered documents, and prohibition of payments.
Other provisions used in this note:

HAMA Sections 2, 3 and 4: who is covered, definitions, overriding effect. Section 30: adoptions before the Act are saved. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act): Sections 2(2), 56, 61 and 63. Guardians and Wards Act, 1890: Sections 24 and 41 (for the contrast with guardianship).
en.meaning:
HAMA does not define adoption. Read together, Sections 6 to 12 show it: adoption is the legal act by which a child is given and taken, with the intent to transfer the child from the family of birth to the adoptive family, so that the child becomes the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes. The JJ Act, which has its own adoption system, defines it in Section 2(2) as "the process through which the adopted child is permanently separated from his biological parents and becomes the lawful child of his adoptive parents with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities that are attached to a biological child". A valid adoption must pass all four requisites of Section 6, one after the other. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. keyPoints: Section 5: an adoption in breach of Chapter II is void. Section 6: four requisites. Spouse's consent is needed (Sections 7 and 8), with exceptions. The child must be a Hindu, unmarried, under fifteen and not already adopted, unless custom permits. Giving and taking is essential; datta homam is not. Section 12: an adopted child is the child of the adopters for all purposes. Section 16 only presumes a registered adoption to be valid; registration is not compulsory under the Act. A widow may adopt in her own right (Section 8); the child becomes her late husband's son too ( Sitabai ). The Act does not apply to Scheduled Tribes unless notified (Section 2(2)).

caseLaws.name: Sitabai v
caseLaws.facts: Ramchandra (1969) Facts. Sitabai's husband died in 1930. In March 1958, after the Act, she adopted Suresh Chandra. The question was whether he became a coparcener with her late husband's brother in the joint family property. Principle. Under Sections 11, 12 and 14, a child adopted by a widow is absorbed in the adoptive family to which she belonged and becomes the son of her deceased husband as well. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It explains the effect of Section 12 on adoption by a widow; the boy took the joint family property as sole surviving coparcener. Addagada Raghavamma v. Addagada Chenchamma (1963) Facts. A widow claimed that her husband had adopted his elder brother's only son in 1905. No document, invitation or expense entry supported it. Principle. A person who alleges adoption to displace natural succession must prove the fact of adoption and its validity. 1964 AIR 136; [1964] 2 SCR 933. Why it matters. It shows why proof of giving and taking matters; Section 16 now presumes in favour of registered documents. Supriyo v. Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which bars unmarried couples from adopting jointly. Principle. The Chief Justice noted that Section 12 of HAMA and Section 63 of the JJ Act deem an adopted child to be the adopters' child for all purposes (paras 337–338, his opinion). The majority did not strike down Regulation 5(3). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It restates the effect of adoption in Section 12.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the result of an adoption that breaks Chapter II?
selfTest.a: It is void (Section 5).

selfTest.q: 2. Is datta homam essential for a valid adoption?
selfTest.a: No. See the proviso to Section 11.

selfTest.q: 3. Can a valid adoption be cancelled?
selfTest.a: No (Section 15).

selfTest.q: 4. A woman aged 30 wants to adopt a boy aged 10. Is the age-gap rule met?
selfTest.a: No. The gap is 20 years; Section 11(iv) requires at least twenty-one.

selfTest.q: 5. Who gives a child of unknown parentage in adoption?
selfTest.a: The guardian, with the previous permission of the court (Section 9(4)).

selfTest.q: 6. Does the JJ Act, 2015 apply to an adoption made under HAMA?
selfTest.a: No (JJ Act, Section 56(3)).

family-law-i-u4-t2.subtitle: From custom and personal law to the 1956 Act and the Juvenile Justice Act, as recorded in the Act and in Supriyo

en.inOneMinute: Classical law. Hindu adoption came from the texts, two special works (the Dattaka Mimamsa and the Dattaka Chandrika), and custom and usage . Its objects were religious (a son to offer funeral cakes and water) and secular (an heir) (Mulla, Section 447). Only a boy could be adopted, and a woman could not adopt to herself. The 1956 Act. The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA) put Hindu adoption into a statute. It ends any old text, rule, interpretation, custom or usage on a matter it covers (Section 4), allows a son or a daughter to be adopted, and saves adoptions made before it (Section 30). Other children. Court guidelines on inter-country adoption ( Laxmi Kant Pandey ) came first, then executive instructions, then the Juvenile Justice Act, which enables adoption among members of all faiths and communities ( Supriyo , Bhat J., para 25). Today. The Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, as amended in 2021, with the Adoption Regulations, 2022, governs adoption outside HAMA; the District Magistrate issues the adoption order.
legalProvision: Section 4, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to apply to Hindus in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 30. Savings. Nothing contained in this Act shall affect any adoption made before the commencement of this Act, and the validity and effect of any such adoption shall be determined as if this Act had not been passed.
Other provisions used in this note:

HAMA, Chapter II (Sections 5 to 17): the statutory law of Hindu adoption . HAMA Section 3(a): "custom" and "usage" mean a rule continuously and uniformly observed for a long time, which has obtained the force of law among Hindus in a local area, tribe, community, group or family. Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act): Sections 2(2), 56, 63, 68(c), 101(6), (7) and 111(1). Supriyo records Section 63 (Chandrachud CJI, para 337). Bhat J. refers to Section 41 of the Juvenile Justice Act (Section 41 of the 2000 Act), which enables adoption among members of all faiths and communities (para 25). Guardians and Wards Act, 1890: Section 7.
en.meaning:
The historical perspective traces how the law of adoption moved from old texts, custom and usage to a statute for Hindus, and then to a law open to members of all faiths. The classical rules are those described in Mulla's Principles of Hindu Law (14th edition); the modern rules are in HAMA and the JJ Act. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. District Magistrate orders"] Text description Before 1956: texts, the Dattaka Mimamsa and Dattaka Chandrika, custom and usage; dattaka and kritrima forms. Branch one, for Hindus: the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (Sections 4 and 30), amended in 1962 and 2010. Branch two, for all faiths: Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines and executive instructions; the Juvenile Justice Act, 2000 with the 2011 and 2015 Guidelines; the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 with the 2017 Regulations; the 2021 amendment and the 2022 Regulations, with the District Magistrate issuing orders. Stage Source of law What it allowed Before 1956 Texts, the Dattaka Mimamsa and Dattaka Chandrika, custom and usage Adoption of a boy, mainly in the dattaka form; kritrima in Mithila 1956 HAMA, Chapter II Adoption of a son or a daughter by a Hindu man or woman From 1984 Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines, then executive instructions Inter-country adoption under court supervision 2000 to now JJ Act 2000, then JJ Act 2015 (amended 2021); CARA Guidelines and Regulations Adoption among members of all faiths and communities
keyPoints: Classical objects: religious (funeral offerings) and secular (an heir) (Mulla, Section 447). Dattaka prevailed all over India; kritrima in Mithila. Classical law: only a boy, of the same caste; a woman could not adopt to herself in dattaka form. Section 4: old texts, rules, interpretations, custom and usage cease on matters the Act covers. HAMA: statutory adoption of sons and daughters; Section 12 gives full status. Section 30 saves adoptions made before the Act. Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines on inter-country adoption (noted in Supriyo , para 25). Juvenile Justice Act: adoption among members of all faiths and communities (Bhat J., para 25). Shabnam Hashmi : the right to adopt was not raised to a fundamental right (quoted in Supriyo , para 307). Since 2021 the District Magistrate issues JJ Act adoption orders; the Adoption Regulations, 2022 are current.

caseLaws.name: Supriyo v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which bars unmarried couples from adopting jointly. Principle. Bhat J. traced the law: court guidelines on inter-country adoption, then executive instructions, then the Juvenile Justice Act for all faiths (para 25). The Court also quoted Shabnam Hashmi (Chandrachud CJI, paras 307–308). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It records the route open to all faiths in the Supreme Court's own words. Sitabai v. Ramchandra (1969) Facts. A widow whose husband had died in 1930 adopted a son in March 1958, after HAMA. Principle. Under Sections 11, 12 and 14, the adopted child is absorbed in the adoptive family and becomes her deceased husband's son too. AIR 1970 SC 343. Why it matters. It shows the full status HAMA gives to an adopted child, even through a widow, which classical law in Mithila would have denied.

selfTest.q: 1. What does Section 4 of HAMA do to old texts and custom?
selfTest.a: They cease to have effect on any matter for which the Act makes provision.

selfTest.q: 2. Which Act made Hindu adoption statutory?
selfTest.a: The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956.

selfTest.q: 3. Which case pioneered the guidelines for inter-country adoption?
selfTest.a: Laxmi Kant Pandey v. Union of India , as noted in Supriyo v. Union of India (para 25, Bhat J.).

selfTest.q: 4. Could a widow in Mithila adopt under classical law?
selfTest.a: No, not even with her husband's express authority (Mulla, Section 452(1)).

selfTest.q: 5. Which form of adoption let a woman adopt a son to herself?
selfTest.a: The kritrima form (Mulla, Section 515).

selfTest.q: 6. Who now issues an adoption order under the JJ Act, and where does an appeal lie?
selfTest.a: The District Magistrate; an appeal lies to the Divisional Commissioner within thirty days (Section 101(6)).

legalProvision: Section 4, Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. Overriding effect of Act. Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act,— (a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or usage as part of that law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; (b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of this Act shall cease to apply to Hindus in so far as it is inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in this Act.

Section 30. Savings. Nothing contained in this Act shall affect any adoption made before the commencement of this Act, and the validity and effect of any such adoption shall be determined as if this Act had not been passed.

family-law-i-u4-t3.subtitle: Eligibility under section 57 and Regulation 5, the effect of an adoption order and the guidelines noted in Supriyo

en.inOneMinute: Two routes. The Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA) covers adoption by Hindus. The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ Act) is a separate system for orphan, abandoned and surrendered children, open to people of every religion, with eligibility rules in Section 57 and in Regulation 5 of the Adoption Regulations, 2022. In-country and inter-country. In-country adoption places a child with parents resident in India. Inter-country adoption sends a child from India to parents living abroad; Indian, non-resident Indian and overseas citizen of India parents get priority (Section 59). Who decides. Since the 2021 amendment, the District Magistrate, not a court, issues the adoption order (Section 61). The Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) frames the Regulations and acts as India's Central Authority under the Hague Convention, 1993 (Section 68). History. Bhat J. notes that guidelines pioneered in Laxmi Kant Pandey v. UOI helped inter-country adoptions, and executive instructions filled the vacuum to some extent ( Supriyo , para 25).
legalProvision: Section 57, Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. Eligibility of prospective adoptive parents. (1) The prospective adoptive parents shall be physically fit, financially sound, mentally alert and highly motivated to adopt a child for providing a good upbringing to him. (2) In case of a couple, the consent of both the spouses for the adoption shall be required. (3) A single or divorced person can also adopt, subject to fulfilment of the criteria and in accordance with the provisions of adoption regulations framed by the Authority. (4) A single male is not eligible to adopt a girl child. (5) Any other criteria that may be specified in the adoption regulations framed by the Authority.

Section 59(1). If an orphan or abandoned or surrendered child could not be placed with an Indian or non-resident Indian prospective adoptive parent despite the joint effort of the Specialised Adoption Agency and State Agency within sixty days from the date the child has been declared legally free for adoption, such child shall be free for inter-country adoption: Provided that children with physical and mental disability, siblings and children above five years of age may be given preference over other children for such inter-country adoption, in accordance with the adoption regulations, as may be framed by the Authority.
Other provisions used in this note:

JJ Act Section 2(49): " prospective adoptive parents" means the person or persons eligible to adopt under Section 57. Section 63: an adoption order makes the child the child of the adoptive parents ( Supriyo , Chandrachud CJI, para 337). Sections 2(3) and 68(c): the Authority is CARA, which frames the Adoption Regulations. Sections 35, 38, 56 to 62, 65 to 68, 80 and 101(6): surrender, legal freedom, the adoption scheme, the roles of the Specialised Adoption Agency and the District Magistrate (since the 2021 amendment), CARA, the offence of unlawful adoption and the appeal. Adoption Regulations, 2022 (G.S.R. 726(E), 23 September 2022): principles, eligible children, eligibility, availability, registration, referral, timelines, inter-country steps, relative and step-parent adoption, grievances, and HAMA adoptions that go abroad. Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption, 1993: Articles 1, 2, 4 to 7, 15 to 17, 19, 21, 23, 24 and 32, summarised below.
en.meaning:
Inter-country adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents living in another. In-country adoption is the adoption of a child within India by parents resident in India. Under the JJ Act, "adoption" is the process through which the child is permanently separated from the biological parents and becomes the lawful child of the adoptive parents, with all the rights, privileges and responsibilities of a biological child (Section 2(2)). Eligibility to adopt under the JJ Act is checked in layers: the Act first, then the Regulations. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Eligibility is checked in layers: first the Act (section 57), then the Regulations (Regulation 5); the adoption order then makes the child the adopters' child (section 63). flowchart TD A["Person or couple wants to adopt

for all purposes"] Text description Start: a person or couple wants to adopt under the JJ Act (sections 56, 58, 59). Check section 57: fit, sound, alert and motivated; consent of both spouses; a single male cannot adopt a girl. If not met, not eligible. If met, check Regulation 5: health and no conviction; two years' stable marital relationship for a couple; age limits and a 25-year age gap. If not met, not eligible. If met, the District Magistrate's adoption order; under section 63 the child becomes the adopters' child for all purposes. Step Question Provision 1 Does the person or couple want to adopt under the JJ Act? Sections 56, 58, 59 2 Do they have the qualities in Section 57 and the consent of both spouses? Section 57 3 Do they meet Regulation 5 (health, record, marital status, gender, age)? Regulation 5 Result The adoption order makes the child the child of the adopters Section 63
keyPoints: Two routes: HAMA, 1956 and the JJ Act, 2015. Section 57: eligibility; both spouses consent; a single male cannot adopt a girl. Regulation 5(3): two years of stable marital relationship for couples; Supriyo (3:2) did not read it down. Regulation 5(4): age limits by the child's age; at least twenty-five years' gap. Indians first: sixty days for a child below five, thirty for older children and siblings (Regulation 8; Section 59(1)). The District Magistrate issues the adoption order; appeal to the Divisional Commissioner within thirty days. An adoption order makes the child the adopters' child (Section 63). Bhat J. notes the Laxmi Kant Pandey guidelines on inter-country adoption (para 25). The Authority under Section 2(3) is CARA, India's Central Authority under the Hague Convention (Section 68(d)).

caseLaws.name: Supriyo v
caseLaws.facts: Union of India (2023) Facts. Queer couples challenged Regulation 5(3) of the Adoption Regulations, which allows a couple to adopt only after two years of stable marital relationship. Principle. By 3:2, the Court did not read down Regulation 5(3). Bhat J. held that Section 57(2) of the Act contemplates joint adoption only by married couples (paras 120–123); the Chief Justice would have read down "marital" (paras 299–317). 2023 INSC 920. Why it matters. It is the Supreme Court's latest word on who may adopt jointly under the Act.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section bars a single male from adopting a girl child?
selfTest.a: Section 57(4).

selfTest.q: 2. What does Section 63 do to an adopted child's status?
selfTest.a: It makes the child the child of the adoptive parents for all purposes, including intestacy ( Supriyo , para 337).

selfTest.q: 3. Which 2023 case decided on joint adoption by unmarried couples?
selfTest.a: Supriyo v. Union of India : by 3:2 the Court did not read down Regulation 5(3).

selfTest.q: 4. A couple's composite age is 98. Can they adopt a child of three?
selfTest.a: No. For a child above two and up to four the limit is 90; they can adopt a child above four and up to eight (limit 100) (Regulation 5(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. When does a normal child below five become available to foreign parents?
selfTest.a: Only after sixty days for Indian, NRI and OCI parents and seven more days for them regardless of seniority (Regulation 8; Section 59(1)).

selfTest.q: 6. Which certificate does CARA issue under Article 23 of the Hague Convention?
selfTest.a: The Conformity Certificate (Regulation 19(1)).

(2) In case of a couple, the consent of both the spouses for the adoption shall be required. If an orphan or abandoned or surrendered child could not be placed with an Indian or non-resident Indian prospective adoptive parent despite the joint effort of the Specialised Adoption Agency and State Agency within sixty days from the date the child has been declared legally free for adoption, such child shall be free for inter-country adoption: Provided that children with physical and mental disability, siblings and children above five years of age may be given preference over other children for such inter-country adoption, in accordance with the adoption regulations, as may be framed by the Authority.
ఈ నోట్‌లో వాడిన ఇతర నిబంధనలు:

JJ Act సెక్షన్ 2(49): "కాబోయే దత్తత తల్లిదండ్రులు" అంటే సెక్షన్ 57 కింద దత్తతకు అర్హులైన వ్యక్తి లేదా వ్యక్తులు. సెక్షన్ 63: దత్తత ఉత్తర్వు బిడ్డను దత్తత తల్లిదండ్రుల బిడ్డగా చేస్తుంది ( Supriyo , Chandrachud CJI, పేరా 337). సెక్షన్లు 2(3), 68(c): అధికార సంస్థ CARA, అది Adoption Regulations రూపొందిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్లు 35, 38, 56 నుంచి 62, 65 నుంచి 68, 80, 101(6): అప్పగింత, చట్టపరమైన స్వేచ్ఛ, దత్తత పథకం, ప్రత్యేక దత్తత సంస్థ, జిల్లా మేజిస్ట్రేట్ (2021 సవరణ నుంచి) పాత్రలు, CARA, అక్రమ దత్తత నేరం, అప్పీలు. Adoption Regulations, 2022 (G.S.R. 726(E), 23 సెప్టెంబర్ 2022): సూత్రాలు, అర్హులైన పిల్లలు, అర్హత, లభ్యత, రిజిస్ట్రేషన్, రిఫరల్, కాల పరిమితులు, అంతర్ దేశ దశలు, బంధువులు, సవతి తల్లిదండ్రుల దత్తత, ఫిర్యాదులు, విదేశాలకు వెళ్లే HAMA దత్తతలు. అంతర్ దేశ దత్తతపై హేగ్ కన్వెన్షన్, 1993: అధికరణలు 1, 2, 4 నుంచి 7, 15 నుంచి 17, 19, 21, 23, 24, 32, కింద సంక్షిప్తంగా.

selfTest.q: 1. ఒంటరి పురుషుడు అమ్మాయిని దత్తత తీసుకోవడాన్ని ఏ సెక్షన్ నిషేధిస్తుంది?
2. దత్తత బిడ్డ హోదాపై సెక్షన్ 63 ఏమి చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: వారసత్వం సహా అన్ని ప్రయోజనాలకూ బిడ్డను దత్తత తల్లిదండ్రుల బిడ్డగా చేస్తుంది ( Supriyo , పేరా 337).

selfTest.q: 3. పెళ్లికాని జంటల ఉమ్మడి దత్తతపై ఏ 2023 కేసు నిర్ణయించింది?
selfTest.a: Supriyo v. Union of India : 3:2 తో కోర్టు Regulation 5(3) ను పరిమితం చేసి చదవలేదు.

selfTest.q: 4. ఒక జంట ఉమ్మడి వయసు 98. వారు మూడేళ్ల బిడ్డను దత్తత తీసుకోవచ్చా?
selfTest.a: లేదు. 2 పైన 4 వరకు బిడ్డకు పరిమితి 90; వారు 4 పైన 8 వరకు బిడ్డను దత్తత తీసుకోవచ్చు (పరిమితి 100) (Regulation 5(4)).

selfTest.q: 5. ఐదేళ్ల లోపు సాధారణ బిడ్డ విదేశీ తల్లిదండ్రులకు ఎప్పుడు అందుబాటులోకి వస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: భారతీయ, NRI, OCI తల్లిదండ్రులకు అరవై రోజులు, సీనియారిటీతో సంబంధం లేకుండా వారికే మరో ఏడు రోజుల తర్వాత మాత్రమే (Regulation 8; సెక్షన్ 59(1)).

selfTest.q: 6. హేగ్ కన్వెన్షన్ అధికరణ 23 కింద CARA ఏ సర్టిఫికెట్ జారీ చేస్తుంది?
selfTest.a: అనుగుణత సర్టిఫికెట్ (Conformity Certificate) (Regulation 19(1)).

family-law-i-u4-t4.subtitle: Who can claim maintenance under the 1956 Act and other laws, and how the amount is fixed

en.inOneMinute: What it is. Maintenance is the support that the law makes one person pay to another. Under Chapter III (Sections 18 to 28) of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956 (HAMA), a Hindu wife, a widowed daughter-in-law, children, aged or infirm parents and certain dependants of a dead person can claim it. How much. The court fixes the amount by the status of the parties, the claimant's reasonable wants and means, and the other factors in Section 23. A claimant who ceases to be a Hindu by conversion loses the claim under this Act (Section 24). Other laws. Maintenance is also given by Sections 24 and 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 (in matrimonial cases), by Section 144 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), which takes the place of Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and by the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005. Nature. In V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy the Supreme Court held that a Hindu woman's right to maintenance is a pre-existing right , not a mere gift.
legalProvision: Section 3(b), Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. "maintenance" includes― (i) in all cases, provision for food, clothing, residence, education and medical attendance and treatment; (ii) in the case of an unmarried daughter, also the reasonable expenses of and incident to her marriage;

Section 18(1). Subject to the provisions of this section, a Hindu wife, whether married before or after the commencement of this Act, shall be entitled to be maintained by her husband during her life time.
Section 22(1). Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), the heirs of a deceased Hindu are bound to maintain the dependants of the deceased out of the estate inherited by them from the deceased.
Other provisions used in this note:

Section 18(2) and (3): the wife's right to live separately without losing maintenance, and when she loses it. Section 19: widowed daughter-in-law, from her father-in-law. Section 20: children and aged or infirm parents. Sections 21 and 22: the nine classes of dependants, and the heirs' duty. Sections 23 to 28: amount; claimant must be a Hindu; alteration; debts first; charge only if created; transfer of the estate. Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, Sections 24 and 25: maintenance pendente lite and permanent alimony . BNSS, Sections 144 to 147: maintenance of wives, children and parents by order of a Magistrate; Section 531 repeals the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. Domestic Violence Act, 2005, Sections 2(a), 2(b), 2(f), 12, 17, 20 to 23, 26 and 36.
en.meaning:
Maintenance is the provision of the basic needs of a person who cannot meet them, by a person whom the law binds to provide them. Section 3(b) says it includes food, clothing, residence, education, and medical attendance and treatment, and for an unmarried daughter also the reasonable expenses of her marriage. Under the Act it is a personal obligation of a living person (wife, widowed daughter-in-law, children, parents), and for dependants an obligation of the heirs, payable out of the estate they inherit. A dependant's claim is a charge on the estate only if one is created (Section 27). Who can claim under the 1956 Act. See Diagram 1 . Diagram 1. Chapter III of the 1956 Act groups claimants by who must pay: a living person, or the heirs out of a dead person's estate. flowchart TD A["Maintenance under Chapter III

Branch one, from a living person: wife from husband (Section 18); widowed daughter-in-law from father-in-law (Section 19); children and aged or infirm parents (Section 20). Branch two, from the estate of a dead person: the nine classes of dependants, from the heirs (Sections 21 and 22). Common rules for both: Sections 23 to 28. Who pays Who can claim Section A living husband His wife 18 A living father-in-law His widowed daughter-in-law 19 A living Hindu His or her children and aged or infirm parents 20 The heirs of a dead Hindu, out of the estate The dead person's dependants 21 and 22
keyPoints: Section 3(b): food, clothing, residence, education, medical care; for an unmarried daughter, marriage expenses. Section 18: wife; may live apart for justified reasons; loses it if unchaste or she converts. Section 19: widowed daughter-in-law, from the father-in-law; ends on remarriage. Section 20: children (while minors) and aged or infirm parents; includes a childless step-mother. Sections 21 and 22: nine classes of dependants; heirs pay out of the estate, in proportion to their shares. Section 23: factors for the amount. Section 24: claimant must be a Hindu. Section 27: a dependant's claim is a charge only if created. Section 28: enforceable against a transferee with notice or a donee. Section 144 BNSS speaks of "any person having sufficient means"; a Magistrate of the first class orders a monthly allowance and may order interim maintenance. Hindu Marriage Act Sections 24 and 25: interim and permanent maintenance between spouses. Tulasamma : maintenance is a pre-existing right.

caseLaws.name: Yamunabai Anantrao Adhav v
caseLaws.facts: Anantrao Shivram Adhav (1988) Facts. In June 1974 a woman went through Hindu rites with a man whose first wife was alive. She left after a week and claimed maintenance as his wife under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Principle. The marriage was void under Sections 5(i) and 11 of the Hindu Marriage Act, a complete nullity, so she was not a "wife" under Section 125. AIR 1988 SC 644 : (1988) 1 SCC 530. Why it matters. The claim to maintenance as a wife depends on a valid marriage. Chanmuniya v. Virendra Kumar Singh Kushwaha (2010) Facts. A widow said she was married by Katha and Sindur to her late husband's younger brother; the High Court held that the essentials of marriage were not performed. Principle. The two-Judge Bench favoured a broad meaning of "wife" in Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but could not depart from earlier two-Judge decisions, and referred three questions to a larger Bench. (2011) 1 SCC 141. Why it matters. It is a reference order, not a final ruling, and shows the debate on who is a wife for maintenance. D. Velusamy v. D. Patchaiammal (2010) Facts. A woman claimed maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as the appellant 's wife; he said he was already married to Lakshmi in 1980. Principle. A relationship in the nature of marriage under the Domestic Violence Act is akin to a common law marriage and needs four conditions and a shared household; the case went back to the Family Court. (2010) 10 SCC 469. Why it matters. It extends relief to women in relationships in the nature of marriage, but not to every live-in relationship. Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma (2013) Facts. From 1992 an unmarried woman lived with a married man who had two children; she knew of his marriage and later claimed relief, including maintenance, under the Domestic Violence Act. Principle. The Court gave eight guidelines and held that her relationship was not in the nature of marriage, so she was not in a "domestic relationship"; the appeal was dismissed, and the Court asked Parliament to legislate. Decided 26 November 2013. Why it matters. It sets limits on maintenance claims by live-in partners. V. Tulasamma v. Sesha Reddy (1977) Facts. A widow, whose husband died in 1931 in a joint family, got a decree for maintenance; in execution, a compromise gave her properties for her life in lieu of maintenance. Principle. Her right to maintenance is a pre-existing right in property; property given in lieu of it falls under Section 14(1), not 14(2), of the Hindu Succession Act, so she became full owner. AIR 1977 SC 1944 : (1977) 3 SCC 99. Why it matters. It shows maintenance as a real right in Hindu law that can ripen into ownership.

selfTest.q: 1. Which section gives a Hindu wife maintenance from her husband?
selfTest.a: Section 18.

selfTest.q: 2. Is a dependant's claim a charge on the estate?
selfTest.a: Not unless one is created by will, decree, agreement or otherwise (Section 27).

selfTest.q: 3. Can a person who converts claim under the 1956 Act?
selfTest.a: No (Section 24).

selfTest.q: 4. Two heirs take ₹12,00,000 and ₹4,00,000 of an estate. Maintenance of a dependant is fixed at ₹8,000 a month. How much does each pay?
selfTest.a: In proportion to their shares (Section 22(3)): the heir with ₹12,00,000 holds three-quarters of ₹16,00,000 and pays ₹6,000; the heir with ₹4,00,000 holds one-quarter and pays ₹2,000.

selfTest.q: 5. Within what time must an application to levy unpaid maintenance under Section 144 of the BNSS be made?
selfTest.a: Within one year from the date the amount became due (proviso to Section 144(3)).

selfTest.q: 6. In Tulasamma , why did the widow become full owner of property given in lieu of maintenance?
selfTest.a: Because her right to maintenance was a pre-existing right, so Section 14(1) of the Hindu Succession Act applied, not Section 14(2).

ఈ నోట్‌లో వాడిన ఇతర నిబంధనలు:

సెక్షన్ 18(2), (3): భరణం కోల్పోకుండా విడిగా జీవించే భార్య హక్కు, ఆమె దానిని ఎప్పుడు కోల్పోతుంది. సెక్షన్ 19: వితంతువైన కోడలు, మామగారి నుంచి. సెక్షన్ 20: పిల్లలు, వృద్ధులు లేదా అశక్తులైన తల్లిదండ్రులు. సెక్షన్లు 21, 22: తొమ్మిది వర్గాల ఆశ్రితులు, వారసుల బాధ్యత. సెక్షన్లు 23 నుంచి 28: మొత్తం; దావాదారు హిందువై ఉండాలి; మార్పు; ముందు అప్పులు; సృష్టిస్తేనే భారం ; ఆస్తి బదిలీ. హిందూ వివాహ చట్టం, 1955, సెక్షన్లు 24, 25: వ్యాజ్యం పెండింగ్‌లో ఉన్నప్పుడు భరణం , శాశ్వత భరణం . BNSS, సెక్షన్లు 144 నుంచి 147: మేజిస్ట్రేట్ ఉత్తర్వుతో భార్యలు, పిల్లలు, తల్లిదండ్రుల భరణం; సెక్షన్ 531 క్రిమినల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1973 ను రద్దు చేస్తుంది. గృహ హింస చట్టం, 2005, సెక్షన్లు 2(a), 2(b), 2(f), 12, 17, 20 నుంచి 23, 26, 36.

selfTest.q: 1. భర్త నుంచి హిందూ భార్యకు భరణం ఇచ్చే సెక్షన్ ఏది?
selfTest.a: సెక్షన్ 18.

selfTest.q: 2. ఆశ్రితుడి దావా ఆస్తిపై భారమా?
selfTest.a: వీలునామా, డిక్రీ, ఒప్పందం, లేదా మరో విధంగా సృష్టిస్తే తప్ప కాదు (సెక్షన్ 27).

selfTest.q: 3. మతం మారిన వ్యక్తి 1956 చట్టం కింద దావా వేయవచ్చా?
4. ఇద్దరు వారసులు ఆస్తిలో ₹12,00,000 మరియు ₹4,00,000 తీసుకుంటారు. ఒక ఆశ్రితుడి భరణం నెలకు ₹8,000 గా నిర్ణయించారు. ప్రతి ఒక్కరూ ఎంత చెల్లిస్తారు?
5. BNSS సెక్షన్ 144 కింద చెల్లించని భరణం వసూలుకు ఎంత సమయంలో దరఖాస్తు చేయాలి?
selfTest.a: మొత్తం బకాయి అయిన తేదీ నుంచి ఒక సంవత్సరంలో (సెక్షన్ 144(3) నిబంధన).

selfTest.q: 6. Tulasamma లో భరణానికి బదులుగా ఇచ్చిన ఆస్తికి వితంతువు పూర్తి యజమాని ఎందుకు అయింది?
selfTest.a: ఆమె భరణ హక్కు ముందే ఉన్న హక్కు కాబట్టి, హిందూ వారసత్వ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 14(2) కాదు, సెక్షన్ 14(1) వర్తించింది.

family-law-i-u4-t5.subtitle: Kinds of guardian, powers over the minor's person and property, custody and the welfare principle

en.inOneMinute: Who is a guardian. A guardian is a person who has the care of a minor's person, property or both. A Hindu minor may have a natural guardian , a guardian appointed by will, or a guardian appointed or declared by a court. Natural guardian. For a boy or an unmarried girl, the father is the natural guardian, and after him the mother. In Githa Hariharan v. Reserve Bank of India the Supreme Court read "after him" to mean "in the absence of" the father, not only after his death. Limits. The natural guardian cannot sell or mortgage the minor's immovable property without the court's permission; a sale without it is voidable. The welfare of the minor is the paramount consideration. Two laws. The Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 (HMGA) is in addition to the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (GWA). Guardianship is different from custody.
legalProvision: Section 6, Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956. Natural guardians of a Hindu minor. —The natural guardians of a Hindu minor, in respect of the minor's person as well as in respect of the minor's property (excluding his or her undivided interest in joint family property), are— (a) in the case of a boy or an unmarried girl—the father, and after him, the mother: provided that the custody of a minor who has not completed the age of five years shall ordinarily be with the mother; (b) in the case of an illegitimate boy or an illegitimate unmarried girl—the mother, and after her, the father; (c) in the case of a married girl—the husband: Provided that no person shall be entitled to act as the natural guardian of a minor under the provisions of this section— (a) if he has ceased to be a Hindu, or (b) if he has completely and finally renounced the world by becoming a hermit (vanaprastha) or an ascetic (yati or sanyasi). Explanation.—In this section, the expressions "father" and "mother" do not include a step-father and a step-mother.
Section 13(1). In the appointment or declaration of any person as guardian of a Hindu minor by a court, the welfare of the minor shall be the paramount consideration.
Other provisions used in this note:

HMGA Section 2: the Act is in addition to, and not in derogation of, the GWA, except where it expressly says so. Section 4: a minor is a person under eighteen; a guardian is a person having the care of the minor's person or property or both, and includes a natural guardian, a guardian appointed by the will of the father or mother, a guardian appointed or declared by a court, and a person empowered under a Court of Wards law. Section 5: the Act overrides earlier Hindu law and inconsistent laws on matters it covers. Section 7: guardianship of an adopted minor son passes to the adoptive father and after him the adoptive mother. Section 8: powers of the natural guardian. Section 9: testamentary guardians . Sections 10 to 12: a minor cannot be guardian of property; a de facto guardian cannot deal with the minor's property; no guardian for the minor's undivided interest in joint family property. GWA: appointment, welfare test, duties, removal and end of a guardian's powers. HMA Section 26: custody, maintenance and education of children in matrimonial cases.
en.meaning:
A guardian is a person in charge of a minor's care and protection. Guardianship covers the minor's person (upbringing, education, health) and the minor's property. A minor is a person who has not completed eighteen years (Section 4(a)). The 1956 Act applies in addition to the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (Section 2). Kinds of guardian of a Hindu minor. keyPoints: Minor means under eighteen (Section 4(a)). Natural guardian of a boy or unmarried girl: the father, and after him the mother; "after" means "in the absence of" ( Githa Hariharan ). Custody of a child under five ordinarily with the mother. Section 8: no sale, mortgage or long lease of the minor's immovable property without court permission; breach is voidable. De facto guardian cannot deal with the minor's property (Section 11). Welfare of the minor is paramount (Section 13). Testamentary guardian: appointment fails if the father dies before the mother but revives if she appoints none; right of a guardian of a girl ends on her marriage (Section 9). Natural guardianship of an adopted minor son passes to the adoptive father, then the adoptive mother (Section 7). GWA: welfare test (Section 17); fiduciary duty (Section 20); removal (Section 39); end of powers (Section 41).

caseLaws.name: Githa Hariharan v
caseLaws.facts: Reserve Bank of India (1999) Facts. The Reserve Bank refused a mother's application for Relief Bonds in her minor son's name without the father's signature; in a second petition, a father claimed to be the only natural guardian in a custody dispute. Principle. "After" in Section 6(a) does not necessarily mean after the father's death; it means in the absence of the father, be it temporary, by total apathy or by inability, and the section survives (para 25). AIR 1999 SC 1149 : (1999) 2 SCC 228. Why it matters. It lets the mother act as natural guardian when the father is absent, apathetic or unable.

selfTest.q: 1. Who is the natural guardian of an unmarried girl?
selfTest.a: The father, and after him the mother (Section 6(a)).

selfTest.q: 2. Is a sale by the natural guardian without permission void?
selfTest.a: No. It is voidable at the instance of the minor (Section 8(3)).

selfTest.q: 3. What did Githa Hariharan decide about "after him"?
selfTest.a: It means in the absence of the father, not only after his death.

selfTest.q: 4. A minor is exactly 16. What is the longest lease of her land a natural guardian can grant without permission?
selfTest.a: Majority comes in 2 years; a lease may not run more than 1 year beyond it, so 2 + 1 = 3 years (Section 8(2)(b)).

selfTest.q: 5. Can a court under the GWA appoint a guardian of the person of a child whose father is alive and fit?
selfTest.a: No (GWA Section 19).

selfTest.q: 6. When does a testamentary guardian's right over a girl end?
selfTest.a: On her marriage (Section 9(6)).

ఈ నోట్‌లో వాడిన ఇతర నిబంధనలు:

HMGA సెక్షన్ 2: స్పష్టంగా చెప్పిన చోట తప్ప, ఈ చట్టం GWA కి అదనం, దానిని తగ్గించదు. సెక్షన్ 4: మైనర్ అంటే పద్దెనిమిదేళ్ల లోపు వ్యక్తి; సంరక్షకుడు అంటే మైనర్ వ్యక్తిత్వం లేదా ఆస్తి లేదా రెండింటి సంరక్షణ ఉన్న వ్యక్తి, సహజ సంరక్షకుడు, తండ్రి లేదా తల్లి వీలునామా ద్వారా నియమించిన సంరక్షకుడు, కోర్టు నియమించిన లేదా ప్రకటించిన సంరక్షకుడు, కోర్ట్ ఆఫ్ వార్డ్స్ చట్టం కింద అధికారం పొందిన వ్యక్తి సహా. సెక్షన్ 5: తాను కవర్ చేసే విషయాలపై చట్టం పాత హిందూ చట్టాన్ని, విరుద్ధమైన చట్టాలను అధిగమిస్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 7: దత్తత మైనర్ కొడుకు సంరక్షకత్వం దత్తత తండ్రికి, అతని తర్వాత దత్తత తల్లికి వెళ్తుంది. సెక్షన్ 8: సహజ సంరక్షకుడి అధికారాలు. సెక్షన్ 9: వీలునామా సంరక్షకులు. సెక్షన్లు 10 నుంచి 12: మైనర్ ఆస్తికి సంరక్షకుడు కాలేరు; వాస్తవ సంరక్షకుడు మైనర్ ఆస్తితో వ్యవహరించలేరు; ఉమ్మడి కుటుంబ ఆస్తిలో మైనర్ అవిభక్త హక్కుకు సంరక్షకుడు లేరు. GWA: సంరక్షకుడి నియామకం, సంక్షేమ పరీక్ష, బాధ్యతలు, తొలగింపు, అధికారాల ముగింపు. HMA సెక్షన్ 26: వైవాహిక కేసుల్లో పిల్లల కస్టడీ, భరణం, విద్య.
te.meaning:
సంరక్షకుడు అంటే మైనర్ సంరక్షణ, రక్షణ బాధ్యత ఉన్న వ్యక్తి. సంరక్షకత్వం మైనర్ వ్యక్తిత్వాన్ని (పెంపకం, విద్య, ఆరోగ్యం), మైనర్ ఆస్తిని కవర్ చేస్తుంది. మైనర్ అంటే పద్దెనిమిదేళ్లు పూర్తి చేయని వ్యక్తి (సెక్షన్ 4(a)). 1956 చట్టం సంరక్షకులు, వార్డుల చట్టం, 1890 కి అదనంగా వర్తిస్తుంది (సెక్షన్ 2). హిందూ మైనర్ సంరక్షకుల రకాలు.
