en.meaning:
The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which Part of the Constitution of India?

Explanation. The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in Part IV, Articles 36 to 51, of the Constitution.

Which Article declares that the Directive Principles shall not be enforceable by any court?

Explanation. Article 37 makes the Directive Principles non-justiciable, while calling them fundamental in the governance of the country.

From which country's Constitution were the Directive Principles of State Policy borrowed?

Explanation. The Directive Principles in Part IV are generally traced to the Irish Constitution of 1937.

Article 36 of the Constitution provides that, for Part IV, 'the State' has the same meaning as under which Article?

en.inOneMinute: Read the full set here, or use the practice card above to test yourself one question at a time.
en.meaning:
The three-fold classification of Directive Principles into socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual groups is:

Explanation. Textbooks sort Articles 38 to 51 into three groups. The Constitution does not use these names, and books differ on a few Articles, such as Article 47.

Which two clauses of Article 39 later became central to the Article 31C controversy?

Explanation. Article 39(b) (distribution of material resources for the common good) and 39(c) (avoiding concentration of wealth) became the pivot of the Article 31C debate.

Article 40, directing the State to organise village panchayats, is regarded as reflecting which philosophy?

Explanation. Article 40 reflects Gandhian ideals of decentralised, village-level self-government, and is the constitutional seed of the 73rd Amendment.

Which Article directs the State to endeavour to secure a Uniform Civil Code?

en.inOneMinute: Read the full set here, or use the practice card above to test yourself one question at a time.
en.meaning:
Which case first established the 'harmonious construction' rule for reading Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together?

Explanation. Chief Justice S.R. Das laid down the harmonious construction rule in the 1957 advisory opinion on the Kerala Education Bill.

In re The Kerala Education Bill reached the Supreme Court through which constitutional route?

Explanation. The President referred the Bill to the Supreme Court for an advisory opinion under Article 143.

In State of Kerala v. N.M. Thomas (1976), the Court read Article 16 together with which Directive Principle?

Explanation. The Court read Article 16's equality guarantee together with Article 46's promise to protect SC/ST educational and economic interests.

Unni Krishnan, J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1993) held that the right to education up to age 14 forms part of which Fundamental Right?

en.inOneMinute: Read the full set here, or use the practice card above to test yourself one question at a time.
en.meaning:
In Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court held that Parliament:

Explanation. By a 6:5 majority, the Court held Parliament cannot amend Part III so as to take away or abridge Fundamental Rights — a ruling later overruled in Kesavananda Bharati.

Which amendment directly reversed Golaknath by amending Articles 368 and 13?

Explanation. The 24th Amendment, 1971 restored Parliament's express power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.

Article 31C, as originally inserted by the 25th Amendment, protected laws implementing which provisions from Article 14/19 challenge?

Explanation. Article 31C originally protected only laws genuinely implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c).

How many Judges heard Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)?

en.inOneMinute: Read the full set here, or use the practice card above to test yourself one question at a time.
en.meaning:
The Fundamental Duties were inserted into the Constitution by which amendment?

Explanation. The 42nd Amendment, 1976 inserted Part IVA and Article 51A, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.

Which committee recommended the introduction of Fundamental Duties?

Explanation. The Sardar Swaran Singh Committee, appointed during the Emergency, recommended a chapter of Fundamental Duties.

Article 51A originally set out how many Fundamental Duties?

Explanation. The original 1976 text set out ten duties, clauses (a) to (j).

Which amendment added the eleventh Fundamental Duty, on a parent's duty to educate a child?

en.inOneMinute: Read the full set here, or use the practice card above to test yourself one question at a time.
en.meaning:
In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (12 January 1988, AIR 1988 SC 1115, the Kanpur Nagar Mahapalika case), the Supreme Court relied on Article 51A(g) for which direction?

Explanation. The Court called protecting the natural environment one of the fundamental duties under Article 51A(g). It used that for the direction on environment lessons in schools.

Which of the following best describes how Article 51A(g) operated in the M.C. Mehta judgment of 12 January 1988?

Explanation. The judgment uses Article 51A(g) only for the environment education direction. It does not use Articles 21 or 51A(g) to close any industry.

For how long each week did the Court direct that lessons on protecting the natural environment be taught in the first ten classes?

Explanation. The Court directed teaching of at least one hour in a week, with free text books and a consideration of short training courses for teachers.

In Rangnath Misra v. Union of India (2003), the Supreme Court:

law-of-torts-u1-t1.subtitle: Meaning, features, objects and scope of the law of torts

en.inOneMinute: The law of torts decides when one person must pay another for a civil wrong. The duty is fixed by law, not by a promise. The usual remedy is money whose amount the court decides. Most of this law is judge-made. It grows as new harms appear, from a leaking gas plant to an online insult. In exams, expect questions on its features, its objects and the debate on "Law of Tort" versus "Law of Torts".
legalProvision: No single Tort Act. India has no code of torts. The subject rests mainly on English common law as adapted by Indian courts, with statutes added on particular points. Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: "tort" is a civil wrong that is not exclusively a breach of contract or a breach of trust. This is the only general statutory description. Statutes on special areas: the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Information Technology Act, 2000 each add rules to the common law. The Constitution: Articles 21, 32 and 226 let the Supreme Court and High Courts award compensation for violation of fundamental rights. This is a public law remedy and is separate from a tort claim.
en.meaning:
A tort is a civil wrong. The word comes from the Latin tortum , meaning twisted or crooked. In law it means conduct that wrongs another person and for which the law gives a private claim for compensation.

The person who commits the wrong is the tortfeasor . The person wronged sues in a civil court. The state does not prosecute , and no punishment follows. The aim is to repair the harm.

The law of torts is the body of rules that says which wrongs carry this liability and how much the wrongdoer must pay. Definitions by Salmond, Winfield and Fraser are explained in the note on the definition of tort.

Where the law of torts sits among wrongs How to read this: start at the top box and follow the lines down. The green box is the subject of this note. Wrongs recognised by law Crimes Wrongs against society. The state prosecutes and the court punishes. Civil wrongs Wrongs against a private person. The injured person sues. Torts A duty fixed by law, owed to people in general. Remedy: unliquidated damages. Breach of contract A duty the parties chose to undertake. Owed to the other party. Breach of trust A duty of a trustee to the beneficiary. Mainly an equitable wrong.
keyPoints: A tort is a civil wrong that is not only a breach of contract or trust (section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963). The duty is fixed by law and owed to people in general, so the right is a right in rem. The usual remedy is unliquidated damages. Objects: compensation, deterrence, protection of rights, fair division of loss. Salmond: fixed list of torts. Winfield: general principle. Courts lean to the wider view. Compensation under Articles 32 and 226 is a public law remedy, not a tort award. Section 36 and section 38, Specific Relief Act, 1963 give injunctions (temporary or perpetual) as a tort remedy. Article 372(1), subject to the rest of the Constitution, continues the law in force before 1950 until a competent authority changes it.

caseLaws.name: Ashby v
caseLaws.facts: White (1703) Facts. A constable refused the vote of a qualified voter of Aylesbury. The jury gave him £5 damages. Principle. A person whose legal right is violated has a remedy at law. A voter wilfully denied his vote may sue the officer. Why it matters. It supports the maxim ubi jus ibi remedium and shows that tort law protects rights, not only losses. Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) Facts. A decomposed snail was found in a ginger-beer bottle bought by a friend of the drinker. She had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle. By 3 to 2, the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the consumer. Lord Atkin stated the neighbour principle. Why it matters. It shows tort law growing by judicial decision to meet new facts. Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) Facts. A mill owner's reservoir burst through old coal workings and flooded a neighbour's mine. Principle. A person who keeps something dangerous on his land must keep it in at his own risk. Why it matters. Courts created a new rule of liability instead of waiting for a statute. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) Facts. Oleum gas leaked from a Delhi factory and harmed people nearby. Principle. The Supreme Court built a rule of absolute liability for hazardous industries, wider than Rylands v. Fletcher. Why it matters. It shows Indian courts shaping tort law to Indian conditions. Rudul Sah v. State of Bihar (1983) Facts. Rudul Sah stayed in jail for fourteen years after he was acquitted. Principle. The Supreme Court awarded him compensation in a petition under Article 32. Why it matters. It marks the public law remedy for violation of fundamental rights, which sits beside tort claims.

selfTest.q: 1. What does section 2(m) of the Limitation Act, 1963 say a tort is?
selfTest.a: A civil wrong that is not exclusively a breach of contract or a breach of trust. 2. Why can a stranger commit a tort but not breach a contract? A tort breaks a duty fixed by law and owed to people in general. A contract duty exists only between the parties who made it. 3. What is the difference between the pigeon-hole theory and the general principle theory? Salmond's pigeon-hole theory limits liability to named torts. Winfield's theory makes any unjustified harm a tort, so new torts can arise. 4. Which Article keeps the pre-1950 law in force? Article 372(1), subject to the other provisions of the Constitution, continues all law in force in the territory of India immediately before the Constitution until a competent authority alters, repeals or amends it. 5. When may a court grant a perpetual injunction against invasion of property under section 38(3)? Where the defendant is trustee for the plaintiff, there is no standard to measure actual damage, money would not give adequate relief, or the injunction prevents multiplicity of proceedings.

legalProvision: ఒకే టార్ట్ చట్టం లేదు. భారతదేశంలో టార్ట్స్ కోడ్ లేదు. ఈ అంశం ప్రధానంగా భారత కోర్టులు తమ పరిస్థితులకు తగ్గట్టు మార్చుకున్న ఇంగ్లీష్ కామన్ లా మీద నిలిచింది. కొన్ని అంశాలపై శాసనాలు అదనంగా ఉన్నాయి. లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 2(m): "tort" అంటే కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. సాధారణ శాసన వర్ణన ఇదొక్కటే. ప్రత్యేక రంగాల శాసనాలు: మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988, వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019, సమాచార సాంకేతిక చట్టం, 2000 ఒక్కొక్కటి కామన్ లా కు అదనపు నియమాలు చేర్చాయి. రాజ్యాంగం: ఆర్టికల్స్ 21, 32, 226 ప్రకారం ప్రాథమిక హక్కుల ఉల్లంఘనకు సుప్రీం కోర్టు, హైకోర్టులు నష్టపరిహారం ఇవ్వగలవు. ఇది పబ్లిక్ లా పరిహారం, టార్ట్ దావా కంటే వేరైనది.
te.meaning:
Tort అంటే పౌర తప్పిదం. ఈ పదం లాటిన్ tortum నుండి వచ్చింది, అంటే వంకర లేదా వక్రమైనది. చట్టంలో ఇది మరొకరికి అన్యాయం చేసే ప్రవర్తనను సూచిస్తుంది, దానికి చట్టం నష్టపరిహారం కోసం ప్రైవేట్ దావా హక్కు ఇస్తుంది.

తప్పిదం చేసిన వ్యక్తిని tortfeasor (టార్ట్ చేసినవాడు) అంటారు. నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తి సివిల్ కోర్టులో దావా వేస్తాడు. ప్రభుత్వం ప్రాసిక్యూట్ చేయదు, శిక్ష ఉండదు. నష్టాన్ని సరిదిద్దడమే లక్ష్యం.

ఏ తప్పిదాలకు ఈ బాధ్యత ఉంటుందో, తప్పిదం చేసినవాడు ఎంత చెల్లించాలో చెప్పే నియమాల సముదాయమే టార్ట్స్ చట్టం. సాల్మండ్, విన్‌ఫీల్డ్, ఫ్రేజర్ ఇచ్చిన నిర్వచనాలు "Definition of Tort" నోట్‌లో వివరించబడ్డాయి.

తప్పిదాల్లో టార్ట్స్ చట్టం స్థానం ఎలా చదవాలి: పైన ఉన్న పెట్టె నుండి మొదలుపెట్టి గీతలను అనుసరించి కిందకు వెళ్లండి. ఆకుపచ్చ పెట్టె ఈ నోట్ అంశం. చట్టం గుర్తించిన తప్పిదాలు నేరాలు సమాజానికి వ్యతిరేకంగా తప్పిదాలు. ప్రభుత్వం ప్రాసిక్యూట్ చేస్తుంది, కోర్టు శిక్షిస్తుంది. పౌర తప్పిదాలు ఒక వ్యక్తికి వ్యతిరేకంగా తప్పిదాలు. నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తి దావా వేస్తాడు. టార్ట్స్ చట్టం విధించిన బాధ్యత, అందరి పట్ల ఉంటుంది. పరిహారం: unliquidated damages. కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన పక్షాలు తామే చేపట్టిన బాధ్యత. అవతలి పక్షం పట్ల ఉంటుంది. ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన ట్రస్టీకి లబ్ధిదారు పట్ల ఉన్న బాధ్యత. ప్రధానంగా ఈక్విటీ తప్పిదం.

selfTest.q: 1. లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 2(m) ప్రకారం టార్ట్ అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. 2. అపరిచితుడు టార్ట్ చేయగలడు కానీ కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన ఎందుకు చేయలేడు? టార్ట్ చట్టం విధించి అందరి పట్ల ఉండే బాధ్యతను ఉల్లంఘిస్తుంది. కాంట్రాక్ట్ బాధ్యత దాన్ని చేసిన పక్షాల మధ్యే ఉంటుంది. 3. pigeon-hole theory, general principle theory మధ్య తేడా ఏమిటి? సాల్మండ్ pigeon-hole theory బాధ్యతను పేరున్న టార్ట్‌లకే పరిమితం చేస్తుంది. విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ సిద్ధాంతం సమర్థన లేని ఏ హానినైనా టార్ట్‌గా చేస్తుంది, కాబట్టి కొత్త టార్ట్‌లు పుట్టవచ్చు. 4. 1950కి ముందు చట్టాన్ని ఏ ఆర్టికల్ కొనసాగిస్తుంది? రాజ్యాంగంలోని ఇతర నిబంధనలకు లోబడి, రాజ్యాంగానికి ముందు భారత భూభాగంలో అమలులో ఉన్న చట్టాన్ని సమర్థ అధికారం మార్చే, రద్దు చేసే, సవరించే వరకు ఆర్టికల్ 372(1) కొనసాగిస్తుంది. 5. సెక్షన్ 38(3) ప్రకారం ఆస్తి ఆక్రమణపై శాశ్వత ఇంజంక్షన్‌ను కోర్టు ఎప్పుడు ఇవ్వవచ్చు? ప్రతివాది వాదికి trustee అయినప్పుడు, అసలు నష్టాన్ని కొలిచే ప్రమాణం లేనప్పుడు, డబ్బు సరిపడా ఉపశమనం ఇవ్వనప్పుడు, లేదా అనేక కేసులను నివారించడానికి ఇంజంక్షన్ అవసరమైనప్పుడు.

law-of-torts-u1-t2.subtitle: Section 2(m) of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the definitions of Salmond, Winfield and Fraser

en.inOneMinute: No single definition of tort satisfies every writer. Three are asked in exams: Salmond's, Winfield's and Fraser's. The Limitation Act, 1963 gives the only Indian statutory description. All of them say the same thing in different words. A tort is a civil wrong, the duty is fixed by law, and the usual remedy is damages that the court measures. Learn each definition word for word, because examiners mark the exact phrases.
legalProvision: Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust. This is the statutory description. No other statute defines tort. The definitions of Salmond, Winfield and Fraser are the views of jurists, and courts treat them as guides.
en.meaning:
A tort is a civil wrong that the law remedies mainly by an award of damages. The word came into English from French and goes back to the Latin tortum , meaning twisted or wrong.

The definitions below describe the same idea from different angles. Salmond starts from the remedy. Winfield starts from the duty. Fraser starts from the right that is infringed.

Three terms recur in all the definitions. They are explained first.

Unliquidated damages . Compensation whose amount is not fixed beforehand. The court decides it after hearing the case. Right in rem. A right good against the whole world, such as the right to bodily safety. Right in personam. A right good only against a particular person, such as the right to be paid under a contract.
keyPoints: Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: a civil wrong not exclusively a breach of contract or trust. Salmond: a civil wrong remedied by a common law action for unliquidated damages. Winfield: breach of a duty primarily fixed by law, owed towards persons generally. Fraser: infringement of a right in rem of a private individual, with compensation at the injured party's suit. The remedy is unliquidated damages, not a sum agreed in advance. The same facts can be a tort and a breach of contract. Essentials: a wrongful act or omission, a duty fixed by law, infringement of a right in rem, and a civil remedy in damages.

caseLaws.name: Donoghue v
caseLaws.facts: Stevenson (1932) Facts. The appellant alleged that a decomposed snail was found in a ginger-beer bottle that a friend bought for the appellant. She had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle. By 3 to 2, the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the consumer. The duty arises from law and not from a contract. Why it matters. It shows Winfield's idea of a duty fixed by law and owed to persons generally. Ashby v. White (1703) Facts. Constables of Aylesbury, acting at an election, refused the vote of a qualified voter. The jury gave him £5 damages. Principle. The House of Lords held that a person whose legal right is violated may sue for damages. Why it matters. It shows a right protected by an action for damages, which is the core of Salmond's and Fraser's definitions. Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) Facts. A mill owner's reservoir burst through old coal workings and flooded a neighbouring mine. Principle. A person who keeps a dangerous thing on his land must keep it in at his own risk. Blackburn J. spoke of anything likely to do mischief if it escapes. The House of Lords spoke of a non-natural use of the land. Why it matters. It shows a duty fixed by law that did not depend on any contract between the neighbours.

selfTest.q: 1. What does "primarily fixed by law" mean in Winfield's definition?
selfTest.a: The law creates the duty. The parties do not create it by agreement. 2. What does the word "exclusively" in section 2(m) allow? The same facts can be both a tort and a breach of contract or trust. Only a wrong that is exclusively one of those is outside tort. 3. What are unliquidated damages? Compensation whose amount is not fixed in advance. The court decides it according to the harm.

legalProvision: లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 2(m): "tort" అంటే కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. ఇదే statutory వర్ణన. టార్ట్‌ను నిర్వచించే ఇతర చట్టం లేదు. సాల్మండ్, విన్‌ఫీల్డ్, ఫ్రేజర్ నిర్వచనాలు న్యాయశాస్త్రవేత్తల అభిప్రాయాలు, కోర్టులు వాటిని మార్గదర్శకాలుగా చూస్తాయి.
te.meaning:
Tort అంటే చట్టం ప్రధానంగా నష్టపరిహారంతో సరిదిద్దే పౌర తప్పిదం. ఈ పదం ఫ్రెంచ్ ద్వారా ఇంగ్లీష్‌లోకి వచ్చింది, లాటిన్ tortum (వంకర లేదా తప్పు) నుండి వచ్చింది.

కింది నిర్వచనాలు ఒకే భావనను వేర్వేరు కోణాల నుండి వివరిస్తాయి. సాల్మండ్ పరిహారం నుండి మొదలుపెడతాడు. విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ బాధ్యత నుండి మొదలుపెడతాడు. ఫ్రేజర్ ఉల్లంఘించిన హక్కు నుండి మొదలుపెడతాడు.

అన్ని నిర్వచనాల్లో మూడు పదాలు పదేపదే వస్తాయి. వాటిని ముందుగా వివరిస్తున్నాం.

Unliquidated damages . మొత్తం ముందే నిర్ణయించని నష్టపరిహారం. కేసు విన్న తర్వాత కోర్టు నిర్ణయిస్తుంది. Right in rem. ప్రపంచమంతటిపై చెల్లే హక్కు, ఉదాహరణకు శారీరక భద్రత హక్కు. Right in personam. ఒక నిర్దిష్ట వ్యక్తిపై మాత్రమే చెల్లే హక్కు, ఉదాహరణకు కాంట్రాక్ట్ ప్రకారం చెల్లింపు పొందే హక్కు.

selfTest.q: 1. విన్‌ఫీల్డ్ నిర్వచనంలో "primarily fixed by law" అంటే ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: బాధ్యతను చట్టం సృష్టిస్తుంది. పక్షాలు ఒప్పందంతో సృష్టించవు. 2. సెక్షన్ 2(m) లోని "exclusively" పదం ఏమి అనుమతిస్తుంది? ఒకే వాస్తవాలు టార్ట్ కూడా, కాంట్రాక్ట్ లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన కూడా కావచ్చు. వాటిలో ఒకటి మాత్రమే అయిన తప్పిదం టార్ట్ వెలుపల ఉంటుంది. 3. Unliquidated damages అంటే ఏమిటి? మొత్తం ముందే నిర్ణయించని నష్టపరిహారం. హానిని బట్టి కోర్టు నిర్ణయిస్తుంది.

law-of-torts-u1-t3.subtitle: Wrongful act or omission, legal damage and legal remedy, with the remedies in tort

en.inOneMinute: A tort has three elements. There must be a wrongful act or omission by the defendant . The act must cause legal damage, which means the violation of a legal right. The law must give a remedy for it. All three must be present for a claim to succeed. Exam questions ask for the elements and for the remedies, both judicial (court orders) and extra-judicial (lawful self-help). Real life tests the same points when a neighbour's act harms you.
legalProvision: Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: a tort is a civil wrong not exclusively a breach of contract or trust. It does not list the elements, which come from decided cases. Specific Relief Act, 1963: sections 5, 7 and 8 allow recovery of specific immovable and movable property. Sections 36 to 42 deal with injunctions , which are the commonest non-money remedy in tort. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, sections 34 to 44: the right of private defence of body and property, which is the nearest statutory source of the self-help remedies. Cattle Trespass Act, 1871: the Indian statute that regulates the seizure of trespassing cattle.
en.meaning:
The elements of a tort are the facts the plaintiff must prove to win. They are three:

a wrongful act or omission by the defendant; legal damage to the plaintiff; and a legal remedy for the wrong.

The third element rests on the maxim ubi jus ibi remedium : where there is a right, there is a remedy. The first two rest on the idea that a lawful act, or a loss without a violated right, gives no claim.

Is there a tort? The three questions How to read this: start at the top. Each question must be answered "yes" to move down. Red text shows where the claim fails. 1. Did the defendant do a wrongful act, or omit a legal duty? No: no tort. A lawful act is not a tort, even if it causes loss. 2. Did the act violate a legal right of the plaintiff (legal damage)? No: damnum sine injuria (loss without legal injury). No claim. 3. Does the law give a remedy for that wrong? No: a moral wrong only. No claim. 4. Result A tort is made out. The plaintiff may claim damages, an injunction or other relief.
keyPoints: Three elements: wrongful act or omission, legal damage, legal remedy. An omission is wrongful only when the law imposes a duty to act. Legal damage means violation of a legal right. Loss alone is not enough. Ubi jus ibi remedium: where there is a right, there is a remedy. Judicial remedies: damages, injunction, specific restitution of property. Extra-judicial remedies: self-defence, expulsion of trespasser, re-entry, recaption, distress damage feasant, abatement of nuisance. Self-help must be prompt, reasonable and peaceful. Intention is not a general element: Wilkinson v Downton (intention), Donoghue v Stevenson (duty of care), Rylands v Fletcher (no personal fault needed). A bad motive does not make a lawful act a tort: Bradford Corporation v Pickles.

caseLaws.name: Ashby v
caseLaws.facts: White (1703) Facts. The constables of Aylesbury refused the vote of a qualified voter. The jury gave him £5 damages. Principle. A violation of a legal right is actionable. Where there is a right, there must be a remedy. A refused vote is actionable even if the vote might not have changed the result. Why it matters. It supports the second and third elements: legal damage and a legal remedy. Gloucester Grammar School Case (1410) Facts. A schoolmaster set up a rival school and charged lower fees. The old school lost pupils. Principle. Loss caused by lawful competition gives no claim. Why it matters. It is the early example of damnum sine injuria, where the second element is missing. Bradford Corporation v. Pickles (1895) Facts. Pickles dug on his own land and cut the water supply that fed Bradford's springs. The town said he did it to force a sale. Principle. A lawful act is not made unlawful by a bad motive. Why it matters. It shows that the first element needs a legal wrong, not just a bad purpose. Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (1892) Facts. A group of shipowners cut freight rates to shut out a rival from the tea trade. Principle. Lawful competition causing loss is damnum sine injuria. Why it matters. It shows loss without legal injury again, in a trade setting. Wilkinson v. Downton (1897) Facts. The defendant, as a practical joke, told the plaintiff falsely that her husband had broken both legs in an accident. She suffered a serious shock, and the jury assessed £100. Principle. A person who wilfully does an act calculated to cause physical harm, and thereby causes it, commits a wrong unless there is a justification. Why it matters. It shows that a wrongful act can be words alone, and that an intentional wrong needs no spite. Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) Facts. A friend bought a bottle of ginger beer for Mrs Donoghue. She alleged that she found the remains of a snail in it and fell ill. The House of Lords decided by three judges to two. Principle. A person must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions that he can reasonably foresee would injure his neighbour. This is the duty of care. Why it matters. It explains the duty that makes an act or omission wrongful in negligence. Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) Facts. Water from the defendants' new reservoir escaped through old shafts and flooded the plaintiff's neighbouring mine. Principle. A person who brings on his land and keeps there something likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it in at his peril. Why it matters. It shows a tort where the first element is met without proof of fault.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the three elements of a tort?
selfTest.a: A wrongful act or omission, legal damage, and a legal remedy. 2. Why does Suresh have no claim against a rival who opens a cheaper shop next door? He suffers loss but no legal right is violated. This is damnum sine injuria. 3. What three limits apply to every extra-judicial remedy? It must be prompt, the force must be reasonable, and it must not cause a breach of the peace. 4. Does every tort require intention to harm? No. Wilkinson v Downton is an intentional wrong, Donoghue v Stevenson turns on duty of care, and Rylands v Fletcher needs no fault. 5. A landowner digs on his own land only to spite his neighbour and cuts off the neighbour's water. Is the first element met? No. Under Bradford Corporation v Pickles a lawful use of land does not become a wrong because of a bad motive.

legalProvision: లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 2(m): టార్ట్ అంటే కాంట్రాక్ట్ లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. ఇది మూలకాలను పేర్కొనదు, అవి తీర్పులు, రచయితల నుండి వస్తాయి. స్పెసిఫిక్ రిలీఫ్ చట్టం, 1963: సెక్షన్లు 5, 7, 8 నిర్దిష్ట స్థిర, చరాస్తుల పునరుద్ధరణకు అనుమతిస్తాయి. సెక్షన్లు 36 నుండి 42 ఇంజంక్షన్ల గురించి, టార్ట్‌లో డబ్బేతర పరిహారాల్లో ఇదే సాధారణం. భారతీయ న్యాయ సంహిత, 2023 సెక్షన్లు 34 నుండి 44: శరీరం, ఆస్తి ప్రైవేట్ రక్షణ హక్కు. స్వయంసహాయ పరిహారాలకు ఇదే దగ్గరి శాసన మూలం. పశువుల అతిక్రమణ చట్టం, 1871: అతిక్రమించిన పశువుల స్వాధీనాన్ని నియంత్రించే భారత చట్టం.
te.meaning:
Tort మూలకాలు అంటే గెలవడానికి వాది నిరూపించాల్సిన వాస్తవాలు. అవి మూడు:

ప్రతివాది తప్పిదపు చర్య లేదా విస్మరణ; వాదికి legal damage; మరియు ఆ తప్పిదానికి చట్టపరమైన పరిహారం.

మూడో మూలకం ubi jus ibi remedium సూత్రంపై ఆధారపడింది: హక్కు ఉన్నచోట పరిహారం ఉంటుంది. మొదటి రెండు మూలకాలు, చట్టబద్ధమైన చర్య లేదా హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన లేని నష్టం దావాకు ఆధారం కాదనే భావనపై ఆధారపడ్డాయి.

టార్ట్ ఉందా? మూడు ప్రశ్నలు ఎలా చదవాలి: పైనుండి మొదలుపెట్టండి. కిందకు వెళ్లాలంటే ప్రతి ప్రశ్నకు "అవును" అనాలి. ఎరుపు అక్షరాలు దావా ఎక్కడ విఫలమవుతుందో చూపుతాయి. 1. ప్రతివాది తప్పిదపు చర్య చేశాడా, లేదా చట్టబద్ధ బాధ్యతను విస్మరించాడా? లేదు: టార్ట్ లేదు. నష్టం కలిగినా చట్టబద్ధమైన చర్య టార్ట్ కాదు. 2. ఆ చర్య వాది చట్టబద్ధ హక్కును ఉల్లంఘించిందా (legal damage)? లేదు: damnum sine injuria (చట్టపరమైన హాని లేని నష్టం). దావా లేదు. 3. ఆ తప్పిదానికి చట్టం పరిహారం ఇస్తుందా? లేదు: అది నైతిక తప్పిదం మాత్రమే. దావా లేదు. 4. ఫలితం టార్ట్ నిరూపితమైంది. వాది నష్టపరిహారం, ఇంజంక్షన్ లేదా ఇతర పరిహారం కోరవచ్చు.

selfTest.q: 1. టార్ట్ మూడు మూలకాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: తప్పిదపు చర్య లేదా విస్మరణ, legal damage, legal remedy. 2. పక్కనే చౌక షాప్ తెరిచిన ప్రత్యర్థిపై సురేష్‌కు ఎందుకు దావా హక్కు లేదు? అతనికి నష్టం కలుగుతుంది కానీ ఏ చట్టబద్ధ హక్కూ ఉల్లంఘించబడలేదు. ఇది damnum sine injuria. 3. ప్రతి న్యాయేతర పరిహారానికి వర్తించే మూడు పరిమితులు ఏవి? అది వెంటనే జరగాలి, బలం సహేతుకంగా ఉండాలి, శాంతి భంగం కలగకూడదు. 4. ప్రతి టార్ట్‌కు హాని చేయాలనే ఉద్దేశం అవసరమా? కాదు. Wilkinson v Downton ఉద్దేశపూర్వక తప్పిదం, Donoghue v Stevenson duty of care పై ఆధారపడింది, Rylands v Fletcher కు దోషం అవసరం లేదు. 5. ఒక భూయజమాని పొరుగువాడిపై కక్షతో మాత్రమే తన భూమిలో తవ్వి పొరుగువాడి నీటిని ఆపేస్తే మొదటి మూలకం తీరుతుందా? తీరదు. Bradford Corporation v Pickles ప్రకారం చట్టబద్ధమైన భూ వినియోగం చెడు ఉద్దేశం వల్ల తప్పిదం కాదు.

law-of-torts-u1-t4.subtitle: From the medieval writs to negligence in England, and from the 1726 Charter to absolute liability in India

en.inOneMinute: English tort law began with royal writs , which were fixed forms of complaint. Judges stretched them to cover new harms, and the Judicature Acts of 1873 to 1875 removed the writ system. Negligence then grew into a general principle. India received English common law through colonial courts. It uses the English rules only as far as they suit Indian conditions, and has added its own rules by statute and by Supreme Court decisions. This topic is asked as a long answer, usually with a timeline of cases.
legalProvision: Judicature Acts, 1873 to 1875 (England): merged the common law and equity courts into one Supreme Court and ended the forms of action. Charter of 1726: set up Mayor's Courts in Bombay, Calcutta and Madras, which applied English law. "Justice, equity and good conscience": the standard that Indian courts used to decide cases with no statute or custom. It lets them take English rules only where suitable. Article 372, Constitution of India: continues the law in force before 26 January 1950 until it is changed. Article 300, Constitution of India: the Union and States may sue and be sued. It carries forward the pre-1950 position on suits against the Government. Section 9, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908: civil courts may try all suits of a civil nature, which lets them hear claims in tort.
en.meaning:
The development of the law of torts is the story of how a list of narrow remedies became a body of general principles. In England the change came through judges working within the writ system and then outside it. In India the law arrived from England and was then reshaped by courts and Parliament.

A writ was a royal order that began a civil action, and each kind of wrong needed its own writ. A plaintiff who chose the wrong writ lost, even if the wrong was real.
keyPoints: England: writ of trespass (direct harm) and trespass on the case (indirect harm). Judicature Acts, 1873 to 1875, ended the forms of action and merged law and equity courts. Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) is the foundation of the modern law of negligence. India: Charter of 1726 and the standard of "justice, equity and good conscience". English rules apply in India only where they suit Indian conditions. India's own additions: absolute liability (M.C. Mehta), public law compensation, special statutes. Pollock's Civil Wrongs Bill of 1886 was never enacted. Before 1932 a maker owed no duty to a stranger to the contract (Winterbottom v. Wright); Donoghue v. Stevenson (3 to 2) removed that barrier. State liability in India runs from section 65 of the 1858 Act, through the 1915 and 1935 Acts, to Article 300(1). M.C. Mehta: "We no longer need the crutches of a foreign legal order."

caseLaws.name: Ashby v
caseLaws.facts: White (1703) Facts. A returning officer refused a qualified voter's vote. The jury gave £5 damages. Principle. The House of Lords held that a violation of a legal right is actionable. Why it matters. An early case that treated the right and the remedy together. Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) Facts. A reservoir burst and flooded a neighbour's mine. Principle. A person who keeps a dangerous thing on his land must keep it in at his own risk. Why it matters. It introduced strict liability after the writ system ended. Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) Facts. A snail was found in a bottle of ginger beer. The drinker had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle. By 3 to 2, the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the consumer. Lord Atkin stated the neighbour principle. Why it matters. It is the foundation of modern negligence. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) Facts. Oleum gas leaked from a factory in Delhi. Principle. The Supreme Court created the rule of absolute liability for hazardous industries. Why it matters. It shows Indian courts building their own tort doctrine. Kasturi Lal Ralia Ram Jain v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1965) Facts. Police seized a bullion dealer's gold. A head constable stole it and fled to Pakistan. Principle. The Supreme Court held that the State was not liable, because seizure was a sovereign power. Why it matters. It shows the colonial doctrine of sovereign immunity carried into India. Nilabati Behera later held that it does not bar the public law remedy. Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) Facts. A young man died in police custody. Principle. The Supreme Court awarded compensation under Articles 32 and 226 as a public law remedy. Sovereign immunity does not apply. Why it matters. It shows compensation for rights violations outside the law of torts.

selfTest.q: 1. What was the difference between trespass and trespass on the case?
selfTest.a: Trespass covered direct and forcible harm. Trespass on the case covered indirect harm that followed from the defendant's act. 2. What did the Judicature Acts, 1873 to 1875 do? They merged the common law and equity courts into one Supreme Court and ended the forms of action. 3. What does "justice, equity and good conscience" mean for tort law in India? Indian courts apply English rules only where they suit Indian society and conditions. 4. Why could a consumer not sue the maker before Donoghue v. Stevenson? Only a party to the contract could sue on it. The maker owed no duty to a stranger, except for articles dangerous in themselves or known to be defective. 5. Which Acts link the Indian State's liability to the East India Company? Section 65 of the Government of India Act, 1858, section 32 of the 1915 Act and section 176 of the 1935 Act, carried on by Article 300(1).

legalProvision: జ్యుడికేచర్ చట్టాలు, 1873 నుండి 1875 (ఇంగ్లండ్): కామన్ లా, ఈక్విటీ కోర్టులను ఒకే సుప్రీం కోర్టుగా కలిపి ఫారమ్స్ ఆఫ్ యాక్షన్ ‌ను రద్దు చేశాయి. 1726 చార్టర్: బొంబాయి, కలకత్తా, మద్రాసుల్లో మేయర్స్ కోర్టులను ఏర్పాటు చేసింది, అవి ఇంగ్లీష్ చట్టాన్ని వర్తింపజేశాయి. "Justice, equity and good conscience": శాసనం లేదా ఆచారం లేని కేసులను భారత కోర్టులు నిర్ణయించిన ప్రమాణం. ఇంగ్లీష్ నియమాలను తగినచోటే తీసుకోవడానికి ఇది అనుమతిస్తుంది. భారత రాజ్యాంగం ఆర్టికల్ 372: 1950 జనవరి 26 కంటే ముందు అమల్లో ఉన్న చట్టాన్ని మార్చే వరకు కొనసాగిస్తుంది. భారత రాజ్యాంగం ఆర్టికల్ 300: కేంద్రం, రాష్ట్రాలు దావా వేయవచ్చు, వాటిపై దావా వేయవచ్చు. ప్రభుత్వంపై దావాలకు సంబంధించి 1950 కంటే ముందున్న స్థితిని ఇది కొనసాగిస్తుంది. సివిల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1908 సెక్షన్ 9: సివిల్ స్వభావం గల అన్ని దావాలను సివిల్ కోర్టులు విచారించవచ్చు, కాబట్టి టార్ట్ దావాలను వినవచ్చు.
te.meaning:
టార్ట్స్ చట్టం అభివృద్ధి అంటే ఇరుకైన పరిహారాల జాబితా సాధారణ సూత్రాల సమూహంగా ఎలా మారిందన్న కథ. ఇంగ్లండ్‌లో మార్పు న్యాయమూర్తులు రిట్ వ్యవస్థ లోపల, తర్వాత దాని వెలుపల పనిచేయడం ద్వారా వచ్చింది. భారతదేశంలో చట్టం ఇంగ్లండ్ నుండి వచ్చి, తర్వాత కోర్టులు, పార్లమెంటు చేతుల్లో రూపం మార్చుకుంది.

రిట్ అంటే సివిల్ దావాను ప్రారంభించే రాజ ఉత్తర్వు, ప్రతి రకం తప్పిదానికి దాని స్వంత రిట్ అవసరం. తప్పిదం నిజమైనదైనా సరే, తప్పు రిట్ ఎంచుకున్న వాది ఓడిపోయేవాడు.

selfTest.q: 1. Trespass, trespass on the case మధ్య తేడా ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: Trespass ప్రత్యక్షంగా, హింసాత్మకంగా చేసిన హానిని కవర్ చేసింది. Trespass on the case ప్రతివాది చర్య వల్ల పరోక్షంగా కలిగిన హానిని కవర్ చేసింది. 2. జ్యుడికేచర్ చట్టాలు, 1873 నుండి 1875 ఏమి చేశాయి? కామన్ లా, ఈక్విటీ కోర్టులను ఒకే సుప్రీం కోర్టుగా కలిపి ఫారమ్స్ ఆఫ్ యాక్షన్‌ను రద్దు చేశాయి. 3. భారతదేశంలో టార్ట్ చట్టానికి "justice, equity and good conscience" అంటే ఏమిటి? భారత సమాజానికి, పరిస్థితులకు సరిపోయినచోటే భారత కోర్టులు ఇంగ్లీష్ నియమాలను వర్తింపజేస్తాయి. 4. Donoghue v. Stevenson కి ముందు వినియోగదారు తయారీదారుపై ఎందుకు దావా వేయలేకపోయాడు? ఒప్పందంలో భాగస్వామి మాత్రమే దానిపై దావా వేయగలడు. స్వతహాగా ప్రమాదకరమైన లేదా లోపం తెలిసిన వస్తువులు తప్ప, ఒప్పందానికి బయటి వ్యక్తికి తయారీదారు duty కలిగి ఉండేవాడు కాదు. 5. భారత రాష్ట్ర బాధ్యతను East India Company తో ఏ చట్టాలు కలుపుతాయి? Government of India Act, 1858 సెక్షన్ 65, 1915 చట్టం సెక్షన్ 32, 1935 చట్టం సెక్షన్ 176, వాటిని Article 300(1) కొనసాగిస్తుంది.

law-of-torts-u1-t5.subtitle: Legal damage, the two maxims, and damages: kinds, assessment and remoteness

en.inOneMinute: A tort needs a wrongful act and legal damage. Legal damage means the violation of a legal right. Plain loss is not enough, and a violated right can be enough even when no loss follows. Two Latin maxims mark the line. Damnum sine injuria is loss without a violated right, and there is no claim. Injuria sine damno is a violated right without loss, and the claim succeeds. In exams, expect these maxims, the cases, and a question on damages and remoteness.
legalProvision: No Indian statute states the rule. The two maxims and the rules of damages come from decided cases. Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: a tort is a civil wrong not exclusively a breach of contract or trust. A wrong needs a violated right to be a civil wrong. Articles 21, 32 and 226, Constitution of India: money compensation for violation of fundamental rights is a public law remedy. It sits beside the tort claim for damages.
en.meaning:
A wrongful act is conduct that breaks a duty the law imposes. It may be an act, an omission or words, and it may be intended, careless or without fault where the law makes liability strict.

Damage in everyday speech is any loss. Legal damage is the violation of a legal right. The two do not always go together.

Damnum sine injuria : damage without legal injury. A real loss occurs, but no legal right is violated. No action lies. Injuria sine damno : legal injury without damage. A legal right is violated but no loss follows. The action lies.

Damages (with an s) are the money the court awards when the claim succeeds. Damage and damages are different words with different meanings.
keyPoints: Legal damage means violation of a legal right. Loss alone is not enough. Damnum sine injuria: loss without legal injury, not actionable. Injuria sine damno: legal injury without loss, actionable per se. A lawful act is not made unlawful by a bad motive. Kinds of damages: nominal, contemptuous, ordinary (general and special), aggravated, exemplary. Damages aim at restitutio in integrum, are awarded once and for all, and are reduced by failure to mitigate. Remoteness: reasonable foresight of the kind of damage (The Wagon Mound No. 1). Thin skull rule applies.

caseLaws.name: Ashby v
caseLaws.facts: White (1703) Facts. Constables of the borough of Aylesbury refused the vote of a qualified voter. The jury gave him £5 damages. Principle. Violation of a legal right is actionable, whether or not the voter's candidate won. Why it matters. The leading case on a violated right being actionable without proved loss, and on there being no right without a remedy. Gloucester Grammar School Case (1410) Facts. A schoolmaster set up a rival school nearby and charged lower fees. The old school lost pupils. Principle. Loss from lawful competition gives no claim. Why it matters. The earliest recorded case on damnum sine injuria. Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (1892) Facts. Shipowners cut freight rates and offered rebates to shut a rival out of the China tea trade. Principle. The combination was lawful because the object was lawful and no unlawful means were used. The rival's loss was damnum sine injuria. Why it matters. Aggressive but lawful competition is not a tort. Bradford Corporation v. Pickles (1895) Facts. Pickles dug on his own land and affected the water supply to Bradford's springs. The town said he meant to force a sale. Principle. A lawful act is not made unlawful by a bad motive. Why it matters. Motive is irrelevant if the act is within the actor's legal rights. P. Seetharamayya v. G. Mahalakshmamma (1958) Facts. Landowners built bunds to protect their land from floodwater. The water was diverted onto the neighbour's crops. Principle. A landowner may reasonably protect his land from flood. The neighbour's loss is damnum sine injuria. Why it matters. An Andhra Pradesh High Court illustration of the maxim. Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (1975) Facts. An owner built sixteen shops without the required notice and sanction. The committee demolished them, allegedly out of spite. Principle. Demolition of an unauthorised structure is lawful. Malice does not make it a tort. Why it matters. It confirms that real loss from a lawful act gives no claim. Bhim Singh v. State of Jammu & Kashmir (1985) Facts. An MLA was arrested at night while travelling to an Assembly session and held in unlawful custody for four days. Principle. The Supreme Court held that his rights under Articles 21 and 22(2) were violated and awarded Rs 50,000. Why it matters. Money compensation for violation of a basic right, though he was already released on bail. It is a public law remedy. Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v. Morts Dock & Engineering Co. (The Wagon Mound No. 1) (1961) Facts. Oil negligently spilled into a bay later caught fire and damaged Mort's Dock. Principle. The Privy Council held that a negligent defendant is liable only for damage that was reasonably foreseeable. Re Polemis is no longer good law. Why it matters. It is the modern test of remoteness of damage.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the difference between damnum sine injuria and injuria sine damno?
selfTest.a: In damnum sine injuria there is loss but no violation of a legal right, so there is no claim. In injuria sine damno a legal right is violated though there is no loss, so the claim succeeds. 2. Why could the voter sue in Ashby v. White even if the candidate he supported won? The right to vote is a legal right. Its wrongful denial is actionable even without loss. 3. What test of remoteness applies today? The defendant is liable for damage of a kind that a reasonable person could foresee, from The Wagon Mound No. 1. 4. What did the House of Lords say in Ashby v. White about a right and its remedy? There is no such notion in the law of England as a right without a remedy. Every injury imports damage in the nature of it, so the voter did not have to prove money loss. 5. What did the Privy Council decide in The Wagon Mound No. 1 about the nuisance claim? It decided nothing on nuisance. It dismissed the negligence claim because the fire damage was not reasonably foreseeable, and sent the nuisance claim back to the Full Court.

legalProvision: ఈ నియమాన్ని పేర్కొనే భారత శాసనం లేదు. రెండు సూత్రాలు, నష్టపరిహార నియమాలు తీర్పుల నుండి వచ్చాయి. లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 2(m): టార్ట్ అంటే కాంట్రాక్ట్ లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. పౌర తప్పిదం కావాలంటే ఉల్లంఘించిన హక్కు ఉండాలి. భారత రాజ్యాంగం ఆర్టికల్స్ 21, 32, 226: ప్రాథమిక హక్కుల ఉల్లంఘనకు డబ్బు పరిహారం ప్రజాచట్టం పరిహారం. ఇది నష్టపరిహారం కోసం టార్ట్ దావాతో పాటు ఉంటుంది.
te.meaning:
తప్పిదపు చర్య అంటే చట్టం విధించిన బాధ్యతను ఉల్లంఘించే ప్రవర్తన. అది చర్య, విస్మరణ లేదా మాటలు కావచ్చు, ఉద్దేశపూర్వకం, నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదా చట్టం బాధ్యతను కఠినంగా చేసినచోట తప్పిదం లేనిది కావచ్చు.

Damage అంటే సాధారణ భాషలో ఏ నష్టమైనా. Legal damage అంటే చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన. ఈ రెండూ ఎప్పుడూ కలిసి ఉండవు.

Damnum sine injuria : చట్టపరమైన హాని లేని నష్టం. నిజమైన నష్టం జరుగుతుంది, కానీ ఏ చట్టబద్ధ హక్కూ ఉల్లంఘించబడదు. దావా నిలవదు. Injuria sine damno : నష్టం లేని చట్టపరమైన హాని. చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘనకు గురవుతుంది కానీ నష్టం జరగదు. దావా నిలుస్తుంది.

Damages (s తో) అంటే దావా విజయవంతమైనప్పుడు కోర్టు ఇచ్చే డబ్బు. Damage, damages వేర్వేరు అర్థాలున్న వేర్వేరు పదాలు.

selfTest.q: 1. Damnum sine injuria, injuria sine damno మధ్య తేడా ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: Damnum sine injuria లో నష్టం ఉంటుంది కానీ చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన ఉండదు, కాబట్టి దావా లేదు. Injuria sine damno లో నష్టం లేకపోయినా చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు ఉల్లంఘన ఉంటుంది, కాబట్టి దావా నిలుస్తుంది. 2. Ashby v. White లో ఓటరు మద్దతిచ్చిన అభ్యర్థి గెలిచినా ఓటరు ఎందుకు దావా వేయగలిగాడు? ఓటు హక్కు చట్టబద్ధ హక్కు. దాని అక్రమ నిరాకరణ నష్టం లేకపోయినా దావాకు అర్హం. 3. ఈ రోజు remoteness కు ఏ పరీక్ష వర్తిస్తుంది? సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ఊహించగల రకం నష్టానికే ప్రతివాది బాధ్యుడు, The Wagon Mound No. 1 నుండి. 4. Ashby v. White లో హక్కు, దాని పరిహారం గురించి House of Lords ఏమన్నది? పరిహారం లేని హక్కు అనే భావన ఇంగ్లండ్ చట్టంలో లేదు. ప్రతి injury తనతో నష్టాన్ని తెస్తుంది, కాబట్టి ఓటరు డబ్బు నష్టాన్ని నిరూపించాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు. 5. The Wagon Mound No. 1 లో nuisance దావాపై Privy Council ఏం నిర్ణయించింది? nuisance పై ఏమీ నిర్ణయించలేదు. అగ్ని నష్టం సహేతుకంగా ఊహించదగినది కాదని నిర్లక్ష్యం దావాను కొట్టివేసింది. nuisance దావాను Full Court కు తిరిగి పంపింది.

law-of-torts-u1-t6.subtitle: How a tort differs from a crime and from a breach of contract, and when one act is more than one wrong

en.inOneMinute: A tort, a crime and a breach of contract are three different wrongs. A tort breaks a duty fixed by law and is remedied by damages. A crime is a public wrong that the State punishes. A breach of contract breaks a duty the parties created by agreement. One act can be more than one wrong. A reckless driver can face a criminal case and a civil suit at once. Examiners ask for the comparison table and for the statement that all torts are civil wrongs but not all civil wrongs are torts.
legalProvision: Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: a tort is a civil wrong that is not exclusively a breach of contract or trust. Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: defines the crimes and their punishments. It replaced the Indian Penal Code from 1 July 2024. Sections 73 and 74, Indian Contract Act, 1872: compensation for breach of contract, and liquidated damages or penalty named in the contract. Section 395, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (earlier section 357, Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973): a criminal court may order that fine money be paid as compensation to the victim. Where no fine is imposed, it may order the accused to pay compensation directly (section 395(3)). It does not replace a civil suit.
en.meaning:
A tort is a private civil wrong. A crime is a public wrong made an offence by law. A breach of contract is a failure to perform a promise made by agreement.

All three are wrongs, but the law treats each differently. The difference lies in the source of the duty, in who starts the case, and in what the court does at the end.

Three wrongs and who acts in each How to read this: each box is one kind of wrong. The text says who brings the case and what the court gives. Tort The injured person sues the wrongdoer in a civil court. The court awards damages. Crime The State prosecutes the accused in a criminal court. The court punishes by fine, prison or both. Breach of contract The promisee sues the party who broke the promise. The court awards damages or orders performance. One act can fall in more than one box, for example a drunk driver who injures a pedestrian. A civil suit does not stop a criminal case, and a criminal case does not stop a civil suit.
keyPoints: Tort is a private wrong and its main remedy is compensation. A court can also grant an injunction (Specific Relief Act, 1963, sections 36 and 38). Crime is a public wrong and the State prosecutes and punishes. Tort duty is fixed by law and owed to persons generally. Contract duty is fixed by agreement. Proof: balance of probabilities for tort and contract, beyond reasonable doubt for crime. One act can be a tort and a crime, and a civil suit is independent of the criminal case. The same facts can give rise to tort and contract claims (White v. John Warwick & Co.). All torts are civil wrongs, but not all civil wrongs are torts. Compensation for violation of Article 21 is a public law remedy, independent of a tort suit and a prosecution (Nilabati Behera).

caseLaws.name: White v
caseLaws.facts: John Warrick & Co. Ltd. (1953) Facts. A newsagent hired a delivery cycle. The saddle slipped and he was thrown and injured. The hire agreement had an exemption clause. Principle. The Court of Appeal held that the clause did not clearly cover negligence, so a claim in negligence could go to trial. Why it matters. The same facts gave a contract claim and a tort claim. Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932) Facts. A snail was found in a bottle of ginger beer. The drinker had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle. The House of Lords held by 3 to 2 that the manufacturer owed her a duty of care, though there was no contract. Why it matters. It shows that a tort duty is fixed by law and does not depend on a contract. Bhim Singh v. State of Jammu & Kashmir (1985) Facts. An MLA of Jammu and Kashmir was arrested in the early hours of 10 September 1985. He was not produced before the Magistrate on 11 September or the Sub Judge on 13 September, though remand orders issued. Principle. The Supreme Court found a gross violation of Articles 21 and 22(2). It awarded Rs 50,000 compensation even though he was already free. Why it matters. The same wrong can be a crime, a tort and a violation of fundamental rights, each with its own remedy. Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa (1993) Facts. A 22-year-old man died in police custody. His mother wrote a letter to the Supreme Court, which was treated as a writ petition. Principle. The Court awarded Rs 1,50,000 and Rs 10,000 costs. It held that compensation under Articles 32 and 226 is a public law remedy, independent of a tort suit or a prosecution, and that sovereign immunity does not bar it. Why it matters. It adds a fourth route to the tort, crime and contract comparison.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the standards of proof in tort and in crime?
selfTest.a: A balance of probabilities in tort, and proof beyond reasonable doubt in crime. 2. Who starts the case in a tort and in a crime? The injured person starts a tort suit. The State prosecutes a crime. 3. Why are not all civil wrongs torts? Breach of contract and breach of trust are civil wrongs that are outside tort. Section 2(m) of the Limitation Act excludes them. 4. In White v. John Warwick & Co., why could the newsagent sue in negligence despite the exemption clause? The clause freed the company from contract liability only. A servant riding the cycle could have sued in negligence, so the company owed a duty of care in tort, and the newsagent need not rely on the contract.

legalProvision: లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 2(m): టార్ట్ అంటే కాంట్రాక్ట్ లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. భారతీయ న్యాయ సంహిత, 2023: నేరాలను, వాటి శిక్షలను నిర్వచిస్తుంది. 2024 జూలై 1 నుండి ఇది ఇండియన్ పీనల్ కోడ్ స్థానంలోకి వచ్చింది. భారతీయ ఒప్పంద చట్టం, 1872 సెక్షన్లు 73, 74: కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘనకు పరిహారం, కాంట్రాక్ట్‌లో పేర్కొన్న liquidated damages లేదా penalty . భారతీయ నాగరిక సురక్ష సంహిత, 2023 సెక్షన్ 395 (గతంలో క్రిమినల్ ప్రొసీజర్ కోడ్, 1973 సెక్షన్ 357): జరిమానా సొమ్మును బాధితుడికి పరిహారంగా చెల్లించాలని క్రిమినల్ కోర్టు ఆదేశించవచ్చు. జరిమానా లేనప్పుడు, నిందితుడే నేరుగా పరిహారం చెల్లించాలని ఆదేశించవచ్చు (సెక్షన్ 395(3)). ఇది సివిల్ దావాకు ప్రత్యామ్నాయం కాదు.
te.meaning:
టార్ట్ అనేది ప్రైవేట్ పౌర తప్పిదం. నేరం అనేది చట్టం నేరంగా చేసిన ప్రజా తప్పిదం. కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన అంటే ఒప్పందంతో చేసిన వాగ్దానాన్ని నెరవేర్చకపోవడం.

ఈ మూడూ తప్పిదాలే, కానీ చట్టం ప్రతిదాన్ని వేర్వేరుగా చూస్తుంది. తేడా బాధ్యత మూలంలో, కేసు ఎవరు ప్రారంభిస్తారన్నదానిలో, చివరలో కోర్టు ఏమి చేస్తుందన్నదానిలో ఉంది.

మూడు తప్పిదాలు, ప్రతిదానిలో ఎవరు చర్య తీసుకుంటారు ఎలా చదవాలి: ప్రతి పెట్టె ఒక రకం తప్పిదం. కేసు ఎవరు ప్రారంభిస్తారో, కోర్టు ఏమి ఇస్తుందో వచనం చెబుతుంది. టార్ట్ నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తి సివిల్ కోర్టులో తప్పిదం చేసినవాడిపై దావా వేస్తాడు. కోర్టు నష్టపరిహారం ఇస్తుంది. నేరం ప్రభుత్వం క్రిమినల్ కోర్టులో నిందితుడిని ప్రాసిక్యూట్ చేస్తుంది. కోర్టు జరిమానా, జైలు లేదా రెండింటితో శిక్షిస్తుంది. కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన వాగ్దాన గ్రహీత వాగ్దానాన్ని ఉల్లంఘించిన పక్షంపై దావా వేస్తాడు. కోర్టు నష్టపరిహారం ఇస్తుంది లేదా నెరవేర్చమని ఆదేశిస్తుంది. ఒక చర్య ఒకటికి మించిన పెట్టెలో ఉండవచ్చు, ఉదాహరణకు పాదచారిని గాయపరిచే తాగిన డ్రైవర్. సివిల్ దావా క్రిమినల్ కేసును ఆపదు, క్రిమినల్ కేసు సివిల్ దావాను ఆపదు.

selfTest.q: 1. టార్ట్‌లో, నేరంలో రుజువు ప్రమాణాలు ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: టార్ట్‌లో balance of probabilities, నేరంలో beyond reasonable doubt. 2. టార్ట్‌లో, నేరంలో కేసు ఎవరు ప్రారంభిస్తారు? నష్టపోయిన వ్యక్తి టార్ట్ దావా ప్రారంభిస్తాడు. నేరాన్ని ప్రభుత్వం ప్రాసిక్యూట్ చేస్తుంది. 3. అన్ని పౌర తప్పిదాలు ఎందుకు టార్ట్‌లు కావు? కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన, ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన టార్ట్ వెలుపల ఉన్న పౌర తప్పిదాలు. లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం సెక్షన్ 2(m) వాటిని మినహాయిస్తుంది. 4. White v. John Warwick & Co. లో exemption clause ఉన్నా న్యూస్‌ఏజెంట్ నిర్లక్ష్యం దావా ఎందుకు వేయగలిగాడు? ఆ క్లాజ్ కాంట్రాక్ట్ బాధ్యత నుంచి మాత్రమే కంపెనీని విముక్తం చేసింది. సైకిల్ నడిపే సేవకుడు నిర్లక్ష్యం దావా వేయగలడు, కాబట్టి కంపెనీకి టార్ట్‌లో duty of care ఉంది, న్యూస్‌ఏజెంట్ కాంట్రాక్ట్‌పై ఆధారపడనవసరం లేదు.

law-of-torts-u1-t7.subtitle: The conditions that make a person liable in tort, and the bases of liability: intention, negligence and no fault

en.inOneMinute: A defendant is liable in tort when the main conditions come together. The core four are these. He did a wrongful act. It caused legal damage. The law attaches a mental element, or none, to that kind of wrong. No defence excuses him. The mental element is the part that varies. Some torts need intention, many need only negligence, and some impose liability without fault. Examiners ask for these conditions as a long answer, so learn the list and the three bases of liability.
legalProvision: No single statute lists the conditions. They come from decided cases and from the statutes on particular torts. Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: a tort is a civil wrong not exclusively a breach of contract or trust. Statutes that fix liability: the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (section 164), the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 each impose liability on set facts.
en.meaning:
The general principles of liability are the common conditions that decide whether a defendant must pay for a tort . They apply across torts, whatever the particular tort is.

A principle is "general" when it applies to most torts and not to one only. The specific rules of assault, nuisance or defamation then add their own special requirements.
keyPoints: Conditions: wrongful act, legal damage, causation, fault where required, capacity, no defence. Fault means intention or negligence. It is the general basis of liability. No-fault liability applies to hazardous activities and under some statutes. Causation has a factual and a legal side. Motive is the reason for an act. Intention is its aim. Motive is generally irrelevant. Capacity and defences can end a claim. M.C. Mehta: absolute liability for hazardous industry, even if all care was taken, and without the Rylands exceptions.

caseLaws.name: Donoghue v
caseLaws.facts: Stevenson (1932) Facts. A snail was alleged to be in a ginger-beer bottle. The drinker had no contract with the manufacturer. Principle. By 3 to 2, the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the consumer. Negligence became a general basis of liability. Why it matters. It shows fault, in the form of carelessness, as the main basis. Rylands v. Fletcher (1868) Facts. A reservoir burst through old mine workings and flooded a neighbour's mine. Principle. A person who keeps a dangerous thing on his land must keep it in at his own risk, whether or not he was careful. Why it matters. It is the early authority for liability without fault. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak Case) (1987) Facts. Oleum gas leaked from a factory in Delhi and harmed people nearby. Principle. The Supreme Court made hazardous industries absolutely liable for harm, with no exceptions. Why it matters. It is the Indian authority for no-fault liability. Ashby v. White (1703) Facts. The constables of Aylesbury refused to let a qualified voter give his vote. The election went ahead without it. Principle. The refusal of a legal right is a wrong that needs a remedy. Why it matters. It supports the second condition: legal damage. Wilkinson v. Downton (1897) Facts. A man falsely told a woman that her husband had broken both legs. She suffered nervous shock. Principle. A wilful act calculated to cause physical harm is actionable. It is "in law malicious" without spite. Why it matters. It is the standard example of intention as the mental element. Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v. Morts Dock & Engineering Co. (The Wagon Mound No. 1) (1961) Facts. Furnace oil discharged from a ship into a bay caught fire and damaged the respondents' wharf. Principle. The defendant is liable only for damage of a kind a reasonable person could foresee. Why it matters. It fixes the legal side of causation. Bradford Corporation v. Pickles (1895) Facts. Pickles used his own land to intercept underground percolating water, and so cut off the town's water supply. Principle. A lawful act does not become unlawful because of a bad motive. Why it matters. It separates motive from the wrongful act.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the main conditions of liability in tort?
selfTest.a: A wrongful act or omission, legal damage, causation, a fault element where the tort needs it, capacity of the parties, and the absence of a defence. 2. How do intention and negligence differ? Intention means the defendant wanted the result or knew it was almost certain. Negligence means he failed to take reasonable care. 3. When is a person liable without fault? For hazardous activities under strict or absolute liability, and under some statutes such as section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. 4. How does absolute liability differ from the rule in Rylands v. Fletcher? Rylands liability has exceptions such as act of God, act of a stranger and the plaintiff's own default. M.C. Mehta held that a hazardous industry is absolutely liable without those exceptions, and the compensation must match the enterprise's size.

legalProvision: షరతులను జాబితా చేసే ఒకే చట్టం లేదు. అవి తీర్పుల నుండి, నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్‌లపై శాసనాల నుండి వస్తాయి. లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 2(m): టార్ట్ అంటే కాంట్రాక్ట్ లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కాని పౌర తప్పిదం. బాధ్యతను నిర్ణయించే శాసనాలు: మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 (సెక్షన్ 164), వినియోగదారుల రక్షణ చట్టం, 2019, పబ్లిక్ లయబిలిటీ ఇన్సూరెన్స్ చట్టం, 1991 ఒక్కొక్కటి నిర్దిష్ట వాస్తవాలపై బాధ్యత విధిస్తాయి.
te.meaning:
బాధ్యత సాధారణ సూత్రాలు అంటే టార్ట్ కు ప్రతివాది చెల్లించాలో లేదో నిర్ణయించే ఉమ్మడి షరతులు. నిర్దిష్ట టార్ట్ ఏదైనా, ఇవి టార్ట్‌లన్నింటికీ వర్తిస్తాయి.

ఒక సూత్రం చాలా టార్ట్‌లకు వర్తిస్తే, ఒక్కదానికే కాకుండా, అది "సాధారణం". అప్పుడు assault, nuisance, defamation వంటి నిర్దిష్ట నియమాలు తమ ప్రత్యేక అవసరాలను జోడిస్తాయి.

selfTest.q: 1. టార్ట్ బాధ్యతకు ప్రధాన షరతులు ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: తప్పిదపు చర్య లేదా విస్మరణ, legal damage, కారణ సంబంధం, టార్ట్ కోరినచోట తప్పిదం అంశం, పక్షాల సామర్థ్యం, రక్షణ లేకపోవడం. 2. ఉద్దేశం, నిర్లక్ష్యం మధ్య తేడా ఏమిటి? ఉద్దేశం అంటే ప్రతివాది ఫలితాన్ని కోరాడు లేదా అది దాదాపు ఖచ్చితమని తెలుసు. నిర్లక్ష్యం అంటే సహేతుక జాగ్రత్త తీసుకోలేదు. 3. తప్పిదం లేకుండా ఎప్పుడు బాధ్యత ఉంటుంది? strict, absolute liability కింద ప్రమాదకర కార్యకలాపాలకు, మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 సెక్షన్ 164 వంటి కొన్ని శాసనాల కింద. 4. Absolute liability, Rylands v. Fletcher నియమం కంటే ఎలా భిన్నం? Rylands బాధ్యతకు act of God, అపరిచితుడి చర్య, వాది సొంత తప్పిదం వంటి మినహాయింపులు ఉన్నాయి. ప్రమాదకర పరిశ్రమ ఆ మినహాయింపులు లేకుండా సంపూర్ణంగా బాధ్యురాలని M.C. Mehta చెప్పింది, పరిహారం సంస్థ పరిమాణానికి తగినట్లు ఉండాలి.

law-of-torts-u1-t8.subtitle: Fault as a basis of liability in tort: its forms, the fault theory, and proof of fault

en.inOneMinute: Fault means blameworthy conduct. In tort, a person is at fault when he acts with intention, with recklessness , or without the care a reasonable person would take. The general rule is that a defendant is liable only if he is at fault. There are exceptions, where the law makes a person liable although he took every care. In exams, expect the fault theory, its contrast with no-fault liability, and how a plaintiff proves fault.
legalProvision: No statute defines fault in tort. The idea comes from decided cases and writers. Section 114, Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (now section 119, Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023): the court may presume facts that are likely, given the common course of natural events, human conduct and business. The word is "may", so the court is not bound to presume. This supports the use of res ipsa loquitur. Statutes with no fault: section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and the Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 make some liability independent of fault. Under the 1991 Act the claimant need not plead or prove a wrongful act, neglect or default (section 3(2)). Section 164, Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, in detail: Sub-section (1) makes the owner of the motor vehicle or the authorised insurer liable to pay Rs 5 lakh for death and Rs 2.5 lakh for grievous hurt caused by an accident arising out of the use of a motor vehicle. Sub-section (2) says the claimant need not plead or establish that the death or hurt was due to any wrongful act, neglect or default of the owner, of the vehicle or of any other person. Sub-section (3) reduces the amount by compensation already paid under any other law. Sub-section (4) says ex gratia payments are not deducted. The older Chapter X, headed "Liability without fault in certain cases", included section 140 (compensation on the principle of no fault). The Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 2019 omitted the whole Chapter with effect from 1 April 2022.
en.meaning:
Fault is conduct for which the law blames a person. It has three forms.

Intention. The person aimed at the result, or knew it was almost certain to follow. Recklessness. The person knew of the risk and went ahead without caring whether harm followed. Negligence. The person did not take the care that a reasonable person would take in the same situation.

The fault theory says that liability in tort should depend on fault. The opposite idea is liability without fault, which makes a person pay although he was careful.
keyPoints: Fault is blameworthy conduct: intention, recklessness or negligence. The general rule: liability follows fault. The plaintiff must prove fault. Res ipsa loquitur lets the court infer it. Contributory negligence reduces damages. Exceptions: strict, absolute, vicarious and statutory liability. No-fault liability rests on risk, not blame. Foresight judged by the reasonable person is the test of carelessness (Wagon Mound No. 1). Intention needs no spite (Wilkinson v. Downton). A lawful act is not made wrongful by bad motive (Bradford v. Pickles). Care is no defence to strict liability: a hazardous activity makes the enterprise liable irrespective of negligence (Shail Kumari).

caseLaws.name: The test
caseLaws.facts: In Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Subhagwanti, the thing that failed was exclusively under the defendant's control. Its failure does not ordinarily happen without negligence. That raises a prima facie case of negligence. The facts found in Subhagwanti. The Clock Tower was about 80 years old. The Chief Engineer said the safe life of the top storey was 40 or 45 years. The mortar had decayed to powder. No earthquake, storm or other natural event was pleaded. The High Court found no evidence worth the name of proper inspections. Any inspections were casual and perfunctory . Taken together, the fall itself "tells its own story" and raised an inference of negligence. Who proves what. The normal rule is that the plaintiff proves negligence. The exception applies where the thing causing damage was exclusively under the defendant's control or management and the happening does not occur in the ordinary course without negligence. The Court relied on the Halsbury statement that a presumption of fault is then raised, which the defendant must overcome by contrary evidence. Result. The trial court (9 July 1953) awarded Rs 25,000, Rs 15,000 and Rs 20,000 in three suits. The High Court (27 November 1959) cut the last two to Rs 7,200 and Rs 9,000. On 24 February 1966 the Supreme Court (V. Ramaswami J.) dismissed the appeals with costs. Latent defects. The Court held that the owner of a structure beside a highway must keep it safe for users of the highway. The owner is responsible "irrespective of whether the damage is caused by a patent or a latent defect". Lack of knowledge of a hidden defect is no defence. Hospital cases. In Cassidy v. Ministry of Health, the Court of Appeal held a hospital authority vicariously liable for negligence of the doctors, surgeons and nurses it employs on a permanent basis. No need to name the careless person. The patient's injury was of a kind that does not ordinarily happen without negligence, and only the hospital's own staff treated him. The patient need not identify which staff member was at fault.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the forms of fault?
selfTest.a: Intention, recklessness and negligence. 2. When can the court infer fault under res ipsa loquitur? When the thing causing harm was under the defendant's control and the accident would not ordinarily happen without negligence. 3. Name two kinds of liability without fault. Absolute liability under M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, and statutory liability under section 164 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. 4. According to Shail Kumari, how does strict liability differ from negligence? In negligence, a defendant who took all reasonable precautions is not liable. In strict liability the precautions taken are not relevant. 5. What need a claimant not prove under section 164(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988? That the death or grievous hurt was due to a wrongful act, neglect or default of the owner, the vehicle or any other person. 6. By what standard does Wagon Mound (No. 1) judge what a person ought to have foreseen? The standard of the reasonable man.

legalProvision: టార్ట్‌లో తప్పిదాన్ని నిర్వచించే శాసనం లేదు. ఈ భావన తీర్పులు, రచయితల నుండి వచ్చింది. భారత సాక్ష్య చట్టం, 1872 సెక్షన్ 114 (ఇప్పుడు భారతీయ సాక్ష్య అధినియమం, 2023 సెక్షన్ 119): సహజ సంఘటనల సాధారణ క్రమం, మానవ ప్రవర్తన, వ్యాపార పద్ధతులను బట్టి సంభావ్యమైన వాస్తవాలను కోర్టు రుజువు లేకుండా నిజమని భావించవచ్చు . చట్టం "may" అంటుంది, కాబట్టి అలా భావించాలని కోర్టుకు తప్పనిసరి కాదు. ఇది res ipsa loquitur వాడకానికి మద్దతు ఇస్తుంది. తప్పిదం లేని శాసనాలు: మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 సెక్షన్ 164, పబ్లిక్ లయబిలిటీ ఇన్సూరెన్స్ చట్టం, 1991 కొంత బాధ్యతను తప్పిదంపై ఆధారపడకుండా చేస్తాయి. 1991 చట్టం కింద క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవారు తప్పుడు చర్య, నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదా వైఫల్యాన్ని చెప్పి రుజువు చేయనవసరం లేదు (సెక్షన్ 3(2)). మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 సెక్షన్ 164 వివరంగా: ఉప-సెక్షన్ (1): మోటార్ వాహన వినియోగం వల్ల జరిగిన ప్రమాదంలో మరణానికి రూ. 5 లక్షలు, తీవ్ర గాయానికి రూ. 2.5 లక్షలు చెల్లించాల్సిన బాధ్యత వాహన యజమానిది లేదా అధీకృత ఇన్సూరర్‌ది. ఉప-సెక్షన్ (2): మరణం లేదా తీవ్ర గాయం యజమాని, వాహనం లేదా మరొకరి తప్పుడు చర్య, నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదా వైఫల్యం వల్ల జరిగిందని క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవారు చెప్పి నిరూపించనవసరం లేదు. ఉప-సెక్షన్ (3): ఇతర చట్టం కింద ఇప్పటికే చెల్లించిన పరిహారాన్ని ఈ మొత్తం నుండి తగ్గిస్తారు. ఉప-సెక్షన్ (4): ex gratia చెల్లింపులను తగ్గించరు. పాత Chapter X శీర్షిక "Liability without fault in certain cases". అందులో సెక్షన్ 140 (no fault సూత్రంపై పరిహారం) ఉంది. మోటార్ వాహనాల (సవరణ) చట్టం, 2019 మొత్తం Chapter ను 1 ఏప్రిల్ 2022 నుండి తొలగించింది.
te.meaning:
తప్పిదం అంటే చట్టం ఒక వ్యక్తిని నిందించే ప్రవర్తన. దానికి మూడు రూపాలు ఉన్నాయి.

ఉద్దేశం. వ్యక్తి ఫలితాన్ని లక్ష్యంగా పెట్టుకున్నాడు, లేదా అది దాదాపు ఖచ్చితమని తెలుసు. Recklessness. వ్యక్తికి ప్రమాదం తెలుసు, హాని కలిగినా పట్టించుకోకుండా ముందుకెళ్లాడు. నిర్లక్ష్యం (negligence). అదే పరిస్థితిలో సహేతుక వ్యక్తి తీసుకునే జాగ్రత్తను వ్యక్తి తీసుకోలేదు.

Fault theory ప్రకారం టార్ట్ బాధ్యత తప్పిదంపై ఆధారపడాలి. దీనికి వ్యతిరేకమైనది తప్పిదం లేని బాధ్యత, అంటే వ్యక్తి జాగ్రత్తగా ఉన్నా చెల్లించాల్సి రావడం.

selfTest.q: 1. తప్పిదపు రూపాలు ఏవి?
selfTest.a: ఉద్దేశం, recklessness, negligence. 2. Res ipsa loquitur కింద కోర్టు తప్పిదాన్ని ఎప్పుడు ఊహించగలదు? హాని కలిగించిన వస్తువు ప్రతివాది అదుపులో ఉండి, నిర్లక్ష్యం లేకుండా ప్రమాదం సాధారణంగా జరగనప్పుడు. 3. తప్పిదం లేని బాధ్యతకు రెండు ఉదాహరణలు చెప్పండి. M.C. Mehta v. Union of India లోని absolute liability, మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 సెక్షన్ 164 లోని శాసన బాధ్యత. 4. Shail Kumari ప్రకారం strict liability, negligence నుండి ఎలా భిన్నం? Negligence లో సహేతుక ముందు జాగ్రత్తలన్నీ తీసుకున్న ప్రతివాది బాధ్యుడు కాదు. Strict liability లో తీసుకున్న జాగ్రత్తలు అసంగతం. 5. మోటార్ వాహనాల చట్టం, 1988 సెక్షన్ 164(2) కింద క్లెయిమ్ చేసేవారు ఏమి నిరూపించనవసరం లేదు? మరణం లేదా తీవ్ర గాయం యజమాని, వాహనం లేదా మరొకరి తప్పుడు చర్య, నిర్లక్ష్యం లేదా వైఫల్యం వల్ల జరిగిందని. 6. ఒక వ్యక్తి ఏమి ముందే ఊహించాలో Wagon Mound (No. 1) ఏ ప్రమాణంతో నిర్ణయిస్తుంది? సహేతుక వ్యక్తి (reasonable man) ప్రమాణంతో.

law-of-torts-u1-t9.subtitle: Intention, motive and mistake in the law of torts, and the torts that need a wrongful intent

en.inOneMinute: Wrongful intent means that the defendant meant to do the act that caused the harm, or knew harm was almost certain. A few torts need it. Most do not. Intention is not motive. Intention is the aim of the act, and motive is the reason behind it. In exams, expect questions on this difference, on mistake as a defence, and on which torts need intent.
legalProvision: No statute defines intention for tort. The meaning comes from decided cases. Rule of evidence, not of statute: a court may infer intention from the act. In Wilkinson v. Downton the judge held that an intention to produce the shock "must be imputed".
en.meaning:
Wrongful intent is a state of mind in which the defendant either wished to bring about the harmful result or knew that it was virtually certain to follow. The act itself must also be wrongful. The result must be virtually certain, not merely possible.

The test looks at what the defendant wanted or knew, not at what a reasonable person would have foreseen. When a court imputes intention from the act, as in Wilkinson v. Downton, it is a way of showing what the defendant meant. The court asks whether the act was plainly calculated to produce the effect. A person who aims at a result intends it. A person who knows it will follow as a certain side effect also intends it for this purpose.
keyPoints: Intention is the aim of the act or knowledge that the result is almost certain. Motive is the reason for acting and is generally irrelevant. Intention is inferred from the act and its natural results. Intent transfers from the intended victim to the person actually harmed. An honest mistake does not defeat trespass or conversion. Assault, battery, false imprisonment and deceit need intent. Negligence does not.

caseLaws.name: Wilkinson v
caseLaws.facts: Downton (1897) Facts. The defendant falsely told the plaintiff, as a joke, that her husband had broken both legs. She fell seriously ill from the shock. Principle. A wilful act calculated to cause physical harm that does cause it is actionable without justification. Intention is imputed from the act. Why it matters. The leading case on intentionally caused harm by words. Bradford Corporation v. Pickles (1895) Facts. Pickles dug on his own land next to the springs that supplied Bradford. The town said he meant to force a purchase. Principle. The House of Lords held that a bad motive does not make a lawful act unlawful. Why it matters. It separates motive from the legal question. Quinn v. Leathem (1901) Facts. Trade union officers used threats and black lists against a butcher to make him dismiss non-union workmen. Principle. A combination formed to injure a person in his trade, and not to advance its own interests, is actionable. Why it matters. It marks the limit of the rule that motive is irrelevant. Mogul Steamship Co. Ltd. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (1891) Facts. Shipowners combined to control the Hankow tea trade, gave rebates to exclusive shippers and cut freights. Principle. Loss from lawful competition is damnum sine injuria, and combining does not turn it into a wrong. Why it matters. It shows when a combination is not a conspiracy. Derry v. Peek (1889) Facts. A prospectus said the tramway company could use steam power. Consent was later refused, and a shareholder sued the directors for deceit. Principle. Deceit needs actual fraud. An honest belief is no deceit, even if held without reasonable grounds. Why it matters. It fixes the mental element of deceit.

selfTest.q: 1. What is the difference between intention and motive?
selfTest.a: Intention is the aim of the act. Motive is the reason behind it. 2. What is transferred intent? If a person intends to harm one person but harms another, his intent transfers to the person harmed. 3. Why did Pickles escape liability in Bradford Corporation v. Pickles? He used his own land within his legal rights, so his bad motive did not make the act unlawful.

legalProvision: టార్ట్‌కు ఉద్దేశాన్ని నిర్వచించే శాసనం లేదు. అర్థం తీర్పుల నుండి వస్తుంది. సాక్ష్య నియమం, శాసనం కాదు: ఒక వ్యక్తి తన చర్య సహజ, సంభావ్య ఫలితాలను ఉద్దేశించాడని కోర్టు వాస్తవాల నుండి అంచనా వేయవచ్చు. Wilkinson v. Downton లో షాక్ కలిగించే ఉద్దేశం "must be imputed" అని న్యాయమూర్తి చెప్పారు.
te.meaning:
Wrongful intent అనేది ప్రతివాది హానికరమైన ఫలితాన్ని తెచ్చిపెట్టాలని కోరుకున్న, లేదా అది దాదాపు ఖచ్చితంగా జరుగుతుందని తెలిసిన మనస్థితి. చర్య కూడా తప్పిదంగా ఉండాలి. ఫలితం సాధ్యమే కాకుండా దాదాపు ఖచ్చితంగా ఉండాలి.

పరీక్ష ప్రతివాది ఏమి కోరాడు లేదా ఏమి తెలుసుకున్నాడు అనేది చూస్తుంది, సహేతుక వ్యక్తి ఏమి ఊహించేవాడో కాదు. Wilkinson v. Downton లో లాగా కోర్టు చర్య నుండి ఉద్దేశాన్ని ఆపాదించినప్పుడు, ప్రతివాది ఏమి ఉద్దేశించాడో చూపే మార్గం అది. ఆ చర్య ఆ ఫలితాన్ని కలిగించేలా స్పష్టంగా ఉందా అని కోర్టు చూస్తుంది. ఫలితాన్ని లక్ష్యంగా పెట్టుకున్న వ్యక్తి దాన్ని ఉద్దేశించినట్లే. ఫలితం ఖచ్చితమైన అనుబంధ పరిణామంగా వస్తుందని తెలిసిన వ్యక్తి కూడా ఈ ప్రయోజనం కోసం దాన్ని ఉద్దేశించినట్లే.

selfTest.q: 1. ఉద్దేశం, motive మధ్య తేడా ఏమిటి?
selfTest.a: ఉద్దేశం చర్య లక్ష్యం. Motive దాని వెనుక కారణం. 2. Transferred intent అంటే ఏమిటి? ఒక వ్యక్తికి హాని చేయాలని ఉద్దేశించి మరొకరికి హాని చేస్తే, అతని ఉద్దేశం హాని పొందిన వ్యక్తికి బదిలీ అవుతుంది. 3. Bradford Corporation v. Pickles లో పికిల్స్ బాధ్యత నుండి ఎందుకు తప్పించుకున్నాడు? అతను తన హక్కుల పరిధిలో తన భూమిని వాడాడు, కాబట్టి అతని చెడు motive చర్యను చట్టవిరుద్ధం చేయలేదు.

law-of-torts-u1-t10.subtitle: Malice in law and malice in fact, and where malice matters in the law of torts

en.inOneMinute: Malice has two meanings in tort. Malice in law means a wrongful act done on purpose, without just cause. Malice in fact means ill will or an improper purpose. The general rule is that malice does not make a lawful act wrongful. Malice matters in a few torts, such as malicious prosecution, and in the defence of privilege. Examiners ask for the two meanings and for the torts where it matters.
legalProvision: No statute defines malice for tort. The meaning comes from decided cases. The rule comes from decided cases. This note uses Bradford Corporation v. Pickles (House of Lords, 1895), Mogul Steamship Co. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (House of Lords, 1892), Quinn v. Leathem (House of Lords, 1901) and Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (Allahabad High Court, 1974). Section 2(m), Limitation Act, 1963: "tort" means a civil wrong which is not exclusively the breach of a contract or the breach of a trust.
en.meaning:
Malice is a word with two technical senses. Courts must know which one is meant.

Malice in law. A wrongful act done intentionally, without just cause or excuse. No ill will is needed. In Wilkinson v. Downton, Wright J. said a wilful act of this kind "is in law malicious", although no motive of spite is imputed to the defendant. Malice in fact. Real spite or a sinister motive behind the act. Lord Brampton describes it in Quinn v. Leathem: "personal spite" or a wish to harm the accused, in a malicious prosecution.

Malice in law looks at the act. Malice in fact looks at the actor's mind.
keyPoints: Malice in law: a wrongful act done intentionally without just cause or excuse. Malice in fact: ill will, spite or improper purpose. A bad motive does not make a lawful act a tort. Malice is an element in malicious prosecution. Malice can defeat a defence of privilege. A good motive does not excuse an unlawful act (Lord Halsbury). Allen v. Flood does not protect a combination to injure a trader (Quinn v. Leathem).

caseLaws.name: Bradford Corporation v
caseLaws.facts: Pickles. The owner of land may divert or appropriate percolating water within his own land, even if his neighbour loses it. His motive, good or bad, does not change his right. Lord Watson said: "No use of property, which would be legal if due to a proper motive, can become illegal". Mogul Steamship Co. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. The shipowners' object was lawful and they used no unlawful means. The rivals' loss gave no claim. Lord Halsbury said the phrases in the evidence about injuring rivals meant only that rival trading would be unprofitable on the shipowners' better terms. If that were malice, he said, "all competition must be malicious and consequently unlawful". He called this a reductio ad absurdum (an argument that proves absurd). Lord Bramwell noted that the plaintiffs did not complain of any act aimed at injuring them from malice or ill will. Quinn v. Leathem. The House of Lords upheld the verdict against the union officers. Allen v. Flood did not apply, since the purpose of the defendants was to injure the plaintiff in his trade, not to promote their own trade interest (Lord Shand). The jury found that the defendants acted wrongfully and maliciously, and awarded 200 pounds against all, with a further 50 pounds against Davey, Dornan and Shaw for the black list.

selfTest.q: 1. What are the two senses of malice?
selfTest.a: Malice in law, which is a wrongful act done intentionally without just cause, and malice in fact, which is ill will or improper purpose. 2. Does a bad motive make a lawful act a tort? No. The House of Lords decided this in Bradford Corporation v. Pickles. 3. Name two places where malice matters. Malicious prosecution and conspiracy. Malice can also defeat a defence of privilege. 4. Why did the owner lose in Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal? He suffered damage but no legal injury, since the shops were built without the notice and sanction the law required. Malice does not enter the scene when the act is legal.

legalProvision: టార్ట్‌కు malice ను నిర్వచించే శాసనం లేదు. అర్థం తీర్పుల నుండి వస్తుంది. ఈ నియమం తీర్పుల నుండి వచ్చింది. ఈ నోట్ Bradford Corporation v. Pickles (హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్, 1895), Mogul Steamship Co. v. McGregor, Gow & Co. (హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్, 1892), Quinn v. Leathem (హౌస్ ఆఫ్ లార్డ్స్, 1901), Town Area Committee v. Prabhu Dayal (అలహాబాద్ హైకోర్టు, 1974) లను వాడుతుంది. లిమిటేషన్ చట్టం, 1963 సెక్షన్ 2(m): "tort" అంటే కేవలం కాంట్రాక్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన లేదా ట్రస్ట్ ఉల్లంఘన మాత్రమే కాని పౌర తప్పిదం.
te.meaning:
Malice కు రెండు సాంకేతిక అర్థాలు ఉన్నాయి. కోర్టులు ఏ అర్థమో తెలుసుకోవాలి.

Malice in law. న్యాయమైన కారణం లేదా మినహాయింపు లేకుండా కావాలని చేసిన తప్పిదపు చర్య. ద్వేషం అవసరం లేదు. Wilkinson v. Downton లో, ఇలాంటి ఉద్దేశపూర్వక చర్య "is in law malicious" అని Wright J. అన్నారు, ప్రతివాదిపై కక్ష మోపబడలేదు . Malice in fact. చర్య వెనుక నిజమైన కక్ష లేదా దురుద్దేశం. Quinn v. Leathem లో Lord Brampton దీన్ని వివరించారు: malicious prosecution లో "personal spite" లేదా నిందితునికి హాని చేయాలన్న కోరిక.

Malice in law చర్యను చూస్తుంది. Malice in fact చర్య చేసిన వ్యక్తి మనసును చూస్తుంది.

selfTest.q: 1. Malice కు రెండు అర్థాలు ఏవి?
